Flydubai jet diverts after hijacking code triggers Israeli scramble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:04:00 UTC
16:04:00 KST

A Flydubai flight carrying more than 170 passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv diverted to Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after transmitting emergency transponder codes, including one associated with a possible hijacking, triggering an Israeli military response before authorities determined the incident was not believed to involve a hijacking.
Flight FZ1073, operated by a Boeing 737 MAX 8, was traveling toward Ben Gurion Airport when it transmitted the international emergency code 7700 and briefly switched to code 7500, which is used to indicate unlawful interference or a possible hijacking.
The aircraft subsequently changed course, descended sharply and headed toward Saudi Arabia, according to flight-tracking data and Israeli media reports. It eventually landed safely at Tabuk Airport.
The unusual flight path and emergency signals prompted Israeli authorities to treat the situation as a potential security threat.
Israeli media reported that the Air Force scrambled fighter jets after the alert, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz held an urgent security consultation with senior defense officials.
The Israeli military also carried out a situation assessment involving the Air Force and other security agencies as authorities sought to determine what had happened aboard the aircraft.
A security source cited by Ynet said there was no confirmed information that the aircraft had been hijacked and that the pilot had activated a distress signal.
The Prime Minister's Office later said the diversion to Saudi Arabia was not believed to have been the result of a hijacking.
The aircraft departed Dubai International Airport early Wednesday on its scheduled service to Tel Aviv. It was carrying roughly 174 passengers, according to reports, including about 27 children.
During the flight, the aircraft transmitted the 7700 general emergency code before briefly transmitting 7500, the code associated with unlawful interference.
The 7500 signal immediately raised the possibility of a hijacking, particularly because the aircraft was headed toward Israel, where security authorities have remained on high alert amid the wider regional security situation.
Flight-tracking data showed the aircraft changing direction and descending to a much lower altitude than its normal cruising level before continuing toward Saudi Arabia. Reports said the aircraft descended to around 15,000 feet.
The combination of the emergency signals, course reversal, descent and temporary concerns over communications intensified the response.
Israeli media initially reported that contact with the aircraft had been lost, although subsequent reports indicated that it was continuing toward Saudi Arabia and was expected to land at Tabuk.
The aircraft eventually landed safely.
The alert prompted an immediate military response in Israel, with fighter jets scrambled as authorities assessed whether the aircraft posed a security threat.
Netanyahu and Katz convened an emergency consultation, while senior military officials assessed the situation with the Air Force.
Other Israeli security bodies were also reported to have been involved in assessing the incident.
Some Israeli reports said departures from Ben Gurion Airport were temporarily affected while the situation was being evaluated.
The response reflected the seriousness with which aviation authorities treat a 7500 transmission. The code is designed to alert air traffic control and relevant security agencies to a possible unlawful interference situation.
However, the transmission alone does not establish that a hijacking has taken place.
As the situation developed, Israeli reports indicated that the incident was not believed to have been caused by a hijacking or an external security threat.
Reports cited by Israeli media suggested that a physical altercation between the pilots may have prompted the emergency signals and the subsequent diversion.
That account remained subject to further verification, however, and detailed official information from flydubai or UAE aviation authorities was not immediately available in the initial coverage.
The Israeli Prime Minister's Office confirmed the broader assessment that the diversion was not believed to have been a hijacking incident.
The aircraft's safe landing in Tabuk brought the immediate security alert to an end.
The incident nevertheless demonstrated how quickly an aviation emergency can escalate when an aircraft transmits a hijacking-related code, particularly on a route involving Israel.
The flight was ultimately diverted well before reaching its planned destination at Ben Gurion Airport.
Rather than continuing toward Israel, the aircraft headed for Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely after the emergency.
Israeli authorities subsequently scaled back their response after determining that there was no confirmed hijacking threat.
The exact circumstances inside the cockpit, including what prompted the emergency transmissions and the aircraft's abrupt change in course and altitude, remained under review.
The incident also highlighted the sensitivity of commercial aviation routes between the United Arab Emirates and Israel, which were established following the normalization of relations under the Abraham Accords.

But analysts expect the two days of talks to end in a deadlock as Trump's tariffs strain relationships while China rejects concerns about its exports, which critics see as driven by excess industrial capacity.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer defended Washington's approach at a Tuesday roundtable in Milwaukee, saying the administration "is not anti-trade."
He added that countries are facing similar challenges with global overcapacity and "non-market policies."
This week, key US trading partners like Canada and the European Union are also expected to push for deeper trade ties outside the United States.
"Don't expect any breakthroughs in Milwaukee," Josh Lipsky of the Atlantic Council think tank told AFP, noting Trump's preference for bilateral negotiations.
Even as G20 partners will be anxious to find ways to cooperate with the world's biggest economy, "they will also be under pressure to voice their concerns with tariffs," added former US trade official Wendy Cutler, now at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
The United States holds the rotating presidency of the G20, which comprises 19 nations plus the EU and the African Union.
'Unfairly targeted'
Trump has unleashed a barrage of tariffs on trading partners since last year, separately targeting sectors like steel and autos.
Although the Supreme Court struck down Trump's country-specific tariffs in February, Washington has since alleged insufficient action against forced labour to slap new tariffs on 60 economies.
These include China, India and the EU.
The president's sectoral duties remain intact too, straining ties.
And Washington is investigating 16 partners over excess industrial capacity, a complaint commonly levied at China. Critics say this floods markets, unfairly suppressing prices.
But ongoing US probes go beyond the world's number two economy, bringing the threat of more tariffs to the EU and G20 countries like Japan and South Korea.
Cutler expects some countries will "mince no words" regarding the investigation, feeling "they are being unfairly targeted."
China "will continue to deny the issue of exporting overproduction," by trying to convince others that it is doing good by providing high-quality and low-priced goods, she said.
"This will be a hard sell," Cutler told AFP, as countries see employment and commercial fallout from waves of Chinese imports.
"Meanwhile, members are wondering how much they should agree to with the Trump administration, given trade policy could change in the US after 2028," Lipsky said, referring to the next US presidential election.
Diversifying
With Trump's trade wars, all eyes are on G20 members' efforts to deepen trade ties outside the US, or strike deals with his administration.
Canada and the EU are expected to try and boost trade and investment with others, as a spat between Ottawa and Washington intensifies.
Canada's international trade minister Maninder Sidhu stressed Ottawa's support for "open, predictable and rules-based trade."
He plans to speak with partners to "reinforce a multilateral trading system," as officials try to diversify an economy they see as too reliant on an increasingly protectionist United States.
Others like India could finalise a long-awaited trade deal with the United States. Observers are also monitoring for signs of further pressure on Iran.
Outside the G20, workers and activists are protesting what they see as the Trump administration's broken promises to improve conditions for workers, farmers and smaller businesses.
John Drew, who chairs the political arm of the United Auto Workers (UAW) union in Wisconsin, laments the loss of manufacturing jobs in the state.
While the UAW does not rule out using targeted duties to protect jobs, he said, Trump's sweeping "use of tariffs has done nothing to bring back jobs and rebuild manufacturing."

F-16s get new friend-or-foe system cleared for service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:02:44 UTC
16:02:44 KST

- BAE Systems' AN/APX-127(V)1 identification friend or foe system received AIMS certification for the U.S. Air Force F-16.
- The company expects to begin delivering the first 90-unit production lot this year.
BAE Systems’ new identification friend or foe system for the F-16 has been certified by the U.S. Department of War, clearing it for use on U.S. Air Force fighters, the company said Sept. 29.
The AN/APX-127(V)1 Combined Interrogator Transponder received AIMS certification, the approval that shows an identification system meets U.S. and NATO standards and can work with allied equipment. BAE Systems said it expects to start delivering the first production lot of 90 units this year. The company did not say which F-16 units will receive them first, who ordered the first lot or how much it is worth.
An identification friend or foe system, known as IFF, lets an aircraft send a coded radio question to another aircraft and receive a coded answer, so a pilot or air defense operator can tell whether it is friendly before deciding whether to fire. The new unit combines the interrogator, which asks the question, and the transponder, which answers it, in one box sized for fighter jets.
The system is certified for Mark XIIB IFF with Mode 5, the encrypted military mode used by the United States and NATO, and Mode S, which is used in civilian air traffic control. BAE Systems said it adds extra receive channels so the aircraft can passively pick up other aircraft’s Mode 5 Level 2 signals, which carry position data, and ADS-B broadcasts, the location signals most civilian aircraft send out. That lets a pilot build a picture of nearby traffic without sending out interrogations of their own.
The unit meets the latest cryptography and cybersecurity requirements, and its open architecture allows new features to be added through software instead of hardware changes, the company said. It fits in the same space as three older BAE combined interrogator transponders, the AN/APX-113, AN/APX-125 and AN/APX-126, which are used on several U.S. and international aircraft, so it can be swapped in without redesigning the aircraft.
“This solution provides added security and real-time information pilots need in a variety of threat environments,” said Seth Guanu, Combat Identification Products program area director at BAE Systems.
BAE Systems says it has delivered more than 1,500 interrogators, 6,000 combined interrogator transponders and 16,000 transponders over more than 80 years. The new system is built at the company’s sites in Greenlawn, New York, and Austin, Texas.

Gene therapy: The breakthrough that inspired Spider-Man | Euronews Tech Talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:02:00 UTC
16:02:00 KST

Although an inspiration for science fiction movies, gene therapy is real. Here is how it works and what could be improved about it.
If you are a science nerd and a Marvel fan, you might have noticed that gene therapy, a promising medical approach to treat diseases by targeting their genetic causes, made an appearance in the latest iteration of the arachnid superhero franchise, Spider-Man: Brand New Day.
In this film, Peter Parker or Spider-Man feels weird. His DNA mutates, and his spider side starts taking over, providing him with new and sometimes difficult-to-control powers.
To manage them, Parker resorts to RNA interference, a real-world gene therapy technique that silences specific gene activity.
But how does gene therapy work? And what are its limitations?
To answer these and more questions, Euronews Tech Talks interviewed Alberto Auricchio, director of the Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine in Naples, professor at the University of Naples and president of the European Society of Gene & Cell Therapy.
How does gene therapy work?
Originally used to treat monogenic diseases, gene therapy is now employed and studied to find a treatment for a wide range of illnesses, including cancer and HIV.
“Gene therapy basically targets the root cause of a genetic disease,” Auricchio explained. This medical approach essentially consists in the introduction of nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) into target cells and tissues for therapeutic purposes.
Nucleic acids can be introduced into target cells either in vivo (directly within the body) or ex vivo (in cells extracted from an organism and then transplanted inside the body). In both cases, delivery is achieved using either viral or non-viral vectors.
Types of gene therapy include gene addition and gene editing, with the latter being further divided into gene silencing and gene correction.
As the names suggest, gene addition consists of adding a gene; gene correction is the fixing of a dysfunctional gene; and gene silencing deactivates a gene.
What’s the state of gene therapy in Europe?
Gene therapy is a complex and evolving field, but it is not only material for science-fiction stories. “We are beyond clinical trials now. There are approved [gene therapy] products that are available to patients,” Auricchio told Euronews Next.
The first in vivo gene therapy approved in Europe was Glybera, which received the European Commission marketing authorisation in 2012 and offers a medical treatment for patients with severe or multiple pancreatitis attacks due to lipoprotein lipase deficiency.
The first ex vivo gene therapy approved in Europe was Strimvelis, which received authorisation in 2016. This drug treats severe combined immunodeficiency due to adenosine deaminase deficiency and was developed at the Hospital San Raffaele in Milan.
What makes gene therapy promising?
Among others, gene therapy has a crucial advantage: it is a durable treatment.
“There are approved gene therapy drugs, for which we have decades of follow-up in patients where we know that the therapeutic effect is stable over decades, and in theory for the lifetime of the individual,” Auricchio explained.
As a matter of fact, gene therapy drugs are designed to be a once-in-a-lifetime treatment, meaning that a single administration should last for a long time.
On the other hand, beyond the scientific difficulties, the main limitation of gene therapy is the economic obstacle.
“These are very expensive drugs to be developed, and those that get to the market have very high prices, some of them matching millions of euros,” Auricchio explained.
For instance, the cost of Strimvelis amounts to €594,000 excluding VAT.
“These drugs are developed for rare diseases in many cases, which are not a very attractive market for typical developers like pharmaceutical companies; the high development cost of this drug is a challenge,” Auricchio said.
Spider-Man: Brand New Day does not explore the economic problem behind gene therapy. Peter Parker is lucky to know the brilliant scientist Bruce Banner or Hulk, who helps him develop his therapy.
But real-life science is often more challenging than a superhero movie.
Euronews Tech Talks is a podcast produced, written, presented and published in English.

I heard one thing loud and clear in Andy Burnham’s landmark speech: the left has won the arguments | Owen Jones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:00:14 UTC
16:00:14 KST

As Andy Burnham delivered his conference speech to the Labour faithful yesterday, it was hard not to recall Jeremy Corbyn’s words after the party’s shattering 2019 election defeat. “I am proud that on austerity, on corporate power, on inequality and the climate emergency,” he wrote for this publication, “we have won the arguments and rewritten the terms of political debate.” Given Boris Johnson’s 80-seat majority, widespread mockery ensued.
But when it comes to rhetoric, who can now deny that the left has won the argument? A Labour prime minister has declared that “Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time”, listing five villains: “Deindustrialisation, deregulation, privatisation, austerity, Brexit.” His speech was infused with class politics, as he condemned a society “run for vested interests, not in the public interest, with power held in too few hands”.
When he committed to break with the “flawed thinking of the last 40 years”, he lumped together Conservative and Labour governments. He has already repeatedly labelled the culprit: neoliberalism. This has long been the received wisdom of the left: that as Clement Attlee’s postwar government established a social-democratic consensus that the Tories upheld for a generation, so Margaret Thatcher bequeathed a settlement that New Labour maintained.
These beliefs were condemned to the fringes of Labour, even though Tony Blair himself eventually confessed: “I always thought my job was to build on some of the things she had done rather than reverse them.” Any mention of neoliberalism was a sure way of provoking an eye-roll from a mainstream politician or commentator. We were denied any debate about an economic system based on extraction rather than investment; an economy based on financialisation rather than making things. Corbynism was an insurgency against all of this – until it crashed on the shores of Brexit.
Add to this the new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, telling those who opposed Israel’s genocide and were infuriated by Labour’s position on Gaza: “You were right.” We should add, too, the disastrous past wars backed by Labour: Iraq, Afghanistan and Libya.
The left should feel vindicated by the political shift taking place. We were right – at home and abroad. We were mocked, demonised and marginalised for making these arguments. Now most of the left’s worldview is embraced by the Labour top brass. This happened after Keir Starmer’s faction based their entire project on defining themselves against the left. As the Labour activist Ali Milani – who was part of Burnham’s team – told me, that strategy nearly brought about the party’s destruction.
Burnham only became prime minister because Labour’s leftwing voters rebelled – by defecting en masse to Zack Polanski’s Green party in the Gorton and Denton byelection, then in local elections in England, Scotland and Wales. That is clearly understood by Burnham’s team, or they would not be so confidently doubling down on their new strategy.
But winning the argument on a rhetorical level is not the same as substance. Burnham is clearly shifting towards state intervention. That’s taking the form of Great British Grid, a new publicly owned network body, and he condemned privatised water as “a symbol of what has gone wrong with Britain”.
The shift in this direction actually began under the last Conservative government. Did Liz Truss not commit to a subsidy for energy bills worth tens of billions of pounds? What of Rishi Sunak being forced to bring railways into public ownership? Starmerism expanded the semi-nationalisation of the railway and founded Great British Energy. Neoliberalism has exhausted itself and governments are being forced to abandon its tenets, whether they want to or not.
But full public ownership of water seems far off, with “public control” acting as a rather flexible label. Burnham has committed to a large-scale building of new council homes and preventing them from being flogged off through right to buy. Yet he has already backtracked on a pledge to spend the government’s entire £39bn affordable homes programme on council and social housing.
Crucially, he remains committed to the suffocating fiscal rules that block the investment Britain’s crumbling infrastructure and starved services need, especially given there remains no promise to hike taxes on the well-to-do.
While committing to a national care service is extremely welcome, scrapping the triple lock on pensions is not. Britain still spends significantly less on pensions than other major European countries such as Germany, France and Spain, and about two million pensioners languish in poverty.
Consider, too, that the Labour parliamentary benches were stuffed with candidates deemed loyal to the Starmer project. The rightwing factionalists who ran the party may currently be sulking on the fringes, but do not underestimate their capacity to inflict damage.
A key difference between Burnhamism and what came before may well be expressed by what Miliband told activists attending a Labour fringe event organised by the soft-left pressure group Mainstream. “Too often in the past, we thought that kicking some of our supporters would do us political credit,” he said, “and we were absolutely wrong.” Offending people “in the progressive community”, he admitted, was sometimes done “deliberately”.
Because of pressure from the streets and the ballot box, Labour has shifted its rhetoric. The substance is a bit more complicated. Where Starmerism defined itself against the left, could this new government be pushed in a more progressive direction? That question has not yet been answered. But the left should indeed feel emboldened. The winds are shifting in our direction.
- 
  Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It, is published on 1 October. Order your copy at the Guardian bookshop

Sixteen English councils spend more than 80% of core funding on social care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:00:13 UTC
16:00:13 KST

Sixteen English councils spent more than 80% of their core funding on adult and children’s social care last year, highlighting the growing financial pressure on other local services.
Guardian analysis of government figures found that councils responsible for social care spent a net £42.8bn on adult and children’s services in 2025-26, equivalent to a record 71.9% of their combined core spending. Adult social care took 44.5% and children’s services accounted for 27.4%. In 2017-18, care costs made up 62.4% of councils’ core spending.
The overspending, which is driven by an ageing population with increasingly complex care needs, rising inflationary pressures and growing children’s social care demand, is pushing many councils to the brink of bankruptcy.
These challenges have led Andy Burnham to make reform of the care system key to his government’s ambitions.
Speaking at the Labour conference on Tuesday, the prime minister announced that the government would begin laying the groundwork for a National Care Service to be introduced after the next election, paid for in part by changing the earnings element of the triple lock.
He has already accelerated a government-commissioned independent review of adult social care carried out by Louise Casey, which initially was due to be published in 2028 but is now expected next year. That review will now shape the form the new care service takes.
Lady Casey delivered a withering critique of the state of the English social care system earlier this year, describing it as held together by “sticking plasters and glue”. She said the country faced a “moment of reckoning” over its failure to meet growing care needs.
Halton in Cheshire had the highest net spending on social care relative to its spending power at 92.9% in 2025-26. Just over half of its core spending was spent on adult social care and 42% was spent on child social care, which includes fostering services.
An official audit of the council published last month found its finances were unsustainable, despite it making cuts and selling off council assets. Halton received £35m in government-approved exceptional financial support this year.
A spokesperson for the council said the demand for services continued to place pressure on their finances. “The council is making necessary changes to drive down spending and improve its long-term financial sustainability,” the spokesperson said. “This includes introducing new ways of working that reduce costs while continuing to deliver good outcomes for vulnerable residents.”
Many of the 16 councils spending the largest proportions of their budgets on social care were forced to apply to the government this year for permission to borrow money to meet the day-to-day costs of running services and balance their budgets. Some cover among the most deprived areas in England, including Blackpool, Middlesbrough and Hartlepool.
Adult care alone consumed more than half of core spending power at 19 councils. That number has more than tripled since 2017-18, when six authorities crossed the same threshold.
Core spending power is the government’s measure of the money councils can use to provide services, combining locally raised income such as council tax and business rates with central government grants. It is not ringfenced, meaning councils can choose how to use it.
Councils in England overspent their 2025-26 adult social care budgets by £715m, and in response have drawn up plans to save £909m, according to the Association of Directors of Adult Social Services. These will include higher charges for care and cuts to adult care services such as daycentres.
Analysis by the King’s Fund found that the recent rise in spending reflected a rise in the number of people being supported – contrasting with 2015-20 when, during a period of cuts to council budgets, increased social care costs were mainly going on the fees to social care providers. As of March this year, 684,920 adults were in long-term care, up from a low of 613,360 in 2021-22.
The King’s Fund’s senior fellow for social care, Simon Bottery, said demand for social care had risen due to England’s ageing population as well as more adults living longer with complex needs.
He said: “Councils are meeting some of the extra costs faced by care providers, while also supporting more people. Those two factors combined account for the extra expenditure and the rising proportion of council funding going on care.
“A higher proportion of council budgets is being spent on adult social care than a few years ago, which means services such as refuse collection, libraries and roads get squeezed. Only about 2% of the population receives adult social care in any one year, but councils are spending a huge proportion of their budgets providing it.
“We need to move to a national system for funding social care to avoid the variation we’re seeing. At the moment, someone may receive support in one local authority but not in the next.”
Dr Wendy Taylor, the chair of the Local Government Association’s health and wellbeing committee, said: “Overall overspend has decreased slightly this year, but it remains high and is impacting spending on other council services. At the same time, councils’ capacity to spend on planned prevention is shrinking, with knock-on effects elsewhere in health and care services.
“Sustained and predictable funding and infrastructure will be essential for the future of adult social care, if councils are to successfully meet growing demand, deliver on their duties under the Care Act and support people to live the independent lives they want to lead.”
The Guardian excluded six councils that had not submitted their spending data for 2025-26.

Edinburgh joins UK universities heading for strikes as cuts spread through entire sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:00:13 UTC
16:00:13 KST

Welcome classes for students at the University of Edinburgh this year didn’t focus on the lectures, seminars and essays expected. Instead, students were told about how their education was going to fit in around the strikes planned for this year, which for many will effectively wipe out a term of teaching.
“This term I’ve got two courses and my dissertation. Currently, I’ve got no teaching for five weeks,” said Theo Warshaw, 22, in his final year studying geography at Edinburgh, where staff are striking over budget cuts and compulsory redundancies needed to bridge what the university’s leaders have said is a £400m shortfall.
“I think it’s a shame that students are the only bargaining chip they really have. But I understand it. I would obviously rather it didn’t happen but I do get it.
“No one goes into academia to drive a Ferrari or live in a mansion. They do it because they love it. They don’t want to be striking. They just want a little bit of job security,” said Warshaw.
But similar conversations are taking place at universities across the UK, as administrators grapple with tuition fees eroded by inflation, a drop in international recruitment and changing patterns of demand as students shift away from arts and humanities subjects towards more vocational subjects in science, law and business.
When University and College Union (UCU) staff in Edinburgh launched their industrial action, their colleagues at the University of Dundee were embarking on a five-week strike. And this week UCU staff at the University of Nottingham announced a further round of strikes starting on Monday 5 October and lasting until the end of the semester in December, a stretch of 10 consecutive weeks.
Strike ballots, marking boycotts and votes of no confidence in leadership punctuated campus life in spring and summer, as universities announced course and department closures and redundancies, leading one UCU officer to note that it was easier to list the universities that had avoided being in dispute with their staff so far.
Lopa Leach, professor of vascular biology and immediate past president of Nottingham’s UCU branch, said: “The word is carnage, it is carnage what they are doing now – at the local level and also at the national, senior management level in the UK. Why are they thinking about the destruction of higher education?”
Nottingham’s industrial action has been brewing since its management declared that an £85m deficit required dramatic restructuring, including a plan announced in May to cut nearly 10% of its 7,000 effective full-time positions and suspending entry to all modern language and music courses for new students.
Nick Clare, the current branch president, said that while the strikes were frustrating for students, the uncertainty was being caused by the university’s demands for restructuring, which had left hundreds of staff unsure of their future, while watching colleagues take voluntary redundancy and leave.
“I met my new master’s students yesterday, and I said: ‘I don’t know if I can teach the rest of this course because my job is at risk and I don’t know if I’ll still be here,’” Clare said.
“They are appalled and they understand that many of the things they like about this university are under threat – the small group teaching, getting to know staff, all the things they appreciate are the things that are going to go.
“So students are angry, but they are angry at what’s happening, not at staff. Honestly I’ve never seen more support or solidarity from our students, having been at Nottingham for more than 10 years. Returning students get it, new students get it, it’s amazing in that regard.”
Clare said that the university’s offer of voluntary redundancy had probably been popular enough to wipe out the deficit, leading him to question why the administration was insisting on going ahead with steeper cuts.
Clare warned of a potential “death spiral” hitting the university if its cuts went too far and harmed its standings in international league tables and research income, causing it to shed students and talented staff.
Leach and Clare both warned that the cuts planned at Nottingham were likely to be repeated across the UK because of the nationwide similarities in funding.
“Sadly, higher education doesn’t seem to be a top priority,” Clare said.
“It’s going to take something bad to happen, it’s going to take a university to go under, a so-called elite institution where the children of MPs or journalists go, for people to take notice. If a Russell group university goes bust people might stand up – we really don’t want that to happen but that’s my fear.”
But for students at Nottingham, Dundee and Edinburgh, the bad news is already very real.
One English literature student at Edinburgh, who asked to remain anonymous, said her GCSEs were cancelled because of Covid. Now her classes have been cancelled due to the strikes.
“I think it’s completely understandable. I’m very sympathetic to their situation. They’ve all been very clear with us about why they need to do it and it’s impacting them as well, because obviously they’re not being paid,” she said.
“But it’s frustrating for me. It’s nerve-racking. I’m in my fourth year, my final year, which is 100% of the degree, marks-wise. I’m stressed, because I know missing out on teaching is a shame. It’s a key part of the education process, and I was looking forward to it.”
Prof Peter Mathieson, the vice-chancellor of Edinburgh, said: “We are extremely disappointed that, despite ongoing discussions, the UCU has announced five weeks’ strike action, which will unfairly and deliberately target our students’ first semester of the academic year.
“While we recognise the right of staff to take this action, I want to assure our students that we will continue to do everything we can to mitigate the impacts of that action on them. In addition, we remain firmly committed to constructive and transparent engagement with our joint unions.”

Former leader of Sharia4Belgium, Fouad Belkacem, applies for asylum in Belgium
In 2015 Fouad Belkacem, who was born in Rumst (Antwerp Province), was sentenced to 12 years’ imprisonment as he served as the leader and founder of the terrorist group Sharia4Belgium.
He recruited and indoctrinated young Muslims in Belgium to prepare them for armed conflict in Syria. He also sought to overthrow democracy in Belgium in order to introduce Sharia law here.
His sentence expires in 2027, at which point Belkacem will be released. He would like to remain in Belgium thereafter. According to information VRT NEWS has received from MP Francesca Van Belleghem (Vlaams Belang), he has now submitted an application for asylum, as he has also lost his Belgian nationality as a result of his conviction.
In principle he cannot simply remain in Belgium once he is released. As he still holds Moroccan nationality, he must, in principle, be extradited to Morocco.
The Office of the Commissioner-General for Refugees and Stateless Persons will now prioritise the processing of his case.
"Model prisoner"
VRT NEWS understands he is said to have behaved in an exemplary manner during his imprisonment. He has already been allowed to leave prison briefly on several occasions on a temporary leave permit. That is said to have gone smoothly. Belkacem also has a Belgian wife and three children here.

Here’s a rundown of all the news you need to start your Wednesday, including new Iran sanctions by the US, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's statements on Brexit, Morocco's king appointing Fatima Zahra Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister, and President Donald Trump's remarks on the Strait of Hormuz.
The US Treasury Department sanctioned 10 individuals and entities in multiple jurisdictions that it said procured weapons and weapons components for Iran's Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics (MODAFL).
"Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran's enablers," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
The department said MODAFL is responsible for weapons research, production and acquisition for Iran's armed forces and oversees organizations developing Iran's ballistic missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he will “lay out to the country” different options for the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU, arguing that Brexit “has done more harm than good.”
Speaking at the annual Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, Burnham said Britain could not have “the clear path we need into the rest of this century” without deciding on its future relationship with the EU, which he described as “still our largest market.”
The UK left the EU in 2020, four years after a referendum in which about 52% of voters chose to leave.
Moroccan King Mohammed VI on Tuesday appointed Fatima Zahra Mansouri as prime minister, making her the first woman to hold the post in the country.
Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) won parliamentary elections on Sept. 23, with 97 seats.
The appointment was announced in a statement by the Ministry of the Royal Household, Protocol and Chancellery.
The king appoints the prime minister from the party winning the most seats in the 395-seat House of Representatives, the lower chamber of parliament, while ministers are appointed on the premier’s proposal.

Yamal opened the scoring early before Croatia drew level, but Marc Pubill restored Spain’s advantage shortly afterwards from a Yamal assist. The Barcelona winger struck again in the second half before Nico Williams completed the scoring late on, extending Spain’s unbeaten run to 40 matches.

Captain Harry Kane added the second to seal Thomas Tuchel’s side’s first victory of the campaign. 
Manchester City were found guilty of serious breaches of Premier League financial rules during a nine-season period, with the club announcing it would appeal the landmark ruling.
An independent commission found City committed breaches between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, including arranging “sham” contracts with commercial partners, misstating accounts and concealing the true state of their finances from auditors and football regulators.
It found the arrangements artificially increased revenues and reduced costs by more than £900 million ($1.2 billion), allowing the club to appear compliant with financial regulations. It concluded City would otherwise have substantially breached Premier League and UEFA spending limits.
Canadian pop star Celine Dion made a surprise appearance at Paris Fashion Week on Monday, performing at a L'Oreal Paris runway show beneath the Eiffel Tower.

The White House Accord on "Super Intelligence," described as a “Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities,” calls on companies developing and deploying frontier models to establish robust internal processes and controls designed to ensure their systems operate as intended and that potential problems are identified and addressed quickly.
According to the accord, each participating company should implement four layers of controls and audits covering model development and deployment.

Users can message or call their dot through ChatGPT on desktop, web and mobile, or message it through Slack and Microsoft Teams. Text messaging is planned for later. The assistant can report progress, ask questions and carry context between the channels, according to OpenAI.

Speaking ahead of an informal meeting of EU energy ministers in Dublin, Jorgensen said the figure highlighted the risks of the bloc's continued dependence on imported energy.
"We have now surpassed €100 billion that we've paid extra for our energy this year without receiving one extra molecule of gas or oil," he said.

Argentine troops get first Israeli ARAD rifles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:58:30 UTC
15:58:30 KST

- Argentina's armed forces formally received their first IWI ARAD 5 and ARAD 7 rifles from Israel to begin replacing FAL and M-16 rifles.
- IWI will train personnel from all three services in October, and a second batch is expected in the first quarter of 2027.
Argentina’s armed forces have formally taken on their first IWI ARAD 5 and ARAD 7 rifles from Israel, the start of a program to replace the FN FAL and M-16 rifles now carried by troops in all three services.
Defense Minister Lt. Gen. Carlos Presti presided over the Sept. 29 ceremony after the Joint Staff completed receipt and acceptance testing of the first batch, which Argentina bought from Israel’s Ministry of Defense, the Argentine Defense Ministry said. The ministry said the new rifles will allow the Army, Navy and Air Force to progressively replace their FALs and M-16s.
The ARAD 5 is built on the AR-15 layout, the design family behind the U.S. M16 and M4, and fires the 5.56×45 mm NATO round. The ARAD 7 is built on the larger AR-10 layout and fires the heavier 7.62×51 mm round used by the FAL. Both come with MEPRO M5 red-dot sights made by Israeli company Meprolight and use a modular design that lets units fit different sights and accessories depending on the mission, the ministry said.
In October, personnel from all three services will take operator and maintenance courses taught by Israel Weapon Industries, the rifles’ maker. The second batch is expected in the first quarter of 2027.
The Defense Ministry did not say how many rifles arrived in the first batch or how many Argentina has ordered in total. Zona Militar, whose team attended the ceremony at the Regiment of Infantry 1 “Patricios” in Buenos Aires, reported that the first batch totals 250 rifles: 50 ARAD 7s for the Argentine Army and 200 ARAD 5s split evenly between the Argentine Air Force and the Navy’s marines. Argentine defense outlet Pucará Defensa reported that the batch is part of an initial order for 1,600 rifles.
Joint Staff chief Adm. Marcelo Dalle Nogare said at the ceremony that Argentina is studying whether to set up a local assembly or production line for the rifles, Zona Militar reported. He gave no timeline and did not name an industrial partner. He said the three services defined their requirements in 2024, joint teams evaluated options in Israel, the United States and Europe in 2025, and Argentina and Israel signed an implementation agreement in June 2026.
Presti said Argentina’s range of operating conditions, from high altitude and extreme cold to heat, humidity, jungle and dust, made the choice difficult, and that the aim was to find the best system for Argentina’s needs.
The FAL, a Belgian design, was built under license in Argentina and has been the standard rifle of Argentine troops for about 70 years, including during the 1982 Falklands War. The rifle purchase is one of several major equipment programs underway, alongside F-16 fighters, armored vehicles, a P-3 Orion patrol aircraft for the Navy and Black Hawk helicopters for the Army.
As of Aug. 31, Argentina had recorded 4.75 billion pesos (about $3.1 million) in spending obligations under the rifle program, according to budget data cited by Zona Militar. The receiving services will run their own operational tests before the rifles are fully issued to units.

Gentle giant Backpack wins Alaska’s Fat Bear Week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:57:52 UTC
15:57:52 KST

Gentle giant Backpack wins Alaska’s Fat Bear Week
The contest, which is in its 12th year, celebrates the resilience of the 2,200 brown bears that live in the preserve on the Alaska Peninsula.
After a week of fierce competition, Backpack emerged victorious as Fat Bear Week champion, the heftiest bear in Alaska’s Katmai National Park and Preserve.
The nonprofit running the longstanding contest announced on Tuesday that the bear, known for his pacifist nature, was the winner with more than 100,000 votes, giving him a close win over Bear 910 with just over 50 percent of the poll.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Hunting endangered animals in the jungles of Myanmar
- list 2 of 3India’s lion numbers soar: Why are some conservationists worried?
- list 3 of 3Photos: Thailand’s soaring captive lion population
The contest, which is in its 12th year, celebrates the resilience of the 2,200 brown bears that live in the preserve on the Alaska Peninsula, which extends from the state’s southwest corner towards the Aleutian Islands. Fat Bear Week was started in 2014 as an interactive way to inform the public about brown bears, the coastal cousins of grizzlies.
Last year’s winner, Chunk — known officially as Bear 32 — clinched his victory at an estimated 1,200 pounds. He was handily defeated in the first round of competition this year by Bucky, who went on to lose a face-off against Backpack, known officially as Bear 89.
The event this year featured 16 bears vying for the heavyweight title in a single-elimination, bracket-style tournament. All voting is done online, and the winner was declared on Tuesday evening after the final poll closed. The public could watch the bears on explore.org’s livestream cameras before deciding on their favourite.
“Fat bears are successful bears,” the nonprofit says on its website. These bears gorge themselves on the abundant salmon that return to the Brooks River starting in late June. It is there that they can stuff themselves to accumulate the fat reserves they will need to survive the winter. To be featured in the contest, the bears must frequent the area around the river.
Son of ex-champion
Backpack is the son of former Fat Bear Week champion Holly, who introduced him to the Brooks River when he was a first-year cub in 2006. His name was inspired by his habit of climbing onto his mother’s back when they swam the river. This year’s fans cheered on Backpack in the contest’s Instagram comments, noting his lineage and reputation as a gentle giant.
“Unlike many large adult male bears, Backpack hasn’t shown much aggression toward his competitors,” his contestant profile reads.
Backpack uses his “quiet strength” rather than brawling and is often seen in wildlife cameras sitting on a rock downstream, appearing to take in the scenery around him.
He defeated Bear 910, who is also the daughter of a former champion: 409 Beadnose.
Adult male brown bears typically weigh between 600 and 900 pounds (270-410kg) in midsummer. By the time they are ready to hibernate after feasting on migrating and spawning salmon, large males can weigh more than 1,000 pounds (454kg). Females are about one-third smaller. Bears may each eat as many as 30 fish a day this time of year, working hard to eat a year’s worth of food in about six months.
During winter hibernation, bears do not eat or drink and can lose one-third of their body weight.
Fat Bear Week’s contestants also included five bear families, in recognition of the record-high number of families and cubs at the river this summer. A mother must feed and protect her cubs while also eating enough calories to sustain herself through hibernation. Cubs often face the risk of attack from other bears due to territorialism or food scarcity.
Bear 132 and her three spring cubs advanced to the semifinals, but lost out to Bear 910.
She has become one of the largest and most experienced mother bears at Brooks River, according to her contestant profile. In mid-July, one of her cubs became separated from the family for several days, wandering the river corridor alone. The cub was reunited with the family a few days later.

Tennessee set to execute first woman in over 200 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:55:46 UTC
15:55:46 KST

Death row inmate Christa Pike, convicted of murdering a schoolmate three decades ago, is due to be executed by lethal injection in Tennessee on Wednesday, becoming the first woman that state has put to death in more than two centuries.
Pike, whose clemency petition highlighting childhood trauma and sexual abuse was denied by Governor Bill Lee, would also be the only person in the modern era of US capital punishment to be executed in Tennessee for a crime committed as a teenager.
The US Supreme Court on Tuesday rejected an 11th-hour bid for a stay of execution, which is set to take place at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, the state capital.
Pike, now 50, was 18 in January 1995 when she, a 17-year-old boyfriend and a third companion lured 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate at their Knoxville Job Corps vocational centre, into a wooded area where they tortured and killed her.
Trial testimony indicated that Pike viewed Slemmer as a rival for the affections of her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp.
Pike and Shipp confessed to the killing, and both were convicted the following year of first-degree murder. Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Their co-defendant, Shadolla Peterson, who was 18 at the time of the murder and had acted as a lookout for the other two, appeared as a witness for the prosecution and received probation.
Currently the only woman on Tennessee's death row, Pike was also convicted in August 2001 of attempted first-degree murder in an assault on another inmate, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction.
In a 226-page petition asking the governor to commute her death penalty to a life sentence without the possibility of parole, her lawyers documented her history as the childhood victim of violence, neglect and sexual abuse, including two rapes at ages 11 and 17. And they cited the diagnoses she received in prison for bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Teen who committed murder 'no longer exists'
Her lawyers also pointed to evidence that Pike's mother drank heavily during pregnancy, contributing to faulty brain development that made it difficult for their client to control her impulses as a young person.
"The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists," her lawyers wrote in response to Lee's denial of clemency. "Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper treatment for her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women."
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, has spoken out in support of the execution.
Executions of female prison inmates are exceedingly rare in the US, with women accounting for just 18 of the 1,683 people put to death since the Supreme Court allowed capital punishment to resume in 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Before Wednesday, Tennessee had executed 17 people.
Pike's case has drawn international attention, with a group of United Nations human rights experts issuing a recent statement calling for commutation of her death sentence.
Sexual violence and trauma experts have also spoken out on her behalf, arguing that the procedures surrounding lethal injection would likely cause Pike to experience severe, traumatic flashbacks of child sexual abuse and rape, adding to the cruelty and anguish of her death.
Tennessee prison officials in May aborted attempts to execute a man convicted of murders after failing to find a suitable vein for a lethal injection.

Drone fell and exploded in Moldova amid Russia's attack on Ukraine; Romania scrambled F-18s
Kyiv • UNN
A drone fell and exploded near the village of Hîrbovăț in Moldova. Romania scrambled two F-18s, but no violation of its airspace was detected.
A drone flew in and exploded near the city of Bender in Moldova on the morning of September 30, amid the Russian Federation's attack on Ukraine. Fighter jets were scrambled again in Romania overnight. UNN reports this, citing data from the police and defense agencies of the countries.
A drone fell and exploded in Moldova
This morning, at around 05:40, police were informed that a drone had been spotted flying at a low altitude over the vicinity of the municipality of Bender. The aircraft later fell in a rural area of the village of Hîrbovăț, in Anenii Noi District, where it exploded. Preliminary reports indicated that there were no casualties
The area was secured, and specialized police units were dispatched to the scene.
"Experts are to examine the object and establish all the circumstances of the incident. Police urge citizens not to approach or touch any suspicious fragments or objects, and to avoid the area until the inspections are completed," the statement said.
The incident was confirmed by Moldova's Ministry of Defense.
"Against the backdrop of massive attacks by the Russian Federation on Ukraine, the national integrated monitoring system reported that today, September 30, at around 05:43, a drone had flown through the national airspace and fallen on the outskirts of the village of Hîrbovăț, in Anenii Noi District, where it exploded," the Moldovan defense agency said in a statement.
The Air Operations Service, as noted, continues to monitor the airspace in coordination with the competent authorities and partners.
As noted, police and representatives of the national army were sent to the scene to investigate the incident.
Romania scrambled fighter jets
"During the night of September 29–30, the radar surveillance system of the Ministry of National Defence detected an aerial target moving east of Izmail, in Ukrainian territory, near the river border with Romania," Romania's Ministry of National Defence said in a statement.
Two F-18 aircraft of the Spanish Air and Space Force, which are on duty as part of enhanced air policing, took off to monitor the situation

Murat Basoglu and Ikram Kouachi
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Iraq on Wednesday announced the end of the US-led international coalition’s mission, marking a transition to bilateral relations with coalition member states, the prime minister’s security adviser said.
In a statement carried by the official Iraqi News Agency INA, Qasim al-Araji called the move an “important milestone,” saying it followed negotiations and understandings that began in July 2021.
US forces completed withdrawal from their remaining positions in Iraq by the end of this month.
He said the new phase would involve “bilateral relations with its countries” aimed at consolidating Iraq’s sovereignty.
Araji credited the victory over ISIS (Daesh) terror group to “the sacrifices of Iraqis and the valor of our armed forces in their various branches and formations,” as well as support from the international coalition and brotherly and friendly countries.
He stressed that ending the coalition’s mission “does not mean the end of the partnership,” but rather a shift toward bilateral relations with its member states.
Security and intelligence cooperation, along with the exchange of information and expertise and capacity-building efforts, will continue “on the basis of mutual respect and shared interests,” he said.
Baghdad and Washington agreed in September 2024 to end the coalition’s military mission in Iraq under a timetable extending through the end of September 2026, with a transition to bilateral security relations between Iraq and member states.
The coalition was formed under US leadership in 2014 after ISIS seized large areas of Iraq and Syria, providing Iraqi forces with air, intelligence and training support during operations against the group.
Iraq announced in December 2017 that it had regained full control of territory seized by ISIS.

The birth of a painting: Artist Merike Estna on creating in public at the Venice Biennale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:51:49 UTC
15:51:49 KST

Estonia artist Merike Estna did something extremely unusual for the Venice Biennale, even by its own standards. Over the past five months, she created paintings live in front of daily visitors. The result is 22 canvases which explore the themes of motherhood and feminism.
Visitors to the Estonian pavilion at this year's Venice International Art Biennale may have been surprised to see the country's representative Merike Estna in person, creating her latest works.
During the past five months, right before people's eyes, she has methodically made The House of Leaking Sky exhibition which consists of 22 large canvases.
"The pavilion shows three monumental works. The long bench that is 26 metres. Then the floor [25,000 tiles] people walk on, which I think of kind of as a mind map for the project and then the painting behind me which I started with empty canvas," Esta told Euronews Culture earlier this month.
Motherhood and female art history
Motherhood and female art history were the inspiration for creating the space. It has an extra significant meaning knowing that Estna recently gave birth. She was still on maternity leave with her younger child while preparing to come to Venice and work on the biggest project in her career for five full months, live in front of the visiting audience.
As curator, Natalia Sielewicz, emphasizes in her curatorial text, Estna braids together meditations on motherhood and the lineages of women artists who carved paths toward artistic self-determination.
"As a working mother herself, she often folds complex iconographies of care, lineage, and inheritance into her practice," she wrote.
Sielewicz reminds visitors of the existence of pittore senza opera - the painter without works, most often embodied by women whose oeuvres were absorbed into patriarchal workshops or erased from official chronicles.
"Marietta Robusti Tintoretta was one of them: a Venetian painter-poet who dressed as a boy to work beside her father, Jacopo Tintoretto, in the heat of the family atelier. Her paintings circulated without her name, her skill credited upward; she died in childbirth before she had the chance to fully step into the light of her own authorship," she wrote.
Living in Venice with her family throughout the Biennale, Estna brings motherhood into the conceptual structure of the project and found the experience to be extremely useful for both her and her children. "It is a complicated city to live with a family and to live with small children," Estna said. "My older kid lost his scooter on the first morning of his arrival [in] the canal. Our youngest only learned to walk a couple of months ago. So it's been a challenge, but also... I really love challenges, I think it always gives us new ideas and drives us, leads us to different thoughts."
Living space
Estna created her studio and exhibition inside of the former Church of Santa Maria Assunta in Venice’s Castello district, which was later used as a community space and gymnasium. These overlapping sacred, civic and everyday histories form an active backdrop for her evolving work.
"This studio space, what Merike created, is really like a living space. The painting has changed and then evolved so much throughout those past five months. It is really active and happy place, I would say. Many people who are living in Venice they keep returning," said Maria Arusoo, Commissioner of Estonian Pavilion at la Biennale di Venezia.
"People really want to ask questions, reflect, talk, just sit around."
For Merike visitors were crucial and she wanted them always to be taken care of. "They're definitely not intruders at the pavilion and the main idea to show the painting how it is born, it only carries when people actually visit and see and so this is an important part of the pavillion".
At first she was anxious, but later on these conditions reminded her of being back at the art academy where she always shared a studio and tried to focus by wearing headphones while others were chatting.
Politics and protests
The 61st Venice Art Biennale kicked off with enormous controversy as several countries and artists protested against the organiser's decision to invite Russia to open its pavilion in Giardini, one of the two main spaces of the Biennale.
Maria Arusoo, Commissioner of the Estonian Pavilion told Euronews Culture that art can never be separated from politics.
"Merike said this really beautiful and sad thing, that we [Estonia] were 60 years not part of this dialogue and not part of the Biennial because of Russia, because we were occupied and we couldn't be part as an independent country. So we won't step back because they decide to join."
The protest against the Russian pavilion ended in front of the Estonian pavilion on the opening day of the Biennale. Estna signed also an open letter against the Israeli pavilion.
The 61st International Art Exhibition of the Venice Biennale closes on Sunday, 22 November 2026.

Pentagon buys Israeli smart rifle sights to shoot down drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:50:40 UTC
15:50:40 KST

- JIATF-401 awarded Smart Shooter a three-year, sole-supplier contract worth up to $150 million for SMASH counter-drone rifle sights.
- The contract supports the task force's Domestic Shield Program to protect U.S. forces and bases at home and abroad.
The Pentagon’s counter-drone task force has awarded Israeli company Smart Shooter a contract worth up to $150 million for its SMASH rifle sights, which help soldiers shoot down small drones with their regular service weapons.
The U.S. Department of War’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401, known as JIATF-401, announced the three-year award on Sept. 29, and Smart Shooter said the next day that it is the only supplier under the deal. The contract is an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity agreement, which sets a ceiling and lets the government place individual orders over time. The quantity, pricing and timing of deliveries will be decided in those orders, and neither the company nor the task force said how many systems the first order will cover.
The contract covers SMASH hardware, software and updates, training and support. It supports JIATF-401’s Domestic Shield Program and related missions overseas, focused on protecting troops, bases and other key sites in the United States and abroad from drones.
SMASH is a fire control system that mounts on a rifle like a scope. It uses artificial intelligence and computer vision to lock onto a target, calculate where to aim and release the shot only when the weapon is lined up to hit. That lets an ordinary soldier hit a small, fast-moving drone that would be very hard to shoot down with iron sights or a standard optic. The rifle can still be used normally against ground targets, and the soldier decides whether to fire. The system can also link to outside sensors and battle management networks.
“Domestic Shield is about giving defenders the tools to stop small, fast-moving drones before they can harm forces, bases, and critical assets,” said Michal Mor, CEO and co-founder of Smart Shooter.
JIATF-401 coordinates counter-drone work across the U.S. military and federal agencies. The task force is led by U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross.
“Our approach allows us to identify the right capabilities for specific operational requirements and rapidly deliver those capabilities to the warfighter,” said U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, director of JIATF-401.
The award is Smart Shooter’s second with the task force, following a contract announced in March 2026. The company says thousands of SMASH systems are already in use across the U.S. Army, U.S. Navy, U.S. Air Force and U.S. Marine Corps, and that it has won a series of new and follow-on orders from those services over the past year. SMASH is also used by forces in Israel, the United Kingdom, Germany and other NATO and allied countries.
JIATF-401 has been signing larger counter-drone deals this year. In May, it gave Perennial Autonomy a three-year contract worth up to $500 million for interceptor drones, including the Merops system that U.S. forces have used against Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones, DroneXL reported.
Smart Shooter, founded in Israel, has offices in the United States, Europe and Australia.

Burnham says he's not getting rid of pensions triple lock, but just adjusting how it works
Andy Burnham has said that it is not accurate to say that he is getting rid of the pensions triple lock.
In interviews this morning, he challenged this description because the plan he announced yesterday means that the value of the state pension will continue to rise in line with prices, earnings or 2.5%.
But under the current system, pensions rise every year either by 2.5%, or by inflation, or by the annual rise in earnings – which is highest.
After 2030, normally they will rise by 2.5% or by inflation. But if that is not enough to ensure that pensions have risen in line with the average increase in earnings since the policy was introduced, they will rise by that amount.
The pensions triple lock is not a benefit; it is an uprating mechanism, and what Burnham announced means that the earnings element of that mechanism will apply according to a new formula.
The change will save money because, under the current system, if the rise in earnings is particularly big one year, as sometimes happens, there is a rachet effect, and the increase gets baked in for future years.
Burnham told Times Radio:
The decision on the triple lock, the adjustment – and it is an adjustment – it’s not getting rid of the whole concept of the triple lock.

It’s important for me to say that we don’t have huge room for manoeuvre.

El Nino is a 'postcard from the future' — and could cause 451,000 excess heat deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:49:00 UTC
15:49:00 KST

El Nino: A deadly 'postcard from the future'
September 30, 2026
Peruvian fishermen gave El Nino its name — "the little boy," or Christ Child — after noticing unusually warm Pacific waters around Christmas that caused the fish they depended on to suddenly become scarce.
But what those fishermen observed locally can have consequences thousands of kilometers away. El Nino can shift temperature and rainfall patterns around the world, bringing extreme heat and drought to some regions and heavy rain and flooding to others.
Researchers now estimate that the unusually high temperatures linked to the current El Nino could cause around 451,000 excess deaths worldwide from June 2026 to February 2027.
The event is a "postcard from the future," Tamma Carleton, head of research at the University of Chicago's Climate Impact Lab, told DW. Land temperatures over the coming months are forecast to run about 1.2 degrees C (2.1 F) above normal.
"For the average person, that's roughly the warming climate change is projected to bring about 20 years from now, arriving all at once," Carleton said.
How does El Nino affect weather worldwide?
Normally, winds blowing west across the Pacific push warm surface water towards Asia and Australia, allowing colder water to rise near South America. During El Nino, which occurs erratically every two to seven years, those winds weaken. Less cold water then rises, and much more of the Pacific stays unusually warm.
The warmer water heats the air above it and fuels rainfall over the central and eastern Pacific. The rising air spreads high in the atmosphere, sending waves that disrupt weather worldwide.
"It is like throwing a stone into a lake," climate researcher Fred Kucharski told DW. "Initially the surface perturbation is local, but then the energy spreads all over the lake through wave propagation."
Kucharski said the effects can cross the tropics within one week and reach higher latitudes in about two. Where the waves travel determines whether a region becomes hotter, cooler, wetter or drier.
The current El Nino developed in June and has strengthened rapidly since. It is now on course to become an exceptionally strong — sometimes called "super" — El Nino.
The Climate Impact Lab says its estimate covers only the first nine months of El Nino, as far as the current seasonal forecasts allow. The event is expected to continue into Northern Hemisphere spring, and its effect on global temperatures could last longer.
"We expect the final number to be meaningfully higher than what we are currently reporting here," Carleton said.
Why can El Nino be so deadly?
The estimate of 451,000 excess deaths covers deaths linked to the direct health effects of unusually high temperatures associated with El Nino.
Extreme heat strains the heart and kidneys, makes it harder for the body to maintain a safe temperature and can worsen cardiovascular, respiratory and other illnesses. As a result, the underlying condition is often recorded as the cause of death rather than the heat that aggravated it.
"Most heat deaths never show up in official statistics as heat deaths," Carleton said.
El Nino can also alter rainfall, contributing to drought in some regions and heavy rain and flooding in others.
Floods can kill, contaminate drinking water and spread disease. Drought can damage harvests and cause water and food shortages.
Deaths from these other indirect effects are not included in the 451,000 projection.
Where will the toll be greatest?
The Climate Impact Lab expects some of the largest increases in deaths in the Sahel, South and Southeast Asia and parts of Latin America. The highest numbers of fatalities are predicted for Nigeria, Sudan, Niger, Chad, India, Indonesia and Brazil.
Many are projected to occur between December and February, meaning much of the expected toll still lies ahead.
"Heat headlines usually focus on Europe and North America," Carleton said. "This event's toll is overwhelmingly in lower-income, already-hot countries, where people have the fewest ways to adapt and where these deaths are least likely to be counted."
Are these lives being significantly shortened?
Some people who die during extreme heat are already frail. This raises an important question: Is the heat cutting their lives substantially short, or merely bringing forward deaths that would have occurred days or weeks later — an effect known as mortality displacement?
The underlying research uses annual rather than daily death rates, which largely filters out deaths brought forward by only days or weeks.
Ben Armstrong, an emeritus professor at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said he could not verify the 451,000 figure. But because the estimate is based on annual mortality data, it largely excludes deaths brought forward by only days or weeks. If the figure is correct, he said, most of those counted "would have lived at least six months longer."
Why predict deaths before they happen?
Scientists have long estimated the death toll from extreme temperatures retrospectively. Better seasonal forecasting is increasingly allowing researchers to look ahead instead.
To produce the estimate, researchers used earlier work showing how death rates change during hot weather in different parts of the world. They combined it with seasonal forecasts showing how hot each place is expected to become.
"Putting the two together lets us estimate the human cost of this event while there's still time to do something about it, rather than counting the deaths after the fact," Carleton said.
Heat warnings, cooling centers and hydration stations, home visits to vulnerable people, protections for outdoor workers and additional health care capacity could all reduce mortality.
The researchers believe targeted interventions could save tens of thousands of lives.
For Carleton, the forecast is a warning to prepare now for the heat that climate change could make commonplace.
"This El Nino gives us a look at future weather in the 2040s," Carleton said. "These temperatures will become normal in 20 years, giving us time and reason to begin investing in adaptive capacity now."
Edited: Carla Bleiker

Gokhan Ergocun
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Germany's import prices soared by 8.3% in August, marking its highest increase rate since December 2022, driven by surging energy costs, official data shows on Wednesday.
The Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) reported that export prices also accelerated by 4.7% compared to August 2025, recording the largest annual increase since February 2023.
On a monthly basis, import prices increased by 1% while export prices rose by 0.4% in August compared to July 2026.
Energy import prices surged by 43% year-on-year in August as the war in the Middle East strongly impacted the sector.
Destatis recorded significant annual import price increases for electricity at 63.9%, mineral oil products at 63.3%, and natural gas at 41.9%.
Imported intermediate goods saw an 11% annual price increase, largely driven by higher costs for non-ferrous metals and semi-finished metal products.
Conversely, imported agricultural products cost 2.4% less and imported consumer goods saw a 0.5% price decline compared to the same month a year earlier.
The Iran war also heavily influenced export prices, pushing energy export prices up by 44.1% compared to August 2025.
Exported intermediate goods registered a 7% year-on-year price increase, significantly impacting the overall export price index.
The two product groups of intermediate and capital goods accounted for nearly 75% of all goods exports.

China factory activity returns to growth in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:45:54 UTC
15:45:54 KST

China’s factory activity returned to growth in September after two months of contraction, official data showed on Sept. 30, offering a modest sign of improvement as Beijing steps up support for the world’s second-largest economy.
The official manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI) rose to 50.1 from 49.8 in August, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while one below that level signals contraction. The index stood at 49.2 in July.
Factory production strengthened, with the production sub-index rising to 51.7 from 50.4 in August. New orders remained in expansion territory at 50.5.
The non-manufacturing PMI, covering services and construction, climbed to 50.2 from 49.0 a month earlier. Construction activity returned to expansion at 50.3, while the services index rose to 50.2.
The composite PMI, which covers both manufacturing and non-manufacturing activity, increased to 50.7 from 49.5.
The figures came as Beijing unveiled additional measures to support an economy still facing weak domestic demand and a prolonged property downturn.
The State Council said earlier this week that it would roll out measures aimed at stabilizing the property market, supporting employment and raising incomes.
The People’s Bank of China followed on Sept. 29 by cutting a key policy lending rate and expanding credit support for infrastructure, technology and smaller businesses.
Authorities also announced an interest subsidy for qualifying first-home mortgages, due to take effect on Oct. 1.
Exports and advanced manufacturing have remained important sources of support for the Chinese economy, with demand linked to the global artificial intelligence boom helping parts of the technology sector.

ATLANTA, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- A pair of Chinese giant pandas landed here for a 10-year stay on Sunday, enabling locals to refresh decades-old bonds after a gap of nearly two years.

Named Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, the pair are in excellent condition and they are doing well, said Rivera in an interview with Xinhua on Monday.
Now it was time for them to adjust to their new surroundings, said Rivera.
The arrival of the giant pandas not only "overjoyed" the staff at Zoo Atlanta but also sparked excitement among local residents and zoo-goers eager to see them.
Zoo Atlanta wasted no time putting up new posters and banners inside and outside the zoo on Sunday.
Meanwhile, as the giant pandas arrived, they were greeted by locals who felt excited for being the first to catch sight of the pair.
Tanya Smith, one of the owners of Ollie's Market and Deli located around the corner of Zoo Atlanta, made a chalk drawing on a community board outside the cafe on Sunday morning.
The drawing depicted two giant pandas surrounded by bamboos, with a big "welcome" to Ping Ping and Fu Shuang alongside the cafe's social media handle.
Smith finished the drawing by adding the Chinese names of the two giant pandas.
"We were all really excited. All the employees came out videoing it and it was really exciting," said Smith.

Deringer added that her eight-year-old daughter Sienna had just named her new panda toy Ping Ping after the new arrivals.

The patrols are meant to further strengthen the orderly management of relevant waters and resolutely safeguard China's territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests, the CCG said.
China has sovereignty over Nanhai Zhudao (the South China Sea Islands), consisting of Dongsha Qundao (the Dongsha Islands), Xisha Qundao (the Xisha Islands), Zhongsha Qundao (the Zhongsha Islands) and Nansha Qundao (the Nansha Islands). Huangyan Dao is located in the Zhongsha Islands.
China has historic rights in the South China Sea. China also has internal waters, territorial sea, contiguous zone, exclusive economic zone and continental shelf, based on Nanhai Zhudao.
The international community has long widely recognized Nanhai Zhudao as part of China's territory. ■

Gene found to help harmful gut bacteria resist antibiotics, disinfectants
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:45:25 CST
15:45:25 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Scientists in Australia have identified a key gene that helps dangerous gut bacteria withstand even hospital-grade disinfectants intended to kill them.
New research reveals that the bacteria Clostridioides difficile has picked up the key gene that gives its dormant spores a free pass against antibiotics and cleaning products, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's Monash University.
Its spores can remain dormant and later activate in suitable environments such as the human gut, posing a particular risk in hospitals where the bacterium can cause potentially deadly diarrhea, according to the study published in Nature Communications.
Researchers found that the antibiotic resistance gene produces a protein that replaces a key spore-building protein, allowing the bacteria to produce tougher spores that can survive hospital-grade cleaning products and high laundry temperatures, potentially making infections harder to control and helping resistant strains spread.
The researchers are now investigating ways to target the spores and address this new type of antibiotic resistance. ■

SEOUL, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's real wages, adjusted for inflation, fell for a fourth straight month amid lingering inflationary pressure, labor ministry data showed Wednesday.
