Interview: El Nino to worsen LatAm's economic woes, warns Chilean expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:13:29 CST
12:13:29 KST

by Cristobal Chavez Bravo
SANTIAGO, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- This year's El Nino phenomenon will exacerbate economic problems in Latin America and the Caribbean, mainly by disrupting rainfall and raising temperatures, a Chilean climatologist has said in a recent interview with Xinhua.
Patricio Gonzalez Colville, a researcher at the Center for Research and Transfer in Irrigation and Agroclimatology at Chile's University of Talca, said El Nino's economic impact would be felt mainly through agriculture.
"The El Nino event affects the economy as a whole. Its main impact is to drastically alter both precipitation, causing floods or droughts, and temperatures, leading to extreme heatwaves with highs exceeding 38 degrees Celsius for several days," Gonzalez said.
Fruit and cereal farming requires moderate weather conditions. "Consequently, the primary impact is felt in agricultural losses, affecting both family farming and access to water," the expert said.
"Many communities will see their food crops diminish, and markets will raise the prices of basic goods due to scarcity. Poverty levels will rise as these communities are unable to sell surpluses and face limited access to irrigation water," he said.
He also warned that unemployment could rise as communities dependent on agriculture may be forced to cut jobs amid growing climate uncertainty and vulnerability.
Gonzalez said the current El Nino warming is classified as "strong" in terms of intensity and is expected to evolve into an "extraordinary" event between November 2026 and January 2027.
Central America faces a "tough" climate outlook with the development of the 2026 El Nino, particularly in the so-called "dry corridor," an extensive strip spanning southern Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and part of Costa Rica.
"El Nino causes extreme droughts in this geographic area. It is estimated that 11 million people who rely almost exclusively on family farming, growing crops such as maize and beans, will face limited access to water. Consequently, the presence of an El Nino event of such extraordinary magnitude threatens to exacerbate the food crisis in this region," he said.
Some 43 million people in Latin America and the Caribbean are undernourished, and the impacts of this event could aggravate the situation in countries such as Colombia, where heatwaves and extreme droughts hurt the country's agricultural economy, he added.
"The most severe scenario could unfold in Brazil, where droughts and water scarcity in the Amazon, the so-called 'lungs of the planet,' could trigger uncontrollable forest fires," said Gonzalez.
"An analysis of past El Nino events shows that Latin American countries tend to bear the brunt of the impact. Their economies rely heavily on agricultural exports," he said, adding that this could result in lower economic returns for these countries.
What's more, climate change "is acting in synergy with El Nino" to raise temperatures, Gonzalez said.
"All signs indicate that the planet has already passed the point of no return regarding this new phase, in which 'normality' is no longer a fixed climatic concept," he concluded. ■

TOKYO, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Japan's total population, including foreign residents, stood at about 122.97 million as of Oct. 1, 2025, down around 3.17 million, or 2.5 percent, from 2020, according to the finalized 2025 census results released by the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications on Tuesday.

Mexico wins arbitration against U.S. parking meter company
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:13:02 CST
12:13:02 KST

MEXICO CITY, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Mexico won an international arbitration case after a tribunal dismissed the complaint brought by a U.S.-based parking meter company and ordered it to pay over a million U.S. dollars in restitution for the legal fees incurred, the Economy Ministry said Tuesday.
Doups Holdings LLC was seeking some 600 million pesos (about 33 million dollars) in damages from the Mexican government after its concessions for installing and operating parking meters in Mexico City, through a local firm, were revoked by the Mexico City Mobility Secretariat.
Doups had filed its claim with the International Center for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) under the rules of the North American Free Trade Agreement, which was in effect at the time.
The ICSID tribunal ruled that it had no jurisdiction over the claim and dismissed the case, ordering the company to pay more than 1 million dollars to cover Mexico's legal and procedural costs.
According to the Economy Ministry, "from the outset of the arbitration, Mexico maintained that the claim suffered from serious deficiencies, specifically regarding the structuring of the subsidiary company that allegedly sustained the damages."
There were issues concerning Doups' control over the subsidiary and its compliance with arbitration procedures, among others, the ministry said.
The ICSID, a World Bank Group institution responsible for resolving international disputes between investors and states, has made the award and additional information regarding the arbitration available.
The ruling marks another instance in which Mexico has utilized international legal mechanisms to defend itself against investor claims brought under investment protection treaties. ■

Still, Watson has mixed emotions about the thought of leaving her home country. “I want to stay here and fight for our safety in Canada,” she said. “The option to come to the US is really important, but we shouldn’t have to need it.”
The Trump administration has imposed stringent restrictions on immigration, including on asylum seekers, but is inviting South African whites – and, potentially, Canadian Jews – to apply for refugee status. Critics accuse Trump of playing politics with refugee status, but some Canadian Jews see it as a lifeline.
Jewish journalist acquires second passport as antisemitism precaution
Talk of Jews feeling compelled to leave Canada gained momentum last week when a well-known Jewish journalist posted publicly on social media about getting a foreign passport. Neil Herland, a newsreader for the national broadcaster, the CBC, wrote on X/Twitter about his encounter with pro-Palestinian protesters outside Toronto’s Meridian Arts Centre, where Yom Kippur services were being held. Herland said that, concerned about rising antisemitism in Canada, he recently acquired his Austrian passport as a safety precaution. (Independent Press Gallery, a press freedom advocacy group, condemned the CBC for reportedly suspending Herland after pro-Palestinian advocates lodged a complaint about his post.)
Some Jews are past the precaution stage. Sheldon Shugal, 64, and his wife are currently researching how to move to the United States.
“If I were able to claim refugee status to come to the US, I’d do it without hesitation,” said Shugal, who lives in Calgary. “I used to love our country… but it’s just not a place that I want to continue to live in.”
Shugal, a property manager, said he has seen increased antisemitism in Canada in the wake of the deadly Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, and the war it launched. He said he and his wife have been struggling to overcome the complexity of acquiring an American visa.
“The Jew-hatred is no longer rising in Canada, it’s fully immersed here,” says Shugal. “It’s not the country I grew up in. I don’t feel affinity to Canada anymore.”
Shugal’s concerns are reflected in the findings of B’nai Brith Canada, which recently reported a 9.3% increase in antisemitic incidents from 2024-2025. According to this report, online harassment has surged dramatically, while Ontario saw the greatest total number of antisemitic incidents out of all the Canadian provinces and territories.
Antisemitic attacks have proliferated. In March of this year, Toronto synagogue Temple Emanu-El was shot at following Purim celebrations. The next week, two more Toronto synagogues were hit with gunfire over Shabbat, causing damage to the buildings, though no injuries were reported. In late April, assailants allegedly fired replica guns at “visually-identifiable” members of the city’s Jewish community, with one of the men sustaining minor injuries.
Shugal said reports of antisemitism have rattled him as well as the pro-Palestinian encampment his daughter encountered on her campus. “There hasn’t necessarily been anything I’ve personally experienced. It’s just what I’ve seen throughout the country,” Shugal said.
Antisemitism main motivator for leaving Canada, immigration lawyer says
Lauren Cohen, an immigration lawyer based in Boca Raton, Florida, said that since the October 7 attacks, about half of her Canadian clients cite antisemitism as a primary reason for wanting to leave Canada for the United States.
“In the past three months, I’ve noticed a very significant increase in the number of people between 55-70 who are contacting me,” said Cohen, who is originally from Toronto. “They have grown children or no children, and they have a little bit more money,” she said. “They want freedom.”
Antisemitism is not the only consideration for her clients, Cohen said. “The economy’s struggling. It’s not just antisemitism,” she said. “That might be the straw that broke the camel’s back, but it’s so many other factors as well.”
Cohen founded the Jewish Community Collective, an organization which helps Jewish Canadians and “displaced Jews” find connection in America. Another option for Jewish Canadians looking to make a new home in the States is Lech L’Tulsa, a program cosponsored by the Jewish Federation of Tulsa that helps settle Jewish newcomers, “designed to help Jewish Canadian citizens relocate to Tulsa.”
Some Canadian Jews do not see greener grass south of the 49th parallel, however. They point to Canada’s more expansive social safety net as one of the many reasons life in the Great White North” is better. “Unquestionably, the answer to whether I’d consider moving to the States is emphatically ‘no,’” said Lawrence Stanleigh, a dentist in Calgary.
“I believe our country is a better place to live,” said Stanleigh, 67. “The US doesn’t have a public healthcare system. Why would I want to leave our safety net for the US?”
Stanleigh said the idea that the United States is a safe haven for Canadian Jews is misleading. “As bad as things are in Canada, I think they’re worse in the United States,” he said. “It’s not a better place for education or for healthcare. The whole idea of moving there for our safety is a fantasy that the Republicans believe in.”
Substituting the United States for Canada is shortsighted, Stanleigh said. “There are failures on behalf of Canadian leaders to stand firm in their support of the Jewish community,” he said. “But as bad as things are, I think they’re worse in the States. Our American cousins are blithely unaware of the problems they have at home.”
Jewish parliament member blames right-wing Jews for attacking government
Anthony Housefather, a Jewish Canadian Member of Parliament representing a riding, or electoral district, in Montreal, is skeptical of the notion that the United States would offer Jews better protection.
“I think this idea is inspired by some right-wing Jews who have decided that their mission is to attack the Canadian government, and to make it look like somehow, Donald Trump and the Republicans are the savior of the Jewish people,” Housefather said in an interview.
Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney are at a low point in their relationship, with tensions over trade intensifying – and Trump seeks opportunities to take potshots at Carney.
Housefather also does not believe that leaving for the United States is gaining traction among Canadian Jews. “There are some people who have decided that Florida or Israel is a greener pasture,” he said. “But that does not represent a significant or a predominant view, and the idea that everybody’s leaving Canada is actually not true.”
The increase in antisemitism is universal – and should be treated holistically, he said. “What I do agree with is everywhere there’s a very serious problem with antisemitism,” he said. “Everywhere Jewish communities don’t feel safe, and all levels of government need to keep doing more.”
Housefather encourages his Jewish countrymen to remain proud Canadians. “Antisemitism has grown to an unacceptable level in this country,” he said. “It doesn’t mean that you should have less pride in being Canadian because there’s a loud, angry, small group of Canadians trying to make us scared.”

Israel's peculiar state of affairs: Arab nations friendlier, Europe's relations fall - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
03:07:56 UTC
12:07:56 KST

An Israeli arriving at Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport today could find wine, dates, or other such souvenirs purchased in the West Bank carrying consequences far more serious than excess baggage.
Since September 22, the Netherlands has prohibited goods originating in Israeli communities in the West Bank, east Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights, including items carried in personal luggage. Intentional violations can result in up to six years’ imprisonment; even unintentional violations can carry a sentence of up to one year.
Israeli passengers have reported having their bags searched, although Dutch Customs claims inspections are risk-based and random rather than systematic.
Israel responded by revoking the diplomatic status of Dutch officials working in Ramallah. Relations with a country once considered among Israel’s closest European friends have consequently reached a remarkable low.
Then there is the fall of relations with the UK. Reports emerged this week that passengers arriving at Luton from Tel Aviv were separated from other travelers and had their luggage searched. The Home Office denied racial profiling, saying searches are based on intelligence. Unlike the Netherlands, Britain’s proposed restrictions on settlement goods have not yet taken effect.
Also, at the Labour conference on Monday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband declared that Palestinian suffering was “a stain on the conscience of the world” and addressed those angered by Britain’s previous approach directly: “We hear you. You were right.”
He went further. Britain, he promised, would “call out ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists,” evidence of war crimes in Gaza and what he called Israel’s “illegal occupation of Palestine.” The government will ban settlement imports and target British financial, construction, and service links to settlements.
Ireland-Israeli relations on all-time low
Ireland almost seems an afterthought. Its relations with Israel have already deteriorated dramatically, with the political hostility now spilling into sport. Ireland’s soccer coach recently declared before the much-disputed match between the two countries, “We are not playing with genocide. We are playing against genocide. We are playing against Israel.”
Yet not all is doom and gloom. Look south and east, and a very different picture emerges.
While European governments erect new barriers, Morocco is preparing to upgrade its relations with Israel to full embassies. They have agreed to expand direct flights, pursue investment and taxation agreements, and arrange reciprocal high-level visits. This has proceeded despite anti-normalization protests across Morocco. More important for Israel is the United Arab Emirates.
On Sunday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu traveled to the UAE at the invitation of President Mohamed bin Zayed. The UAE publicly confirmed the visit, which is noteworthy after years when sensitive contacts were often kept deliberately quiet.
Europe should see irony in situation
Europe should contemplate the irony here. Some Muslim-majority states that live in Israel’s neighborhood increasingly see cooperation with the Jewish state through the prism of shared strategic interests: Iran, Islamism, security, technology, trade, and regional stability.
Their governments certainly disagree with Israel, sometimes sharply, and Morocco’s protests demonstrate that normalization remains contested by some sectors of the population. But in general, their response is engagement.
In parts of Europe, meanwhile, relations with Israel are moving in the opposite direction. Governments face large domestic constituencies demanding increasingly punitive measures against Israel, and Miliband’s appeal to “millions of people in this country” demonstrated how directly domestic politics now intersects with foreign policy. The resulting picture is extraordinary.
In Abu Dhabi, an Israeli prime minister can spend hours discussing common threats with an Arab leader. In Morocco, governments are working toward ambassadors, investment and more flights. In Amsterdam, Israelis wonder whether customs officers will inspect their suitcases for a bottle of Judean wine.
There is something deeply strange about an Israel increasingly able to discuss its future with Arab and Muslim states while its citizens face growing suspicion and restrictions in European countries that once regarded friendship with Israel as essential.
Some in the Middle East have carefully cultivated bridges with Israel. Europe should think very carefully before it starts tearing its own down.

Executives of Iconic American Companies Reflect on How They Stay on Top
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
03:05:32 UTC
12:05:32 KST

A panel of executives spoke on Tuesday at a TIME100 Talk titled "Built to Last: The Enduring Power of Iconic American Brands" about the ways in which their companies have been able to adapt and dominate their industries throughout the years.
Included on the panel were Scott Kirby, chief executive officer of United Airlines; Ruth Porat, president and chief investment officer of Alphabet, the parent company of Google; and Bill Ford, executive chair of automotive company Ford, which sponsored the event.
Each panelist spoke about the unique approaches their companies have taken to remain relevant and an asset to consumers across generations.
Ford said prioritizing his employees and the communities his company impacts is chief among his values.
“We take care of each other. We take care of our communities. We take care of our country,” he said. “Those values are timeless. And it’s different than culture because cultures change and cultures evolve. But I think the values that underlie that culture are what really have sustained us for our whole lifetime.”
Porat stressed “a commitment to long-term investing” and “relentless focus on innovation.” She said that “we should never take innovation for granted.” In this spirit, the founders of her company, she explained, created something called “20% time,” which allows employees to dedicate a fifth of their workload to an idea that is deemed great. “And out of that was born Gmail and our first AI entity, Google Brain,” Porat said. Alongside encouraging innovation, she continued, is setting ambitious goals.
“If we achieve 60% of the objectives we set out in a year, that is success,” she said. “Because if we achieve 100% it just means we have not been audacious enough. We haven’t set the goal high enough.”
Kirby attributed the long-term success of United Airlines to it being what he described as a “brand loyal airline.” This has entailed focusing on four areas of the business: “the reliability, the service, the hard product, and the technology.”
“We need to wow them consistently,” he said. “I wanted them to get on an airplane and be surprised with something new that we have done.”
The United CEO acknowledged that maintaining a high standard in each of these areas has been no easy feat, particularly during the COVID pandemic, which he described as the “most existential financial crisis that ever existed in aviation.” Despite disruptions to his company, his priority is to protect his employees.
After reflecting on how they’ve succeeded in the past, the panelists were also asked about their visions for the future.
“My number one goal, my north star for the company, is actually going to be to set the company up so that there’s never again a furlough at the airline,” Kirby said.
Part of Porat’s vision for the future lies in expanding Alphabet’s business infrastructure into space, where on Thursday the company will launch an AI data center.
“It’s an attempt to continue to ask a question that our technical infrastructure team has been asking for a long time, which is how can we build as efficiently as possible using resources as wisely as possible to deliver the best experiences as possible,” Porat said about the launch. “This is a tiny little step. We still call it research.”
Ford hoped for a lot more of the same, and again stressed the value of his product for customers.
“I think what gets me most excited is the fact that we will still be the most American car company 25 years from now,” he said, “and that we’ll be making our customers' lives better, and hopefully give them back their most precious asset, which is time.”
TIME100 Talks: Built to Last: The Enduring Power of Iconic American Brands was presented by Ford.

Pentagon chief set to announce 20% cuts to senior officer positions
WASHINGTON – US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is set to announce a 20% cut in the number of positions for generals and admirals when he speaks with hundreds of junior service members at Quantico, Virginia, two US officials told Reuters on Sept 29.
Hegseth will give a speech on Sept 30 in front of hundreds of junior officers and enlisted officials, updating them on his priorities for the military.
The officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said Hegseth will announce plans to cut the billets for general and flag officers by 20%. Those are one- to four-star generals and admirals. That is an increase from the minimum 10% cut Hegseth laid out in 2025.
Rather than firing people, one of the officials said, the rank of some future jobs would change, while billets for others would be cancelled.
Separately on Sept 29, the Pentagon released a memo signed by Hegseth which directed that the Department of Defence will no longer appoint civilians as tenured college faculty at the US Military Service Academies. The memo cast the directive as an effort to refocus military academies on “warfighting”.
Hegseth has moved quickly to reshape the department, firing senior officers across the military and dealing with niche personnel issues. In 2025, he ordered a 20% reduction in the number of four-star officers.
The event on Sept 30 will come a year after Hegseth slammed “fat generals” and diversity initiatives in front of US military generals and admirals during a speech at Quantico.
In 2025, US President Donald Trump also delivered an address at Quantico and floated the idea of using deployments to US cities “as training grounds for our military”.
The remarks by Hegseth, a former Fox News personality, and Trump, a former reality television star, resembled a reality TV format, as top US military officials were summoned on short notice.
Addressing an auditorium full of top brass who flew in from around the world at the time, Hegseth defended his firings of flag officers, including the top US general, who was black, and the navy’s top admiral, who was a woman. He said the officers he relieved were part of a broken culture.
“If the words I’m speaking today are making your hearts sink, then you should do the honourable thing and resign,” Hegseth said. REUTERS

AI driving up innovation investment, says UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:54:00 UTC
11:54:00 KST

AI driving up innovation investment, says UN
- Artificial intelligence is driving record corporate R&D spending and fuelling global economic growth, with innovation investment expected to reach US$3.4 trillion in 2026, outpacing GDP growth.
- Venture capital deals are fewer but larger, with AI making up 77% of VC deal value in early 2026, signalling strong focus on AI startups despite cuts in traditional sectors.
- Switzerland leads global innovation rankings for the 16th year, while China and India have risen significantly; top innovation clusters remain dominated by Asian and US cities.
AI generated
GENEVA – Artificial intelligence is fuelling a rebound in investment in innovation, with corporate research and development spending reaching record highs, the United Nations said on Sept 29.
The UN’s World Intellectual Property Organisation said more money was going into venture capital (VC), even as the number of VC deals was shrinking and becoming increasingly concentrated on AI firms.
World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO), the UN patent and innovation agency, said AI was shortening the paths of discovery and fuelling much of the world’s economic growth.
“AI is not just a breakthrough technology; it’s going to change the way that we innovate and create,” WIPO chief Daren Tang told reporters.
“A new generation of deep-science start-ups is translating breakthroughs into products and transforming fields such as life sciences, space, robotics and clean energy.”
Tang said innovation investment had remained resilient in 2026 and was even “beginning to see growth again”.
Global research and development is expected to reach US$3.4 trillion (S$4.35 trillion) in 2026, growing faster than gross domestic product growth, while corporate R&D reached a record US$1.5 trillion in 2025, up 5.8%, said WIPO.
Venture capital’s AI focus
And while the number of venture capital deals dropped for the fourth straight year, their value rose by 28% to US$510 billion in 2025.
AI accounted for 53% of global VC deal value in 2025, and 77% in the first half of 2026.
“AI might reverse this productivity slump that we have seen for the last 15 to 20 years in high-income economies,” said Sacha Wunsch-Vincent, co-editor of WIPO’s annual Global Innovation Index.
If applied correctly, artificial intelligence would help every sector, he told reporters.
“The open question here really is how can we broaden this innovation spurt beyond this one technology only, which is currently mostly LLM (large language models). We see a lot of the traditional big R&D spenders – pharma, cars, construction – cutting back on their R&D spend,” he noted.
Tang said he hoped AI was “a rising tide that lifts all boats because... a healthy innovation ecosystem needs to be able to have strength in as many areas of technology as possible.”
Global country rankings
For the 16th consecutive year, Switzerland led the Global Innovation Index, which tracks innovation drivers in the world’s economies.
Sweden and the United States retained second and third place for the fourth year running, followed by South Korea and Singapore.
China has meanwhile shot up from 35th place in 2013 to 10th position, while India rose from 66th to 38th place during the same period, the report showed, also highlighting big jumps up by the likes of Vietnam, Turkey and the Philippines.
The top five innovation clusters remain unchanged in 2026, led by Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou, followed by Tokyo-Yokohama, San Jose-San Francisco, Beijing and Seoul, the report showed.
Further down, Osaka-Kobe-Kyoto and Paris overtook Los Angeles, which dropped two places to 12th.
Most of the big risers were in China, with Ningde the most prominent, up 24 places to 75th.
Outside China, Miami rose six places to 61st, while Chennai climbed five places to 79th.
The biggest fallers were Pittsburgh and Oxford, which both dropped eight places to 84th and 85th, respectively. AFP

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked nine Chinese military aircraft, seven naval vessels, and six official ships around Taiwan between 6 a.m. on Tuesday and 6 a.m. on Wednesday.
Five of the nine People’s Liberation Army aircraft entered the country’s southwestern air defense identification zone, according to the MND.
In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems to monitor PLA activity.
So far this month, the MND has tracked Chinese aircraft 232 times and ships 312 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

Iran appeals to US voters as American troops leave Iraq
Unknown

Iran appeals to US voters as American troops leave Iraq
BAGHDAD/WASHINGTON, Sept 30 - Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps urged Americans to vote out US President Donald Trump's allies in Congress as US forces were due to withdraw from their remaining bases in neighbouring Iraq on Wednesday in a departure celebrated by Tehran.
Meanwhile, Qatar continued to promote its shuttle diplomacy aimed at ending the seven-month-old war between Iran and the United States. Trump once again predicted a swift surrender for Iran.
The 26-page letter by the Guards, published on Tuesday, urges Americans to use their political power to remove current leaders from office and reject US support for Israel and military intervention abroad.
While the missive was unlikely to sway US voters who may not even see the text published by Iranian media, it identifies issues that US political analysts say are working against Trump and the Republican Party ahead of November 3 congressional elections, when the opposition Democrats could retake control of one or both legislative chambers, potentially impeding Trump's political agenda.
"Remove from power the evil, deceitful, and violent politicians who are responsible for America’s current state," the letter said. "Make sure your politicians understand that the world has changed."
Trump campaigned in 2024 pledging to avoid new wars, end existing conflicts and bring down inflation, but the war with Iran, which Trump launched alongside Israel, has contributed to higher global fuel prices and spread in the Middle East.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll published September 21 found just 17% of respondents approved Trump's handling of the cost of living - the top issue Americans say will determine how they vote in November. Only 34% approved of the strikes on Iran.
Trump, who broke with Republican orthodoxy in 2016 when he called the US invasion of Iraq a major mistake, allowed the final withdrawal from Iraq on Wednesday, which was agreed in 2024 by former President Joe Biden.
The withdrawal comes 23 years after US-led forces toppled Saddam Hussein, then triggered upheaval that culminated with the rise of Islamic State.
QATARI MEDIATION
The US war in Iran has drawn in Iranian allies in the region, including the Houthis in Yemen, Hezbollah in Lebanon and militias in Iraq, which Riyadh blamed for the September 10 attack that knocked the East-West Pipeline in Saudi Arabia offline.
Iran, which says its ultimate aim is to force American forces to leave the entire Middle East, casts the US withdrawal from Iraq as a triumph for its "axis of resistance" of allied armed groups across the region.
The US and Iran have not found an off-ramp from the war despite rounds of talks and several ceasefires.
Negotiations appeared to intensify during last week's UN General Assembly meeting in New York, but have so far not yielded any agreement to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of global oil and liquefied natural gas passed before the war started in February.
Qatar has again emerged as would-be peacemaker after previously playing a supporting role in producing a June memorandum of understanding that led to a brief ceasefire. US and Iranian officials spoke separately with Qatari mediators on Monday, but it was unclear if exchanges took place on Tuesday.
"We are exchanging messages between the parties, and we're working towards establishing a common ground in order to get into a deal that would save all of us from the repercussions of the conflict," Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari told reporters.
Trump meanwhile repeated his position that Iran must not obtain a nuclear weapon and that the war would be over soon.
The conflict has degraded Iran's conventional forces and damaged its already ailing economy, but Tehran has fought back with missile and drone strikes on US allies in the Gulf and by restricting oil tanker traffic in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, which has pushed up world energy prices.
"I don't know if they are going to give up yet but they'll give up," Trump told reporters on Tuesday.
"They are doing very poorly," he added.
At the United Nations General Assembly last week, Iran floated a peace proposal that would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in fighting.
Trump on Saturday rejected the plan although Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that Washington had not officially relayed a US rejection through mediators.
Trump has cited weakening Iran's nuclear capabilities as one of his war objectives, along with ending its ability to attack its neighbours and creating conditions for Iranians to topple their leadership.
Iran, which does not have nuclear weapons, denies seeking them. The US is nuclear-armed. Tehran says it has the right to develop nuclear technology for peaceful purposes as a party to the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. REUTERS

A source of tension since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Latvia’s Russian-speaking community has faced renewed questions over identity, loyalty, and Moscow’s influence.
As parliamentary elections loom on Oct. 3, many Russian speakers in the eastern Latgale region said they had no desire to be “saved” by Moscow.
“We do not need help from Russia here. We can solve our problems ourselves,” 45-year-old local resident Igors Nazarovs told AFP as a band played on the city’s main street.
This is a separate culture – a separate land
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly claimed that the rights of Russian speakers in the Baltic states are being violated, rhetoric that has raised concern in Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia.
His language has echoes of claims Moscow made about Russian speakers in Ukraine’s Donbas region before launching its invasion.
Russian world
Daugavpils, Latvia’s second-largest city, has around 80,000 residents, roughly 90% of whom are Russian-speaking.
Putin Envoy Talks Post-War Energy Deals as US Weighs Belarus-Style Sanctions Plan for Russia
Some Russian speakers there, including Inna Plavoka, said Russia’s war against Ukraine forced them to reconsider their own identity.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, “my life was divided into a ‘before’ and an ‘after,’” she told AFP.
“Today, I clearly identify with Latvia and with this country, in no way with Russia.”
Plavoka, editor-in-chief of the independent Daugavpils media outlet Tchaika, or “Seagull,” said she believes a growing number of Russian speakers now feel the same way.
Before the war, she still knew people who believed Putin would come to Latvia “to save them” by offering them “Russki mir” – a phrase that can be translated as both “the Russian world” and “Russian peace.”
Today, she said, she no longer knows anyone who openly says: “Yes, I want that.”
Recent drone crashes on Latvian territory have also changed attitudes, she added.
“Everyone understands what this ‘Russki mir’ really means.”
Portraits of Lenin and Stalin
Affection for Moscow, however, remains among some older members of Latvia’s Russian-speaking population.
At the offices of the Latvian Russian Community association, Aleksei Vassiliev, a candidate from the Russian-speaking Harmony party, proudly pointed to portraits of Soviet leaders Vladimir Lenin and Joseph Stalin.
“This is the history of people who lived in the Soviet Union,” he said.
While insisting that he is attached to Latvia, Vassiliev criticized the status of so-called “non-citizens” – permanent residents, mostly Russian-speaking, who did not meet the full requirements for Latvian citizenship and hold no other nationality.
Many either failed or did not take the Latvian language and history examinations required for citizenship.
They make up nearly 9% of Latvia’s population and are not permitted to vote.
“If they were allowed to vote and if they voted as a bloc, they would be the largest parliamentary group in parliament,” Vassiliev said.
He also criticized measures adopted by Riga since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine aimed at reducing Russian influence, including the transition toward Latvian as the main language of instruction and the removal of Soviet monuments.
Kremlin influence and economic frustration
In Latgale, the poorest region of the Baltic states, some Russian-speaking residents also criticize European support for Ukraine.
Their complaints often appear rooted more in local economic hardship than in direct support for the Kremlin.
Seeking votes from that electorate, Vjaceslavs Stepanenko, leader of the local branch of the populist Suverena Vara party – accused by critics of pro-Russian sympathies – attacked European assistance to Kyiv.
“It would be nice if this aid from European countries were for us,” he said.
Only a few meters away, center-right MP Juris Vilums of the United List handed out his own campaign leaflets.
Led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, the party is leading in opinion polls and is expected to play a central role in forming Latvia’s next governing coalition, while maintaining the country’s broadly centrist and pro-Western course.
Vilums argued that Russian influence persists in parts of eastern Latvia largely because local residents lack alternative sources of information.
“The major problem... is propaganda,” he said.
“For now, we don’t have any Russian-language media at the national level,” Vilums added, noting that residents near the border can easily receive Russian or Belarusian radio broadcasts.
While one part of Latvia’s Russian-speaking population “is already integrated,” he said, “another part is not, and I’m afraid it never will be.”

Australia has an edge many countries don't and should help the world, spy chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:48:18 UTC
11:48:18 KST

in brief
- The Australian Signals Directorate has revealed that it has access to high-level, non-public AI models.
- Australia should use its privilege and power to help others defend against AI attacks, the country's top cyber spy chief says.
Australia's top cyber spy chief has said the country has a "technical edge" in dealing with the risks posed by frontier artificial intelligence models and should be training other nations to defend against them.
Speaking after a recent apology by United States technology firm OpenAI for a breach of Australian Medicare data by one of its experimental AI models, Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) chief Abigail Bradshaw said Australia's Five Eyes membership has resulted in key advantages from powerful US tech companies.
The director-general of the ASD, which manages the country's national cyber security and foreign intelligence gathering, told ABC Radio National on Wednesday that her team had been granted access to developmental AI models over six months ago.
"Australia has enjoyed a rare level of engagement with the frontier labs," she said. "We have had an incredible alliance starting with the Five Eyes Intelligence Alliance."
Few other nations have been granted access to high-level, non-publicly available AI models, which Bradshaw said her team has been using to shore up government systems ahead of the rest of the world.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Now, the country should be sharing that information with others, she stated.
Five Eyes is an intelligence-sharing alliance of Australia, New Zealand, Canada, the United Kingdom and the US, which developed after World War Two.
In June, the alliance released a three-page document saying the pace of AI development means major operational shifts are "months away, not years" and that organisations should "assume breaches will occur".
"For the last 80 years, we have enjoyed a technical edge as a consequence of our membership and our partnership in the Five Eyes alliance," Bradshaw said.
She noted, however, that "a new partnership" is required between governments, research groups, industry, and frontier AI companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind due to the nature of the threat.
The ASD Cyber Security Partnership Program, which aims to address the issue, was reported as having 133,000 members last year, but Bradshaw said this has now grown to 150,000 as organisations come together to share information about AI.
OpenAI apology 'not insignificant'
Last week, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced at the United Nations General Assembly that an OpenAI model had breached a Medicare site.
The incident took place in June, but the company didn't realise until August and failed to notify the government until 10 September.
The company issued a formal apology on Tuesday, pledging technical support and the establishment of a local task force to advise on AI safety. Its newest frontier model, GPT-6.1 Astra, was shelved over safety concerns.
In response, the government has launched a rapid review of the incident and issued a directive to all federal departments to conduct an immediate stocktake of legacy IT systems. A review of existing security reporting laws is also taking place.
Bradshaw said the apology and cooperation of OpenAI is encouraging.
"Look at the content of what OpenAI have set out there; that is not insignificant," Bradshaw said.
"In fact, that is consistent with our experience, with our engagement with not just OpenAI, but the other labs, Anthropic and others, over the last six months.
"That's a really important precedent for the way this relationship proceeds into the future."
Engagement with frontier AI companies is a "two-way street", Bradshaw said, but added that the technology could also provide advantages if those relationships are managed well.
"Cyber security is like painting the Sydney Harbour Bridge," she said. "It never stops."

An attempted attack on RAF Fairford in Britain, which is used by the U.S. Air Force and from which American bombers took off for strikes on Iran, was foiled after one of the suspects called police himself, Britain’s Daily Mail reported Tuesday. It remains unclear why the suspect called the emergency services, and investigators are examining whether he wanted to back out of the alleged plot or whether the call itself was part of the plan.
After the call was made to the 999 emergency number, armed police rushed to the scene in Gloucestershire and arrested the suspects. Officers removed their clothing over concerns they could be wearing suicide vests. No such devices were found, and suspected explosive materials in the suspects’ vans were found to be unusable.
British media initially reported that a farmer returning from a party encountered the suspicious vehicles near the base early Sunday, became concerned and called 999. The Daily Mail later reported that the masked men the farmer described were apparently armed police officers who had arrived at the scene.
Counterterrorism chief Laurence Taylor earlier told reporters that the police response that morning had been based on a range of information.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham convened a COBRA meeting, the British government’s emergency response committee, on Monday afternoon and urged the public not to speculate while authorities worked to establish the full facts.
One line of inquiry is whether the incident, which has been linked to Iran, was not in fact a foiled terrorist attack but rather an intelligence-gathering operation, an exercise or a kind of “calling card” intended to send a message to British and U.S. authorities.
Counterterrorism police said earlier that the vans found near the base did not contain explosives but fuel.
British police raised further questions about the incident Monday when they announced that all five suspects who had been arrested had been released on bail. Police said the men were suspected of planning a terrorist attack, but their release has prompted significant questions about the case.
All five are British citizens from London, ages 23 to 25. Taylor said investigators were keeping an “open mind” about whether there was a “geopolitical” motive behind the alleged plot, amid reports that investigators were examining whether Iran had sent the five suspects to attack RAF Fairford.
The base is used by the U.S. Air Force and, during the war, American bombers took off from there to carry out strikes in Iran.
Iran has denied involvement in the incident. In a statement, the Iranian Embassy in London said the Islamic Republic “completely rejects and strongly condemns the malicious and baseless speculation” surrounding the arrests near the base, adding that such speculation would only “fuel Iranophobia in Britain.”
British police had declared a “major incident” in the village of Whelford, near RAF Fairford, and hours later it emerged that five men had been arrested there on suspicion of planning a terrorist attack.
Three vans were found in their possession and bomb disposal experts were called in because of materials initially believed to be explosives. Photos taken by a local resident showed the suspects lying shirtless on a sidewalk with their hands cuffed behind their backs as British security forces searched them.
It later emerged that the suspects had been arrested only about 320 meters, or 350 yards, from the base. British media reported Tuesday night that security forces were examining the possibility that Iran had sent them to carry out an attack after Tehran threatened in July to target bases such as Fairford if U.S. aircraft continued taking off from them to bomb Iranian territory.
During the latest war, Britain initially prevented the United States from using British bases to carry out strikes on Iran. Then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer later allowed U.S. forces to launch strikes on the Islamic Republic from those bases, targeting missile sites, particularly those used to launch Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

US ban on diesel fuel exports could whip up gasoline prices, expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:44:00 UTC
11:44:00 KST

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. A possible US ban on diesel fuel exports after storages have been filled could force refineries to cut operations, which would reduce gasoline and jet fuel production and boost their prices, Oleg Nikolayev, an expert at the Institute for the Economy of Growth, Stolypin P. A. and a member of the General Council of Delovaya Rossiya, told TASS.
Earlier, CNBC reported that a US ban on diesel fuel exports could drive up European prices to unprecedented highs. Over the past few months, about half of the diesel fuel supplied to Europe came from the US, experts note. However, most European oil traders doubt that Washington will take such a step because it will pose a serious challenge to the US oil companies.
"Once all possible volumes of diesel fuel storages are filled (and this will happen in about a month), refineries will be forced to reduce oil refining. That is, there will be less gasoline and jet fuel in America, and their prices will start to rise. The situation is called 'pulling out the nose and getting the tail stuck,'" Nikolayev said.
According to him, the measure could backfire.
"A possible ban on diesel fuel exports from the United States would have too many negative side effects for the United States itself," he said.
Nikolayev said that a significant portion of the US diesel fuel is exported.
"It is worth recalling that over the past 20 years, the United States has transformed from a net importer of petroleum products into the world’s largest exporter of diesel fuel. American oil refineries currently produce about 5.1-5.2 million barrels of diesel per day, and up to 30% is exported," he said.
Damage to producers
According to the expert, the ban will also hit revenues of US producers.
"The export revenue of American producers from diesel fuel amounts to about $150 million per day, or $55 billion per year. If the ban is imposed, then 1.5 million barrels per day will either have to be stored or sold on the domestic market at falling prices," he said. "For the voter, this will have a temporary effect (although there’s little that will save the Republicans in the upcoming elections anyway), but the industry giants will perceive it as nothing less than the president’s hand reaching into their pockets," Nikolayev concluded.

NEW YORK - In the annual battle of the big bears, only one can be the winner.
For 2026, 89 Backpack was crowned the winner of Katmai National Park and Preserve’s Fat Bear Week.

Participants vote on which bear they believe is the chunkiest chunk of them all in a sports-style bracket.

David Shoebridge named new Greens leader after hotly contested ballot
In short:
The party held an unprecedented ballot for the leadership.
David Shoebridge won seven votes to Mehreen Faruqi's four.
What's next?
Disappointed Greens have called for future leadership votes to be opened up to the broader party membership.
David Shoebridge has been chosen as the new leader of the Greens, emerging victorious from a hotly contested three-way race, with Steph Hodgins-May elected deputy.
In an unprecedented ballot for the party, which in the past has chosen its leaders by consensus, Senator Shoebridge defeated former deputy Mehreen Faruqi and long-serving senator Sarah Hanson-Young, the manager of Greens business in the Senate.
The decision was made by the 11-member party room in Sydney today after the shock resignation of Larissa Waters, who on Monday revealed she was stepping down from the role to deal with chronic kidney disease.
Greens whip Nick McKim took the rare step of announcing the full results of the ballot, with Senator Shoebridge ultimately winning seven votes to four over Senator Faruqi after preferences.
Senator Hodgins-May defeated Vanessa Bleyer six votes to five. Jordon Steele-John also nominated for the deputy position.
Senator Shoebridge is the sixth leader in the environment-focused party's history.
He said he wanted the Greens to "fill the vacuum that has been left by the Labor Party rushing to the right".
"We're here to beat down One Nation, and we're here to replace Labor and return hope and faith to politics," he said.
Senator Shoebridge has served as a senator for New South Wales since 2022.
He is a former barrister and member of the NSW parliament.
Announcing a "new face" for the Greens, Senator Shoebridge said the party would take up the fight against "corporate greed", naming the gas lobby, AUKUS, artificial intelligence, and fossil fuel billionaires as issues of concern.
"This is an extraordinary moment in politics, and we can all feel it," he said at a press conference today.
"We can feel that politics as usual is not providing the answers that people are desperately calling for now."
Senator Shoebridge's deputy, Senator Hodgins-May, entered parliament just two years ago after a career as an environmental lawyer.
She said she was part of a generation who has grown up not having the opportunities to live the kind of life they deserved.
She said she had a "bold vision" for the party and was determined to grow the movement.
"I'm incredibly excited, I'm energetic, and I'm optimistic about the opportunities that this moment brings. I'm ready to roll up my sleeves and work hard," she said.
Both senators foregrounded material concerns for everyday Australians amid cost-of-living pressures, while vowing to combat the climate crisis.
Faruqi disappointed
In a sign of divisions within the party, Senator Faruqi put out a statement on social media expressing her disappointment.
"Of course, I am disappointed the party room chose another direction, and know many others will feel the same way," she said.
"I did not stand again for Deputy Leader today because, on reflection, I believe I can best play my part in that action outside the constraints of the leadership team."
She said she had long advocated for Greens leaders to be elected by members "with enough time for thoughtful deliberation on who is best to grow our party".
"I share members' frustration that the opposite happened this week," she said.
"Without a member vote, we cannot call ourselves a grassroots party. I call on the new leadership team to set a timeline for one member, one vote."
Her comments echoed sentiment circulated in an open letter by former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather, who was ousted from his Griffith seat at the last election.
Mr Chandler-Mather argued opening up the vote to rank and file would demonstrate grassroots democracy, and hoped to emulate the overseas success of left-leaning movements like those under Zohran Mamdani in New York and Zack Polanski in the UK.
Senator Hanson-Young has not yet commented publicly on the result.
Waters sad to step aside
In her first public remarks since her resignation, Senator Waters became emotional and said it had been an "incredible honour" to lead the party.
"It's with great sadness that I'm not able to continue in that role due to my health getting worse," she said.
Senator Waters rose to the leadership after the shock election defeat in 2025, when then-leader Adam Bandt lost his long-held seat of Melbourne.
The Queensland senator was in the role for 16 months, and said she would be returning as a "humble backbencher" after taking medical leave.
She said she was proud to see the party polling higher despite a surge in right-wing politics.
"It's been a wild ride, and I want to thank all of the team for their support," she said.
"We've got a lot of work to do. The country's in a state, and people deserve politicians that work for them, not work for corporate interests."
Senator Shoebridge paid tribute to her leadership during a challenging time for The Greens.
"Bloody hell, she rose to the occasion. Led with compassion, led with principle, showed what collective leadership can do," he said.
Senator Hodgins-May also paid tribute to Senator Waters, describing her as "a source of inspiration".
She added Senator Faruqi would continue to be a "ferocious champion" for Greens causes.

Mexico seeks extradition of former official in Israel over 2014 student disappearance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:35:58 UTC
11:35:58 KST

Jorge Antonio Gonzalez Rocha
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum announced Tuesday that her administration is seeking the extradition of Tomas Zeron de Lucio, a former top security official linked to the disappearance of 43 students who is living in self-exile in Israel.
In 2014, 43 students from the Ayotzinapa Rural Teachers' College in Iguala, Guerrero were disappeared by local police and criminal groups, allegedly with the backing and protection of high-ranking Mexican government figures, including military officers and intelligence and security officials, according to the Presidential Commission for Truth and Access to Justice in the Ayotzinapa Case.
From the disappearance of the students until 2020, the government maintained that the attack had been carried out exclusively by criminal groups, a fabricated account promoted by the administration of former President Enrique Pena Nieto and challenged by the government of Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, who had promised to solve the case if he won the 2018 elections.
Zeron de Lucia, then director of the now-defunct Criminal Investigation Agency (AIC), was key to efforts to protect government officials as well as police and military personnel involved in the crime.
In 2020, Mexico's Attorney General's Office issued an arrest warrant against him for the crimes of enforced disappearance and torture after the official version fabricated during the Pena Nieto administration was refuted.
The disgraced former criminal intelligence chief relocated to Israel in 2019, where he has lived ever since.
During her morning press conference following the 12th anniversary of the mass disappearance of the students on Sept. 26, President Sheinbaum announced that her government had made changes within Mexico's Attorney General's Office to secure Zeron's extradition, a request that has gone unaddressed since 2020.
“And in the case of extraditions, the Attorney General's Office has, at this time, even changed personnel within the office to accelerate all extradition processes, both from the United States and from Israel, which is where Tomas Zeron is. And work is underway on this,” she said.
Although the Mexican government has offered Zeron immunity in exchange for his cooperation, he has remained in self-exile in Israel, while the lack of an extradition treaty between the two countries has stalled the Mexican government's requests.
Sheinbaum said she sent a letter directly to Israeli President Isaac Herzog requesting Zeron's extradition to no avail.
“He replied to us that he had raised this with the judiciary but that it fell outside the scope of his authority,” she said.
According to investigations carried out following the rise of the ruling Morena Party, which culminated in its historic landslide victory during the 2018 general elections, Zeron as head of the AIC ordered the fabrication of evidence and the torture of witnesses to extract false testimonies that upheld the official version of events at the time, holding the criminal syndicate Guerreros Unidos as the sole perpetrator while shielding government officials.
Zeron's extradition would mark a major accomplishment in Sheinbaum's handling of the case, which so far has alienated the relatives of the 43 students.
The parents of the Ayotzinapa victims have maintained that the government of Lopez Obrador and the current Sheinbaum administration have failed to fulfill their promises to clarify the case, arguing that protection continues to be afforded to senior military commanders allegedly involved in the state crime.
Lopez Obrador and Sheinbaum have maintained the innocence of the armed forces, despite extensive evidence gathered by independent investigative groups documenting that the military had infiltrated a soldier into the ranks of the students to monitor them and that military troops dressed in civilian clothing were surveilling the students before their disappearance.
Twelve years after the mass disappearance, the parents still do not know the whereabouts of their children, the reasons for their disappearance or who ordered the attack.

Her allegations surfaced again two weeks ago after the student, identified in a lawsuit as Jane Doe, sued seven men, the university, her sorority and the fraternity.
The case has led to fierce debate across the internet and drawn attention to the persistent problem of sexual assault on college campuses.
The district attorney for Tompkins County, home to Cornell in Ithaca, New York, said he would consider presenting the case to a grand jury. In 2024, immediately after her report, he declined to do so.
Here is what we know about the Cornell case.
What do we know about Jane Doe?
Because she is anonymous in the lawsuit, most of the details about her life are unknown.
Her lawyer has said she is from a small town about 1,610km away from Cornell.
She arrived at the university as an undergraduate in August 2022, then dropped out after she said she was raped in 2024.
She was 20 years old at the time and had been a member of the Tri-Delta sorority.
Her lawyer said she is struggling with the aftermath of the incident and is not in college.
What does the lawsuit say happened?
On Oct 19, 2024, according to the lawsuit, the woman was raped repeatedly over nearly seven hours at the Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca.
The lawsuit states that she started her night drinking vodka at the sorority house.
Around 8.30pm, she took an Uber to an event her sorority was hosting at a bar.
Although the bouncer correctly identified her as underage, she claims she was served at least one alcoholic beverage.
By about 11pm, she had decided to walk about a mile to Chi Phi’s fraternity house to see a man she considered a friend.
Once she arrived, according to the lawsuit, the man and his fraternity brothers gave her a beer, marijuana, rum and ketamine.
In the lawsuit, she claims she had not tried ketamine before and was pressured into snorting it.
The lawsuit then details a series of sexual assaults and continued drug use involving her friend and six other men.
At about 1.42am, one of the men sent a message to the Chi Phi Snapchat group inviting others to join in, using a crude term for female genitalia, according to a screenshot included in the lawsuit.
How did the police respond?
With the encouragement of friends, Jane Doe reported the incident to Cornell’s police department on Nov 8, 2024.
The Cornell police sent a crime alert to campus, stating that a victim had reported being “sexually assaulted by several males” and “coerced into consuming ketamine and other drugs” at a fraternity house.
In a message to campus before that Thanksgiving, Cornell’s president said that the university police department was continuing its criminal investigation, and that a second, administrative investigation into the allegations was under way.
Some time that month, the Cornell police asked the Tompkins County district attorney’s office to review a statement from Jane Doe.
Criminal investigators advised the police that they did not think they could bring criminal charges under New York state law based on the statement.
Jane Doe’s lawyer said that after she gave her initial statement, no police or criminal investigators contacted her again.
It is unclear whether the police interviewed the men involved, or whether Jane Doe was told that her criminal case was not being pursued.
On Sept 28, the district attorney – who has released only excerpts from Jane Doe’s initial six-page statement – said that the statement did not make clear that she was forced into the sexual acts or that she was incapacitated, though she was under the influence of drugs and alcohol.
How did Cornell respond?
The university immediately placed the fraternity, and the seven men she named in the lawsuit, on interim suspensions, the suit said.
Meanwhile, Cornell’s administrative Title IX justice process swung into motion to determine any potential discipline for the accused men.
In May 2025, at least 12 hearings were held before a panel of faculty and staff, according to the woman’s lawsuit.
The accused men “were afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell”, according to the lawsuit.
Cornell does not deny that essays – which it calls reflection papers – were part of the punishment that the panel decided on for some of the men.
But it stated on Sept 28 that it was not the only consequence for any of them.
Cornell, citing student privacy rules, declined to give details about how the individual men were punished.
It said on Sept 28 that it gave the men “a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions”.
Thomas Giuffra, the lawyer who represents Jane Doe, has said in interviews that only two of the men were expelled, and that his client did not feel justice had been done.
What has been the fallout from the lawsuit?
Millions of people have viewed the lawsuit or heard influencers and celebrities discuss the allegations online, bringing attention to the ongoing problem of sexual assault at Cornell and other college campuses.
The mayor of Ithaca said on Sept 28 that he is proposing a ban on permits for Cornell events until the university reforms its sexual assault policies.
The pressure and attention pushed the Tompkins County district attorney to reopen the criminal case.
A criminal investigator has reached out to Jane Doe’s lawyer, meaning that there could still be criminal charges in the case.
Governor Kathy Hochul has called for an independent investigation of Cornell’s handling of the case.
The names and photographs of the seven accused men are widely circulating online, as part of a mass movement that some see as a grassroots effort to bring accountability, and others view as a form of harassment of men not yet charged with any crime. NYTIMES

Heatwaves, wildfires expose a third of world to extreme ozone pollution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:31:15 UTC
11:31:15 KST

Heatwaves, wildfires expose a third of world to extreme ozone pollution
Heatwaves and wildfires helped expose 34 percent of the world’s population to “extremely poor” ozone air quality in the first eight months of 2026, according to a European Union report published Wednesday. Asia recorded the highest exposure, while ozone pollution remained difficult to curb despite decades of progress in reducing other harmful emissions.
Heatwaves and wildfires combined with human-caused emissions this year to expose one third of the world's population to extremely high levels of ozone pollution, a European Union report said on Wednesday.
In a new analysis covering the first eight months of 2026, the European Union's Copernicus Climate Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) highlighted the close relationship between climate change and air pollution.
When heat and sunlight react with airborne emissions from wildfires, vehicles and industry, they create ground-level ozone pollution, which can damage lung tissue, cause breathing problems, trigger asthma attacks and lead to other health issues.
Despite progress in cutting the most harmful air pollutants in recent decades, ozone has proved more difficult to tackle as climate change fuels the conditions that favour its formation.
Read moreFrance puts out massive fire that torched 42,000 hectares and smouldered for 69 days
This year's ozone pollution was driven in part by record-breaking heatwaves and wildfires that seared Europe and North America and sent smoke well beyond their borders.
Indonesia has experienced major wildfires, while the warming El Nino weather pattern, which started in June and is due to peak later this year, could drive more fires in southeast Asia, according to the analysis.
"Air pollution does not stop at borders. It can travel thousands of kilometres, crossing continents and oceans and affecting air quality far from its source," CAMS director Laurence Rouil said in the Atmosphere Watch report.
'Extremely poor' air
CAMS uses satellite data and computer models to track air pollution and wildfires.
The report found that 34 percent of the global population was exposed to "extremely poor" air quality between January 1 and September 15, meaning concentrations of ozone were well above the World Health Organization's exposure guidance.
The WHO's guideline sets 100 micrograms of ozone per cubic metre as the maximum recommended level of exposure, averaged over eight hours.
Read moreWildfires, heatwaves threaten global air quality and health, UN warns
Another 17 percent of the world breathed "very poor" air, while five percent was exposed to "good" levels of ozone.
Asia has the highest rate of exposure to ozone pollution, with 53 percent of its population breathing "extremely poor" air. Another 22 percent was exposed to "very poor" ozone.
The continent's widespread emissions are driven by industrialisation, economic development and transport, as well as wildfires and the burning of agricultural residue.
New Delhi, Dhaka, Chinese megalopolis Chongqing and Pakistan's Lahore were among cities whose ozone levels were "extremely poor".
Two thirds of the population in North America and 45 percent in Europe were exposed to "poor" or "very poor" air quality.
EU regulation has been effective in reducing emissions from air pollutants, except for ozone, the report said.
Read moreFrance recorded 'hottest summer ever' in 2026, environment minister says
Ozone pollution is linked to 60,000 premature deaths per year in Europe, Ian Marnane, an official at the European Environment Agency, told a media briefing.
Ozone levels in North America also remained "relatively unchanged" despite ambitious emissions reduction policies, the report said.
Smoke from forest fires, crop burning and cooking are significant contributors to Africa's air pollution while Saharan dust travels as far as Europe.
Eight percent of Africa's population endured "extremely poor" air quality this year. It was "very poor" or "poor" for 19 percent of the continent.
Ozone levels were very high in the Brazilian city of Sao Paulo and extremely elevated in Rio de Janeiro but the air quality was "good" or "fair" for 81 percent of South America's population.
One bright spot was Oceania, including Australia and New Zealand, where 66 percent of the population enjoyed "good" ozone levels and 34 percent lived under "fair" conditions.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

US Senate blocks resolution seeking report on Americans killed in West Bank
The resolution cites a ‘lack of accountability’ by Israel’s government and an ‘inability to secure justice’ by the US.
The United States Senate has blocked a resolution that would have required President Donald Trump’s administration to report on the killing of nine Americans in the occupied West Bank and on Israel’s treatment of Palestinian children in military detention.
The resolution failed 47-53 on Tuesday, with senators voting largely along party lines.

It was brought to the floor by Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, and cited a “lack of accountability” from the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and an “inability to secure justice” from the US government.
Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania was the only Democrat to vote against advancing the resolution, while Senator Rand Paul, a Republican from Kentucky, joined Democrats in supporting it.
Van Hollen forced the vote under the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, which allows individual members of Congress to demand a formal State Department report on the human rights practices of any country that receives US security assistance.
In a social media post after the vote, Van Hollen pledged to continue to press for justice.
“Tonight, 47 Senators supported my resolution to get accountability for the 9 Americans killed on the West Bank & for Palestinians who face injustices daily. That’s more support than we’ve ever had in this fight,” he wrote on X.
“Republicans blocked us, but we won’t stop until we get justice.”
Nine Americans killed
The resolution called for an unclassified report within 30 days of adoption. It would have detailed investigations into the deaths of the Americans, the treatment of US citizens held in Israeli prisons, and the conditions facing Palestinian children in Israeli military detention.
The measure cited the deaths of nine American citizens in the occupied West Bank since January 2022, including Shireen Abu Akleh, a Palestinian-American journalist and Al Jazeera correspondent who was shot in the head and killed in May 2022 while reporting in the city of Jenin.
It also included Aysenur Ezgi Eygi, who was shot in the head and killed by an Israeli soldier in September 2024, and Sayfollah Kamel Musallet, who was beaten to death by Israeli settlers in July 2025.
The others were Amer Mohammad Saada Rabee, who was 14; Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohamed Ahmad Alkhdour, both 17; Omar Assad; Khamid Ayyad; Nasrallah Abu Siyam; and Khamis Rabee Jabara.
The resolution also noted the arrests of several Palestinian-American children by Israeli forces.
Among them was Mohammed Ibrahim, a 16-year-old from Florida, who was arrested in February 2025 and held in pretrial detention for nine months without contact with his family. It noted that US embassy officials and lawyers who met him told his family that he had lost nearly a quarter of his body weight, contracted scabies, and was beaten and tortured.
Other Palestinian Americans who remain in custody include Adam Wajeh Abdelfattah Karakrah, 16, and Sama Safi, 20, a student detained in June in raids targeting students at Birzeit University.
The resolution cited rights groups that have documented the deaths of at least 44 Palestinians in Israeli military camps since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023. Those groups, it said, have documented widespread abuses, including beatings, sexual violence, harassment and threats, “pointing to systemic and deliberate mistreatment”.
It also went on to note a sharp escalation in Israeli settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank, and stressed that there have been no convictions for the killings of Palestinian civilians by Israeli settlers since 2020.

Why Nirvana and Midnight Oil made the cut in Songs that Changed the World
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:25:40 UTC
11:25:40 KST

Why Nirvana and Midnight Oil made the cut in Songs that Changed the World
In the new book Songs that Changed the World, author Andrew Clarke was aiming for a top 40, but couldn't do away with any two songs.
Here he tells the ABC's pop culture journalist why some songs made the list and others didn't.
You start the book with Strange Fruit. I want to talk about artists paying a personal price for their songs that change the world. You write in the book about Billie Holiday's final moments as well as some of what she went through in life. Tell me about that.
She did become public enemy number one. I mean, a Black woman singing about lynching in the United States was very confrontational, but she was a huge star and she had the power to do it. But the FBI and all the entities didn't really like that. So, she spent a lot of time being interviewed by police.
And you wrote that she didn't receive the medical treatment that she was due when dying in hospital.
Absolutely … the evidence is there to say that she could have got lots of things to help her, but no-one was willing to do that for her, and a lot of it was the pressure from the FBI.
It's pretty obvious why this particular song is on the list, but can you tell me what's going on in this song and why it's so powerful?
It is [written by] Abel Meeropol, who [was] a Jewish poet in New York City, and he saw a photograph of lynchings in Indiana, and he was so taken by that that he wrote this poem, which was later turned into the song Strange Fruit … the fruit is actually the Black people swinging in the trees as they're being lynched and the visual imagery of it is quite confronting.
When you go from that to something like Smells Like Teen Spirit, it seems like quite the jump. Why do both songs belong side by side in this book and tell me why the Nirvana classic made it in there?
I think the beauty of this is that the 42 songs tell different stories in most cases. Smells Like Teen Spirit is really about a disaffected youth finding a voice and finding some power, and maybe just understanding that they are a bit cranky at times … and that's the teen spirit because "you might think I'm just a stoner or lazy, but that's just the way we are and you guys need to understand it because we've got the power".
Would you describe this as a song that doesn't really have political messaging but still has an impact socially?
Oh, absolutely. And there's a couple of songs in this book like that that weren't designed to be political but the message in it was so strong and connected so strongly. Smells Like Teen Spirit [is a] song that connected to a generation in many ways. People I know who don't like that style of music still love that song. And … it gave people [the] feeling that it's OK to feel disaffected. But let's just get people to understand that we can still be productive, useful, and loved.
It appears in a lot of different places in pop culture. I hear the riff every day when I tune into The Breakfast Club — a radio show out of New York on a station that plays mostly hip hop and R&B — but I did go back and listen to the song after reading that part in your book because you mentioned that the lyrics, a lot of them don't even really make sense, and you're absolutely right.
It's pure genius when you think about it. It's just that great abstract way of thinking that older people didn't understand at the time.
Let's jump on to Beds are Burning. Tell me about this song and its impact, as well as the impact of Midnight Oil.
It's an interesting one because Midnight Oil had always been political to a degree, but this ramped it up. It's written specifically around the dispossession of the Pintupi people and it was the first time, I think, in Australia that anybody had really in a public way spoken about Aboriginal land rights, so something that we'd buried and hidden and didn't even want to talk about suddenly became something that we were singing along with … so it really brought that way of thinking into the mainstream.
There's something about having a catchy tune you're singing along to, but then it has this potent message.
It is good, isn't it? That's where some of these songs in the book, not just this one, hook you in without you knowing. You get entrapped by the music or entrapped by the melody, and then underneath it all are these great lyrics that are telling you a story and trying to ask you to think. And subconsciously, whether you like it or not, if you like the sound of that song, you are going to start to take in the lyrics in a way that you don't even understand.
It did make me wonder though why a song like Treaty by Yothu Yindi didn't make the list. Are there songs, Australian songs, that could have made the list but just missed out?
Oh, absolutely. Treaty is one of them, clearly. There's I was Only 19 by Redgum, Khe Sanh by Cold Chisel — they were all on the list that we considered. And hopefully we get to a point where we do a second book and they'll be in there.

"Thirty years ago, Atlanta welcomed the world. The 1996 Centennial Olympic Games changed this city," Dickens said. "When the flame returns to the U.S., Atlanta will be ready. Ready to welcome it from Greece. Ready to celebrate the spirit of the Games together as a community. And ready to send it forward toward Los Angeles and the next chapter of America's Olympic story."
Organizers said the complete route will be revealed in 2027, with the relay scheduled to begin in spring 2028 and conclude at the LA28 opening ceremony. ■

S. Korea's production, consumption, investment fall in August
