Environmental Impact Assessment: How eDNA can revolutionize Taiwan’s biodiversity research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:31 UTC
01:49:31 KST

Last year, a Taiwanese-Japanese team of scientists described a new species: the Yuchi music frog (Nidirana shyhhuangi), an amphibian previously thought to be an isolated population of the Ryukyu music frog (Nidirana okinavana).
Careful comparison of body sizes, patterning, and vocalizations convinced the researchers they were looking at different species, meaning that Nidirana shyhhuangi — found at only two locations in Nantou County — is a critically endangered Taiwan endemic. According to a press release issued by NTNU’s Center of Public Affairs, this discovery “shows that even on an island as small as Taiwan, the richness and complexity of biodiversity are still widely underestimated.”
In the last two decades, various technological leaps have made the detection and identification of species easier than ever. Among them, environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding is one of the most transformative.
Photo courtesy of the National Institutes of Applied Research
Every plant and animal within an environment sheds genetic material in forms such as feces, urine, feathers, spores or pollen. Some of these traces last just a few hours, but viable DNA fragments have been extracted from the teeth or bones of creatures that died over 1,000 years ago.
So far, most eDNA studies have focused on what can be learned by analyzing a location’s soil or water. But an article in June last year on the University of Florida’s online news hub quoted David Duffy, a professor of wildlife disease genomics at the university, as saying that a great deal of informative DNA can be found in the air.
“That means you can study species without directly having to disturb them, without ever having to see them. It opens up huge possibilities to study all the species in an area simultaneously, from microbes and viruses all the way up to vertebrates like bobcats and humans, and everything in between,” Duffy said.
Photo: Steven Crook
TECHNOLOGICAL PROGRESS
Filters fine enough to catch all but the very smallest bacteria — which are less than 1/200th of the width of a human hair — have been around since the 1960s. Only recently, however, have scientists gained access to sufficient computational power to process the enormous amounts of data a single study can generate. Computers are now able to compare eDNA sequences against vast reference databases such as GenBank (maintained by the US National Institutes of Health). In addition to producing a list of the species found at a particular place, bioinformatics software suites can estimate species abundance and biomass.
Even though the Yuchi music frog was identified using more traditional methods, Taiwanese researchers have embraced the potential of eDNA metabarcoding.
Photo courtesy of the National Academy of Marine Research
Lin Yen-ting (林晏廷), an expert on invasive fish species (see “Taiwan’s freshwater invaders” in the Aug. 26, 2026 Taipei Times), has applied the technology to the piscine population of New Taipei City’s Feitsui Reservoir (翡翠水庫).
According to a paper authored by Lin, an assistant professor in the Master’s Program in Biodiversity at National Taiwan University, and seven other specialists, eDNA demonstrated “superior sensitivity” compared to traditional survey methods such as gillnetting (Environmental and Sustainability Indicators, September 2025).
Damming a waterway to create a reservoir — in the case of Feitsui, the Beishi Creek (北勢溪) was impounded — changes it from a lotic (flowing) to a lentic (still) system. This leads to “profound alterations in aquatic environments and shifts in species composition [which] often favor species adapted to stagnant waters…The result is often species replacement, altered community structures, and declines in ecological stability and native biodiversity,” Lin and his coauthors point out.
Traditional sampling at Feitsui had previously documented 23 fish species, while eDNA analysis not only matched this count but detected 13 additional species. Capture methods appear to be biased toward “large-bodied, invasive taxa” while metabarcoding favors “native and small-bodied species,” the paper states. At the same time, the authors express concern that among the species detected exclusively through eDNA were the Florida or largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides) and the blue tilapia (Oreochromis aureus). Both are “high-risk invasive species.”
While there can be no doubt as to “the dominance of invasive species and the evident shift in community structure,” the authors take heart from the fact that native fish haven’t entirely disappeared from the reservoir. The evidence they present indicates “these species continue to exist — albeit potentially in lower abundance or occupying less-sampled habitats — suggesting that invasive species, while impactful, have not entirely displaced native fauna.” Feitsui Reservoir’s native fish populations may, they speculate, benefit from ecological connectivity between the reservoir and upstream tributaries of the Beishi Creek.
Metabarcoding demonstrates “both time and cost efficiency” compared to older sampling methods, Lin’s team writes, but it’s not without its drawbacks. Depending on their life stages, activity levels and stress levels, individual organisms shed varying amounts of DNA. Temperature, UV radiation and microbial activity influence the rate at which DNA degrades, while running water can move it far from the source fish. This makes it “difficult to infer community structure solely based on eDNA data [and] accurately estimating abundance remains a major challenge in fish surveys using eDNA methods.”
BLUE OCEANS, GREEN FIELDS
Even in the open ocean, metabarcoding produces useful data. Scientists at National Sun Yat-sen University’s Department of Marine Biotechnology and Resources recently used it to better understand the boundary between tropical and subtropical marine communities.
They took samples of seawater from 10 coastal locations, including Taiwan’s north and northeast coasts, the Penghu archipelago, Siaoliouciou (小琉球) and Green Island (綠島). In July paper in Marine Environmental Research, they explain that hard corals and benthic organisms (those that dwell on or close to the seabed) were more evident in southern waters, whereas the richness of copepods (small crustaceans) was highest in the north.
Rice fields cover a major part of Taiwan’s lowlands, and rice is a crop of great importance. It’s hardly surprising, then, that local researchers have been conducting eDNA biodiversity surveys to assess the presence of native and non-native pests across cultivation phases.
Rice fields are “ephemeral wetlands particularly vulnerable to invasive species,” according to an April paper in Ecology and Evolution. To study these habitats, the authors collected water and soil samples from eight rice fields in Chiayi County, generating 1.01 million usable DNA sequencing reads. After excluding unclassifiable results, 93 percent of the reads were matched to arthropods (a group that includes agricultural pests such as stem borers and planthoppers) and nearly 6 percent to annelids (segmented worms). Rotifers — microscopic swimming organisms — and mollusks made up most of the remainder.
The paper concludes that, despite the limited number of samples, the study provided “valuable insights into the pest community.” The detection of the Asiatic rice borer (Chilo suppressalis), the Formosan termite (Coptotermes formosanus) and the golden apple snail (Pomacea canaliculata) “are highly concerning.” Humans who live near paddy fields may be alarmed to know the scholars also found “high abundances of Culex tritaeniorhynchus, a vector of Japanese encephalitis virus.”
Metabarcoding offers distinct advantages over conventional biomonitoring, which in rice fields relies on dip nets, funnel traps and taxonomic expertise. As the technology advances, analyzing water, soil or leaf swabs will become increasingly accessible to ordinary farmers. By providing a real-time picture of field biodiversity, metabarcoding could make it possible to target pests more precisely — and reduce farmers’ reliance on broad-spectrum pesticides.
Steven Crook, the author or co-author of four books about Taiwan, has been following environmental issues since he arrived in the country in 1991. He drives a hybrid and carries his own chopsticks. The views expressed here are his own.

Japan’s efforts could redraw  the global oil map
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:26 UTC
01:49:26 KST

Among the world’s top fuel-consuming nations, Japan is the most energy insecure. Its import-dependency ratios are scary: It buys overseas 99.9 percent of the oil it needs; 99.7 percent of the coal; and 97.8 percent of the natural gas. So Tokyo springs into action after every major energy shock to reassess its supply sources, making it a bellwether of global trends. The direction it is signaling this time? Run away from the Middle East.
Where Japan goes, others in Asia often follow. South Korea, another major energy importer, has already announced plans to reduce its reliance on the Middle East. India has been less vocal but was trying to diversify even before the war in Iran.
Beyond creating a major conundrum for Middle Eastern suppliers, the shift goes against geographic, economic and historic reasoning. The Middle East and Far East are relatively close, so it makes commercial sense — particularly when the cost of shipping is high, as it is now — that oil flows from one region to the other. And so it has done for decades.
Illustration: Mountain People
Despite its deep sense of energy vulnerability after the 1973-74 oil crisis, and again in 1979, Japan trusted the Middle East, buying more than 90 percent of its crude from the region. With the benefit of hindsight, the policy was — to borrow a phrase from Nobuo Tanaka, a former senior energy official in Japan who later ran the International Energy Agency (IEA) — a “mistake.”
The official message is, of course, more diplomatic. However, read between the lines and it is obvious that Japanese officials are trying to rectify what they see as a policy failure. The key is “diversifying procurement sources and transport routes,” according to a cabinet document. The goal, while unquantified, is clear: to “break free from a structural vulnerability where recurring energy supply instability and constraints act as a bottleneck for Japan’s economic growth.”
The documents talk about supporting construction of new pipelines to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, which would allow it to keep buying crude from the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia without having to worry as much about instability in Iran. Japan still appears to be headed for a major supply shift.
The Japanese government is discussing the plan, and a formal announcement including import targets and taxpayer money to support it might come before year-end. Seoul, meanwhile, has already set a quota and vows to reduce its oil supply from any region to 50 percent of the total. The Middle East accounts for more than 75 percent of South Korean oil imports.
Japan might not have the numbers sorted, but it is not waiting for the end of the war to make changes. In July, according to the latest monthly data available, the US was its main provider of oil, accounting for 37 percent of petroleum imports. It is worth repeating because it reflects the power of the US shale revolution along with the latest upheaval in the global oil market: Washington is today the biggest oil supplier to Tokyo. Mexico and Latin America provided another 3 percent.
Turning those one-off statistics into sustained flows would not be easy. If history serves as any guide, Japan has demonstrated it can shift its oil consumption when it senses its national security is at stake. Back in the late 1970s, the country consumed more than 5.5 million barrels a day, generating more than 60 percent of its electricity burning crude and fuel-oil. Betting heavily on coal, nuclear and liquefied natural gas, it pushed oil out of its power industry almost entirely. By last year, Japanese oil consumption had fallen to a 55-year low of less than 3 million barrels a day.
Reducing dependency on the Middle East would be easier if overall Japanese oil demand drops. The fewer barrels it needs to buy, the easier it is to shift purchases. If the mantra in the 1970s and 1980s was “get oil out of electricity,” the next objective should be more radical: get oil out of transportation.
It was Japan that gave the world the first mass-produced hybrid car, Toyota Motor Corp’s Prius. Hybrids have made huge inroads since then, helping to reduce gasoline consumption by about half over the last two decades. Japan, the world’s fourth-largest car market by sales, lags in adoption of pure electric vehicles. Having developed hybrids first, its car manufacturers did not push nearly as hard as China’s into full electrification.
The result is that today only about 2 percent of new cars sales in Japan are full EVs, well below the 28 percent average in Europe, and even trailing the US and Canada. The IEA believes the high share of the population living in apartments with limited access to private parking, in combination with a limited charging network, are holding back EV sales in Japan. That makes EVs an important lever for reducing oil imports, which would make diversification easier. So alongside its plans to finance pipelines to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, Tokyo should work harder to boost EV sales, with a focus on expanding its EV charging infrastructure.
It could try to reduce oil usage in heating. Rural Japan relies on kerosene stoves, an oddity among industrialized nations. If Tokyo manages to limit its gasoline and kerosene demand, what would be left is diesel and other petrochemical feedstock. As the world’s fourth-largest chemicals producer, it imports huge amounts of refined petroleum products used in plastics and other materials.
The oil market’s algebra, however, is unyieldingly zero-sum. If Japan succeeds, it would have to elbow its way into markets others consider their own, such as West Africa and the Americas, the traditional hunting grounds of European refiners. And producers in the Middle East would need to find new customers. Trouble is, who would like to boost its reliance on Middle Eastern oil. That would not be Tokyo’s problem to solve. However, it is another way in which Japan could change the global oil map for good.
Javier Blas is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering energy and commodities. He is coauthor of The World for Sale: Money, Power and the Traders Who Barter the Earth’s Resources. Government to subsidize new marriage leave

Unknown Publisher

The government is to fully subsidize wages for the additional six days of paid marriage leave that become available tomorrow, the Ministry of Labor said yesterday.
The measure is part of an 18-point government policy package aimed at encouraging people to have children. It would extend paid marriage leave from eight days to 14.
Under current regulations, employees must generally take the up to eight days of leave within three months, beginning 10 days before the date of marriage, and employers are required to pay the wages. With the employer’s approval, a worker could extend the window for up to a year.
Photo: CNA
Employers are required by law to pay employees for all paid leave, but to encourage companies to support the new policy, the ministry would allow employers to apply for subsidies covering wages for the additional six days of marriage leave, Department of Labor Conditions and Employment Equality Director-General Huang Chi-ya (黃琦雅) said.
The subsidy is part of the ministry’s Guidelines for Wage Subsidies for Marriage, Maternity and Paternity Leave under the Family-Friendly Workplace Program (友善育兒職場婚孕產假薪資補助要點), which is also to take effect tomorrow.
The applications must be filed within two years of paying workers for marriage leave, Huang said.
Liu Hsiu-ling (劉秀玲), director of the Ordinary Accident Benefits Payment Division at the Bureau of Labor Insurance, said that wage subsidies for prenatal examination leave and paternity leave for prenatal examinations must be applied for through the bureau.
After paying the wages, employers can apply online using their organization credentials through the bureau’s e-service system, or download and complete an application for the marriage leave wage subsidy from its Web site and submit it by registered mail or in person.

Help SMEs use AI to their advantage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:24 UTC
01:49:24 KST

Taiwan’s export orders surpassed US$100 billion for the first time last month, reaching a record US$102.96 billion and amounting to an increase of 71.4 percent year-on-year. Sustained demand for artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing has fueled growth in semiconductors, servers and related supply chain industries.
Although this is certainly a commendable achievement, behind these impressive figures lies a more pressing question for the nation to consider: Can the economic momentum generated by the AI boom extend to Taiwan’s vast community of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs)?
Taiwan holds a crucial position in the global AI hardware supply chain, but for many SMEs, AI use remains limited to chatbots, copywriting or personal productivity support. What truly affects a company’s competitiveness is whether it can integrate AI into its everyday operations.
For example, can customer service be made more efficient? Can repetitive workloads involving quotations and administrative data be reduced? Can inventory and sales information be organized more quickly? Can employees shift time spent on routine tasks toward serving customers and creating value?
The next stage of Taiwan’s AI policy should not focus solely on chips, computing power and large-scale investment — it should also assist SMEs in streamlining their processes, developing talent, managing data and putting AI into practical use.
What Taiwan’s SMEs truly need might not be expensive AI systems, but a path to digital transformation that is affordable, accessible and genuinely useful.
Taiwan’s export orders surpassing US$100 billion demonstrates that the nation has already secured an important position in the AI wave. The next step is to enable more SMEs to use AI to boost productivity, which would help ensure that the benefits of AI become more than just growth export figures, allowing them to instead translate into enhanced corporate competitiveness and higher value work.
Taiwan has already proven its ability to manufacture AI technology — now, it has to empower the nation’s vast network of SMEs to properly utilize it.
Liu Dian-ke is a pharmacist and a doctoral student of business administration at National Chung Cheng University.

AI might displace 11m US employees, McKinsey says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:23 UTC
01:49:23 KST

An artificial intelligence (AI) job apocalypse might not be the biggest threat to US workers in the next decade. The larger challenge could be helping millions of people move into new jobs, according to a study by consulting firm McKinsey & Co.
About 11 million US workers, about 7 percent of the workforce, might need to change jobs by 2035 because of AI-related displacement, said the report released yesterday.
That means the number of US workers who change occupations each year — historically about 215,000 — might triple over the next decade. The transition would be difficult for many, with six out of seven workers facing substantial retraining and loss of income, McKinsey said.
Photo: EPA
Workers are not “interchangeable units,” the report says. “Job opportunities can be abundant and yet leave millions of workers without work if those positions require different skills, credentials, locations or pay structures than current jobs.”
The McKinsey study found that full-time employees most likely to have to change jobs are concentrated in three groups: Office and administrative support, retail and sales, and transportation and logistics. That includes jobs such as customer-service representatives, cashiers and warehouse workers. Many are low-income workers, whom the report says would be almost eight times as likely as higher earners to have to change jobs.
Like many projections of its kind, the analysis hinges on factors that are difficult to predict, including how quickly companies adopt AI and how that affects demand for workers across industries. The research accounts for broader trends shaping labor demand, including the country’s aging population. Given that uncertainty, the authors estimate that 6 million to 16 million workers might need to switch occupations.
Earlier labor market transformations, such as the US move away from agriculture, unfolded far more gradually, but there is precedent for this pace of change: The rate of projected job changes is similar to what US workers experienced during the COVID-19 pandemic, said Tanguy Catlin, a senior partner at the McKinsey Global Institute and one of the report’s authors.
“We did it during COVID for two years,” he said. “You would need to presume that we can sustain it for about 10 years.”
One factor the report did not consider, Catlin said, is whether demand for workers could fall faster in some occupations than it rises in others.
“We don’t know whether it’s going to be painless,” he said.
The report outlines several ways federal, state and local governments could help workers make those transitions, including providing more detailed and timely labor-market data and funding retraining programs.
“The education system has been developed over time really to focus mostly on youth,” Catlin said. “But what can be done to continue to upskill the existing workforce, people who need to change occupations? Those are the questions we wanted to tee up for public debate.”

AMD buys firm founded by researcher Li Feifei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:19 UTC
01:49:19 KST

Advanced Micro Devices Inc (AMD) on Monday announced that it has acquired World Labs, an artificial intelligence (AI) company founded by Li Feifei (李飛飛), one of the field’s most prominent researchers, sometimes referred to as “the godmother of AI.”
The deal is valued at about US$8.2 billion and would make Li, a Stanford computer science professor, chief scientist at AMD.
The all-stock transaction is expected to close by the end of the year, subject to regulatory approvals, the companies said in a statement.
Photo: Reuters
“The more you understand end to end, the better system you are going to build,” AMD chief executive officer Lisa Su (蘇姿丰) said in a Bloomberg Television interview.
“That’s why we are acquiring World Labs,” Su said. “To have access to the world-class talent Feifei has brought together and bring it together with AMD’s capabilities around hardware, software and systems.”
Li founded World Labs to develop what she calls “spatial intelligence” — technology that can simulate 3D environments from images, video and text. The company researches so-called world models, which work differently from the popular AI systems that generate text and images. Instead of creating new content, world models learn how the physical world actually works so they can simulate and predict what happens.
The research has applications in robotics and virtual simulations.
“Now that we have tangible proof of the possibilities, we want to do everything we can to accelerate the future,” Li said in a blog post. “To do this requires scaling our efforts, widening our reach, and getting closer to the hardware.”
AMD this month became the latest equity to reach a US$1 trillion valuation due to the massive investment boom over AI.
Even with the latest surge, AMD’s valuation significantly trails rival chip company Nvidia Corp, which recently agreed to acquire high-profile AI start-up Hugging Face in a deal valued at about US$13 billion.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:17 UTC
01:49:17 KST

Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have launched a joint TV channel as part of the three junta-run nations’ struggle for hearts and minds against a Western media they accuse of being “imperialist.”
Russia-backed Tafouk TV represents another battleground in the Sahelian countries’ campaign against the West since the trio fell to military coups between 2020 and 2023.
“We had to strike back ... to ensure that these platforms could spread our own narrative,” Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs Abdoulaye Diop said at the channel’s launch this month.
Photo: AFP
Tafouk TV, whose name means “Sun” in the Tamasheq language spoken by the nomadic Tuaregs, is accessible through Canal+, which is widely available online and throughout west Africa. Setting the tone, its opening credits theme tune is inspired by the music of traditional Dozo hunters.
The logo for its “Communication Intervention Brigade” show is a winged shield incorporating a camera, microphone and pen.
“When plotters attempt to destabilize the state, the battle plays out not just in the barracks, but also on our screens, in newspaper columns and on social media,” said presenter Abdoul Niang, Tafouk TV’s news director and a cyberactivist with close ties to Mali’s military leadership.
His guest to help “decipher” the French media’s coverage of a thwarted mutiny in Niger last month was pan-African influencer and fellow Sahel junta supporter Franklin Nyamsi.
The three juntas have all turned their backs on the West, especially former colonial ruler France, in favor of closer ties with Russia. Despite invoking the need to end years-long jihadist violence in their countries to justify seizing power, none of the juntas have succeeded in halting the deadly unrest.
The trio are also regularly accused of clamping down on criticism. Several foreign correspondents have been expelled and the military governments have suspended most major Western media outlets for reporting on losses by the armies, contradicting official accounts of battlefield successes.
Broadcasting from the Malian capital, Bamako, Tafouk TV produces three news bulletins a day dedicated to current events in the junta-led governments.
The three countries formed their own confederation called the Alliance of Sahel States after quitting a regional west African grouping.
“From now on in the battle of narratives, the people of the Sahel ... are no longer passive consumers of false and manipulated stories coming from fake news factories,” Niger’s state television said as the channel went on air.
Its line-up promises shows on factchecking, geopolitics and news from the front, broadcast in French and English, as well as several regional languages, including Bambara and Hausa. Tafouk TV is openly backed by Russia: In June, Moscow’s ambassador to Mali, Igor Gromyko, hailed the channel’s “role in the fight against disinformation and cognitive warfare.”
A month later, the channel signed an agreement with the parent company of Russia Today in Niamey. RT said the deal covers “content exchanges, sharing of expertise and joint coverage of major current events in Russia and the Sahel countries.”
Tafouk TV’s launch followed the December debut of the AES-wide Daande Liptako radio station.
It broadcasts from Burkina Faso’s capital, Ouagadougou, on the frequency formerly home to Radio France Internationale (RFI), now banned across the alliance. A joint official press agency based in Niamey is expected to be set up soon, too.
“Tafouk TV is far more than a television channel. It’s the AES’s communication weapon,” a Burkinabe analyst said.
However, a former Nigerien lawmaker insisted that the “television channel must not become a propaganda tool.”
“We also need genuine, open debates where any and all opinions can be expressed,” the lawmaker added.

Science parks post record revenue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:15 UTC
01:49:15 KST

The nation’s three major science parks posted a combined revenue of NT$3.54 trillion (US$111.1 billion) in the first half of this year, up 29.27 percent year-on-year and a new record, the National Science and Technology Council (NSTC) said in a report released yesterday.
The council attributed the strong performance to explosive demand for artificial intelligence (AI) chips and cloud services, driving a new wave of growth in the semiconductor industry, the report said.
The Hsinchu Science Park (新竹科學園區) recorded a revenue increase of 36.03 percent annually to NT$1.12 trillion, Central Taiwan Science Park (中部科學園區) posted revenue growth of 20.63 percent to NT$643.63 billion and Southern Taiwan Science Park (南部科學園區) grew 28.57 percent to NT$1.77 trillion, it said.
Photo: CNA
From January to June, the three science parks saw two-way trade rise 50.98 percent year-on-year to NT$4.75 trillion, while investment totaled NT$366.1 billion, up 1,317.43 percent from the previous year, it added.
The council said the three parks’ revenue is expected to grow steadily, thanks to continued development of AI applications and advanced semiconductor process technologies, as well as manufacturers’ efforts to deepen customer relationships and enhance their international competitiveness.
Based on current trends, the three parks’ total revenue is projected to top NT$7.56 trillion this year, the council said.
Of the parks’ six major industries, the integrated circuit industry led in revenue in the first half of the year, as robust demand for AI and high-performance computing drove sales up 29.57 percent year-on-year to NT$2.93 trillion, the report said.
The optoelectronics industry ranked second, with an increase of 6.3 percent to NT$237.87 billion during the period, benefiting from increased orders for fiber optic communication modules and continued sales growth in uninterruptible power systems, it said.
Revenue of the computer and peripherals industry rose 82.49 percent to NT$164.1 billion on strong orders of servers and related equipment, and that of the communications industry grew 13.01 percent to NT$36.15 billion amid strong sales of key networking components, the report said.
The precision machinery industry’s revenue increased 37.65 percent to NT$118.34 billion, as the AI boom boosted demand for automation systems, and precision equipment and components, it said.
Biotechnology industry sales were up 17.44 percent to NT$29.98 billion, driven by effective marketing strategies of medical device makers and new drug developers, coupled with sales contributions by contract development and manufacturing organizations, it said.

OpenAI will not release its newest artificial intelligence (AI) model, known as Astra 6.1, after internal testing by the ChatGPT-maker revealed it did not meet safety standards, the company confirmed on Monday.
The news comes one day before the AI giant hosts an annual developer conference known as OpenAI DevDay in San Francisco, where it is expected to make several announcements — but it is unclear if a new version of Astra will be among them.
Astra 6.1 was an improvement over previous models in some aspects, but “it didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it’s done,” OpenAI safety systems head Saachi Jain said in a statement. “We want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that’s in the company, or when we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment.”
Photo: Reuters
The AI Security Institute, an initiative under the British government, published a study on Monday showing that GPT-6 Astra went off the guardrails more often during testing than its predecessors, GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.5.
In simulations, GPT-6 spontaneously carried out cyberattacks at rates significantly higher than those observed for the other two interfaces, the study showed.
Concerns about AI safety have escalated in the past few months after models developed by OpenAI and rival lab Anthropic PBC were involved in security incidents during testing. Agents built with OpenAI’s models have inappropriately accessed Web sites maintained by US federal agencies, an Australian government health statistics portal and Hugging Face, a repository of AI models.
OpenAI on Monday apologized for not properly responding to the Australia incident, which involved its AI models accessing government Web sites without authorization.
“We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” OpenAI said in a blog post, adding that the company would explain “what we know, what we have changed, and what we will do to rebuild trust with the Australian people.”
“Our aim was to give affected agencies a detailed account once our investigation was complete,” the ChatGPT-maker said. “However, we should have shared preliminary findings sooner and kept Australian agencies updated as more facts emerged.”
Separately, Anthropic has warned investors of potential “existential risks to humanity” in the prospectus for its highly anticipated initial public offering (IPO) of shares, the Financial Times reported yesterday.
Citing people with knowledge of the so-called S1 filing to go public, the report notes the possibility of powerful AI models to operate beyond their predicted parameters, despite safety controls.
The IPO filing also gives financial details of the company created just six years ago, including plans to spend a massive US$518 billion on AI infrastructure and computing power in the coming years.
It said operating losses hit more than US$8 billion last year, as development costs far outstripped revenue of US$4.6 billion.

ENGLISH DIGEST 實用美語(空中美語)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:14 UTC
01:49:14 KST

At first glance, quinoa looks like just another grain on a supermarket shelf, but this tiny seed carries a history far richer than most people realize. Botanically, it belongs to the same family as spinach and beets. It is not a true grain at all, but a seed humans have relied on for thousands of years.
Quinoa originated in the Andes Mountains of South America—particularly in Peru, Bolivia and Chile—where it has been cultivated for over 5,000 years. For the Inca civilization, quinoa was far more than a food source. They called it chisaya mama, meaning “the mother of all grains,” and regarded it as a sacred crop. So central was quinoa to Inca culture that the emperor himself would sow the first seeds of the season as a ritual.
The arrival of Spanish explorers in the 16th century, however, dealt a devastating blow to this ancient tradition. Conquistador Francisco Pizarro, intent on erasing Inca culture, ordered quinoa fields to be destroyed and replaced with European crops such as wheat and barley. As a result, quinoa was pushed to the margins of mainstream agriculture, surviving only in remote mountain communities where Indigenous farmers quietly preserved the seeds.
Photo: Freepik / 照片：Freepik
In recent decades, quinoa has gained recognition for its impressive nutritional profile. It is rich in protein, fiber, vitamins and minerals, and it is especially valued for containing all nine essential amino acids. This feature is relatively uncommon in plant-based foods and has contributed to quinoa’s reputation as a highly nutritious choice. In addition, its gluten-free nature has made it particularly appealing to consumers with specific dietary concerns.
Today, quinoa is grown on nearly every continent and celebrated worldwide as a superfood. The reason why it has captured global attention is that it meets the demands of modern health-conscious consumers while honoring an ancient and enduring legacy.
乍看之下，藜麥只是超市貨架上另一種普通的穀物，但這顆小小的種子所承載的歷史遠比多數人想像的更加豐富。從植物學的角度看來，它與菠菜和甜菜屬於同一科。它完全不是真正的穀物，而是人類數千年來賴以維生的種子。
藜麥起源於南美洲的安地斯山脈——特別是在秘魯、玻利維亞和智利——在此已被栽種超過五千年。對印加文明而言，藜麥遠不只是一種食物來源。他們稱其為「chisaya mama」，意為「穀物之母」，並將其視為神聖的作物。藜麥在印加文化中佔據如此核心地位，以至於皇帝本人會親自播下當季的第一批種子以作為一種儀式。
然而，16世紀西班牙探險者的到來對這項古老傳統造成毀滅性的打擊。征服者法蘭西斯科・皮薩羅一心想要消除印加文化，下令摧毀藜麥田，並改種小麥和大麥等歐洲作物。結果，藜麥逐漸被排擠至主流農業的邊緣，僅存於偏遠的山區社群中，由原住民農民默默保存著種子。
近幾十年來，藜麥因其卓越的營養價值而逐漸受到重視。它富含蛋白質、纖維、維生素和礦物質，尤其因為含有全部九種人體必需胺基酸而備受推崇。這一特性在植物性食物中相對罕見，也使藜麥贏得高營養價值選擇的美譽。此外，藜麥不含麩質的特性使其特別吸引有特定飲食需求的消費者。
如今，藜麥幾乎已遍植各大洲，並在全球被譽為超級食物。它之所以能引起全球關注是因為它滿足了現代重視健康的消費者之需求，同時也傳承了古老且持久的傳統。
MORE INFORMATION
superfood n. 超級食物（對健康非常好的食品）
quinoa n. 藜麥
botanically adv. 植物學方面地
beet n. 甜菜
Inca adj. 印加的
devastating adj. 毀滅性的
barley n. 大麥
nutritional adj. 營養的
amino acid n. 胺基酸
dietary adj. 飲食的
KEY VOCABULARY
1. cultivate v. 栽種；培育；培養
Mike’s early life and childhood cultivated a sense of responsibility in him that he still has today.
邁克的早年生活和童年使他培養出至今依然有的責任感。
2. civilization n. 文明
Ruins left behind by ancient civilizations are studied today so modern people can learn from them.
現代人研究古文明所留下的遺跡以從中學習。
3. sow v. 播種
Farmers sow seeds in early spring to ensure a healthy summer harvest.
農夫在早春播種，以確保夏季能有健康的收成。
4. explorer n. 探險家
The explorer has traveled to every continent on Earth, including Antarctica.
那位探險家去過地球上每一洲，包括南極洲。
5. mainstream adj. 主流的
The artist refused to follow mainstream trends and created unique styles.
這位藝術家拒絕追隨主流潮流，創作出獨特風格。
6. indigenous adj. 本土的；土生土長的
The indigenous people of Australia had their land taken from them by British settlers hundreds of years ago.
澳洲原住民在數百年前被英國移居者搶走土地。
7. preserve v. 保存；保護
Good traditions should be preserved while bad and outdated ones should be discarded.

Civil groups call for equal parental leave to prevent workplace discrimination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:13 UTC
01:49:13 KST

Civil groups yesterday urged the Legislative Yuan to increase maternity leave and paternity leave by the same amount to avoid workplace discrimination against women.
President William Lai (賴清德) in May unveiled an 18-point population strategy to combat the nation’s low birthrate, titled “Taiwan Population Strategy 2.0: Family Support.” One new measure would be to extend maternity leave from the current eight weeks to 12 weeks, while leave for partners is set to be extended from seven to 14 days.
The proposal is being reviewed by the legislature, with some lawmakers proposing a 14-week maternity period.
Photo: CNA
Maternity leave is not simply “the longer the better,” and must be increased in tandem with paternity leave to avoid discrimination in the workplace, the Childcare Policy Alliance said.
Extending maternity leave without extending paternity leave leaves the entire female workforce at a disadvantage, the alliance said, citing a study from Brazil last year.
The study of 14,767 workers who took leave and 423,926 of their colleagues showed that women’s overall promotion rate dropped by 17 percent and average income decreased by 3.5 percent, while the proportion of women in highly skilled positions decreased by 5 percent.
Meanwhile, the study showed that men’s promotion rate rose from 3.35 percent to 6.23 percent.
The study shows that extended maternity leave puts the entire female workforce at a disadvantage, as employers might not hire women due to costly maternity leave policies, Childcare Policy Alliance spokesman Wang Chao-ching (王兆慶) said.
Spain grants equal parental leave for men and women, Wang said, adding that the key to increasing the birthrate is encouraging dual-parent caregiving and encouraging men to take a more active role in childcare.
Spain also grants wage subsidies during childcare leave, he said.
Government proposals should consider how to encourage fathers to participate in childcare responsibilities and break the misconception that it is solely a woman’s duty, Alliance of Educare Trade Unions member Chen Hui-ching (陳惠菁) said.
New policies should ensure women do not have to leave the workforce because they have children, Taiwan Labour Front secretary-general Yang Shu-wei (楊書瑋) said.
Additional maternity leave should preserve women’s choice as long as their health is not compromised, he said.
Moreover, the wage costs of additional leave should be covered by the government through social insurance or subsidies, he added.

India uses corals, seagrass to shield against rising seas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:12 UTC
01:49:12 KST

Under a blazing sun, workers crouch on a shrinking island off India’s southern coast, threading bright green seagrass shoots onto wooden frames before anchoring them onto the ocean floor.
Restoration work on Kariyachalli island hopes to rebuild its natural defenses with artificial reefs, transplanted corals and seagrass meadows, in a bid to slow erosion and protect the mainland from surging seas.
“If you are not able to provide that resilience, you are absolutely at the mercy of vulnerabilities of storm surges, cyclonic storms or sea-level rise and also erosion,” senior state official Supriya Sahu said.
Photo: AFP
Agence France-Presse reporters traveled by boat to the protected island after being granted exclusive access by the Indian foreign ministry.
Kariyachalli, which is part of a chain of 21 islands in southern Tamil Nadu state, has lost more than 80 percent of its landmass over the past half century and could disappear entirely by 2036 if erosion is left unchecked.
Government estimates show Kariyachalli shrank from 20.85 hectares in 1969 to just 3.14 hectares last year.
The coral reefs in the Gulf of Mannar, where Kariyachalli and other islands are located, also play a vital role in softening the impact of natural disasters, such as the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.
More than 8,000 people were killed in Tamil Nadu during the tsunami, but marine scientists say these ecosystems acted as a crucial natural barrier and prevented a much larger disaster from happening.
“This was because these tiny islands, seagrass and coral beds absorb the impact,” said K. Diraviya Raj, an associate professor at the Suganthi Devadason Marine Research Institute.
The Gulf of Mannar is among Asia’s richest marine environments, home to coral reefs, endangered dugongs and hundreds of fish species, but decades of human activity and climate change have steadily weakened the ecosystem.
Coral mining in the 1960s and 1970s severely damaged reefs around the islands. Pollution, overfishing and coral bleaching caused by warming seas have also added pressure.
Around Kariyachalli, reef cover fell from roughly 500 hectares in 2005 to 197 hectares in 2021.
The restoration, part of a US$4.79 million state conservation program, includes the deployment of about 8,500 artificial reef modules around the island.
The bulky structures, each weighing several tonnes, are being lowered into carefully selected locations around Kariyachalli. Designed using data on seabed conditions, currents and wave patterns, they are intended to break the force of incoming waves while creating new surfaces for corals to colonise.
Experts are also transplanting corals and restoring seagrass meadows that help stabilise sediments and provide nursery grounds for marine life.
The deployment phase is expected to finish by the end of this month, after which the site would be monitored for at least four years.
For local residents, the project offers a chance to earn some extra money.
Among them is saltpan worker Devkani, 47, who travels 25 minutes by boat from the mainland to prepare seagrass frames.
“We had to borrow loans earlier at high interest rates to make ends meet during lean months at saltpans,” she said. “But this year because of this sea-based work, we didn’t have to.”
Though there have been some strides, scientists acknowledge that warming oceans have created significant challenges to reef restoration.
A severe bleaching incident hit the region in 2024, killing large numbers of corals and raising questions about whether restoration efforts can keep pace with climate change.
Researcher Raj said that the worsening outlook makes intervention even more necessary.
“What we are doing is restoring corals to keep the biomass intact,” he said.
“So, in a way corals will adapt themselves for this deteriorating scenario of changing climatic conditions and will survive to form the future reef,” he said.
Scientists are also searching for naturally heat-resistant coral species that might better withstand future marine heatwaves.
There are already signs of encouragement elsewhere in the Gulf of Mannar.
On nearby Vaan Island, restoration involving about 10,000 artificial reef modules helped recover part of the lost landmass. On Shingle Island, transplanted corals endured a 2024 bleaching event better than older colonies.
“Vaan island restoration results were very promising,” wildlife warden Akhil Thampi said. “That’s why we went towards Kariyachalli island restoration.”
However, for seagrass worker Martina, the reason to support the project is personal.
“Growing seagrass increases the reproduction of fish and saves the ecosystem,” said Martina, 29, who goes by one name.
“This is useful to us and improves our livelihood,” she said.

Taiwan’s men’s 4x100m relay team on Monday night won silver at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, winning Taiwan’s first medal in an Asian Games relay since 2010 while breaking the national record in the event with a time of 38.32 seconds.
Lai Po-hsiang, Chen Wen-pu, Huang Zuo-jyun and Yang Chun-han finished behind China, which won in 38.17 seconds. South Korea took bronze in 38.43. Taiwan’s previous national record was 38.41, set in June.
The silver was Taiwan’s third athletics medal at this year’s Games, following Fu Chao-hsuan’s men’s high jump gold on Sunday and Lin Chung-wei’s men’s 400m hurdles bronze earlier on Monday.
Photo: Reuters
Lai kept Taiwan in contention on the opening leg before passing to Chen, who ran the back straight. Huang closed the gap around the bend, and anchor Yang overtook South Korea to secure second place.
Yang, 29, was competing at his fourth Asian Games and won a medal for the third consecutive games. He said the team had felt good after Sunday’s heats and believed gold was within reach.
“I had even thought of what I would say if we won gold,” Yang said, adding that the silver — his first Asian Games relay medal — was nevertheless special.
Photo: AP
Huang became tearful after the race as he thanked his mother, who died in March. He said he had prayed to her after experiencing a physical problem following the heats, hoping he could finish the final and help the team win a medal.
Chen also raced through injury. He said a torn plantar fascia in his left foot, sustained in July, had kept him from training in spikes until two weeks before the Games and still made every step painful.

Groups question nuclear review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:11 UTC
01:49:11 KST

Thirty-four civic groups issued a joint statement yesterday after the Nuclear Safety Commission (NSC) completed its review of a plan to restart the Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant, calling for broader participation by experts from different fields and greater transparency about the composition of the review committees.
The commission completed the review on Thursday last week.
The issue should not be included in the referendum accompanying the upcoming November general elections so that it would not be treated as political authorization for the restart of the plant, the groups said.
The statement outlined four demands.
First, it called for broadening the range of experts involved in reviews of the plant to include specialists in geology, seismology, climate, compound disasters, emergency medicine, transportation, public health and public safety.
Second, it called for the full names of review committee members and experts, their professional backgrounds, selection procedures and conflict-of-interest disclosures to be made public, saying major nuclear safety decisions should not be confined to nuclear and engineering experts.
Third, Taiwan Power Co should comply with the approved restart plan and submit an implementation-results report to the NSC for review.
Lastly, the groups said that deciding whether the Ma-anshan plant should be restarted is not simply a matter of nuclear engineering and technical feasibility, but should account for geology, climate impacts and compound disasters.
The statement was jointly issued by Citizen of the Earth, Taiwan, the Pingtung Environmental Protection Union and the Green Citizens’ Action Alliance.
Residents living near the plant should be included in discussions and planning, as they would be the first impacted by a disaster or accident, the groups said.
Completing the review of the 708-page restart plan in six months, from March to September, was a very rapid process, they said.
The document did not contain all of the information needed to determine whether the plant should be restarted, adding that even if the plant were restored to functionality, it would not guarantee the safety of nuclear power generation, they added.
The Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant ceased operation on May 17 last year, when the operating license for its second and final reactor expired.

Dead ambassador to Nicaragua’s book makes waves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:05 UTC
01:49:05 KST

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs yesterday said Taiwan worked until the last minute before breaking diplomatic ties with Nicaragua in 2021 in response to a former ambassador to Nicaragua’s claim that Taiwan voluntarily gave up diplomatic relations, revealed in a posthumous publication.
On Dec. 9, 2021, Nicaragua severed its diplomatic ties with Taiwan for the second time, switching its recognition to China.
In 1985, Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega’s government first ended 55 years of diplomatic relations with Taiwan and switched recognition to China, but after Ortega was replaced in 1990, ties with Taiwan resumed, which were maintained by Ortega when he returned to office in 2007.
In a posthumous autobiography published this month, former ambassador to Nicaragua Jaime Wu (吳進木) said that “Taiwan chose to stand with the US and voluntarily gave up Nicaragua,” the Chinese-language China Times reported on Monday.
Wu had been ambassador to Nicaragua twice — from June 2007 to June 2011, and again from July 2017 to November 2021 — retiring on Nov. 17, 2021. He was granted Nicaraguan citizenship on Dec. 10, 2021, a day after Nicaragua cut ties with Taiwan. Wu died in April last year.
The China Times cited Wu’s autobiography as saying that Taiwan-Nicaragua relations had been steady when he retired, and that the main reason Nicaragua cut ties with Taiwan the next month was because former president Tsai Ing-wen’s (蔡英文) administration did not congratulate Ortega when he secured his re-election in November that year.
Regarding the report, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Chen Ming-chi (陳明祺) told reporters that the ministry was well-informed about all diplomatic situation, but sometimes when China is engaging in secret diplomacy, the parties involved maintain strict confidentiality.
Regarding Nicaragua severing diplomatic ties with Taiwan, he said the government “worked hard until the last minute” to maintain ties with all of its diplomatic allies, but “sometimes the situation leaves us no choice.”
The ministry is aware of China investing significant resources and effort into poaching Taiwan’s allies, he said, adding that the ministry’s understanding of the situation regarding Nicaragua cutting ties with Taiwan is not the same as Wu’s, and the information has been submitted to the Control Yuan.
Foreign ministry deputy spokeswoman Chen Yi-chun (陳怡君) said when asked for comment that Deputy Minister Chen Ming-chi and the government have a full grasp of the status of all diplomatic allies, and would work hard in their dealings until the last moment.
The Ortega-led Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN) had pursued liberation and public welfare, but after Ortega came to power, he established a dictatorship, cracking down on press freedom and civil society groups, she said.
During the 2021 presidential election, Ortega fabricated charges to persecute opposition candidates and potential challengers, violating citizens’ fundamental rights to political participation and betraying his public ideals, as well as the Nicaraguan people’s desire for democratic governance, she said.
“Ortega disregarded the long-standing friendship built on Taiwan’s years of continuous assistance to Nicaragua’s development, and turned to China after the election,” she said, adding that to maintain national dignity, Taiwan severed diplomatic relations with Nicaragua at the time.
The Control Yuan has already issued its findings from an investigation about Wu’s claims in his autobiography, she said.

Malaysia begins repatriation of Burmese nationals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:05 UTC
01:49:05 KST

Malaysia yesterday began repatriating Burmese nationals, including women and children, under a voluntary program, despite warnings from the UN refugee agency and rights groups that conditions in the country remain unsafe.
The 1,476 people being sent back are among 5,000 Burmese nationals who are to be repatriated in stages from Malaysia, where as of Aug. 15, 10,388 Burmese nationals were being held at immigration detention depots nationwide, the Malaysian Ministry of Home Affairs said.
Buses believed to be carrying Burmese returnees arrived at a stadium in Manjung town in Malaysia’s central Perak state early yesterday, amid tight security. Ships believed to be from Myanmar were docked at the nearby Lumut naval base.
Photo: AFP
Home ministry official Makhzan Mahyuddin was quoted by national Bernama news agency as saying the returnees comprised 1,370 men, 79 women, 20 boys and seven girls, aged eight to 60.
The ministry said they would be sent back safely on two Myanmar navy warships and a hospital ship. It is unclear if any of the returnees were minority Muslim Rohingya, who are rejected by the Myanmar government. The ministry did not provide further details of their identities and circumstances, but stressed their return was voluntary.
“This move also sends a clear signal that the government is serious about addressing irregular migration and the issue of undocumented foreign nationals through law enforcement, repatriation and more systematic management and data collection,” the ministry said in a statement.
The UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and rights groups slammed the repatriation, saying the security and humanitarian situation in parts of Myanmar remains volatile and returnees could face serious risks, such as persecution and forced military conscription in an active war zone.
Myanmar is involved in an armed conflict and political instability following the military’s seizure of power in 2021.
Malaysia is home to about 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the UNHCR, including about 126,000 Rohingya who make up one of Southeast Asia’s largest refugee communities. Despite hosting them, Malaysia is not a party to the UN Refugee Convention and treats refugees as undocumented migrants.
The government recently launched a system to register refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia and to build a biometric database, as it seeks to manage and regulate the population independently from the UNHCR.
Rohingya have faced growing public hostility in Malaysia due to their growing numbers, fueled by concerns over jobs, public services and security.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has defended the repatriation policy as a diplomatic effort to find a long-term solution, saying Malaysia cannot host refugees indefinitely and Myanmar must take responsibility for its citizens.
Anwar said he plans to invite Burmese President Min Aung Hlaing to Malaysia to discuss the long-running refugee and undocumented migrant issue that has dragged on for decades.
“I am inviting him to say that we can be friends and trade, we can accept Myanmar, but Myanmar must accept them back,” he said in a podcast posted online on Sept. 16. “To me, that’s better diplomacy than just shouting angrily at Myanmar.”

Students losing their minds over AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:04 UTC
01:49:04 KST

Taiwanese writer Chu Yu-hsun (朱宥勳) this month spoke out about the difficulties of judging literary competitions when nearly 40 percent of the novel submissions he reviews appear to be generated by artificial intelligence (AI). He said he would refuse to serve as a judge for any literary award that does not explicitly prohibit the use of AI in creative writing.
The use of AI in creative and academic work has become increasingly common. My son, who attends National Chengchi University, says he is exasperated after working to complete assignments on his own, only to receive lower grades than classmates who used AI. Professors might have told students not to use the technology, but they still struggle to identify AI-generated work when grading assignments.
Schools cannot simply allow students to misuse AI to the point that their intellectual and creative abilities stagnate. Concrete measures must be taken to prevent human thinking from being replaced by AI and to preserve education as a process that stimulates creativity.
An important first step should be to encourage more handwriting in schoolwork. Work produced with pen and paper is more likely to be the student’s own, and can help with stimulating thinking and creativity. It could also help foster patience, self-cultivation and emotional regulation as broader life skills.
Schools should also increase the number of written-response questions in assessments. Students would spend more time practicing with pen and paper, developing the fluency and creativity needed to perform well and earn higher marks in examinations.
Reading is, of course, also important. Teachers can take advantage of opportunities to have students read aloud, not only in Chinese-language classes, but also in other subjects. Outside of classes, students could read written materials during morning sessions, class meetings and club activities. Reading can improve students’ comprehension, while reading aloud strengthens their ability to express themselves and helps cultivate literacy.
AI might not be stoppable, but schools still have options to provide students opportunities to develop necessary cognitive skills. Such measures would not only prevent intellectual decline and promote creativity, but also cultivate the kind of self-development needed to navigate the world.
Chen Chi-nung is former principal of Kuohsin Junior High School in Nantou County.

Economy stays strong for a ninth straight month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:04 UTC
01:49:04 KST

Taiwan’s economy maintained its strong momentum last month, with booming demand for artificial intelligence (AI) hardware continuing to drive exports and industrial activity, while improving consumer sentiment pointed to broader confidence in the expansion.
The National Development Council’s (NDC) business climate monitoring score stayed at 41 points last month, unchanged from July and remaining at a level signaling a booming economy for a ninth straight month, tying the historical record for the longest period from February to October set in 2021.
All nine components of the indicator maintained their signals, the council said yesterday.
Photo: CNA
“Exports performed the strongest,” NDC Department of Economic Development Director Chen Mei-chu (陳美菊) told a news conference.
Wholesale, retail and food services reached record highs, while more companies said they expected business conditions to improve over the next six months, she said.
The leading index rose 0.51 percent last month, while the coincident index gained 0.36 percent, indicating that the expansion retained momentum, the council said.
Higher capital spending by US AI and cloud computing companies, mass production of new servers and chips, and spillover demand for some traditional industries should continue to support exports, Chen said.
Investment is expected to continue to be supported by expansion across Taiwan’s AI supply chain, particularly in advanced manufacturing and packaging, she said.
A stable labor market and strong corporate earnings could encourage companies to raise wages and dividends, while elevated stock prices might support consumer spending through a wealth effect, Chen said.
The strength of the economy was reflected in household sentiment, with the consumer confidence index rising 3.76 points to 68.77 this month, its highest level since April last year, a survey by the National Central University’s Research Center for Taiwan Economic Development (RCTED) showed yesterday.
All six components improved, with confidence in stock investments posting the biggest gain, climbing 7.7 points to 35.42, its highest level since November last year, the center said.
The gauge measuring sentiment toward home purchases jumped 8.81 points to 98.84, its biggest monthly gain since 2020, after the central bank eased lending restrictions on second-home buyers, it said.
Sentiment toward stock investment remained relatively subdued, despite the TAIEX reaching record highs earlier this month, RCTED executive director Dachrahn Wu (吳大任) said.
He cautioned that consumer surveys measure individual sentiment and might not track actual market movements.
Confidence in Taiwan’s economic outlook rose 5.82 points to 87.02, while sentiment toward household finances and employment improved.
National Central University economics professor Yau Ruey (姚睿) said that robust demand for AI hardware has supported Taiwan’s exports, prompting research institutions to raise their forecasts for GDP growth to between 10.3 percent and 11.6 percent this year.
Nevertheless, risks remain.
The NDC cited uncertainty over Middle East tensions, US tariff policy and monetary policy in major economies, while Yao warned that a rebound in oil prices to about US$100 a barrel could keep inflation elevated.
Strong demand from the cloud-computing boom could add upward pressure on prices, Yao said.

US recognizes Taiwan’s value: analyst
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:03 UTC
01:49:03 KST

The US would not abandon Taiwan in exchange for soybeans and Boeing jets, a US analyst said yesterday, as US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) ended their summit in Washington.
The White House understands that Taiwan might be its most important partner and therefore unlikely to take on any course that jeopardizes its relationship with the nation, said Hudson Institute senior fellow Riley Walters, in an interview.
Taiwan makes the semiconductors and artificial intelligence servers that are critical to the US economy and worth more than any amount of soybeans or jets the US could sell to China, he said.
Trump and Xi likely conducted much of their dialogue about Taiwan behind closed doors and any understandings they might have achieved would be kept secret, Walters said.
US officials have said that Trump has made no changes to Washington’s Taiwan policy, he said.
The US government has always considered trade and economics its most important issue, especially Trump, whose attention was focused on getting an agreement to cut tariffs on nonsensitive goods worth US$30 billion, Walters said.
Trump had reasons to attempt to reduce the US economy’s inflation ahead of the midterm elections, although whether slashing tariffs would achieve that goal remained to be seen, he said.
The political motive could explain the communications between the two countries and in the US-China Board of Trade, enabling Washington to make progress on some level, he said.
Washington and Beijing produced different versions of agreements reached during the talks, indicating the two sides need to improve their communication and understanding of each other’s goals, Walters said.
Separately, an academic said the Trump-Xi meeting had no tangible effect on US arms sales to Taiwan.
Tamkang University assistant professor of international affairs and strategic studies professor Ma Chun-wei (馬準威) made the remarks at a conference on the impact of the summits on US-China relations at National Chengchi University.
Ma, recently returned from a visit to the US, said that DC-based think tanks continued to advocate for policies to oppose China and support Taiwan, regardless of their party alignment.
Production capacity shortfalls in the US defense industrial base, managing tensions for Trump and Xi’s many meetings this year, and concerns over Taiwan’s ability to effectively defend itself all played a role in delaying US arms sales, he said.
The policy circle in Washington concurred that China was unlikely to invade Taiwan in the short and intermediate terms, making Taiwan less of a priority in the US’ eyes, he said.
Ma said the Council on Foreign Relations’ Web site has downgraded the risk of a conflict in Taiwan from high to medium.
Although Trump and Xi confirmed to have discussed Taiwan, the US Department of State and US Ambassador to China David Perdue said that no changes had been made to Washington’s stance on Taiwan, he said.
Washington’s Taiwan policy continued to be based on the Shanghai Communique, Taiwan Relations Act and the “Six Assurances,” Ma cited them as saying.
US policy to export arms to Taiwan likely would remain unaltered over the long term, but the nation should stay alert for personal remarks and decisionmaking from Trump that could alter US policy, he said.
Beijing’s strategy in the summits is to shift the narrative of US policy under the guise of conflict management and de-escalation, National Chengchi University associate research fellow of international relations Tzeng Wei-feng (曾偉?) said.
Xi demanded that the US treat China as an equal and oppose Taiwanese independence under Beijing’s definition of the term, while Trump was committed to strategic ambiguity, including arms sales to Taiwan, he said.
However, the risk of Trump’s transactional approach to international relations causing changes to the US policy on Taiwan and China is a risk that the nation should not ignore, he said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:01 UTC
01:49:01 KST

Aerospace company Aerospace Industrial Development Corp (AIDC) yesterday said that it had participated in the Agency of Corrections’ first-ever counter-drone drill earlier this month.
The drill, which took place on Sept. 18 at Changhua Prison, was part of a wider exercise to test the preparedness of the Ministry of Justice’s anti-riot Ching An Squad.
Under the agency’s scenario, one drone carrying contraband for an airdrop had breached the prison compound. The system broadcast warnings and collected evidence.
Photo courtesy of Aerospace Industrial Development Corp
After the drone’s operator was autonomously located, a squad member neutralized the drone using a jammer.
The drill was staged in response to emerging challenges facing the security of correctional facilities, given modern technological advancements, the agency said.
The counter-drone system deployed in the drill was capable of "smart" detection, combining active radar, a radio frequency detector and jammers, and had a detection range of 5km, AIDC said in a statement.
The "smart" detection feature allows the operator to identify the make of incoming drones and locate their pilots, AIDC said.
In addition, the counter-drone system is powered by artificial intelligence, which prioritizes targets with higher threat levels when there are multiple inbound threats, AIDC added.
The system debuted at last year’s Taipei Aerospace & Defense Technology Exhibition and has since been continually refined, AIDC president Chuang Hsiu-mei (莊秀美) said.
The system is "100 percent" free of Chinese components and poses no threats to information security, Chuang said.
It adopts an open-ended structure, allowing for rapid integration with sensors and other equipment made by other manufacturers, making it highly flexible and scalable, she added.

16:48:57 UTC

British police on Monday said that five men arrested near an air base used by the US to strike Iran were released on bail, as Washington asserted a “foreign actor” was involved in the suspected bomb plot.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the “hands of a foreign actor” were involved in the incident in which the five were arrested on suspected explosives and terrorism offenses.
British police declared a major incident at the RAF Fairford base in western England following the arrests early on Sunday, and the government held a national emergency meeting.
Photo: AP
However, the police on Monday released the five on bail, but said the investigation was not over and they were examining whether individuals acting for a foreign state were involved.
A source familiar with the matter said that the three large white vans the men appeared to travel in had not contained viable explosives.
The source said Sunday’s police response had not been intelligence-led — an indication that the five were not under direct surveillance — but security had been beefed up at the base, suggesting there was information it was being targeted.
“What happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It’s one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor. I won’t get into great detail about that yet,” Rubio told the Fox News network’s Hannity program late on Monday.
He provided no evidence and did not give specific details.
US President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that the incident “might be” connected to Iran, and that he would not have released the suspects on bail.
“I wouldn’t have done that,” Trump said.
The five arrested are all British nationals in their early 20s from London. They were detained in the early hours on Sunday after police were alerted by a local farmer to the three white vans parked near RAF Fairford.
Local residents have said security was significantly beefed up at the base in the days leading up to Sunday. A local farmer told reporters that one neighbor, driving past the base on Saturday night, had been ordered by US security personnel to stop and put their hands out of their car.
The farmer, who asked not to be named, called the police after she returned home at about 1am and found three large vans parked in the road, one with a fake telephone number on it, and a group of hooded and masked men running away.
Yesterday morning, a large cordon remained around the base and roadblocks were in place, although local media reports said residents from nearby homes that had been evacuated were returning.
Western governments have warned in recent years of the threat of hostile actors from Iran, Russia and elsewhere organizing destabilizing activity or hiring proxies to carry out plots.
Britain raised its national terrorism threat level to its second highest in April after a series of anti-Semitic incidents in north London, meaning an attack is considered highly likely.
It has also imposed sanctions on people and entities linked to Iran, accusing them of involvement in hostile activity, including plotting attacks and providing financial services to groups seeking to destabilize Britain and other countries.
Iran has denied involvement in attacks or plots in Britain and elsewhere, and on Monday denied any involvement in the incident at Fairford.

====================================================================================================

AI will be wrong more and more without reliable journalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:48:56 UTC
01:48:56 KST

In her 1967 essay “Truth and Politics,” the philosopher Hannah Arendt said “Freedom of opinion is a farce unless factual information is guaranteed and the facts themselves are not in dispute.” The news supplied by trustworthy journalists has long been a source of that information, without which democratic societies cannot function effectively. However, as people increasingly rely on AI chatbots for news, siphoning traffic and profits from outlets often operating on a shoestring budget, good journalism is at risk of disappearing.
The paradox is that trusted news sources are essential to AI’s credibility. Failure to recognize this dependence might result in AI tools destabilizing the already precarious journalism industry further at a moment of profound upheaval and democratic erosion. Mariya Gabriel, UNESCO’s Assistant Director-General for Communication and Information, said at the World News Media Congress in June: “Support for journalism is not a luxury. It is democratic infrastructure.” Around the same time, UNESCO translated that principle into practice by unveiling its Draft Guidance on Fair Compensation for News, with the final version expected later this year.
AI firms have a responsibility to help sustain the institutions producing the information that their models train on and reproduce, because every AI-generated answer depends on knowledge that someone first had to discover, verify, report, edit and publish. An analysis of more than 680 million individual citations across popular chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini found that journalism accounts for 27 percent of them, rising to 49 percent for queries about recent events. Without verified information from outside sources, AI systems do not just give inaccurate or out-of-date information, but degrade as well.
Supporting journalism could help AI firms win the public’s confidence, as only 20 percent of people worldwide trust chatbot answers. That caution looks justified. A study last year by the European Broadcasting Union and the BBC evaluated more than 3,000 responses from leading AI assistants and found that 45 percent contained at least one significant issue, and that 31 percent had serious sourcing failures.
UNESCO’s proposal seeks to address this problem by establishing a framework rooted in shared responsibility while protecting human rights and media freedom. This approach, which regards journalism not simply as an industry but as a public good whose sustainability underpins access to reliable information, advocates the use of bargaining codes, competition remedies, public and platform-financed funds, and collective licensing. These tools would be paired with transparency and attribution obligations and protections for smaller and local media.
The real strength of UNESCO’s proposal is that it shifts the debate away from copyright toward the public interest in preserving sources of accurate, trusted information. The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) endorses that framing of the issue. For two decades, the internet rested on a workable bargain: publishers invested in journalism, and tech platforms helped audiences discover it. The arrival of AI chatbots that answer questions directly instead of sending users to the publishers who invested in finding the answers has broken that bargain.
We must create a new value-exchange model. As the New York Times publisher A.G. Sulzberger told delegates at June’s World News Media Congress, AI companies should “support the healthy, sustainable flow of the information and ideas and creativity” that powers their technology. This is not charity; it is enlightened self-interest. Every AI firm is one misinformation crisis away from discovering the difficulty of rebuilding broken trust. Algorithms cannot replicate independent news publications’ verification process and professional editorial judgment.
Fair compensation should not be viewed as a regulatory burden. It is an investment in trusted information, democratic resilience and the long-term credibility of AI — a technology that, contrary to the popular narrative, news publishers and journalists are embracing. For example, investigative reporters are using AI to analyze thousands of documents and public records, helping them identify patterns, connections and anomalies that would otherwise take weeks or months to uncover. This gives them more time to do what the technology cannot: verify the findings, cultivate sources, ask difficult questions and establish what actually happened.
Building a future in which AI and journalism can thrive is a responsibility that must be shared by publishers, policymakers and tech companies. UNESCO has taken an important step toward making this future a reality, and its guidelines deserve broad global support. The success of the AI ecosystem is going to be determined not only by the sophistication of its algorithms, but by the continued existence of trusted, diverse and economically sustainable news sources.
Stig Orskov is CEO of WAN-IFRA, representing 20,000 publications in more than 120 countries.
Copyright: Project Syndicate
If Taiwan falls, the true battle moves from the beaches into the concrete streets. Western analysts fixate on the invasion phase. They end wargames when missiles stop flying and submit policy papers after the fate of a beachhead is decided. This narrow focus ignores the grim reality of “the day after.” To address this blind spot, the Irregular Warfare Center (IWC) published a seminal study on March 5, 2026, titled China’s Way of Occupation: Implications for Taiwan. Authored by Jan K. Gleiman and others, the report analyzes Beijing’s actions in Tibet, Xinjiang (East Turkestan), and Hong Kong to expose a chilling playbook
Beijing has for decades insisted that Taiwan is a matter to be settled between China and the US — or, preferably, by China alone. The strategic environment around Taiwan is making that increasingly difficult. The clearest evidence this week came not from Washington or Beijing, but from Tokyo. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Tuesday met with US President Donald Trump before his summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平). Taiwan is expected to feature prominently in US-China talks, particularly as Beijing presses Washington over arms sales to Taipei.
