N Korea DMZ landmine blasts violation of truce: Seoul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:48:55 UTC
01:48:55 KST

The blasts that wounded three South Korean soldiers last week were apparently caused by North Korean mines, Seoul said yesterday, accusing Pyongyang of an armistice violation and warning of “corresponding measures.”
One soldier lost a foot due to the explosions in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), the heavily mined buffer zone that has divided the two Koreas since their 1953 armistice.
The northern and southern boundaries of the zone are among the world’s most heavily fortified frontiers and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two Koreas, which remain technically at war.
Photo: EPA
South Korean Minister of National Defense Kang Shin-chul spoke before a parliamentary hearing a day after his ministry said North Korean mines were “highly suspected” of causing the two explosions on Monday last week.
“This is a clear violation of the armistice agreement, and since North Korea bears responsibility, we will take corresponding measures,” he said.
The military “has a range of necessary measures at our disposal, and we will implement them in stages,” he added, without giving details.
The minister said that dense vegetation in the area had hampered the work of mine detectors, and that South Korean forces were in the DMZ to clear the area in advance of an operation with the UN Command.
That operation would assess terrain changes caused by North Korean forces south of the Military Demarcation Line, which marks the nations’ effective border.
Hong Sung-pyo, senior researcher at the Seoul-based Korea Institute for Military Affairs, said it was reasonable to conclude that the mines were North Korean.
“In practical terms, the only forces operating in the DMZ area are the South Korean, US and North Korean militaries,” he said.
“Given the interoperability between South Korean and US forces, there would be little reason for the US military to have laid any mines there,” he said.
Yang Jin-hyeok, director of operations for South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, told lawmakers that a site investigation yesterday discovered an unexploded North Korean plastic anti-personnel mine.
Since 2024, after North Korean leader Kim Jong-un designated South Korea as his country’s “principal enemy,” Pyongyang’s military has laid mines and built anti-tank barriers along the frontier as part of efforts to permanently seal it off.
During the operation, Pyongyang also blew up the northern parts of inter-Korean roads no longer in use.
Kang said that the North Korean mines linked to last week’s incident were believed to have been laid as part of Pyongyang’s border fortification work.
There was no mention of last week’s blasts on North Korean state media.
In a 2015 incident, two South Korean soldiers were seriously wounded in a landmine blast on the southern side of the DMZ, with one losing both legs.
Seoul concluded that North Korean troops had crossed the Military Demarcation Line to plant the mines, an accusation Pyongyang denied.
The incident prompted South Korea to resume anti-Pyongyang loudspeaker broadcasts along the border.
However, Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, said that there is “very little South Korea can realistically do” in retaliation for the latest blasts.
“Resuming loudspeaker broadcasts would do more harm than good, particularly because residents in border areas would bear much of the disruption,” he said.
“That effectively leaves Seoul with few options beyond demanding an apology from North Korea and seeking assurances that such an incident will not happen again” — unless it is willing to risk heightened military tensions and further escalation, he added.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:48:50 UTC
01:48:50 KST

Mauricio Pochettino has branded Manchester City’s era of sustained success “a period of deception” after they were reportedly found guilty of breaking the English Premier League’s financial rules.
City are believed to have been found guilty of breaching the vast majority of the 115 charges brought against them.
News of the decision, reached by an independent commission, was widely reported on Friday last week, but no official announcement has been made by the Premier League.
Photo: Nathan Ray Seebeck-Imagn Images
City have strenuously denied the charges and their chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak on Saturday said he is still confident of proving the club’s innocence.
City have won a host of trophies, including the Premier League and UEFA Champions League, since the takeover by their Abu Dhabi-based owners in 2008.
US manager Pochettino spent seven years in the Premier League as Chelsea, Tottenham Hotspur and Southampton boss.
The Argentine believes City’s guilt has done massive damage to the club and the Premier League.
“Whatever punishment, it’s impossible to turn back time,” Pochettino told reporters. “It’s done a lot of damage. Many clubs followed the rules, and some didn’t.”

Photo: AP

Former US president Bill Clinton completed US$8.7 billion in arms sales over two terms from 1993 to 2001, while former US president George W. Bush approved US$15.6 billion over two terms from 2001 to 2009, the data showed.
The Obama administration approved arms sales of US$14 billion over two terms from 2009 to 2017, while former US president Joe Biden approved US$5.7 billion in a single term from 2021 to last year, the data showed.

16:48:49 UTC
01:48:49 KST

Vietnamese authorities have “abducted” two pro-democracy Vietnamese activists in Cambodia, their campaign group said yesterday, after Hanoi said they and another man from the outlawed organization were arrested.
Communist Vietnam permits little to no dissent within its borders and critics say its security apparatus stretches abroad, with wanted dissidents previously abducted in Thailand and Germany.
Rights group Viet Tan said its members were “abducted” by Vietnamese authorities in Cambodia, forcibly brought to Vietnam and detained on “fabricated” terrorism charges.
They are Nguyen Duc Thuan, a Norwegian citizen, and Australian national Tran Hiep, also known as Ho Pham Hiep Huy. They were reported missing since Sept. 18, when they were traveling to meet with other Vietnamese activists in Cambodia.
Vietnam’s Ministry of Public Security confirmed late on Monday that Thuan, 52, Hiep, 51, and a third Vietnamese man, Thai Cong Truong Son, 46, were detained on charges of terrorism and forging documents.
Viet Tan has not identified Son as a member of the group.
The ministry said the men attempted to enter Vietnam illegally from Cambodia on the night of Sept. 18.
It said the three “confessed” to being Viet Tan members and “carrying forged documents to illegally enter Vietnam to conduct terrorist and sabotage activities.”
The terrorism charge carries a maximum sentence of 15 years in jail.
Viet Tan’s US-based executive director Duy Hoang said that Thuan and Hiep had no intention of entering Vietnam.
“Essentially, they’re being charged with belonging to Viet Tan,” Hoang said.
“It’s clear that Hanoi wants to crack down on dissent, whether it’s from inside of Vietnam or outside,” he said.
“It’s unacceptable to have a regime that can just kidnap opponents,” he said, adding that Vietnam “needs political change.”
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese yesterday told reporters his government was engaging directly with Hiep’s family and providing consular assistance.
More than 160 political prisoners are detained in Vietnam, Human Rights Watch said.
Campaigners say previous cases of “transnational repression” by Vietnam include the 2017 kidnapping of fugitive Vietnamese executive Trinh Xuan Thanh from a Berlin park, and the 2023 abduction of Vietnamese blogger and government critic Duong Van Thai in Thailand.
Both men were seeking asylum outside Vietnam, but were ultimately returned and jailed.
Hoang said he believed the recent detentions were the first of a person with non-Vietnamese citizenship being “abducted outside of Vietnam because of that person’s political activities.”
“This is not a normal missing persons case,” he said.
“These are long-time human rights activists ... and we’re worried for their safety,” he said.

Xi’s narrative of WWII obscures the ROC’s role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:48:45 UTC
01:48:45 KST

When Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) discussed US-China cooperation during World War II (WWII) at a White House state dinner on Thursday last week, he left out a name central to that history: the Republic of China (ROC).
“Over 80 years ago, the Chinese and American people stood shoulder to shoulder in a fight against Japanese militarist aggressors,” Xi said at the dinner hosted by US President Donald Trump.
China did fight alongside the US, but its government at the time was the ROC, now based in Taiwan. The People’s Republic of China (PRC) was founded in 1949, four years after the war ended.
Photo: Yang Mien-chieh, Taipei Times
Leaving the ROC unnamed was likely aimed at helping Beijing portray the wartime alliance as part of the PRC’s own history, Taiwanese academics said yesterday at a forum in Taipei on the summit.
Wang Hsin-hsien (王信賢), director of National Chengchi University’s Institute of International Relations, said Xi stood to gain if the alliance came to be remembered simply as one between “China” and the US.
Repeated use of such language by Washington could make “the erasure of the Republic of China ... very apparent,” Wang said.
The White House’s own fact sheet, issued on Friday, also referred simply to “China.”
“The two leaders recalled that United States and China were allies in World War II and fought side by side to win the war,” it said, without identifying the ROC.
The US’ de facto embassy in Taiwan was more specific when in a post in September last year commemorating the war’s end, American Institute in Taiwan Director Raymond Greene referenced the First American Volunteer Group, nicknamed the “Flying Tigers,” who fought alongside the ROC Air Force.
The Mainland Affairs Council on Friday protested Xi’s remarks, saying they did not reflect that it was the ROC that fought alongside the US.
Institute for National Policy Research vice president Kuo Yu-jen (郭育仁) on Saturday said that Xi’s comments had two goals.
One of them was to “suggest that the Republic of China has completely disappeared and been replaced by the People’s Republic of China,” he said.
The other was for Xi to highlight Japanese wartime militarism through his reference to fighting “Japanese militarist aggressors” amid strained China-Japan relations.
He linked it to Tokyo’s campaign for a permanent UN Security Council seat and its call to remove the UN Charter’s “enemy state” clauses, which refer to countries that fought against the charter’s signatories during WWII.
Days before Xi’s remarks, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called for those clauses to be remove in a UN General Assembly address that also urged Security Council reform.
Tzeng Wei-feng (曾偉?), an associate research fellow at the National Chengchi University’s Institute of International Relations, said that despite the WWII remarks, he saw no clear sign that the visit had immediately changed Washington’s Taiwan policy.
However, he said he was concerned how language used in prominent diplomatic settings could spread and endure.
He pointed to the 1972 Shanghai Communique, in which the US “acknowledged” that people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait maintained there was one China and that Taiwan was part of China.
Beijing’s later portrayal of that wording as US “recognition” of its position showed how an interpretation of diplomatic language could spread and endure, Tseng said.
“Xi isn’t saying this just for Trump to hear,” he said. “He’s saying it for the whole world to hear.”

EDITORIAL: The haunting voices of Hong Kong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:48:44 UTC
01:48:44 KST

Freedom of expression is a precious gift from the times, civilization and history, Hong Kong writer Hon Lai-chu (韓麗珠) said on Wednesday last week when she received the Golden Tripod Award, the highest honor in Taiwan’s publishing industry, for her novel Flesh Mountain (祼山).
“As a Hong Konger these days, I deeply feel that the freedom to write and publish should not be taken for granted,” she said.
She said that for a reason. Hon, who rarely speaks publicly or accept interviews in Hong Kong because it could result in serious consequences, resigned from her long-running columnist post at the Chinese-language Hong Kong daily Ming Pao earlier this month after two of her articles were rejected in the same week. The editor cited concerns over “sensitive issues.” She called the rejections a “re-education” effort that she refused to accept.
The article, which she on Sept. 10 posted on Facebook, discussed John Berger’s novel From A to X: A Story in Letters, about A’ida and her imprisoned lover, Xavier. She also addressed the independent bookstore raids in July and called for sustained awareness of injustice. Hon said it would be safer to write about “food, weather and cats,” but the happenings in Hong Kong were too painful for her to ignore even though she has been living abroad the past few months.
“A totalitarian regime is not built by one person, but by generations of every single individual who hands over the sides of them that resonate with the regime,” she wrote, adding that she refused to do so.
Hon is not the first Hong Konger to receive the Golden Tripod Award for writing about the struggles of ordinary people in the territory’s turbulent times. In 2024, novelist Leung Lee-chi’s (梁莉姿) The Melancholy of Trees (樹的憂鬱) and poet Liu Wai-tong’s (廖偉棠) The Letter After the Kalpa (劫後書) won Best Literature Book. They were both published in Taiwan.
Flesh Mountain, which was also shortlisted for the Taiwan Literature Awards for Books, follows three “bare lives” after two social movements shook an “empty city” and the lives of two generations. “Bare life,” a concept developed by Italian philosopher Giorgio Agamben, refers to a human existence stripped of all political rights, legal status and social identity. It is human life reduced to pure biological existence, completely exposed to the unchecked power and violence of the state.
When the sovereign power, which has the capacity to declare a “state of exception,” suspends the law, individuals inside that jurisdiction are no longer protected by legal rights. They are placed in a legal vacuum where the state can act upon their bodies with absolute authority.
Hong Kong’s National Security Law, which Beijing forced on the territory in 2020 after a year of democracy protests and unrest, essentially put Hong Kong in a “state of exception.” It bypassed the Legislative Council, which was later filled with “patriots” in an “electoral overhaul,” giving police sweeping new powers and handpicking judges. It allowed for closed-door hearings, trials without juries and a higher bar for bail. These all go against the tradition of common law that has long been observed in Hong Kong, not to mention that the chief executive has been empowered to certify “other offenses” endangering national security, despite the law already broadly defining the four types of offenses: subversion, secession, collusion with foreign forces and terrorist acts.
Under this state of exception, every member of society is put in a legal vacuum where they are deprived of basic human rights and exposed to the violence of the state apparatus. The territory has become an open prison where state power is left unchecked.
The fire that broke out at the Wang Fuk Court housing complex in November last year, killing 168 people, was a painful example of how unchecked power — amid allegations of collusive tendering, rubber-stamp inspections and unauthorized proxy votes — could reduce people to bare life. No government official has yet been criminally charged for the blaze. Meanwhile, residents said they were not allowed to put up signs calling for Wang Fuk Court to be rebuilt.
Last week’s Mid-Autumn Festival was supposed to be a time for family reunion, and yet, it is an impossible dream for some. As Hon said in her speech, in times like these, when people often feel isolated, connections between people and nations are of utmost significance.
If Taiwan falls, the true battle moves from the beaches into the concrete streets. Western analysts fixate on the invasion phase. They end wargames when missiles stop flying and submit policy papers after the fate of a beachhead is decided. This narrow focus ignores the grim reality of “the day after.” To address this blind spot, the Irregular Warfare Center (IWC) published a seminal study on March 5, 2026, titled China’s Way of Occupation: Implications for Taiwan. Authored by Jan K. Gleiman and others, the report analyzes Beijing’s actions in Tibet, Xinjiang (East Turkestan), and Hong Kong to expose a chilling playbook
Beijing has for decades insisted that Taiwan is a matter to be settled between China and the US — or, preferably, by China alone. The strategic environment around Taiwan is making that increasingly difficult. The clearest evidence this week came not from Washington or Beijing, but from Tokyo. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Tuesday met with US President Donald Trump before his summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平). Taiwan is expected to feature prominently in US-China talks, particularly as Beijing presses Washington over arms sales to Taipei. However, focusing only on what Trump might or might not concede misses the
On the surface, a radio interview with Democratic Progressive Party and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) hosted by television producer Wang Wei-chung (王偉忠) on Sept. 10 came across as an old-time city resident putting questions to a candidate on the campaign trail. Beneath that, however, it was an encounter between two distinct Taiwanese experiences, two generations and two different political vocabularies. Wang grew up in a military dependents’ village. His parents came to Taiwan with the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) government, carrying with them the legacy of war, displacement, the loss of a homeland, and an identification with Chinese culture

The nation has spent four decades mastering semiconductor manufacturing, and now finds itself at the center of the fastest redrawing of Asia’s trade map in a generation. What Taiwan does with that position, at home as much as abroad, would shape its economy for decades to come. The scale of the shift is striking. The overall trend remains positive as the number of crash-related deaths, including those from drunk-driving incidents and those involving motorcycles, older people, children and adolescents or pedestrians, all declined compared with the same period of 2023, the minstry said.
Deaths of children and adolescents and among people involved in alcohol-related crashes both fell by more than 54 percent, it added.
However, the number of fatal crashes involving older people increased compared with the same period last year, Department of Railways, Highways and Road Safety Director-General Wu Tung-ling (吳東凌) said.
The increase was concentrated in Taoyuan, Taichung and Hualien County, where 50 percent of fatal crashes involving older people were related to motorcycle crashes and 20 percent were due to collisions involving pedestrians, Wu said.
Crashes commonly occurred when motorcycles were turning left at intersections or pedestrians were crossing the road, he said.
The fourth quarter of the year is historically the peak period for fatal crashes involving older people, the ministry said, with shorter daylight hours and larger day-night temperature differences.
It advised older people to wear bright clothing or reflective accessories when going out in the early morning or late at night.
Drug-driving incidents occurred often so far this year, with 23 people killed in the first six months of the year and seven in July alone, ministry data showed.
Beginning in July, the method for counting drug-driving incidents was changed, National Police Agency Traffic Division section chief Chen Chi-feng (陳其鋒) said.
Statistics were expanded to include not only instances in which the first party involved in the crash was under the influence of drugs, but also when a crash involved a second party who was drug-driving and committed a traffic violation, to more accurately count drug-driving crashes, he said.
The news system recorded 105 drug-driving crashes in July, falling to 89 last month, Chen said.

'White House oppressing both Iranians and Americans'
IRGC letter to American people urges break from US war policies
TEHRAN — The Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) has published a 26-page open letter to the American people this week, urging them to break with the foreign policy of their government and to reconsider what they have been told about U.S. wars in West Asia.
The letter is addressed to scholars, students and media workers. It says the American public is not the target of Iran's resistance. Rather, the target is a political class that turns war into a business and uses the country's power against people in the region and at home.
"The men enthroned at the White House oppress both Iranians and Americans," the letter states.
The letter is signed by the IRGC's public relations office and circulated in English and Persian. Its central message is that Americans have been misled about Iran and about their own government's role in the region.
Much of the document calls on Americans to separate themselves from the "U.S. war machine." It asks university communities to refuse research and media work that helps plan or justify attacks that kill civilians. It says silence in the face of such policies makes Americans complicit in decisions taken in their name. "This is not a call for hostility toward Americans, but for them to hold their own leaders accountable," the letter reads.
The letter then lists historical grievances that it says explain the hostile nature of Iran-U.S. ties. It begins with the U.S.-orchestrated 1953 coup in Iran, which installed a dictator and created the roots of decades of hostility. It points to the Iran-Iraq War, which it explains was an American-backed effort to destroy Iran's new government through Saddam Hussein. It also cites the 1988 downing of Iran Air Flight 655 by the USS Vincennes, calling it a crime that was rewarded instead of punished.
The letter adds that these policies continue through sanctions, covert operations and support for armed groups opposed to Iran. It asks Americans to "test that record against what they have been told about Iran by their own media and politicians."
On its designation as a "terrorist" organization by the U.S. government, the IRGC rejects the label as a political tool used by Washington to isolate and silence its opponents. It says the American people should see the IRGC "not as a threat but as the main line of defense against Western and Zionist domination." Iran's resistance is regional and defensive, the letter says, while U.S. power is expansionist and driven by interests outside the region.
The document is written from the position of an Iran that, it says, has survived a major military aggression launched by the United States and Israel on February 28, 2026. The letter devotes several pages to that aggression. It says the war failed to break Iran's will or change its course, and that the "outcome has exposed the limits of American military power in the region."
From that experience, the IRGC draws a larger conclusion: the United States is a declining power, and Iran's doctrine and worldview have already won a moral and strategic victory.
"It is perfectly clear which of the two leaders God supports," the letter says, contrasting Iran's leadership with a "self-enriching" elite in Washington.
The IRGC also accuses American politicians of treating foreign wars as financial opportunities. It notes that some trade stocks based on the outcomes of conflicts. It says the same leaders who speak of democracy and human rights have little concern for the Americans who bear the costs of war. That charge, the letter says, should unite Americans and Iranians rather than divide them.
The closing section is a warning. "America's crimes have turned the world into a powder keg that is ready to explode," the letter states. It says the American public has the power and the responsibility to stop a course that is unsustainable and dangerous for West Asia and for the United States itself.
The letter ends by invoking the Golden Rule, found in the Talmud and the Gospels, and calls on Americans to demand immediate change before more conflict spreads.

LONDON, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The European Union (EU) has paid an extra 100 billion euros (about 113.3 billion U.S. dollars) for the same volume of fossil fuel imports since the start of the U.S.-Iran war, EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen said Tuesday.
He was speaking at a meeting of the bloc's energy ministers in Dublin, in Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the EU.

His remarks came after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to impose a ban on diesel exports last week, pushing up already high prices for refined oil products. Nevertheless, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright later expressed skepticism about the merits of a full diesel export ban, and Jorgensen said he was happy about this.

EU member states are currently discussing measures to prepare for a winter of high energy prices. Jorgensen has urged member states to consider ways to cut demand, continue filling gas storage facilities to at least 80 percent of capacity, and adopt "targeted and temporary" measures to address high prices. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: Doolittle Raid fragment returns to China, completing shared China-U.S. wartime history
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
00:43:50 CST
01:43:50 KST

HANGZHOU, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- A small piece of metal from a Doolittle Raid bomber during World War II was reunited on Monday with fragments from its sister aircraft, reviving memories of a heroic rescue that has linked China and the United States for more than eight decades.
The fragment from B-25 bomber No. 8 was donated by George Retelas, a descendant of a Doolittle Raid participant and a representative of the USS Hornet Museum in California, to the Doolittle Raid Memorial Hall in Quzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province.
On April 18, 1942, a group of 16 U.S. bombers took off from the USS Hornet and bombed Japan in retaliation for the attack on Pearl Harbor.
After the raid, 15 planes heading for an airport in Quzhou ran out of fuel and crashed in various localities in east China. B-25 bomber No. 8 was the only one that diverted to the Soviet Union.
Chinese villagers risked their lives to rescue the parachuting airmen and helped them evacuate to safety. Of the 75 airmen aboard the planes, 64 were rescued by the Chinese people.
Their rescue, however, came at a tremendous cost. Many locals were suspected of sheltering the Americans, and some were tortured or even killed by Japanese soldiers.
In China, the Doolittle story has long been regarded as a symbol of the friendship forged between the Chinese and American peoples during their joint fight against fascism.
Today, the memorial hall in Quzhou preserves fragments from 11 of the 16 bombers, while the wreckage of five others was not found. China has designated the memorial hall as a new national patriotic education base.
"The fragment enriches this unique collection," said Tong Lijuan, director of the memorial hall, noting that the memorial hall will properly preserve and document the artifact, conduct further research and put it on display at an appropriate time.
Tong added that it will help tell the story of how Chinese and American people worked together during World War II to resist fascism and safeguard peace.
Retelas' connection to the raid runs deep. For him, the return of the fragment represents both a piece of history and a part of his family story.
His grandfather was a U.S. Navy sailor who helped load bombs onto the USS Hornet before the mission.
"My grandfather and those men in Alameda couldn't believe that they were part of history," Retelas said, adding that they would only learn later that the bombers were preparing for the first U.S. air strike on Japan after the attack on Pearl Harbor.
"That mission meant so much to Americans at that time because it boosted morale. At that point in World War II, it seemed like there was no hope. And the success of the Doolittle Raid gave people hope," he said.
Decades later, while volunteering at the USS Hornet Museum, Retelas discovered a 16mm film reel donated by a descendant of one of the Doolittle Raiders. The footage captured the Raiders training with their B-25 bombers before the mission.
Around the same time, he received an invitation to travel to China.
"What if we could exchange? What if we could create a cultural exchange to bring our two countries a little bit closer through the shared memory and sacrifice of our two peoples?" he recalled.
That discovery led him to Quzhou for the first time in 2025. He brought the film to the Doolittle Raid Memorial Hall as part of a cultural exchange and was given a fragment from B-25 No. 9, Whirling Dervish, recovered in China.
The visit changed his perception of China.
"China had always been a mystery to me as a place. But now I've found myself falling in love with the people," he said. "I know what that friendship felt like when those Doolittle Raiders were rescued by Chinese people. They must have had that same feeling of affection."
Back at the USS Hornet Museum, Retelas came across a plaque containing a fragment from B-25 bomber No. 8. The piece had been recovered in Russia in the early 1990s and eventually entered the U.S. museum's collection.
Knowing that Quzhou held pieces from several other bombers that reached China, he saw an opportunity. "So why not complete the collection?" he said.
The donation closed a circle that began with his grandfather more than 80 years ago. "As a grandson of a sailor who helped load those bombs and to be here, now, eight decades later, to help bring those aircraft back together in a very sentimental way, is very heartwarming," he said.
During his visits to Quzhou, Retelas also befriended local volunteers who helped recover fragments from Doolittle Raid bombers.
"They're like a version of me I see over in China," he said. "Seeing someone that you see a little bit of yourself in across the Pacific brings that ocean closer."
Retelas is working on a documentary called The Great Doolittle Raid Rescue, focusing on descendants, witnesses and volunteers who have helped keep the story alive. He hopes the film will reach wider audiences on both sides of the Pacific.
The 16 U.S. bombers that left the Hornet in 1942 could not be physically reunited, as the whereabouts of five remain unknown.
But for Retelas, the small fragment from bomber No. 8 has already brought together something else: a family memory in California and a wartime story preserved in China. It also carries the weight of shared history and the friendship across the Pacific. ■

Gaza flotilla organisers’ hunger strikes reach critical stage in Tunisia
The Global Sumud Flotilla (GSF), a pro-Palestine campaign group that has sought to challenge Israel’s blockade of Gaza, issued a warning on Tuesday, saying that the lives of a number of its detained activists in Tunisia are in danger after they launched hunger strikes to protest against their detention on what they say are trumped up charges.
The four Gaza solidarity campaigners known collectively as the ‘Sumud 4’: Wael Naouar, Ghassen El Henchiri, Ghassen Boughdiri and Nabil Channoufi.
They have been held since March 2026 on charges of financial misconduct, which they strongly deny.
GSF stated that their attempts to oppose their detention by hunger strike had reached a “catastrophic breaking point”.
GSF stated that Boughdiri is "unable to walk or speak clearly, his condition is critical, with the refusal of water placing him at immediate risk of acute organ damage and death", after he spent 20 days without food and water.
According to the group, Boughdiri collapsed at Mornaguia Prison, where he is currently being held, before he was able to meet his mother during a visit.
Meanwhile, organiser Ghassan El Henchiri, also on day 20 of his hunger strike, has lost 20 kilograms.
El Henchiri is experiencing blurred vision, severe cognitive difficulties and a compromised immune system that leaves him unable to respond to basic medication.
Wael Naouar, a GSF steering committee member, was reportedly rushed to hospital last week following a 38-day hunger strike.
Bassem Trifi, the head of the Tunisian League for the Defence of Human Rights (LTDH), previously commented that Naouar was “in a very critical health condition and on the verge of death”.
GSF further stated that Naouar has since remained hospitalised under a strict state-imposed information blackout, while claiming that authorities continue to deny his family and legal defence team access to information about his condition or his medical records.
GSF also stated that Naouar and Nabil Channoufi have temporarily suspended their hunger strikes following medical intervention, while El Henchiri and Boughdiri continue theirs.
“The Tunisian state is allowing civil society organisers to face organ failure and death in custody for the sole ‘crime’ of organising civilian aid to challenge the siege on Gaza,” the statement read.
"We hold the President of the Republic, the Ministry of Justice, and the General Directorate of Prisons fully and directly responsible for their safety, their access to urgent medical care and their lives."
The four activists are in pre-trial detention.
They are facing accusations of misusing funds raised for GSF after the Gaza-bound flotilla set sail last September and was intercepted by Israel, which then detained and deported the activists to the North African country.
The detentions have since garnered international outcry, triggering an open letter backed by prominent pro-Palestine advocates, including climate activist Greta Thunberg, Irish hip-hop trio Kneecap and Game of Thrones actor Liam Cunningham, calling for “the immediate and unconditional release of the Sumud 4”.
The Tunisian government has previously rejected claims that the prosecutions are political.
Since President Kais Saied launched a power-grab in 2021 which effectively ended democracy in Tunisia, hundreds of political opponents and dissidents have been arrested.
Said however has said in response to the backlash that freedoms are guaranteed, the judiciary is independent and no one is above the law.
The Sumud 4’s detention comes as Tunisia cracks down on international NGOs in the country.
Human Rights Watch said it had documented what it described as the “weaponisation” of financial and criminal investigations by Tunisian authorities against civil society activists- with at least 47 people connected to NGOs have been prosecuted.
In addition, 14 have been convicted and sentenced to prison in 2025.
The Global Sumud Flotilla, launched in 2025, has made several attempts to break Israel’s blockade of Gaza and deliver aid to the enclave.
However, all were either intercepted by Israeli forces in international waters or stopped by local authorities in Egypt or Libya.
In May, an attempt to break the siege saw the mass abduction and detention of hundreds of activists by Israeli forces.
A number of GSF campaigners later reported instances of torture, including beatings and sexual assault by Israeli personnel.

Taiwan's debate over textbooks highlights calls to preserve traditional Chinese culture
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
00:43:36 CST
01:43:36 KST

TAIPEI, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- At a Taipei bookstore, books on finance, business and modern literature dominate the shelves, while history books are relegated to a quiet corner, offering a glimpse of why concerns are rising over young people's waning interest in traditional Chinese culture.
A female staff member at the bookstore said she could not recall a recent sale of "The Romance of the Three Kingdoms," one of China's must-read classics.
"I find that our young customers prefer buying introductory books on Egyptian and Western European history, probably to prepare for traveling abroad," she said.
Concerns about the changing reading preferences are part of a wider discussion in Taiwan over the island's education curriculum and textbooks, which critics say have increasingly marginalized classical Chinese literature and disrupted the teaching of Chinese history.
"There may have been some exaggeration about Taiwan students who don't know a well-known chapter in 'The Romance of the Three Kingdoms,' but to some extent this is not entirely alarmist," said Chang Fu-kung, vice chairman of Taiwan's Publishers Association.
Interest in Chinese classics in Taiwan has been declining, and the root cause may lie in changes in educational ideology, he said.
With "education reform" starting in the 1990s amid a rising secessionist narrative, the changes to curriculum and textbook guidelines in Taiwan have been highly political, aimed at removing Chinese cultural elements and severing historical ties with the Chinese mainland.
Taiwan adopts a textbook selection system in which the education department issues guidelines on what should be included in textbooks, and schools can then choose from different editions of textbooks that follow the guidelines.
With the implementation of the 2019 guidelines, the number of recommended classical texts for senior high school students has been reduced to 15 from 30 recommended by the previous guidelines. Several landmark works that are important for Chinese identity and values are no longer on the recommended list.
Textbooks for subjects such as Chinese language and history compiled under the guidelines have also drawn criticism for reducing both the proportion and depth of study of classical works, while weakening the continuity and systematic presentation of history.
In a junior-high history textbook, for example, the year 1624, when Dutch colonists occupied parts of southern Taiwan, is presented as an important starting point for Taiwan's so-called "period of international competition." By contrast, the 1662 victory of a historic campaign by Zheng Chenggong, a Chinese military leader, to recover Taiwan from the Dutch, is described briefly as an attack on a Dutch stronghold in Taiwan.
Before the 2019 textbook guidelines, Chinese history was taught as a separate subject in Taiwan's middle schools, with students studying it over several semesters. History textbooks generally followed a chronological structure, starting from the birth of Chinese civilization and covering various imperial dynasties before reaching contemporary history.
Since the late 1990s, however, curriculum revisions have reduced the content and classroom hours devoted to Chinese history. Under the current senior high school curriculum, Chinese history is taught as part of a broader East Asian and regional history, completely separated from the history of Taiwan.
Tuan Hsin-i, secretary-general of a local association for promoting Chinese language education, noted that the guidelines had "broken up the timeline of history and how the geography textbook defines region, and minimized teaching materials on Chinese culture and from the classics."
This has deconstructed students' sense of national identity, leading to a situation in which some under 20 are unfamiliar with Sun Yat-sen, a great forerunner of China's democratic revolution, and those under 30 are unfamiliar with the 1911 Revolution, which put an end to more than 2,000 years of feudal rule in China, let alone Qin Shi Huang and Emperor Wu of Han Dynasty, both living before the Common Era, she noted.
Some teachers worry that without a systematic grounding in history, students may end up understanding only the words in a classical text but not the world in which the text was born.
Ou Gui-zhi, who used to work as a teacher at Taipei First Girls High School, said the reduction in classical texts, together with fewer hours devoted to Chinese-language courses, could deprive students of opportunities to explore traditional values and reflect on responsibility and integrity through classical literature.
Wang, a freshman at Ming Chuan University, experienced this firsthand. During a trip to the Chinese mainland in July, he visited the Yellow Crane Tower in the central Chinese city of Wuhan, a historical site frequently featured in ancient Chinese literature.
He said he could only vaguely recall a few lines in a famous ancient poem, while knowing little about when the poem was written or what it meant. "I felt sorry that I could not fully appreciate the beauty of the site," he said.
"Out of helplessness, some parents and teachers in Taiwan have even compiled their own Chinese language and history textbooks," said Lin An-wu, former dean of the College of Humanities, Communication and Social Sciences of Tzu Chi University. "I hope that the difficult situation facing education could prompt broader and deeper public discussion."
"Education should not sever people from their cultural roots. Only by looking at ourselves through the perspective of our own Chinese culture can we understand where we should go," Ou said. "Classics should not be forgotten." ■

by sportswriters Cao Yibo, Wang Qinou, Yang Fan
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Two days before her first race at the 2026 Asian Games, 17-year-old Chinese sprinter Chen Yujie slept until almost noon.
It was hardly the image of a title contender on the eve of competition, but little about Chen fits the mold.

Along the way, Chen showed fans a high school student who is just as comfortable joking about her cat as she is chasing sprint records.
A "NERVOUS" ROAD TO GOLD
Chen had been too young to compete at the Hangzhou Asian Games three years ago. Instead, she carried the torch for one leg of its journey through her hometown, Ningbo in Zhejiang province.
This time, she arrived in Nagoya as one of the favorites, fresh off a national championship win in 11.08 seconds in August that broke the Asian junior record and stood as the world's best mark of the season.
"This time I'm here as an athlete, and I want to approach it with a learning mindset," she said. "I'll treat the veterans on the track, whether from China or other teams, as people to chase and learn from."
As for whether she was a favorite, she added: "I won't pay attention to what people say. Let the result speak for itself."
Chen won her 100m qualifying heat in 11.41 seconds, technically sound but, by her own admission, short of her best after steering clear of a lane-drifting habit she'd spotted in Singapore's Shanti Pereira.
The semifinal proved more nerve-wracking; Chen matched that time but nearly missed a rival closing from the left while tracking another to her right. "I was so scared!" she told Xinhua after the race.
That tension gave way to a viral moment back home: a video of Chen napping under a small blanket at the training track, which fans took as proof of a generation confident enough to nap its way through Games-eve nerves.
Speaking to Xinhua on the eve of the Mid-Autumn Festival, she admitted the days before the final had felt strangely calm. "I've actually felt pretty normal, even calm, calmer than at domestic meets," she said, joking that she may have gotten so nervous she came out the other side of it.
"Before the race, my parents told me to relax," she said. "If I run well tomorrow, I'll celebrate the festival when I get home. If not, well, we'll still celebrate."
She did run well. In the women's 100m final on September 25, Chen led from the gun and crossed the line in 11.06 seconds, a Games record 0.09 seconds faster than the previous mark, set in 2002. The win kept the Asian Games title in China's hands, three years after Ge Manqi's victory in Hangzhou.
Wrapped in the Chinese flag, Chen shouted to the cameras: "Mom, Dad, I made it!"
"I've gone from being a challenger to a defending champion, and holding on to that title won't be easy," Chen said. "I want to keep a challenger's mindset and set my sights on the World Championships and the Olympics. I hope women's sprinters from China and across Asia can do even better on those stages."
SILVER, EXHAUSTION, GOLDS
Two days later, Chen returned for the 200m final and ran into Pereira again, this time with the title on the line. The Singaporean defended her crown in 22.78 seconds, with Chen taking silver in 22.93.
"Coming off the bend, I glanced over at her, and that probably cost me a little focus, because I really wanted to stay with her," Chen said. "My bend running has always been one of my weaker points in Asia. I honestly didn't expect to keep pace with her through the turn, but doing that used up the energy I needed for the finish."
Chen had nothing but respect for the winner: "She defended her Asian Games title, and I think that makes her a rival truly worth respecting."
There was little time to dwell on it. With the relay heats looming that same night, exhausted Chen made the call to sit out the first round.
"Today's race really took a lot out of me," she said. "I'm not racing the relay heat tonight; I'm genuinely worn out. But I know the responsibility is on my shoulders, and whatever happens, I'll do my part and give what I have to give."
Three days later, she delivered on that promise, anchoring China's women's 4x100m relay team to gold in 42.96 seconds alongside veteran Liang Xiaojing and Asian Games newcomers Liu Guoyi and Liu Xiajun.
It was Chen's third medal of the Games.
"These past three years of building chemistry as a team, everyone out there was fighting for that shared title, that gold medal," Chen said. "That sense of unity is what let me run the anchor leg without too much pressure, and just settle into the race."
On Tuesday, Chen closed out her Games with a fourth medal, anchoring China to mixed 4x100m relay gold despite taking the baton in second place.
"What I achieved at the Games is a real motivator," Chen said. "Now that it's done, I can already start looking ahead to the next one."
THE "KID SISTER" WITH HER SIGHTS ON THE WORLD
Off the track, Chen has become known in China for an unfiltered honesty rare among athletes her age. She talks openly about her parents watching from home and her mischievous cat chasing her around the house, which is why fans call her "kid sister."
Asked how she feels about her nickname, "kid sister," she brushed off any sense of being singled out: "People like me enough to give me a cute name like that. But as China keeps growing stronger, you're going to see more 'kid sisters' and 'kid brothers' show up in every field. I'm not the only one."
"I don't really feel like a star, I'm just a girl," she added.
Competing abroad taught her the gap between reading about the world and standing in it. She landed once in Lima, Peru, introduced in books as a rainless city, only to find it raining. "If you only read about things in books, what you understand is one-sided," she said. "You have to go there yourself and feel what it's really like."
It is also why, for all the records already behind her, Chen keeps talking about the ones still ahead.
She has said many times that winning national titles in China carry little weight on the world stage, where the real contenders run in the 10-second range.
"I don't need to break 11 seconds by some specific date," she said earlier this year about the milestone every Chinese sprint fan is waiting for. "If I treat it as a target I must hit, and then don't hit it, my whole rhythm gets thrown off. What matters more is doing every step right in training, and 11 seconds might just take care of itself."
Asked what winning golds in Nagoya meant to her, Chen, who turns 18 in December, called it the best gift she could give herself heading into adulthood, and a beginning, not an end.
"I want to set my sights on the world stage," she said, "and help Chinese and Asian women's sprinting achieve even more there." ■

Beyza Binnur Donmez
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
UN Human Rights Chief Volker Turk on Tuesday deplored Myanmar military airstrikes that reportedly killed at least 50 people at a crowded market in Rakhine State, warning that the toll could rise.
The strikes hit Kyauktaw township around midday Monday, killing vendors, customers, transport workers and other civilians, including women and children, according to the UN human rights office.
At least 58 others were reportedly injured in what the office described as "one of the deadliest attacks" in Rakhine since the February 2021 military coup.
The market contained more than 200 shops operated by members of several communities, including Rakhine, Rohingya, Hindu and Daingnet, and was crowded when the strikes occurred.
"This latest attack raises serious concerns about respect for international humanitarian law with respect to the conduct of hostilities," Turk said, stressing that parties must respect the principles of distinction, proportionality and precautions in attack.
He also pointed to reports of arbitrary arrests, torture, sexual and gender-based violence, enforced disappearances, forced labor and recruitment in Rakhine.
The attack came hours before Malaysia began implementing a plan to deport around 5,000 Myanmar nationals, prompting Turk to call for the process to be halted immediately.
"This is no time to return anyone forcibly to a country plagued by egregious human rights violations and abuses," he said.
The human rights chief said conditions in Myanmar remain "far from safe and sustainable," urging other countries to support refugee-hosting nations, including Malaysia and Bangladesh, with alternative solutions.
He concluded by reminding states of their obligations under the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits states from returning people to countries where they face persecution, torture, serious harm, or other serious human rights violations.

Is Syria's ancient Jabal Kawkab volcano waking up?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:39:06 UTC
01:39:06 KST

Breadcrumb
Is Syria's ancient Jabal Kawkab volcano waking up?
Mysterious vapours emerging from the ground near an ancient volcanic formation in northeast Syria have prompted scientists to investigate whether recent seismic activity disturbed the geology beneath the area.
Videos from Jabal Kawkab, around 15 kilometres east of Hasakah, showed white vapour rising from cracks in the ground, alongside reports of subsidence in the surrounding area.
The phenomenon sparked speculation on Syrian social media that the ancient volcano could be reawakening, particularly after an earthquake was felt across parts of northern Syria last week.
But geologists have cautioned that there is currently no evidence of renewed volcanic activity, with several other possible explanations being investigated.
Syrian authorities have now sent specialist teams to Jabal Kawkab to examine the cracks, measure the emissions and determine what is happening beneath the surface.
Is Jabal Kawkab waking up?
Jabal Kawkab is an ancient volcanic formation rising from the plains east of Hasakah.
Its volcanic origins made the appearance of vapour particularly striking, but scientists say images of emissions from the ground are not sufficient to demonstrate that magma or renewed volcanic activity is involved.
One preliminary explanation being examined by Syrian geologists is that groundwater could be travelling through newly opened fractures and reaching warmer layers underground, producing vapour at the surface.
Scientists are also investigating whether recent seismic activity contributed to the appearance of the cracks or altered existing underground pathways.
Dr Abdul-Moneim Issa Hassan, a geology lecturer at Homs University who is originally from Hasakah, has urged caution over claims that the phenomenon is volcanic.
Hassan said the nature and source of the emissions could not be determined from videos alone and called for gas analysis, measurements of soil and rock temperatures and geophysical surveys of the area.
He also pointed to possible non-volcanic explanations linked to the history of the site.
The area around Jabal Kawkab includes an old rubbish dump and has previously been used for military purposes, meaning buried waste or other material could also potentially be responsible for the emissions.
Determining the composition and temperature of the gases will therefore be crucial in establishing whether their origin is geological, environmental or linked to human activity.
Scientists investigate
Syria's General Establishment of Geology and Mineral Resources has dispatched specialists to examine the site and investigate underground cavities and fractures.
Local environmental authorities are also preparing to analyse the emissions.
However, the legacy of Syria's war has complicated even a geological investigation.
Before environmental specialists can safely work across the affected area, mine-clearance teams are checking it for unexploded ordnance and other remnants of war.
Hasakah's Environment Directorate has said the area has been cordoned off while the investigation continues, with residents and journalists urged not to approach the affected sites.
The different teams are expected to examine the composition of the gases and the geology beneath the mountain before determining the most likely cause.
For now, there is no indication from Syrian geological authorities that Jabal Kawkab is undergoing a volcanic eruption or that one is imminent.
The appearance of vapour shortly after seismic activity has nevertheless drawn attention to a geological feature that has remained dormant for thousands of years.
Establishing whether the earthquake played any role will require scientists to determine whether new fractures were created, existing faults shifted or the timing of the two events was simply coincidental.
Until laboratory analysis and geophysical surveys are completed, scientists say the origin of the mysterious vapours remains unresolved.

====================================================================================================

CCAs and Autonomy Gain Momentum as Focus of Future Force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:37:09 UTC
01:37:09 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—For the past four years, the idea of autonomous drone warfare like Collaborative Combat Aircraft has been discussed as a future concept, rather than near-term reality.
But now that promised vision appears imminent, with the Air Force promising at least 1,000 such drones by 2032.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink kicked off AFA’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber conference by promising the service will have at least 500 CCAs by then. And going a step further, he also predicted USAF will field an additional 500 Massed Modular Aircraft—a new semi-autonomous aircraft intended to inherit the MQ-9 Reaper’s strike and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions, but at a lower price.
These new aircraft will complement the high-end sixth-generation bomber and fighter now in development.
“The F-47 and B-21 are phenomenal aircraft,” Meink said. “They will be able to do things no other aircraft have ever done before. However, they’re not going to fully meet the mass or scale of combat power we need. But when we pair manned aircraft with lower-cost autonomous systems, we will be able to unlock combat power at scale.”
Industry has heard the Air Force loud and clear, and at this year’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference, the concept was on full display, with vendors large and small touting their MMA and CCA offerings.
General Atomics Aeronautical Systems and Anduril Industries, as they did last year, highlighted their FQ-42A and FQ-44A aircraft, which represent the first series—or increment—of CCAs. Meink confirmed the FQ-42A’s nickname will be Fury and disclosed the FQ-44A’s nickname will be Vengeance.
Lockheed Martin, the world’s largest defense contractor and the maker of the manned F-35 Lightning II and F-16 Fighting Falcon, built its display around a fullscale model of its tailless Vectis CCA drone, predicting the aircraft will fly in 2027. And in a sign of how bullish Lockheed is about the burgeoning CCA market, Lockheed said it would build five Vectis drones before it even has a contract.
Swarm Aero, a California startup, unveiled a full-scale model of Gamera, a Group 5 drone about the size of an MQ-9 Reaper that it wants to offer for the MMA mission. And Shield AI displayed its roughly half-size model of X-Bat, an autonomous drone design powered by an F100 engine that would take off and land vertically. General Atomics, the grandaddy of drone makers, released images of its new Wildfire drone, another candidate for the MMA program.
But it is the FQ-42 and FQ-44 CCAs that are drawing the most near-term attention, as plans emerge for their move from test articles to production. General Atomics announced it is ready to produce six FQ-42s a month to meet Air Force requirements and could ramp up higher if needed. Anduril, which moved the FQ-44 into production in March at its Arsenal-1 facility in Columbus, Ohio, said it has capacity to build 150 annually.
Meink said Sept. 14 that the Air Force wants to field an initial 100 MMA drones by 2029, upping the service’s previous estimates. When asked about those expanded plans, he noted the aircraft’s projected low cost—$10 million or less for a bare airframe—and the importance of being able to combine strike and recon.
The MQ-9 mission “is a very important mission,” Meink said. “We’re looking at how we do that with a mix of different platforms. … The ability to bring low-cost mass is a driver here, and we expect these to be significantly cheaper than even the MQ-9s or the CCA.”
Pricing for an MQ-9B, the larger, next-generation model now available, depends on sensors and other factors, but starts around $25 million. The Air Force is now aiming for a $20 million price target for CCAs, again for just the aircraft.
Meink said the Air Force anticipates multiple MMA types produced by different manufacturers, similar to its competitive approach to developing CCAs. Asked if 500 MMAs is a ceiling or a floor, Meink said it would depend on budget, but “I think it should probably be much higher than that.”
The Air Force plans for CCAs to develop iteratively over time, as technology and innovations advance. The next increment in the cycle is still in the conceptual stage, but officials expect to define the objectives in mid-2027 and to winnow the competitive field to six or fewer.
Gen. Dale White, director of critical major weapon systems for the Air Force, told reporters at the conference the Air Force and industry are still hashing out what the second CCA increment will look like.
“It’s getting defined as every day goes by,” White said. In addition to acquisition leaders like himself, operators are also getting a say in what they want, and that’s going to increase over time because conditions aren’t uniform from region to region.
“The challenges I may have in the Indo-Pacific theater could be very different [from those] in the [U.S. Central Command] theater and different again in the [European Command] theater,” White said. “So how do we take all of those different requirements and make sure we have a [CCA] capability that can address many different mission sets across many different requirement centers?”
Operational Use
As autonomy advances, the Air Force is pushing ahead with new operational concepts. The Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit at Creech Air Force Base, Nev., is the epicenter for that work. Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich, the portfolio acquisition executive for fighters and advanced aircraft, said the unit is operating CCAs “multiple times a week” as it develops and applies new thinking.
In December, CCAs will be included in a large-force engagement exercise for the first time, at Emerald Flag at Eglin Air Force Base, Fla.
EOU commander Lt. Col. Lyndon Bartlett said that will be CCAs’ “first dip of the toe in an actual force integration,” a crucial step.
“That will, in [my] mind, be the first time that we will ever do some CCA end-to-end kill chain live,” Bartlett said. “That’s the first time we’ll ever be integrated in a fourth- and fifth-gen combined [offensive counter-air] push. It’ll be small, but those type of building blocks are where, I think, you get the intangibles like trust in the CCA.”
In 15 months since its June 2025 establishment, Bartlett said, his team members have been “pleasantly surprised” by the ease of maintenance of the unmanned CCAs, and what a comparatively small footprint they require compared to a manned jet.
In a series of recent Agile Combat Employment exercises, Bartlett said, “we’re at a one-to-one maintainer-to-airplane ratio, which is crazy small.” That is a small fraction of what a manned fighter jet typically requires.
That simplicity matches well to the concept of “cross-functional” Airman generating CCA sorties even when those duties are beyond their standard job descriptions.
“Because they’re a little bit simpler, because their role is so focused, what we found is that any [Airman] can be trained to generate sorties, to load weapons,” Bartlett said. “We’ve done some of those things already, and we’re going to do a lot more experimentation over the next couple of years.”
The EOU now has both FQ-42 and FQ-44 airframes, with Anduril’s model arriving in August and General Atomics’ in September.
Jason Levin, Anduril’s senior vice president for air dominance and strike, said his company’s Fury prototype took part in two exercises with the EOU.
The July exercise, at Creech, demonstrated that a single Air Force operator could launch and recover an aircraft on his own after just a few hours of training.
“The Air Force was operating mission autonomy by themselves, which was a first,” Levin said. “They were flying multiple times a day, operating mission autonomy without Anduril personnel–they were on-site kind of helping, but it was really the Air Force operating that.
Fury also flew in the same airspace as crewed fighters during the exercise, using its mission autonomy, which helped to build trust among the Airmen flying with it.
General Atomics, meanwhile, said Vengeance has flown in formation with piloted F-35A Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle jets, en route to future test flights in which fighter pilots will command the drones.
Lt. Gen. Jason Hinds, commander of U.S. Air Forces in Europe-Air Forces Africa, said his command is thinking of how to incorporate CCA operations, including using them to boost—or even take over—USAFE’s integrated air missile defense mission.
“You don’t always have to have a human in a cockpit to be able to defend against a one-way attack drone or defend against a cruise missile,” Hinds said. “You could use a CCA to be able to conduct that mission set.”
If a hostile nation invaded a NATO ally, said Hinds, who also commands NATO’s Allied Air Command, the Air Force could also use CCAs to attack adversaries’ air defense systems, or attack invading forces.
NATO allies—particularly Germany, the Netherlands, and some Scandinavian countries—are watching CCA experiments, Hinds said, with some taking their own steps toward the concept. Hinds predicted Sweden, among others, will start to experiment with CCAs in the European theater in the next few years.
“You’re going to see a lot more interest from other nations inside Europe,” Hinds said.
As the autonomous era begins, Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s Chief Modernization Officer, said during a panel discussion that the service faces a massive cultural shift—one he acknowledged will face significant pushback from today’s pilots.
“I can imagine a day in the future, 10 years [from now], maybe more, where a CCA autonomy algorithm does a better job flying a fighter airplane than I did as a captain,” Niemi said. “That hurts my ego a little bit. But at the same time, I see that this trend is happening, and we’ve got to find a way to do that.”
Meink challenged attendees to come up with an operational concept that was more challenging than urban driving, suggesting that the progress in self-driving cars over the past decade has proven that such skills can be automated. Niemi agreed.
But experienced pilots counter that there are a host of differences between flying combat operations and driving in a controlled urban environment, ranging from speed to the addition of flight’s vertical dimension. Autonomous driving, which has taken years longer to perfect than most experts predicted a decade ago, has vastly more data to pull from than CCA operators do, pilots say.
Most importantly, the incentives are different. On the road, drivers are doing their best to act responsibly and predictably. In combat, however, rival pilots are doing their best to be disruptive and surprising. Those are challenges that could take time to master.
But Niemi is undeterred in his future vision and convinced those pilots are wrong. “As you institutionalize these capabilities,” he said, “it’s not too surprising that maybe fighter pilots are not too enthusiastic about the idea of fielding a capability [that] will start to replace some of what they do—how they define themselves.”
Pentagon Editor Chris Gordon contributed reporting.

UN urges US, Russia to pursue new nuclear arms control deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:37:00 UTC
01:37:00 KST

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has called on the US and Russia to negotiate a successor framework to the New START Treaty, warning that growing nuclear arsenals and weakening safeguards are increasing risks to global security.
"The United States and the Russian Federation must negotiate a successor framework to New START," Guterres said at a UN General Assembly plenary meeting marking the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons on Tuesday.
The New START Treaty expired earlier this year, leaving, for the first time in more than half a century, no binding limits on strategic nuclear arsenals, according to Guterres.
“This undermines not only the security of those who possess nuclear weapons, but the entire international community," he said.
The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) was signed on April 8 2010, in Prague by the United States and Russia and entered into force on February 5 2011. It replaced the 1991 START I treaty, which expired in December 2009, and superseded the 2002 Strategic Offensive Reductions Treaty (SORT), which terminated when New START entered into force, according to the US-based Arms Control Association.
Guterres warned that nuclear arsenals are being expanded and modernised while technological advances are increasing the risks of mistakes and miscalculations.
"Nuclear arsenals are being expanded and modernised. The rattling of nuclear sabres is growing louder. Advances in technology are increasing the odds of mistake and miscalculation," he said.
He also pointed to the failure to reach a substantive consensus of the 11th Review Conference of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons and the UN Disarmament Commission's inability to produce substantive recommendations during its latest three-year cycle.
"These are not simply diplomatic disappointments — they are warning signs. And the lights are flashing red," Guterres said.
He said nuclear disarmament is "a binding legal obligation" under the Non-Proliferation Treaty and urged all nuclear-weapon states to reduce the role of nuclear weapons in their security policies through confidence-building measures that ensure transparency.
Nuclear stockpile expected to grow
UN General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman said the global inventory stood at more than 12,000 nuclear warheads as of January 2026.
He said between 2,100 and 2,200 warheads are kept in a state of high operational alert on ballistic missiles capable of being launched at very short notice.
"For the first time since the end of the Cold War, the global stockpile is expected to grow again, as new and more modern warheads enter arsenals faster than retired ones are dismantled," Rahman said.
He said global military expenditure reached nearly $3 trillion in 2025, marking the 11th consecutive annual increase.
"As long as nuclear weapons exist, the danger of their use by design, by accident, or by miscalculation, will remain," Rahman said.
He described the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons as "the cornerstone" of global efforts to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons and advance nuclear disarmament.

Yemen mobilisation call signals escalation backed by Saudis

Breadcrumb
Yemen mobilisation call signals escalation backed by Saudi coordination
A call for military mobilisation by Yemen's government is a sign of growing escalation in the country but has yet to translate into preparations for a new offensive against the Houthis, a leading Yemeni analyst has told The New Arab.
The mobilisation call was issued on Monday by Presidential Leadership Council (PLC) chief Rashad al-Alimi amid heightened tensions with the Houthi movement and signs that Saudi Arabia is taking a more direct role in managing its Yemeni allies.
Al-Alimi called for military forces aligned with the government to increase their readiness and mobilise against the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of northern and western Yemen.
The announcement comes amid renewed speculation over a possible attempt by anti-Houthi forces to alter the military balance after years in which Yemen's main front lines have remained largely frozen.
Maysaa Shuja al-Deen, a senior researcher at the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies, told The New Arab that there was so far little evidence that the announcement had resulted in mobilisation on the ground.
"I think the call for mobilisation is one of the signals of escalation in Yemen, alongside the fatwa of the Saudi mufti," Shuja al-Deen said.
"I haven't seen anything in practice showing that there is any kind of mobilisation."
"Nothing in practice is happening in response to this call," she added.
Saudi Arabia's Grand Mufti recently issued a religious ruling calling for support for Yemen's internationally recognised government against the Houthis, another indication of increasingly confrontational rhetoric towards the group.
Shuja al-Deen said Al-Alimi's mobilisation call was unlikely to have been issued independently of Riyadh.
"Definitely this call was in coordination with Saudi Arabia," she said.
Saudi Arabia intervened militarily in Yemen in 2015 at the head of a coalition seeking to restore the internationally recognised government after the Houthis seized Sanaa.
Years of fighting failed to dislodge the group from the capital, and Riyadh subsequently sought negotiations with the Houthis as it attempted to extricate itself from the conflict, which has caused one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world.
Recent developments, however, have raised questions over whether Saudi Arabia is again preparing for a more assertive role.
Shuja al-Deen said the most important change was not greater cohesion among Yemen's notoriously divided anti-Houthi factions, but Riyadh's determination to exercise much closer control over them.
"I don't think the government now is more united, but definitely the Saudis are now more determined to manage the situation closely," she said.
She contrasted the current approach with earlier periods of fighting, when she said Riyadh had not followed developments as closely or been as thoroughly prepared.
"I think the preparations of the Saudis are bigger than the last time," she said.
Shuja al-Deen also said Riyadh appeared to be increasingly relying on new Salafi leaders as part of its preparations.
The PLC brings together a collection of factions with often competing political and territorial ambitions, and divisions among anti-Houthi forces have repeatedly complicated attempts to establish a unified military strategy.
Saudi Arabia has traditionally been the internationally recognised government's principal external sponsor, while the UAE has developed close relationships with several other armed factions, particularly in southern Yemen.
Shuja al-Deen said Riyadh's current role went significantly beyond simply providing weapons or financial assistance.
"It's everything under their supervision - definitely close supervision," she said.
"It's not only about military support. It's everything under their supervision."
Whether the mobilisation announcement will develop into a significant military build-up remains unclear.
For now, Shuja al-Deen said there was a gap between increasingly confrontational rhetoric and developments on the ground, suggesting the call should be understood as a warning of possible escalation rather than evidence that a new offensive is already underway.

Russia to cut welfare, education funding in 2027, as spending soars on war in Ukraine
- Russia will cut funding for welfare, education, healthcare, and infrastructure by around 6-7% in 2027 to fund rising military expenses amid the ongoing war in Ukraine.
- Defence spending is set at 17.1 trillion roubles in 2027, a 27% rise from the original budget and the highest since 2022, with increased tax hikes and borrowing planned.
- Debt-servicing costs will increase by 21.6% in 2027, reaching 9.4% of total spending, reflecting high interest rates and growing borrowing, despite cuts in non-military budgets.
AI generated
MOSCOW - Russia will cut funding for welfare, education and health care in 2027’s state budget, in addition to previously announced tax hikes, to help cover soaring military spending, fiscal documents obtained by Reuters showed.
Russia plans to spend 17.1 trillion roubles (S$259 billion) on defence in 2027, around 27% more than the 13.5 trillion roubles originally budgeted and the highest figure since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022.
Funding for social policy, which covers items such as state pensions, payments to war veterans and maternity benefits, will shrink by 7% in 2027.
Funding for education will fall by 6% and healthcare funding by 6.8%, compared with the initial plan.
Spending under the “national economy” section, which includes road construction and other infrastructure projects, as well as subsidies for agriculture and other sectors, will shrink by 7.4% in 2027.
Russia’s budget situation has gradually deteriorated throughout its four and a half years of war in Ukraine, as the country has had to tap its fiscal reserve fund, increase borrowing and raise taxes to keep up with growing military spending.
Russia is drawing up a three-year budget in an attempt to improve long-term planning, but it has had to revise figures sharply upwards each year and has repeatedly missed its annual deficit targets.
The federal budget does not incorporate regional and municipal budgets, which account for a significant share of social spending.
The new tax hikes in the 2027 draft budget, as well as a larger-than-expected increase in utility tariffs planned for 2027 and announced after this month’s parliamentary election, have angered even some Kremlin supporters.
The new State Duma, in which the pro-Kremlin United Russia party will hold a constitutional majority, is expected to approve the new budget, with authorities saying that winning the war in Ukraine takes priority over other needs.
While overall non-military spending is shrinking, the share of debt-servicing costs in the Russian budget is rising due to high interest rates, which the central bank maintains to fight inflation, and increased borrowing plans.
The documents show that debt-servicing costs will rise by 21.6% in 2027 compared with the initial plan, reaching 9.4% of total spending in 2027 and increasing further to 10.6% in 2029. REUTERS

BAE friend or foe system certified for US Air Force F-16
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:30:44 BST
01:30:44 KST

BAE Systems has received AIMS certification for a new Identification Friend or Foe unit fitted to the United States Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcon, clearing the equipment for use on a standard shared across American and NATO forces, according to the company.
The AN/APX-127(V)1 Combined Interrogator Transponder consolidates the interrogator and transponder functions into a single box, an arrangement the company says suits highly manoeuvrable aircraft where space is at a premium. It keeps the same form factor as the units it replaces, making it a drop-in substitute for the AN/APX-113(V), AN/APX-125(V) and AN/APX-126(V), which are in service on a range of American and international platforms.
Seth Guanu, combat identification products program area director at BAE Systems, said: “We are investing in the next generation of our IFF technology to support our customers’ missions for today and tomorrow. Our multi-domain systems are designed for high-performance; easily upgradeable; and meet size, weight, and power objectives for existing and emerging platforms. This solution provides added security and real-time information pilots need in a variety of threat environments.”
According to BAE Systems, the unit is AIMS Mark XIIB certified with Mode S and Mode 5 for secure and encrypted exchange, and carries additional receive channels for passive acquisition of Mode 5 Level 2 and Automatic Dependent Surveillance Broadcast In. The open systems architecture is intended to allow capability to be added through software rather than hardware changes, which the company says reduces the risk and cost of keeping the equipment current.
Identification Friend or Foe is the means by which an aircraft or ship establishes whether a contact is friendly before a weapon is released, and the consequences of getting it wrong are the reason the field attracts the attention it does. Mode 5 is the current encrypted NATO standard, introduced to replace the older Mode 4 across the alliance, and it uses cryptographic keys that have to be loaded and managed rather than a simple coded reply.
Work on the unit is carried out at BAE Systems facilities at Greenlawn in New York and in Austin, Texas, through the company’s American business rather than its British operations. Deliveries against an initial production lot of 90 units are expected to begin this year.
