Brexit has done more harm than good: British PM Burnham
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:29:50 UTC
01:29:50 KST

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will “lay out to the country” different options for the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU, arguing that Brexit “has done more harm than good.”
Speaking at the annual Labour Party Conference in Liverpool on Tuesday, Burnham said Britain could not have “the clear path we need into the rest of this century” without deciding on its future relationship with the EU, which he described as “still our largest market.”
The UK left the EU in 2020, four years after a referendum in which about 52 percent of voters chose to leave.
The prime minister said he would use the opportunity around the summit to set out the choices available to Britain.
“And there are different options, and I will see if we can find consensus around one, which will give us clarity about our position and the future of the continent that we live in,” he said.
Burnham also announced that Labour's next manifesto would contain a commitment to change the UK's electoral system.
He said he was creating a “new national commission on electoral reform” and invited all political parties to take part in its work.
“In past years, you have voted twice to support electoral reform. I hear you, I agree with you,” Burnham said.
“We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so that everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard,” he added.
‘Political price'
Burnham promised to put Britain "on a new path" and unveil policies on water, housing, energy and education.
"When we pull as one, there is nothing we can't do," he said. "Today, we draw a line on a decade of division. We stop doomscrolling on posts running Britain down. And we put the country on a new path."
He acknowledged he "may pay a political price" for his announcements but said "someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off."
Burnham said Environment Secretary Angela Eagle would introduce a "strengthened Water Bill" including the repeal of "Margaret Thatcher's ideological ban on public ownership of water companies."
"Water is a symbol of what has gone wrong with Britain," he said, criticising sewage dumping, high prices and problems with infrastructure.
He, however, did not announce plans to nationalise any individual water companies.
Housing, energy and education
Burnham said the government could introduce legislation making it easier to reclaim homes from negligent landlords.
He also pledged to bring down energy prices and asked the energy secretary to speed up efforts to decouple green energy prices from gas prices.
On education, he promised to "rebuild a system of comprehensive education in this country with parity between academic and technical."
Burnham criticised the political direction taken since the 1980s, saying: "Homes, water, energy, transport, care, healthcare - broken up and sold off."
"The British right talk about taking back control. Never let them forget, they are the ones that gave it away in the first place," he said.
Growth and fiscal rules
Burnham said his economic strategy would involve nationalisation and devolution, arguing that greater control over essential services could help create conditions for business growth.
He confirmed that the government would stick to its fiscal rules "to get borrowing and debt down."
The premier said the party would maintain its 2024 general election manifesto commitment not to make changes in the current period, while changes could be considered if Labour remains in power beyond the 2029 election.

Iran waits for US response to peace proposals as Trump denies making concessions
Iran put forward ideas for reaching a new peace agreement with the US through Qatari mediators, Iranian state media reported on Monday, while US President Donald Trump denied reports that he had offered Tehran concessions to end the war.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is currently in New York, where he has discussed a number of ideas with Qatari mediators to be presented to the US. He denied reports that Tehran had shown flexibility on the nuclear issue.
On Tuesday, Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed Al-Ansari said efforts were still underway to arrange meetings between the US and Iran.
“We are carrying messages between the parties to build common ground,” he said.
Al-Ansari, however, warned against Iranian threats to target infrastructure in Gulf countries, saying: “Iranian attacks on our countries are unjustified aggression, and we did not choose to be a party to this war.”
He added that “any threat to infrastructure is a violation of the principles of international law and good-neighbourly relations.”
Araghchi said a seven-point plan had been conveyed to the US through Qatari mediators, adding that Iran was still waiting for an official response despite Trump’s statements.
Following a report by Axios that Trump was prepared to ease sanctions on Iran and release frozen funds in exchange for concrete steps regarding Iran’s nuclear programme, the US president angrily denied the claim.
“This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform on Monday.
Araghchi added that Iranian officials met one of the Qatari mediators on Monday and discussed ideas for paving the way towards implementing Iran’s conditions. He said the mediators would present the ideas to the US side before conveying Washington’s final response to Tehran.
Araghchi expressed hope that the US response would arrive on Tuesday, adding that he would leave New York for Tehran within hours and that Qatari mediators would know how to deliver the response as soon as they received it.
The Iranian foreign minister added that Iran’s position on its nuclear programme remained unchanged and that Tehran had shown no flexibility on the issue.
He said the current discussions were limited to the Strait of Hormuz and that the strategic waterway would only be reopened if a series of conditions communicated by Iran were met.
According to officials who spoke to the Associated Press, the proposal currently under discussion involves reopening the Strait of Hormuz and lifting the US blockade on Iranian ports, followed by the lifting of sanctions on Iran.
A draft of the agreement indicates that the strait would be reopened under a separate understanding discussed between Iran and Oman, with no fees imposed on ships. The agreement would temporarily regulate the movement of vessels through the strategic waterway.

Between two chokepoints: Egypt's growing Red Sea dilemma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:28:23 UTC
01:28:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Between two chokepoints: Egypt's growing Red Sea dilemma
Seven months into the US-Israel war on Iran, Egypt finds itself increasingly exposed to the pressures of a wider regional conflagration.
The Houthis’ recent offensive to consolidate control over Bab al-Mandeb poses serious risks for Cairo, which has already experienced the economic fallout of Houthi attacks on maritime traffic.
In late 2023, when the Houthis targeted commercial shipping in response to Israel’s war on Gaza, the campaign sharply curtailed traffic through the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.
According to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the turmoil reduced Egypt’s Suez Canal revenues by over $6 billion in 2024.
Traffic through the canal has since recovered, with transits exceeding 1,200 in both July and August. August also marked the busiest month since December 2023.
Prolonged disruption could, however, once again constrain one of Egypt’s key sources of foreign currency. A deterioration in Red Sea security would also carry wider economic, political, and security consequences for the broader region.
Houthis seek to maximise Red Sea gains
The Houthis’ expanding offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including their capture of strategically important territory around Mocha and the islands of Mayun (Perim) and Hanish, is aimed at cementing their position around Bab al-Mandeb.
“They know that holding the coast for long may be difficult, which is why they are trying to entrench themselves by securing the highlands overlooking Bab al-Mandeb and cutting the strategic lines connecting Aden and Taiz, which would obstruct the ability to send reinforcements to Mokha,” Yasmeen El Eryani, Executive Director for Knowledge Production at the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, told The New Arab.
This strategy also reinforces a broader trend in contemporary conflict: the weaponisation of economic interdependence. Recent months have demonstrated the extent of the global economy’s dependence on a limited number of strategic infrastructure networks and maritime chokepoints.
This asymmetry has created opportunities for conventionally weaker actors to generate outsized political gains. Iran’s use of the Strait of Hormuz underscored the strategic leverage that can be derived from weaponising maritime chokepoints.
That logic is particularly relevant to the Red Sea, where the Houthis are closely watching developments around the Strait of Hormuz with a growing awareness that they do not need uncontested control of the entire maritime corridor to impose real costs on global shipping and energy markets. The ability to generate sufficient uncertainty can itself become a major strategic tool.
“The Houthis don’t yet want to strangle all shipping, rather, they seek to leave open the possibility that things could go in that direction if certain demands aren’t met. For now, it serves them better if the threat remains veiled,” Alia Brahimi, Non-resident Senior Fellow at the Atlantic Council, told The New Arab.
Prospects of prolonged disruption weigh heavily on Cairo’s strategic calculations. Consistent with its cautious posture since the US-Israel war on Iran began, Egypt has approached the latest escalation with strategic restraint.
In response to the latest round of Houthi attacks, Cairo established a specialised crisis cell to monitor developments and doubled down on regional diplomacy. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to Cairo in mid-September reflected continued close bilateral coordination.
Multilaterally, the regional quartet (R4), comprising Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan, remains active, convening for the sixth time on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty also met with his Omani counterpart, stressing Egypt’s solidarity with Saudi Arabia and affirming Cairo’s commitment to supporting regional de-escalation.
“Egypt has much to lose from further escalation of regional hostilities, particularly in the Red Sea. This suggests Cairo will likely continue pursuing an intermediary role alongside other regional actors with similar interests, including Oman, Pakistan, Turkey, and Qatar,” Giorgio Cafiero, CEO of Gulf State Analytics, told The New Arab.
The Houthis’ growing confidence, however, cannot be separated from Iran’s broader regional strategy. With Hamas and Hezbollah’s capabilities severely degraded, the Houthis have become a vital lever for Tehran to exert pressure and project power across the region.
Interconnected regional conflict theatres
The Houthis’ increasingly assertive approach to Bab al-Mandeb comes at a strategically significant moment, ahead of the US midterm elections.
With peace negotiations stalled and fears of renewed hostilities mounting, “the Houthis gave themselves a tight timeline to conduct the Bab al-Mandeb operation because, for it to yield optimal results for the Houthis and Iran, it needed to happen ahead of the US midterms, so that it could be used as leverage in Iran-US negotiations,” El Eryani told The New Arab.
These developments illustrate how multiple theatres can be exploited simultaneously, through allied groups, with far-reaching economic and security repercussions.
Previously relatively shielded from the direct effects of the Iran war, Egypt now faces growing challenges from escalating tensions in the Red Sea. Cairo has thus far avoided isolating or antagonising any regional players.
This caution is reinforced by the legacy of Egypt’s 1960s intervention in Yemen, which cost the lives of more than 10,000 Egyptian soldiers and shaped a longstanding preference for diplomatic engagement and close coordination with regional partners over direct military intervention.
Egypt is likely to remain aligned with regional partners, providing political and potentially targeted military support, as it did through naval participation in the 2015 Operation Decisive Storm and through its membership in the Saudi-led Multinational Maritime Defence Alliance, established earlier this year to strengthen maritime security and protect international shipping and energy routes in the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandeb, and Gulf of Aden.
“But the pressure to act is being applied from many directions, and the real risk is that Egypt accidentally becomes entrapped by the escalatory logic of the conflict more generally,” said Brahimi.
The limits of regional alliances
The Houthis’ attacks on Saudi Arabia marked the first real test of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, struck last month between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan. The test revealed the enduring challenges of activating joint regional defence frameworks.
While signatories mobilised rhetorically in response to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, whether that translates into a coordinated joint response remains to be seen.
Egypt remains outside the framework, but this challenging landscape will likely further complicate Cairo’s prospective role in joint defence frameworks, particularly Article 5-style agreements that create commitments to direct intervention.
Any decision to intervene would require caution. Cairo is navigating the Red Sea on two simultaneous fronts, as an economic lifeline and a strategic theatre in which competing regional interests intersect. This creates significant constraints on the scope of direct Egyptian involvement.
These dynamics leave Egypt with a narrow set of options. Further escalation in the Red Sea would expose the Egyptian economy to direct economic and security risks, but the costs of direct intervention remain high.
Cairo is therefore likely to continue relying on its diplomatic channels, intelligence-sharing networks, and naval capabilities while closely monitoring developments.
Ultimately, Egypt’s strategy will be shaped by how far the Houthis and the wider Iran war expand, and how directly the conflict spills over into Egypt’s strategic interests.
Hana Elshehaby is a Senior Research Assistant for the Middle East Council on Global Affairs. She is also a Non-Resident Fellow at the Institute for Middle East Options

The Pardon of Elor Azaria: Killing, maiming, and culpability in the Israeli law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:27:58 UTC
01:27:58 KST

Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s recent decision to pardon a former Israeli soldier who summarily executed an incapacitated Palestinian a decade ago is more than a gesture toward one individual, and it is not an innocent attempt to “heal the divisions” between Israelis surrounding a case that convulsed Israeli society a decade ago. It is a political act that continues a long tradition of legitimizing the killing of Palestinians. The pardon does more than clear the remaining stain from the soldier’s record. It once again blurs the line between an unlawful killing and conduct that the state is prepared first to tolerate, then to justify, and ultimately to absolve and thereby implicitly condone.
In March 2016, Elor Azaria, then an Israeli soldier, shot Abdel Fattah al-Sharif in the head as he lay wounded and unarmed on the ground in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank. The shooting was filmed, and the scene was widely circulated. An Israeli military court convicted Azaria of manslaughter. His sentence—an astonishingly lenient eighteen months in prison—was subsequently reduced, and he was released after serving two-thirds of it. He later declared that he would do exactly the same thing again. Nevertheless, Herzog has decided to pardon him.
The president’s position carries considerable public weight. In a 2017 Peace Index poll, 64 percent of Jewish Israelis supported a pardon for Azaria, reflecting the broad consensus that once a person is defined as a mehabel, they forfeit their right to live. Yet in a subsequent survey, when respondents were asked whether they agreed with President Reuven Rivlin’s decision to reject Azaria’s pardon request, only 50 percent opposed his decision.
Therefore, in the current public climate, the Herzog’s message to present and future soldiers could hardly be clearer: even if they are filmed killing a Palestinian who no longer poses a threat, and even if they are convicted, the political system may ultimately erase the stigma attached to their actions.
Incidents of this kind should not be understood as momentary deviations from the Israeli state’s norms. The pardon forms part of a long history that began with leniency toward those who perpetrated massacres during Israel’s establishment in 1948 and the accompanying mass expulsion of Palestinians. It continued in the years that followed, when Israel pursued an unofficial policy of shooting Palestinian refugees who attempted to return to their homes, their land, or the property they had left behind. This unofficial open-fire policy turned the new border into a lethal instrument for making the results of the expulsion permanent.
Even when Jews were convicted of killing Arabs, the state knew how to respond with understanding. Israeli presidents Chaim Weizmann, Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, Yitzhak Navon, and Chaim Herzog (the current president’s father) granted pardons or reduced the sentences of Israeli soldiers and police who had killed Arabs. Each case was explained by reference to its supposedly exceptional circumstances: prevailing security tensions, the defendant’s personal history, his service to the state, the passage of time, or the need for reconciliation. Yet the accumulation of such cases reveals a pattern. The judicial process ostensibly draws a moral boundary, while the power of pardon retroactively strips the crossing of that boundary of its full significance.
The pardons, reduced sentences, and failures to prosecute associated with the perpetrators of the 1956 Kafr Qasim massacre, members of the Jewish Underground in the 1980s, and the policemen who killed a dozen Palestinian citizens of Israel in October 2000 all belong to the same pattern—a pattern that prepared the ground for the genocide that has unfolded since October 2023.
The killing of Palestinians has never been separate from their dispossession. It was one of the means through which dispossession became possible and, later, one of the tools through which it was maintained. A territory cannot be emptied of its inhabitants, its expelled population prevented from returning, its land confiscated, and another population settled in its place without the continuing threat of violence. Not every Palestinian must be killed for violence to serve its purpose. It is enough for the possibility of being killed to remain palpable—and for Palestinians to know that their lives are exposed and that those who kill them are unlikely to face serious punishment.
From this perspective, the pardon of Azaria complements the enduring Zionist aspiration to reduce the Palestinian presence in the land as much as possible. Herzog signals to soldiers on the ground that killing a Palestinian need not permanently stain their futures. There may be a trial and perhaps even a short prison term, but ultimately the state will know how to welcome them back into its embrace. The pardon transforms what is presented as an aberration into part of the state’s moral order. The “civilized” language of the pardon presents the erasure of responsibility as a humanitarian gesture while making the person who was killed disappear. Al-Sharif vanishes from the story, while the killer’s future, feelings, and rehabilitation become the focus of concern.
The decision also has an ethnic and class dimension that should not be ignored. Azaria, the son of a Mizrahi family from the working-class city of Ramla, carried out the killing on the ground. Herzog, a descendant of a prominent Ashkenazi family of European origin and a former partner in one of Israel’s most powerful law firms, now legitimizes Azaria’s act in the decorous language of the establishment. One man pulled the trigger; the other speaks of reconciliation, rehabilitation, the passage of time, and mercy.
This does not mean that Azaria is a victim who bears no responsibility. It means that a social division of labor is at work. Members of the lower classes are sent to perform the work of policing and occupation, which necessarily entails sporadic killing, while the legal and political elite translates the consequences into clean, respectable language.
This division of labor enables Israel’s liberal center to distinguish itself publicly from the crude rhetoric of the far right while still legitimizing the results of its actions. Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s far-right national security minister, can openly turn Azaria into a hero. Herzog has no need for such rhetoric. The “civilized” language of the pardon is, in fact, more effective: it presents the erasure of responsibility as a humanitarian gesture while making the person who was killed disappear. Al-Sharif vanishes from the story, while the killer’s future, feelings, and rehabilitation become the focus of concern.
The pardon therefore tells us not only how Israel treats one soldier, but also how it understands the relationship between Jews and Palestinians. A Palestinian life may be taken, and after enough time has passed, even the conviction for taking that life may be erased. This is how the imagination of erasure operates: first the person is erased from the landscape, and then responsibility for that erasure is itself erased.
Herzog’s decision is not a belated conclusion to the Azaria affair. It is another link in a historical chain connecting the shooting of refugees who tried to return home, pardons for Jews who have killed Arabs since 1948, and the continuing effort to make the land less Palestinian.

Sweden’s newly elected parliament formally opened in Stockholm on Tuesday, marking the start of the 2026-2027 parliamentary year as parties continued efforts to form a government following the election.
King Carl XVI Gustaf declared the Riksdag open at the speaker’s request during a ceremony attended by members of the royal family, the prime minister and parliamentary officials, according to public broadcaster SVT. The ceremony followed a service at Stockholm’s Storkyrkan church.

Disagreements over potential coalition partners remain a central obstacle. Centre Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist reiterated that her party would not join a government including the Left Party, citing differences over economic policy.
Andersson urged parties to reconsider their positions and compromise, while Left Party leader Nooshi Dadgostar said the Centre Party needed to decide which political bloc it would support. Green Party leader Amanda Lind called for the parties involved in a potential center-left coalition to meet.
On the other side, Sweden Democrats leader Jimmie Akesson maintained that his party would demand ministerial posts in any government it supports. Christian Democrats leader Ebba Busch called for votes on prime ministerial candidates to help move the process forward.

Nuclear weapons in space would break law, says Britain
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:26:51 BST
01:26:51 KST

Orbital weapons of both kinds pose a growing threat to the space-based services Britain and its allies depend on, and any attempt to put nuclear weapons in orbit would be highly destabilising and contrary to international law, the Ministry of Defence stated in a written answer.
Lord Coaker, Minister of State at the department, was answering Baroness Bennett of Manor Castle, the Green Party peer, who asked what assessment the government had made of the danger of orbital weapons, kinetic and otherwise, following what she described as the disclosure by the United States of its aggressive space capacity, and what steps ministers plan to take to prevent a new arms race in space.
The minister replied: “The Government recognises that orbital weapons, both kinetic and non-kinetic, pose a growing threat to critical space-based services vital to the UK and its allies. We are concerned by reports of efforts to deploy nuclear weapons in space, which would be highly destabilising and contrary to international law. The Government supports a behaviour-based, risk-reduction approach to maintain a safe, secure and sustainable space environment. We work closely with international partners to promote responsible conduct, uphold existing legal frameworks and prevent escalation.”
He continued: “Through the UK Space Strategy and Defence Investment Plan, the Government is investing in the resilience and protection of UK and allied space assets to ensure freedom of action in space and safeguard long-term sustainability. We remain committed to international cooperation and the development of norms that reduce risk and preserve stability in this increasingly contested domain.”
The same minister had declined a week earlier to say whether Britain itself has anything in orbit. Lord Lee of Trafford, the Liberal Democrat peer, asked on 22 September whether the United Kingdom has any weapons in space, and if not whether there are plans to deploy any.
Coaker replied: “We do not comment on specific Defence capabilities, including whether such capabilities are deployed in space, nor on future operational plans where doing so would risk undermining national security. We do however recognise that space is important to military operations and is becoming more congested, contested, and competitive. The Government is committed to collaborating with allies and partners to promote internationally agreed norms, avoid unintentional escalation and conflict, and ensure that space remains open, safe, and sustainable.”
He added: “In addition, the UK’s national security depends on freedom of action in space, including the ability to protect UK and allied space assets. As set out in the UK Space Strategy and Defence Investment Plan, the Government is investing in capabilities to strengthen resilience and support the protection of UK interests in space, while continuing to operate responsibly and in accordance with international law.”

Hamas, Islamic Jihad and a powerful ex-Fatah official form an unlikely electoral alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:26:24 UTC
01:26:24 KST

Hamas and the allied Palestinian Islamic Jihad group have agreed to form an unlikely electoral coalition with a former top Fatah official who has close ties to the United Arab Emirates, Israel's closest ally in the Middle East, Palestinian officials told The Associated Press.
The alliance could be well positioned to threaten the dominance of President Mahmoud Abbas' Fatah party over the internationally recognized Palestinian Authority — but only if the first national elections in 20 years actually happen, which is very much in doubt.
Abbas has said parliamentary elections will be held Nov. 28 in Gaza and the West Bank. But he has repeatedly delayed elections, most recently in 2021, when Fatah appeared headed for defeat. When Hamas won the last elections, in 2006, Israel and Western countries boycotted its government, fueling months of unrest that led to its takeover of Gaza the following year.
Islamic Jihad Deputy Secretary General Mohammed al-Hindi confirmed the formation of the electoral alliance in a rare interview with The Associated Press in Istanbul on Monday. He said it would support “a unified national list” that could be made up of independent figures rather than members of the groups.
It would include a bloc led by Mohammed Dahlan, a former Fatah security chief who was exiled in 2010 after a bitter falling-out with Abbas and had previously been driven from Gaza by Hamas. Dahlan has since cultivated close ties with the UAE, where he serves as an adviser to the ruler.
The UAE was the driving force behind the 2020 Abraham Accords, and Dahlan himself has extensive contacts with U.S. and Israeli officials, making him an unlikely ally for Hamas and Islamic Jihad, which have fought Israel for decades. The alliance appears to be rooted in shared frustration with Abbas.
New alliance takes aim at Abbas
Abbas’ leadership of the Palestinian Authority, which has limited autonomy over parts of the West Bank, is deeply unpopular among Palestinians who see it as autocratic, corrupt and ineffective.
The 90-year-old Abbas has clung to power since his own mandate expired in 2009, while Hamas continues to control parts of Gaza three years into a brutal war with Israel.
Dimitri Diliani, spokesperson for Dahlan’s Reformist Democratic Faction, confirmed the electoral alliance in a statement that took a swipe at Abbas’ leadership, saying “the Palestinian Authority has failed Gaza and the Palestinian people everywhere.”
He said several other Palestinian groups are also part of the alliance and there are efforts to bring “all other factions and independent professionals into uniting around one national rebuilding program.”
Hamas said in August that Dahlan and Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya had met in Cairo and discussed ways to “end the monopolization of national decision-making and formulate a comprehensive national strategy.”
Hamas and Fatah officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Past attempts at Palestinian unity have failed
Al-Hindi said the decision to launch the alliance came after attempts to bring together all factions in a “dialogue for internal consensus on the overall Palestinian issue” failed to bear fruit.
There have been multiple attempts over the years to bring Hamas and Islamic Jihad into the Fatah-led Palestine Liberation Organization, the highest body representing the Palestinian cause internationally, but all have foundered.
A main sticking point has been the PLO’s recognition of Israel. While Hamas officials have said they are willing to accept a Palestinian state in Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem — territories Israel seized in the 1967 Six-Day War — they have stopped short of recognizing Israel, while Islamic Jihad takes a harder line.
Both are considered terrorist groups by the U.S. and other Western countries, which have voiced support for Palestinian democracy over the years while rejecting any government that includes Hamas. Fatah and Hamas are the most popular factions by far, though many Palestinians are frustrated with both.
Al-Hindi said his group — which has historically not participated in elections run by the Palestinian Authority — will not directly run any candidates but will “support a national list that is agreed upon.”
Violence is ongoing in Gaza and the West Bank
The scheduled elections come at a precarious time.
In the West Bank, attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians have intensified. In Gaza, a ceasefire that took effect in October 2025 has halted the heaviest fighting, but the Israeli military has seized control of more of the territory and continued strikes, which it says are in response to threats.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the start of the war, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. Hamas started the war with its Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, in which terrorists killed some 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and took 251 others hostage.
Under a U.S. plan for implementing the ceasefire, armed Palestinian groups were to give up their weapons while Israel would withdraw from the enclave. Al-Hindi said his group, along with Hamas, had agreed to the plan and blamed Israel for blocking it.
“When Israel’s obligations in the first phase (of the agreement) are achieved, we will move on to talk about the second phase, which includes the issue of weapons,” al-Hindi said.
Islamic Jihad official says Oct. 7 came as a surprise
Islamic Jihad took part in the Oct. 7 attack and held Israeli hostages, but al-Hindi said the group was not involved in planning the attack or given forewarning by Hamas. The night before, he said, Islamic Jihad members held a commemoration of the group’s founding and many stayed up late.
“In the morning, we were surprised by the media reporting what happened, but as a resistance movement, we were quick to participate in these confrontations,” he said.
With tens of thousands dead, Gaza largely reduced to rubble and most of its population displaced, al-Hindi acknowledged that “some voices began to express doubts and say, ’What has the resistance brought down on the Palestinian people?'”
But he insisted that the Oct. 7 attack had been necessary to prevent the plight of the Palestinians from being completely sidelined as the UAE and other Arab countries had moved to normalize relations with Israel.
He also acknowledged that Iran — long a main source of support for Palestinian terrorist groups — is now preoccupied by the ongoing war and a U.S. economic blockade. But al-Hindi said his group will continue with or without Iranian support.
“As long as there is no political horizon to solve the Palestinian issue and attempts continue to flee from the Palestinian cause in the region, the future will be resistance,” he said.

Saudi Arabia restarts Yanbu oil loadings after pipeline resumes operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:25:08 UTC
01:25:08 KST

Saudi Arabia resumes oil tanker loadings from its Red Sea port of Yanbu after restarting operations on the East-West pipeline, according to trade sources and shipping data.
Saudi Aramco notified customers on Monday of its October loading schedule from Yanbu, an Asian refining source said. The refiner also loaded a cargo from the port late last week.
Yanbu loadings were halted earlier this month after a drone attack on the pipeline, which Saudi Arabia blamed on Iraqi militias. The pipeline was shut on September 11, before operations resumed last Tuesday.
Crude flows recover
Satellite imagery from the European Space Agency also indicated that oil loading had resumed at Yanbu and the nearby Al Muajjiz terminal.
“ESA satellite imagery captured over the Red Sea on September 27 shows Saudi Arabia loading nearly 10 million barrels of crude oil at Yanbu and Al Muajjiz,” vessel-tracking firm TankerTrackers.com said on X.
The company also identified refined-product loadings and 40 tankers in the area.
Two trade sources estimated crude loadings from Yanbu at about 2 million barrels per day since last week.
Pipeline throughput is currently about 2 million barrels per day, according to an industry source, compared with its 7 million barrels per day capacity.
Kpler expects flows to rise to 3-4 million barrels per day in the coming days, although a return to the pre-attack rate of about 5.5 million barrels per day could take another month.
Kpler said crude inventories at the Yanbu terminal rose by about 1 million barrels on September 22, the first increase since the attack.
Middle East exports show signs of recovery
The restart of Yanbu loadings adds to signs of increasing Middle East oil shipments following a recovery in exports through the Strait of Hormuz.
Crude loadings at Egypt’s Sidi Kerir terminal also resumed on September 22 after a 10-day halt, although tankers remain queued offshore as restrictions continue to limit access for much of the commercial fleet, Kpler said.

EU tells Ukraine to focus on reforms to unlock funding, as Kyiv faces mammoth budget hole

- Ukraine faces a US$20 billion deficit this year and seeks faster EU payments, but EU demands clearer explanations and reform progress before releasing more funds.
- EU explores options like advancing loan payments and tapping frozen Russian assets, while calling on other allies to help cover Ukraine's financing gap for a stable state.
AI generated
BRUSSELS - The European Union told Ukraine on Sept 29 to continue reforms in order to unlock billions in funding this year, as Kyiv warns it faces a mammoth budget shortfall.
Brussels is currently paying out instalments of a €90 billion (S$130 billion) loan that is meant to help the war-torn country keep afloat to the end of 2027.
But Ukraine’s government has said it still needs some US$20 billion (S$25.5 billion) to cover a yawning deficit this year and has urged the EU to speed up the payments.
EU officials say they are looking into options for Ukraine’s funding needs.
But they say Kyiv has not fully explained its figures for the shortfall and should first focus on pushing through reforms to unlock funds already on the table for this year.
“Our message to our Ukrainian friends is clear – deliver the agreed reforms, so we can continue supporting you financially,” EU enlargement commissioner Marta Kos told a gathering of donors with Kyiv in Brussels.
“Reforms matter. They build trust. They give Ukraine’s partners confidence that our support is being used effectively.”
In a letter to Ukraine’s parliamentary speaker this month, Brussels said, “over 20 billion euros in EU financial assistance remains available” for Kyiv before the end of 2026 provided that it carries out reforms.
Black hole
Coming against a backdrop of a string of high-profile corruption scandals in Ukraine, diplomats in Brussels say there is a greater scrutiny of the demands from Kyiv.
They insist there is still a firm willingness to ensure there is enough money to see the country through a tough winter.
In an interview over the weekend, Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky told local media the deficit was US$27 billion, but Kyiv would find US$7 billion from savings domestically.
One option for the 27-nation EU to plug the black hole could be bringing forward more payments under the €90 billion loan.
But that could cause the fund to run dry sooner than expected before the end of 2027.
With expectations growing that Ukraine will eventually need more funds, several EU countries have revived calls to tap frozen Russian central bank assets.
So far, there has not been real progress on the issue as Belgium, where the bulk of the money is held, is still firmly opposed.
The EU, meanwhile, is also trying to push other supporters of Ukraine such as Britain, Canada and Japan to also help plug the financing gap.
“The coming months will require action from all of us. We need to give Ukraine the predictability it needs to keep the state functioning,” Kos told the donor meeting.
“We are delivering our share.” AFP

The cabinet of Madhya Pradesh has sanctioned horizontal reservations for ex-Agniveers aiming to join various uniformed services, such as the police force.
The Madhya Pradesh cabinet has approved a 20% horizontal reservation for former Agniveers in several uniformed services and cleared schemes and projects worth more than Rs 24,500 crore, the state government said.The decisions were taken at a cabinet meeting chaired by chief minister Mohan Yadav at the state secretariat.The reservation will apply to recruitment for police constables, the Special Armed Force, jail guards, forest guards and excise constables. It will be available across the General Category and reserved categories, including Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes.Under the approved policy, former Agniveers will receive 20% horizontal reservation in police constable recruitment, while Home Guards will get 10% and ex-servicemen 5%.For the Special Armed Force, the allocation will be 20% for former Agniveers, 10% for Home Guards and 5% for ex-servicemen. In jail guard recruitment, 20% will be reserved for former Agniveers, 15% for Home Guards and 5% for ex-servicemen.The same allocation will apply to forest guard recruitment. For excise constable posts, former Agniveers will receive 20% reservation, Home Guards 10% and ex-servicemen 5%.The cabinet approved Rs 5,329.17 crore for payment of honorariums to around 76,000 guest teachers over five years, from 2026-27 to 2030-31.
It also cleared Rs 348.7 crore for school uniforms and Rs 3,245.8 crore for health centres and drug control, according to the official cited by PTI.The cabinet approved the construction of the Damoh-Katni four-lane road at a cost of Rs 4,470.30 crore and allocated Rs 3,580.22 crore to the Rural Development Fund.It also approved the continuation of major irrigation projects in Banda, Datia, Neemuch and Sagar, along with the Kanh Diversion Project in Ujjain, ahead of the Simhastha Kumbh Mela in 2028.The Rs 348.7-crore allocation for school uniforms will be transferred directly to the bank accounts of parents or students enrolled in government schools from Classes 1 to 8 during the 2026-27 academic year.The government also plans to use guest teachers to fill vacant posts in government primary, secondary, high and higher secondary schools. Madhya Pradesh currently has around 76,000 guest teachers, the official said.
Under the Centre’s Agnipath scheme, Agniveers serve in the armed forces for four years, including six months of training. The scheme provides for retaining 25% of each batch in the Army, Navy and Air Force, while the remaining personnel are released after their tenure.

Syrian city of Douma bans grooms from their own wedding parties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:23:06 UTC
01:23:06 KST

Breadcrumb
Syrian city of Douma bans grooms from their own wedding parties
Grooms in the Syrian city of Douma have been banned from entering women-only wedding celebrations, with local authorities threatening legal action against men who turn up at their own brides' parties.
The decision by Douma City Council in the Damascus countryside prohibits "the groom entering women's celebrations in the halls of Douma city", according to a copy of the order published by the council.
It means that even the groom himself cannot enter the women's section of a wedding celebration.
In socially conservative parts of Syria, weddings are usually segregated by gender. However at the end of the women's party the groom usually enters to meet the bride and take her home.
The council warned that anyone violating the ban could face legal measures, although it did not specify what those measures would be or what penalties could be imposed.
The order was approved during a council meeting on 22 September but emerged publicly on Monday, prompting debate over why a local authority was regulating who could attend private wedding celebrations.
The council has not publicly explained the reason for the ban or when it will come into force.
Syrian fact-checking platform Ta'akkad said it contacted the council asking about the reasoning behind the decision, its legal basis, how broadly it would be applied and what action could be taken against those breaking the rule.
It had received no response by the time its report was published.
The decision has also prompted questions over whether local councils have the legal authority to regulate social customs in this way.
The council cited Syria's Local Administration Law No. 107 of 2011, but critics have questioned whether the powers it grants local authorities extend to imposing restrictions on private social practices.
The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said the decision had divided opinion, with supporters viewing it as a way of organising weddings and protecting the privacy of women-only celebrations.
Opponents, however, questioned both the council's authority to impose the restriction and how it could threaten legal measures without clearly defining either the offence or the punishment.
The Douma decision is not the first attempt by a local authority in the Damascus countryside to regulate men's attendance at women-only weddings.
In May, the local council in Badda issued a broader order banning men from entering women's wedding halls, including the groom and male relatives of both the bride and groom.
Unlike the Douma decision, the Badda order explicitly invoked religious considerations, saying the restriction was intended to prevent mixing between men and women.
The latest controversy comes amid a wider debate in post-Assad Syria over the extent to which local authorities should be able to regulate social behaviour and customs.
For grooms planning weddings in Douma, however, the immediate implication is simpler: when the women's party begins, even the man getting married may have to wait outside.

Former prime minister Naftali Bennett warned on Tuesday that the IDF would collapse due to a lack of manpower if haredim (ultra-Orthodox) are not drafted during the next government’s term, following the October elections.

He made the remarks at Hostages Square in Tel Aviv, where families of October 7 victims built a sukkah for the holiday called the “Sukkah of Failure.”
Bennett’s B’Yachad party is one of the leading parties in the opposition bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu in the October elections.
“I am here today at Hostages Square, which symbolizes the terrible failure of the October 7 government, which has yet to be investigated. Everyone who was part of this failure must immediately step down,” Bennett said.
Bennett says he will form an October 7 commission of inquiry in the next government
The former prime minister has vowed that, if he is part of the next government, he will seek to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the government’s failures surrounding October 7.“Everyone is focused on the warnings Netanyahu ignored before October 7, but when the next disaster happens, no one will be able to say they were not warned about this one.”
“The IDF is on the verge of collapse. The chief of staff has raised 10 red flags, saying the IDF is short 20,000 combat soldiers, but Netanyahu is ignoring them and dismantling the IDF,” he added.
Bennett said that he has gone into the field and spoken with officers and soldiers who told him that the shortage of combat soldiers “is already costing us soldiers’ lives.”
“They say soldiers are being wounded and killed by drones because there are not enough observers and snipers to protect them. The long reserve-duty rotations are wearing down the soldiers’ operational readiness, and that too is costing us casualties,” he noted.
Bennett also said that during combat, “they are forced to abandon positions they have already captured because there is no one to hold the ground, and then they have to recapture them at the cost of bloodshed.”
“Voting for the draft-evasion coalition is a direct vote against IDF soldiers and against those who serve.
Bennett: 'We will enlist everyone'
“We will enlist everyone, stop funding draft evaders, and strengthen the IDF,” he added.
The haredi parties – Shas and United Torah Judaism – have encouraged Netanayhu’s coalition to advance legislation that critics argue would not increase haredi enlistment.
The haredi parties boycotted coalition voting during the government’s term, stating that they would not cooperate with Netanyahu’s coalition until there was advancement with the contentious legislation they had been pushing for.
The IDF has repeatedly warned of an urgent manpower shortage after three years of war.
In March, IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir said the IDF could soon collapse if no solution was found for the manpower shortage.
Bennett has drawn a red line against forming a coalition with the haredi parties, and called for reversing contentious haredi-backed legislation passed by the outgoing government.
He has also taken a hardline stance toward haredi conscription to the IDF, as his party’s platform seeks to cut all state funding for anyone evading military service and bar any exemptions from the IDF.

Campaign centers on five commitments
The campaign centers on five core commitments: affirming that Jewish safety, including the safety of Zionist Jews, is nonnegotiable; recognizing the right of Jews to define their own identities; supporting Jewish sovereignty in Israel; welcoming the full participation of Jews in American political life; and providing an affirmative vision for a better future in the Middle East.

Nonnegotiable Michigan leaders are also asking El-Sayed to publicly reject and walk back rhetoric that stigmatizes and incites violence against Jewish Michiganders, that invokes longstanding anti-Jewish tropes and stereotypes, casts Jewish political participation as nefarious or corrupt, or scapegoats Israel and Jews for the suffering of Michiganders.”

"It would help reintegrate Russia into the global economy and broaden Trump's talks with the Kremlin beyond the intractable war in Ukraine, which his envoys have failed to end after more than a year of diplomacy...create a path for the US to sign lucrative deals involving Russian oil, diesel, rare earth minerals, and other commodities, [and] as a bonus, the release of prisoners on humanitarian grounds could bolster Trump's case for his long-coveted Nobel Peace Prize," the report said.
However, this approach "is likely to outrage the Ukrainians, Europeans, and even many of Trump's allies on Capitol Hill," the report noted.
This is because "any potential business deal between the US and Russia would risk funneling money to the Russian military even as it continues to terrorize Ukraine and threatens a wider war against US allies in Europe," the report added.
Earlier in September, Trump signed a law co-authored by the late senator Lindsey Graham that authorized the president to "impose severe sanctions on Russia and its trading partners," the report highlighted.
Coale used his successful experience negotiating with Belarus, Lukashenko
Coale, who proposed the strategy, was formerly Trump's envoy to Belarus, Russia's closest ally. During his talks with Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, Cole achieved the release of hundreds of political prisoners from Belarusian jails in exchange for easing sanctions and promising to buy potash fertilizer.
Trump has therefore given Cole his "blessing" to do the same with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said during his visit to New York for the United Nations General Assembly that he would try his best to "block" any attempt to lift sanctions on Russia before the war ends, but "it's difficult."
However, Trump's envoys do not see a way to conduct business with Russia without first achieving at least a partial ceasefire in Ukraine, one of the negotiators told The Atlantic.
"Economic ties usually result in normality," Coale told The Atlantic, adding that, in his view, such deals could help bring the Ukraine-Russia War closer to a ceasefire by easing tensions between Russia and the West.
The White House has nominated Coale to serve as the special presidential envoy for hostage affairs, with full ambassadorial rank and privileges, pending Senate confirmation, the report noted.
"The president and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we'll ultimately get a peace deal done," a White House official said when asked to comment on Coale's mission.
According to the report, Coale plans to coordinate his efforts with Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff, who has met with Putin at least seven times since the start of the war.
Most recently, on September 5, Putin expressed gratitude to Witkoff and Jared Kushner for their attempts to negotiate a peace deal following meetings in the Kremlin.
"I'd like to tell you that we find it comfortable to work with you, and, of course, we have a very high level of trust doing this work," Putin told them.

As US leaves Iraq definetly, Baghdad sees withdrawal as 'symbol of sovereignty' - analysis

01:15:32 KST

ISIS invaded Iraq in the summer of 2014. It swept across the Sunni cities of Iraq, preying on the anger among locals who resented then-premier Nouri al-Maliki. Maliki was close to Iran and was thought to be suppressing Sunni Arabs.
The Islamic State conquered the city of Mosul in June 2014, and in August, it began massacring the Yazidis in what would become an eventual genocide. It went on to decimate Iraq’s military. Thousands of military vehicles, many of which were supplied by the US, fell into ISIS’s hands.
Iraq asked the United States for help. The US left Iraq in 2011, but the Obama administration nonetheless wanted to help. Thus, three years after its departure, the US returned to Iraq, this time to join the fight against ISIS.
Today, over a decade later, the US is leaving Iraq again. The Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported: “September 30 represents a significant historic milestone in Iraq’s path toward completing its national sovereignty and strengthening the independence of its political and economic decision-making.”
Iraq is treating this like a victory over America. Instead of thanking the US for its help, Iraq is treating the US like it’s the problem, not ISIS.
INA noted: “The importance of this step extends beyond its security and political dimensions to highlight the state’s ability to capitalize on this transition to improve the economic environment.
“Experts and lawmakers see the success of this phase as dependent on the ability to uphold the rule of law, provide a secure environment for investors, and undertake structural reforms that strengthen the confidence of domestic and foreign capital in the Iraqi economy.”
Why does Iraq think the US leaving is good?
Why is it like this? The US assisted, trained, and equipped the Iraqi army. US soldiers fought ISIS and helped Iraq recover. Only just recently, Iraq’s prime minister was in the US, seeking energy investments and other deals. So why is the coalition deemed the problem, instead of getting the applause it deserves?
Iraqi Parliament member Nasser Turki told INA that “September 30 represents an important historic day, marking the withdrawal of all foreign forces from Iraq, and this will have a positive impact on attracting foreign investment opportunities.” He added that “the state’s strategic plans will focus on working in the service, economic, industrial, and agricultural sectors while taking into account the interests of its people.”
The Security Media Cell, a confab of Iraqi security news that is also official and run by Lt.-Gen. Saad Maan, said: “Sovereignty Day represents a new chapter in Iraq’s relations with the countries of the world, based on shared interests in accordance with Iraq’s vision and the interests of its people. It reflects the ability of the state and its institutions to assume responsibility for protecting the country and confronting security challenges, thereby strengthening citizens’ confidence in the security and military institutions.”
Meanwhile, The National in the United Arab Emirates noted that the US and Iraq signed a deal to transfer diplomatic and logistical facilities at Baghdad airport to the Iraqis. This site had often been targeted by Iran and Iran-backed militias. In fact, Iran has attacked Iraq more than 1,000 times, primarily targeting the Kurdistan Region. Iranian-backed militias in Iraq executed over 600 attacks against other groups.
Iran's influence in Iraq also impacts withdrawal
Another angle to America’s withdrawal from Iraq is Iran. Iran still believes the US has far too much influence in Iraq. Iran wants the US away from Iraq and the Gulf, and will view its departure as a win.
Rudaw Media reported that Hossein Shariatmadari, representative of Iran’s supreme leader, accused Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi on Tuesday of accepting and implementing US sanctions against Iranian airlines.
Rudaw also noted that the “Kurdistan region’s Peshmerga Affairs Ministry on Monday warned that the planned withdrawal of US-led coalition forces from Iraq on September 30 comes at a ‘sensitive time,’ as Baghdad and Washington proceed with a joint agreement to end the military mission in the country, including operations in the Kurdistan region.”
Meanwhile, Iranian-backed militias have hinted at their increased role. This comes as they’re supposed to be disarming. However, Hezbollah “warned Monday that it would shoot down ‘hostile’ aircraft violating Iraqi airspace after the US-led Global Coalition completes its military withdrawal from Iraq this week,” Rudaw said.
Currently, the Kurdistan Region appears to lack some of the defenses the coalition had provided in the past. It’s still unclear how many of their air defenses remain. In the past, Baghdad has refused to provide the Kurdistan Region with air defenses. Thus, the US’s departure has left many Kurds feeling concerned.
North Press media wrote that “Kurdish leader Masoud Barzani warned of the repercussions and dangers of the withdrawal of US and international coalition forces from Iraq, according to Kurdistan 24.”
It remains to be seen what comes next. However, Iraq depicting the US’s withdrawal as a victory points to its failure to value America’s contributions. It is unclear what Iraq will do after the US has left its shores, and when – or how – Iran could take advantage of it.

From ruins, regrowth: Artists answer October 7 with humanity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:15:18 UTC
01:15:18 KST

An exhibition at the Bible Lands Museum, born of a Jerusalem Biennale open call, gathers artists who had to find their way back to the studio after the massacre, and asks whether a people, like a tree, can grow again.
Six artists have contributed their own views of life, death and humanity to mark the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre. Curated by Yael Boverman-Attas, the exhibition "As Humankind," which opened to the public on September 24, has brought life back to the Bible Lands Museum's garden in Jerusalem.
In the weeks after October 7, some of the artists now showing in the garden could not make anything at all.
"It just shut your mouth," Galit Shvo, one of the featured artists, told The Jerusalem Post. "I couldn't work."
The exhibition took shape during the Israel-Hamas War, when Dr. Risa Levitt, the museum's executive director and acting chief curator, approached Boverman-Attas, an artist, designer, curator and researcher, with a vision for a show in its garden, "which is so beautiful," the curator told the Post. A call for works for the Jerusalem Biennale followed. Boverman-Attas gathered a group of artists, applied, and was accepted.
"Since then, it was a kind of journey that we went through," the curator said. "I think the war actually brought a new way to look at art."
Some of the pieces were made years before the war and are now being seen from a new perspective, while others were built on site. According to the curator, a single idea connects them.
"In every piece of art that I chose for this exhibition, I could see the growth," she said. "We were searching for an optimistic message. We were searching for hope, and we were searching for regrowth."
The title "As Humankind" comes from a poem and a verse in Deuteronomy that compares humankind to a tree, a comparison that holds "in many senses," Boverman-Attas said. "One of them is their ability to grow, to regrow after the disaster," she told the Post.
Trees cut from a single plate
Shvo's folded iron trees stand among the garden's plantings. The series grew out of four years of sketches and a fascination with branching.
"It's a process that started four years ago, in all kinds of sketches, and my interest in bifurcation and splitting," Shvo told the Post. "It's an algorithm that is mutual to trees, to growth, and also to a nuclear explosion, a chain reaction."
Asked what about October 7 had inspired the work, Shvo pushed back on the premise. "They didn't inspire me," she said. "The only thing I could do was work with children."
With the help of volunteers, Shvo cut small trees that the children folded, painted, and wrote on, "especially kids that were away from home." Only months later, when invitations to exhibit arrived, did she return to the studio and begin creating "other variations of splitting, of growing algorithms."
"It really took me a lot of time to find myself again in this horrible situation and start working," Shvo said.
Four rooms, a broken heart
Tel Aviv artist Sharon Pazner, a trained architect, built the exhibition's largest ruin out of the wreckage of her own studio.
The piece, Four Rooms, began with the footage of destroyed homes that emerged after October 7. "I thought I'd make a piece called Four Rooms, like the four rooms of our heart," she told the Post. "Like a broken heart and a broken house."
The material came from a crisis of faith in her own work. "I was so traumatized, as we all were, but I was thinking that to be an artist after such a tragedy was kind of absurd," she said. "It was kind of depressing, because I thought I could never create again."
Each brick in Four Rooms was cast individually in fresh concrete and embedded with fragments of earlier works she had come to see as irrelevant, along with small objects she had cast in her studio and pieces of broken industrial blocks.
"To overcome the pain and the feeling of art being irrelevant, first of all, I had to make my art relevant," Pazner told the Post. "My art couldn't be the same after the 7th of October."
For Boverman-Attas, the work reads as an archaeological site. The four-room plan echoes an ancient Israelite building form, while the bricks hold fragments of dolls and objects linked to Pazner's activism during the war. "If you take a very close look, it seems like they're all kind of crashed into the ruins," the curator said. "She's asking us to feel and to look at the details."
Reaching for the apple
Not every work in the garden was made in response to the war. Eva Avidar's figure straining toward an apple on a tree was made about a decade ago, as the artist tried to come to terms with "my new body, the new me."
The sculpture captures a single instant of desire. "I wanted to feel this extreme pleasure of sweetness in the mouth," Avidar told the Post, describing the moment when "the tree that was holding the apple disappears, and only the essence of the bite is the experience."
The curator saw something else in it after October 7. "I felt that she's really talking about the war, about how we all ache, how we all feel the pain and how we are all trying to achieve the fruit of Eden," Boverman-Attas said.
The figure's pose, she noted, is impossible. "If she bites the apple, it will fall. If she tries to hold it, she will lose her balance. And I felt that this is so much how we feel about the situation, so fragile, so on the edge, and so full of hope to try and make things better."
Relics for a distant future
Gabriel Klasmer, primarily an abstract painter, is showing a figurative sculpture made from an unlikely material: compressed shopping bags, bound with tape and wrapped in cling film.
"Living especially in Israel, you accumulate lots of plastic bags very quickly from all the shops," Klasmer said. "This is a very discarded material. But on the other end of it, it is a very highly sophisticated material."
The work, Klasmer said, touches "a very deep human aspect, but it's also a very political aspect."
Between life and death
Max Epstein carves with archaic tools: axes, knives and fire. For 17 years he has co-run a community animation studio where children and teenagers make films and develop "their own voices."
His newest work here, whose title translates roughly as Roadside, draws on the ancient Greek herm, a roadside marker topped with the head of a god, which the Romans later turned into portraits of a territory's owner.
"For me it was important to create a portrait of a man who is [suffering] from inside, physically and mentally," Epstein told the Post, "and to try to point to the border between the suffering and the silence before, and the silence after death."
"Art has no right to escape from the world," Epstein said. Most of the works in the garden, he added, are dealing with "the current period, which has a lot of pain."
Reflecting on what art means after October 7, Pazner offered an optimistic view. "I see this work as an optimistic work, first of all, because it exists, because I could make art again," she said. "But more importantly, I wanted to show that despite the many losses we have, they're still here with us. We haven't forgotten them, but we must continue."

‘New path’: UK’s Burnham promises huge expansion of public services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:13:04 UTC
01:13:04 KST

‘New path’: UK’s Burnham promises huge expansion of public services
UK prime minister tells his first Labour Party conference ‘fundamental rethink’ needed to set Britain on right course.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised to put the United Kingdom on a new path of equitable growth during his first Labour conference speech as leader of the country and party.
Covering a range of topics including healthcare, pensions, electoral reforms, affordable housing and publicly-owned utilities, Burnham on Tuesday said it was time for the UK to opt for drastic change and reject a slow and painful demise.
“Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time,” Burnham told delegates, adding that he was “ready to do things my predecessors wouldn’t”.
“I will make a break with the direction of the past 40 years and put Britain on a new path, build a new economy and a new politics. That is the case I make to you today,” he said.
Burnham, who replaced Keir Starmer as the UK prime minister in July, said there was a “sense of the powers-that-be pulling against the people, not with them”.
“More of the same isn’t good enough,” said the former mayor of Manchester, where the party conference was held. He added that it was time “to break the mould today”.
Social reforms
This year’s Labour Party conference brought together legislators and party members alongside trade unions and businesses in one place.
“This country isn’t where any of us would want it to be,” Burnham said.
Much of Burnham’s speech addressed the need for social reforms with a focus on caregivers and healthcare, including building a “National Care Service … free at the point of use”.
He said it will be “a person-centred, high-quality” service where “everyone contributes and everyone is covered” and care “is about people not profit”, does not erode savings and gives “proper recognition” to care workers.
There was also talk of adjusting the so-called “pension triple lock” that sets state pension rises. He said changes will be made by April 2030, after the next general election.
Burnham said low-income pensioners would not pay income tax in the current Parliament. The planned changes meant pensioners would receive annual rises to their state pension without additional care charges, “so that pensioners will always share in the rising prosperity of the nation”.
He also spoke on the need to make housing more affordable, confirming his party’s intention to make it easy for young people to own a home by reducing the deposit needed to buy property.
There was also mention of returning control of utilities, such as water and electricity, back to the public, by scrapping “[former Prime Minister] Margaret Thatcher’s ideological ban on public ownership of water companies”.
On electricity, Burnham announced a new publicly-owned “Great British Grid” that will “challenge the private sector operators” to “increase competition, drive down costs and speed up delivery”, and make it easier to connect to the electricity grid.
Russia, Iran ‘threats’
Burnham’s speech also focused on foreign policy issues, saying he will “stand up to” Russian and Iranian “threats”.
“I will be steadfast in my support for Ukraine and stand up to threats wherever they come from, whether Russia, Iran, or anywhere,” he said.
On Israel, the occupied West Bank and Gaza, Burnham praised his foreign secretary’s approach, since assuming office in July.
“We will be principled in our leadership in securing a two-state solution between Israel and Palestine, as [Foreign Secretary] Ed Miliband has done,” he said.
Al Jazeera’s Milena Veselinovic, who was listening to the British prime minister at the conference, said Burnham’s speech was laced with “a lot of fiery rhetoric”.
“Britain finds itself in a very dire position when it comes to finances,” said Veselinovic, adding that there is immense pressure on Burnham’s new government as it prepares to introduce its first budget at the end of October.
The UK annual consumer price inflation (CPI) reached 3.1 percent in the 12 months to August, ticking up from 2.9 percent in July, according to the Office of National Statistics.
Veselinovic said Burnham is aware he may have to “pay a political price for all the reforms he’s promising”, but that he also understands, “somebody has to rip out the plaster on that because the costs are too high”.
‘Remarkable speech’
Danny Sriskandarajah, the chief executive officer of New Economics Foundation, said Burnham delivered “a remarkable speech”.
“Andy Burnham has this knack to be able to come across as authentic, as genuine,” Sriskandarajah told Al Jazeera.
Burnham, Sriskandarajah said, “was tearful at moments”.
“He was honest about what challenges Britain faces. But he also generates a sense of hope which I think is much needed,” he said.
Sriskandarajah said the challenge for Burnham will be to fund the promises he made in the speech.
“All of these things that he wants to do will cost money, which means they’ll have to raise those resources somewhere,” he said.

Rail in today’s world – full of challenges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:12:26 UTC
01:12:26 KST

After years of Polish road hauliers dominating European markets, the time may have come for Polish rail companies to play an increasingly strong role in European logistics as well. We talk about the opportunities and challenges of today’s rail market with Marcin Witczak, President of the Management Board of Laude Smart Intermodal.
Can Polish rail companies make a stronger entry into the European freight market and, over time, play a role comparable to that of road transport firms? Which transport directions in Europe are the most promising? Where do we see bottlenecks?
Absolutely, yes. The European Union still allows several countries to effectively restrict market entry. That does not serve the markets, and the customer pays for it by buying a more expensive, lower-quality service. I am referring to Belgium and France, among others. For Poland to become a leader, it should have financial support from institutions such as PFR, BGK or ARP to fund the outlays needed to enter foreign markets. I am not only thinking of acquisitions. I also mean the purchase of rolling stock, licence fees and investment in our own terminals abroad.
For Laude Smart Intermodal, being a leader means above all delivering the most innovative solutions. Meeting that challenge requires enormous outlays. In rail, nothing can be done “at half the cost”. Every investment here means really big money, and the vast majority of rail companies cannot generate such funds on their own.
To sum up: as a country and as a logistics sector, we have the necessary potential, technical capacity and infrastructure in Poland. But to make a stronger push onto European rail routes, we need solid capital backing. And we are not talking about hundreds of millions here, but billions of zlotys. I am convinced, however, that this money would be sensibly invested.
In a word, can Europe’s railway lines take on more freight in the coming years?
Definitely. Rail infrastructure in the European Union is ready for it. As it is renovated and expanded, it will cope with more trains and more cargo. What is missing, both in Poland and in Europe, is the ability to run longer trains on a much larger number of routes. I mean trains at least 750 metres long.
Before we charge onto European routes, we have to deal with a potential threat hanging over our railways from “stray Russian drones”. We are talking about terminal security. Is Laude planning or considering protection of its Zamość terminal against such drones?
That in turn raises the question of whether we, as carriers, can protect ourselves against threats during transport in the border zone. That is the first point. Going a step further: are we considering using drones ourselves to counter threats to our terminals?
So let us start at the beginning, with our terminal in Zamość. The Laude terminal is located in a closed zone that is already protected today by the authorities appointed for that purpose. State services are responsible for protecting critical facilities, and they have the right tools, training and knowledge. The private sector has no access to weapons or military technology and no way of buying them. In any case, I am not sure that allowing companies to take independent action involving weapons would be the most sensible solution.
I would like to stress that drones should already be patrolling rail routes today, just as they patrol critical infrastructure.
A question has come up in public debate: since the Russians are systematically destroying Ukrainian rolling stock, mainly locomotives, can Poland help Ukraine in some way? Are there equipment reserves that could be handed over or sold to Ukraine?
Realistically, there are no such reserves. What I can see is handing over the entire LHS rolling stock fleet and quickly replacing it with new stock. LHS is preparing to renew its fleet anyway, but I don’t think it planned to transfer its existing stock to Ukraine. That is why the whole process is moving rather slowly. Still, I think nothing prevents us from looking at this strategically and deciding to hand over the broad-gauge locomotives and wagons we have to our Ukrainian partners. On our side, we would need to shorten, as far as possible, the approval procedures, for example for diesel locomotives on the only broad-gauge line in use in Poland.
Of course, supporting our eastern neighbours with locomotives would be crucial. It is a realistic solution, but we are talking about a minimum of two years to implement it. With political will, though, that period could probably be shortened very considerably. This matters because, to my knowledge, Poland does not have even a dozen or so broad-gauge locomotives, let alone several dozen, set aside in deep reserve. Nor do I really see any possibility of buying them on the open market.
I see sense in joint action on this by Poland and the Baltic states, including Finland. They are in a better position because they still run on broad gauge, so they have the right facilities. Such action, supported by simpler procedures and shorter testing periods, would be a step towards real help for Ukraine. Cooperation with these countries would also strengthen the resilience of the whole region to potential disruptions. This is a war, and we have to think outside the box. I encourage exactly this approach; otherwise we stand no chance. The purchase of new equipment could be subsidised from the Solidarity Corridor programme.
Finally, let us not forget that we all hope and expect that one day not only our wagons and containers, but also our locomotives and entire trains will run into Ukraine. So we too will need locomotives adapted to broad gauge.

Russian state media on Tuesday cited the ministry as saying the Tu-95 plane crashed during a training flight in an uninhabited area of Amur, a region bordering China.
The plane was flying without ammunition, according to the TASS state-run news agency.
Interfax news agency quoted Russia’s military as saying that an Aerospace Forces commission had been dispatched “to the crash site to establish all the circumstances of the incident”.
Unverified social media videos of the purported crash aftermath showed large amounts of smoke rising from the burning aircraft.
The Tupolev Tu-95 is a large, Soviet-era bomber aircraft that can carry, launch and deliver nuclear weapons.
It was first flown in 1952 but was only introduced into service in 1956 and remains in use, often by the Russian military in routine military exercises.
This is not the first time aircraft have gone down in Russia’s Far East. In July last year, an Antonov An-24 plane crashed in poor weather conditions on its way to the town of Tynda, killing all 48 people on board.
