Indian firm building $15bn Trump-announced steel mill has deep Russia ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:19:51 UTC
23:19:51 KST

Indian firm building $15bn Trump-announced steel mill has deep Russia ties
Russian cash helped Essar, the firm behind the steel factory, manage major debts. Now the group is investing in the US.
As United States President Donald Trump announced a $15bn steel megaplant while seated at his Oval Office desk on Monday, he had a lineup of mostly US politicians standing behind him – from cabinet members to elected representatives from Iowa, where the mill is to be built. There was one exception: an Indian man with a receding hairline and a lilac pocket handkerchief, standing behind the US president’s right shoulder.
Ravi Ruia is a cofounder of the Essar Group, which owns Mesabi Metallics, the Minnesota-based firm that is building the steel mill, expected to be the US’s largest. A decade earlier, in October 2016, his brother Shashi was in the photo frame with a different president during the signing of another major deal: Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Steel and metallics are not Essar’s only association with minerals and natural resources. The conglomerate had been involved in oil for years, before selling one of India’s largest private oil refineries to a Russian-led consortium in 2016 for nearly $13bn. Essar Oil was rebranded as Nayara Energy.
Today, Nayara Energy is half-owned by Russian gas major Rosneft, which is under heavy US and European sanctions over Moscow’s war on Ukraine. Nayara has also emerged as a supplier of petroleum products to Russia at a time when the country is facing a fuel crisis following multiple Ukrainian attacks on its oil and gas depots.
As part of a 99-year deal, Nayara is continuing to use Essar’s branding in India, where the company runs thousands of petrol stations. Nayara is under European Union sanctions.
The White House is touting the Iowa steel project, unveiled weeks before the US midterm elections, as a major economic win for Americans, promising hundreds of jobs and billions of dollars in revenue. And there is no evidence that the steel project is in violation of any Russia-specific US sanctions.
But Trump’s announcement of a megaproject with an Indian firm closely tied to Russian investments under Western sanctions underscores how the US has struggled to isolate Moscow economically despite an unprecedented economic pressure campaign.
And the timing of the steel mill announcement raises questions, because it comes days after Trump signed a law that empowers him to punish countries that buy Russian oil with up to 100 percent tariffs. India is Russia’s second-largest oil buyer. But the legacy Indian conglomerate that best epitomises the country’s links to Russian energy is now also behind the US’s biggest steel factory.
What’s the steel factory project about?
The new project would integrate its iron ore mining operations in Minnesota’s Mesabi Iron Range with the upcoming steel complex in Iowa.
The White House and the company’s announcements said the Iowa steel plant is expected to create at least 1,750 permanent jobs – “while continuing to work with suppliers and businesses throughout Iowa and the Midwest” – and support up to 6,000 construction jobs.
Washington also noted that the mill will produce 7.5 million tonnes of steel per year in its first phase, with production expected to rise to 10 million tonnes. Steel production is expected to begin in 2030.
The first phase of the project is expected to generate $95bn in total economic impact during construction and its first 10 years of operation, according to the White House.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told reporters that “these are your 232 tariffs, the steel tariffs at work”. He added: “Without those tariffs, this mine and steel plant doesn’t get built.”
Trump chipped in, too. “Soon after my inauguration, I imposed powerful 50 percent tariffs on all foreign steel, and now our steel industry is roaring back to life,” he said. “Everyone’s building their plant here because they don’t want to pay tariffs.”
But the steel project is also evidence of how countries and companies have skirted US economic pressure – and how it gives them leverage to continue to do so.
What are Essar’s ties to Russia?
Essar Oil, the group’s energy arm, began refining crude in 2008 at its refinery in Vadinar on the coast of the western Indian state of Gujarat.
But by 2016, the company was in deep debt, listed as a defaulter by the Reserve Bank of India, the country’s central bank, and desperately looking for a buyer who would take over its oil operations. The timing was opportune. President Putin was at the time trying to get Rosneft, Russia’s energy giant, to offload some stakes in exchange for foreign capital.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi played matchmaker, helping stitch together a series of deals between 2014 and 2016 that helped Rosneft and Essar. First, Indian public sector oil majors bought stakes in Rosneft, giving it the cash it needed. Rosneft, in turn, joined hands with other investors to buy the Vadinar refinery, freeing Essar from its debts.
Essar Oil became Nayara Energy – a company in which Rosneft owns a 49 percent stake, and United Capital Partners, a Russian asset management company, owns another 49 percent. The buyers paid Essar $12.9bn for the deal. As part of the agreement, Nayara got to use Essar’s branding – including on thousands of petrol stations across India – for 99 years.
Is Nayara under Western sanctions?
Yes. The EU imposed sanctions on Nayara in July last year as part of the broader 18th package of sanctions against Russian oil.
That banned the import of petroleum products processed using Russian crude oil and restricted the refinery’s access to EU shipping insurance, as well as financial and other services.
Nayara’s Vadinar refinery in western India has been processing only Russian oil since other suppliers backed out following the sanctions. Since then, Nayara has relied on international traders to import crude and export refined fuels.
In July this year, Nayara Energy sold petroleum to Russia as Ukrainian attacks targeted oil refineries across the country, triggering a fuel crisis.
In recent months, Ukrainian forces have targeted Russian oil facilities, setting them ablaze and causing long lines for fuel across the country, including in the capital, Moscow. The fuel crisis, unprecedented for Russia, one of the world’s biggest energy producers, has led to rationing in many regions.
These Russian links have brought Nayara Energy under wider scrutiny, prompting companies, including SAP, to suspend services to the refiner, citing sanctions and obligations under EU law.
Nayara challenged the move in the Delhi High Court, which ordered SAP India to restore its services earlier this month.
Are Essar or the steel plant violating any sanctions?
While Nayara is under EU sanctions, Essar does not face any US or EU sanctions.
In October 2016, after Essar struck its deal with Rosneft and United Capital Partners to sell the Vadinar refinery, the US – at the time under the Barack Obama administration – said the agreement did not violate any sanctions.
“I don’t think we see any violation of any US-EU sanctions stemming from this deal,” State Department spokesperson Mark Toner said at the time. Essar also said the deal was compliant with US sanctions.
There is no evidence of any sanctions breach in Essar’s investment in Mesabi, or in the planned investment to set up the steel factory in Iowa.
But Rishika Chauhan, a researcher at the Centre for Science and Security Studies (CSSS), King’s College London, who focuses on sanctions, said Essar’s investments in the US now make it “more predisposed to American arm-twisting, as sanctions and other actions can be taken more easily on the conglomerate’s assets and investments in the US now, and US laws can be used on it”.
Chauhan noted that sanctions on Russia and Iran have “a provision to impose new tariffs on the states that import from certain countries that purchase Russian energy or facilitate Russian oil sanctions evasion”.
“Essar can certainly come under the purview of these and many other US sanctions laws and executive orders,” she told Al Jazeera. “It isn’t a simple exercise, but sanctions and tariffs are often used by Trump as leverage to get what they want.”
Essar’s relations with Russia have also attracted scrutiny elsewhere, including in the United Kingdom, where the Ruia brothers have long had major investments.
At the time of the sale of the Vadinar refinery to Russian buyers, the Russian bank VTB also gave Essar a $3.9bn loan for debt reconstruction.
The bank was hit by major US and EU sanctions in February 2022, right after Russia’s full-fledged invasion of Ukraine. Reporting published in April 2026 by The Guardian and investigative journalism platform SourceMaterial showed that Essar moved the VTB loan to Mauritius, a tax haven, allegedly to avoid the sanctions. Essar owns the Stanlow oil refinery in the UK.
Why is the timing of the steel plant announcement significant?
Trump’s Republican Party is heading for crucial midterm congressional elections in November, while his approval rating has been plumbing all-time lows in the face of voter concerns about inflation, cost of living and the US-Israel war on Iran.
In his second term, Trump has made tariffs and the revival of US manufacturing a cornerstone of his economic vision, claiming that higher barriers to imports will drive investment back to the US.
Moreover, Washington introduced legislation that would allow the president to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on imports from countries that continue economic engagement with Russia or Iran, aiming to put pressure on those buying Russian energy.
New Delhi is particularly exposed since it became one of the largest buyers of discounted Russian crude after the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Trump imposed an additional 25 percent tariff on Indian imports in 2025 over the issue, before removing it in February 2026 after India committed to stop buying Russian crude.
Russia has remained India’s largest source of crude, although purchases have declined as the threat of US penalties has grown. The Reuters news agency reported that India imported approximately 2.1 million barrels per day of Russian crude in August.
There is also a recent parallel to underscore the incentives for investment in Trump’s US. In May this year, Washington moved to dismiss the criminal fraud and bribery charges against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani, while his lawyers had told the Justice Department that his group was prepared to invest $10bn in the US. A federal judge subsequently dismissed the criminal case in August.
Chauhan said capital investment in Trump’s US does provide an incentive to companies looking to distance themselves from dealings with Russia, but it does not guarantee a shield from Washington’s weaponisation of sanctions and tariffs. “Sanctions politics is quite interesting and cannot be taken at face value; laws and executive orders are a starting part, but many other parts of this moving machinery need to be understood,” he added.

OpenAI hack sparks crackdown on weak government websites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:17:17 UTC
23:17:17 KST

Government orders cyber system crackdown in wake of OpenAI breach
In short:
Home Affairs has directed all government departments and agencies to review their cyber systems for weaknesses against AI threats.
Acting Home Affairs Minister Richard Marles says government systems must keep up with the rapid changes sparked by artificial intelligence.
What's next?
Critical systems will need to be reviewed by the end of the year under the two-stage process.
The OpenAI Medicare breach has prompted an urgent bolstering of government cyber systems to ensure resistance against AI threats.
New details have also been revealed about OpenAI's notification to the government, sent months after its agent went rogue and gained unauthorised access to the Medicare statistics portal administered by Services Australia.
Following the incident all government departments and agencies have been required to take stock of how their systems may be exposed to risks posed by AI and other emerging technologies.
On Wednesday Home Affairs issued a directive advising departments to target older software and technology.
Systems of Government Significance will be prioritised and a review is due by the end of the year.
Less vital systems will be assessed by the end of March next year.
Acting Home Affairs Minister Richard Marles stressed the importance of constantly reviewing the systems in a rapidly changing environment.
"AI is changing the environment in which we operate at extraordinary speed. Government systems need to keep up," he said in a statement.
"We can't wait for an old system to fail before replacing it. We need to identify vulnerabilities and deal with them before they can be exploited."
The breach has sharpened Labor's plans to impose reporting requirements on artificial intelligence companies.
Australia is set to introduce legislation for national standards to put "guardrails on AI", which would include mandatory standards for data centres, before the end of the year.
A rapid review into the OpenAI breach is due to conclude within weeks and the findings are expected to inform the national standards.
New details about OpenAI government disclosure
OpenAI has faced scrutiny over the two-month delay in informing the government about the Services Australia breach, as well the nature of the disclosure.
The website targeted was a legacy system that has since been shut down, with the data moved to a more secure address.
A copy of the letter obtained by ABC reveals the framing to the government, which was notified of "security vulnerability identified" during a review of the agent's activity.
"An OpenAI model identified a way to make the server carry out instructions sent through the public reporting interface, without a private account or password," the notification said.
"It was able to access this to read portions of internal program files and settings, obtain a list of files, and create and read back a small test file on the server."
OpenAI has since admitted the agent took actions the company "did not intend" during the incident.
On Tuesday the ChatGPT maker apologised for the breach which was carried out by an internal-only model that did not have the safeguards used in publicly available products.
In a blog post on OpenAI's website, the company said it intended to "rebuild trust with the Australian people".
"We are sorry and working to do better in the future," the post said.
"This is a new kind of cyber incident which represents an emerging global challenge."
Abigail Bradshaw, the director-general of the Australian Signals Directorate, welcomed the apology and noted the company's commitment to report preliminary findings early and to pause the release of the next model to ensure the guardrails are right.
Ms Bradshaw said Australia enjoyed a "rare" level of engagement with frontier artificial intelligence labs to ensure vulnerabilities are patched.
She added that several government systems had been "fortified" in the past six months, including the Australian Bureau of Statistics ahead of the recent census, and said there had already been a 30 per cent reduction in government legacy software technology.
She said entities needed to be prioritising security over availability.
"We say, reduce your attack surface. What that means is, if you have a system that doesn't need to be connected to the internet, then segregate that system and isolate it," she said.
"The process of cyber security is like painting the Sydney Harbour Bridge. It never stops."

Hassett: 'We're still working our way out from' Biden Covid spending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:15:52 UTC
23:15:52 KST

The U.S. is still dealing with the impact of Covid 19-related stimulus spending from former President Joe Biden's first year in office, National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said Tuesday as he defended the Trump administration's handling of the economy.
"That's really the big mistake that we're still working our way out from," Hassett contended on CNBC's "Squawk Box."
The comment came in the final weeks of a midterm election cycle centered on widespread concerns about affordability and inflation, with Democrats appearing poised to make gains in Congress.
A Senate Majority PAC memo circulated Tuesday morning urges Democratic candidates to keep affordability "front-and-center," citing battleground polling that found attacks tying Republicans to higher prices for healthcare, utilities, gas and other everyday expenses tested more strongly than corruption arguments on their own.
The memo, based on an August survey of 1,800 likely voters across nine Senate battleground states, argues Democrats should explicitly connect political decisions and corporate influence to higher household costs.
"The strongest reason to vote against a Republican continues to be that they have raised our costs," the memo says.
President Donald Trump and his top officials regularly defend their administration's record by contrasting it favorably with the Biden era, or blaming the former president's policies for creating lingering problems.
Nearly two years since the 2024 presidential election, those claims appear to be losing some potency, with recent polls showing voters increasingly disapprove of Trump on the economy and in general.
After a CNBC host brought up Covid, Hassett argued that Trump's first administration approved the right amount of pandemic-related stimulus, but that heavy spending continued under Biden.
"We wanted to fill the hole, but not do more than that," Hassett said of Trump's first term, which overlapped with the spread of Covid in March 2020. "What Biden did is he took all that spending and he decided to spend it on other things, even though we didn't need it."
"When President Trump left office last time — talk about affordability — inflation was one and a half percent," he said.
"And then it took off when they helicopter-dropped money by keeping as a baseline the Covid spending, and that's really the big mistake that we're still working our way out from," Hassett argued.
Biden signed the $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan in March 2021, and many economists say it exacerbated U.S. inflation, though there is debate about the extent of its impact.
Inflation under Biden rose sharply during his first two years in office, peaking around 9% in summer of 2022. It declined to 3% by the time Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, and has crept higher this year as the U.S. war against Iran and Russia's continuing conflict in Ukraine heap pressure on global energy supplies.
— Luke Fountain contributed to this report.

Rosatom proposes new 1,000-megawatt nuclear power unit in Armenia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:15:14 UTC
23:15:14 KST

Burc Eruygur
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom has proposed building a new 1,000-megawatt nuclear power unit in Armenia as Yerevan considers offers from international partners, its head said Tuesday.
Rosatom Director General Alexey Likhachev made the remarks following talks with Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan in Yerevan.
Likhachev said the talks followed agreements reached during Pashinyan's earlier discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin.
He said the talks were “deep in terms of expertise and broad in scope,” adding that nuclear energy has a future in Armenia “for decades to come,” according to Russian media.
“The task now before us is to formulate the most competitive proposal in the coming months so that Armenia can select a partner and vendor for the construction of a new unit,” Likhachev said, according to Russian state news agency Tass.
“We have submitted a concrete proposal to the Armenian government for a 1,000-megawatt unit based on our best-in-class VVER-1000 design,” he added.
Likhachev said Armenia is also considering extending the Armenian Nuclear Power Plant’s service life until 2046. Rosatom is prepared to carry out the necessary work if Yerevan proceeds, he added.
“However, beyond technical feasibility, we must also consider economic viability,” he said, adding that extending the plant's operations would require substantial investment.
The ANPP was commissioned in 1976 and is located about 30 kilometers (18.6 miles) west of the Armenian capital and around 16 kilometers (10 miles) from Türkiye's eastern border with Armenia.
The plant currently has a single operational power unit. Another was shut down following a 6.8-magnitude earthquake in 1988 that killed at least 25,000 people and left hundreds of thousands homeless.
Rosatom said in a statement following Tuesday's talks that the two sides also discussed extending the ANPP's operating license until 2036, as well as prospects for new nuclear power generation capacity in Armenia.
Pashinyan's office said Yerevan is considering proposals from international partners for the construction of a new nuclear power unit and expects to make a decision “in the near future.”
“Nikol Pashinyan emphasized that the final decision would be based exclusively on economic considerations, taking into account price, quality, safety, timelines, and guarantees,” the statement said.
His office added that Likhachev presented proposals for a new nuclear power plant as well as small- and medium-capacity power units and possible mechanisms for their implementation.

Pakistan’s Escalating Response to Cross-Border Terrorism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:14:00 UTC
23:14:00 KST

Tensions are on the rise between Pakistan and Afghanistan once again as both countries have traded fire as well as accusations over the past few days. The current flare-up is a direct consequence of a terrorist attack on a mosque in the north-western Pakistani town of Kohat on September 18, in which at least 31 people, including 16 police personnel, were killed and over 100 injured.
After neutralizing the attackers after an hours-long gun battle, Pakistan launched retaliatory airstrikes against the alleged positions of the Hafiz Gul Bahadur-led Ittehad ul Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), which had claimed responsibility for the attack, and its ideological ally, the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), in Paktika and Kunar provinces of Afghanistan on September 21. Pakistan claimed to have killed 28 terrorists in those strikes.
Instead of engaging Pakistan’s border posts with machine guns and mortars like in most previous instances, the Taliban government of Afghanistan launched drones against Pakistan from its territory in the early hours of September 23. Eight of the drones were downed by Pakistan’s air defenses, according to Pakistani authorities.
The Afghan drone incursions did not cause any casualties or damage to civilian or military infrastructure in Pakistan; the spokesperson for the Pakistani president dismissed them as unfrightening “flying toys.” Even so, Islamabad conducted fresh air raids in Afghanistan, targeting 10 different locations in the early hours of September 24. Pakistan’s information minister confirmed that the second round of strikes was indeed a response to the Afghan drone incursions.
Quite ironically, the Kohat terrorist attack came a day after Turkiye’s intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin, arrived in Islamabad following his trip to Afghanistan. Kalin was continuing Turkiye’s effort to mediate a long-term peace between the two countries. Kabul had already expressed its lack of enthusiasm toward the Turkish mediation when the Taliban’s Supreme Leader Mullah Hibatullah Akhunzada refused to see Kalin in Kandahar, reportedly calling him “Westernized.” Then Islamabad’s identification of one of the suicide bombers as an Afghan national and the subsequent events sealed the fate of the ongoing peace efforts by Turkiye and Qatar.
While Pakistani and Afghan security forces continue to trade fire across the border and accusations in the media, the question on many a mind right now is whether any meaningful mediation between the two countries is possible any time soon. The short answer seems to be “no.” Here is the longer explanation for it.
Looking at Pakistan’s kinetic responses to terrorist attacks that its officials associated with terrorist safe havens across the border in Afghanistan, one can discern a break from the past since October last year. Even though Islamabad has been alleging an Afghan connection to earlier terrorist attacks as well, its kinetic responses were sparse and cautious.
Pakistan’s first reported use of force inside Afghanistan since the Taliban’s return to power in August 2021 occurred in April 2022, following a terrorist attack in the North Waziristan district bordering Afghanistan. At the time, Pakistan’s Foreign Office did not even acknowledge the airstrikes, even though the Taliban government of Afghanistan complained to the United Nations Security Council about them and initiated limited cross-border retaliatory fire against Pakistani border posts.
Two years later, in March 2024, Pakistan once again responded with airstrikes inside Afghanistan after a terrorist attack in North Waziristan. This time, Pakistan’s Foreign Office was quick to acknowledge the attack but its spokesperson hastened to add that Islamabad “respect[ed] the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Afghanistan and look[ed] forward to working together” with Afghanistan. In a subsequent press briefing, the Foreign Office even clarified that its actions were not against the government or the people of Afghanistan.
The response of the Taliban government of Afghanistan was also measured. Even though it claimed that it had conducted cross-border strikes against Pakistani posts, which was corroborated by the local population, the damage to personnel and infrastructure was limited. Like in April 2022, the crisis de-escalated quickly.
In December 2024 Pakistan conducted another round of airstrikes inside Afghanistan in response to a terrorist attack. Even though the airstrikes came at a time when Pakistan’s Special Representative for Afghanistan Ambassador Muhammad Sadiq was on his first visit to Kabul after resuming his responsibilities in the position, the aftermath followed a somewhat similar pattern to April 2022 and March 2024.
In October 2025, however, things changed significantly. Pakistan not only conducted an airstrike in the heart of Kabul targeting the head of the TTP, but responded to Afghanistan’s cross-border retaliatory fire on Pakistani border posts with much more intensity than the previous instances.
This led to a quick escalation of the conflict, forcing Qatar and Turkiye to make frantic efforts toward a ceasefire as well as a longer-term rapprochement. While the ceasefire held for a time, negotiations on the signing of a longer-term peace deal between Afghanistan and Pakistan remained unsuccessful, resulting in a tense diplomatic impasse that has persisted ever since.
Things got even worse in February 2026, when Pakistan initiated a long-term military operation aimed at neutralizing terrorists inside Afghan territory through the sustained use of air power.
Thus October 2025 marked a break from the past and February 2026 made the use of coercive power a norm. The reason for the new normal was the failure of months of bilateral and trilateral diplomacy starting in March 2025, when Sadiq travelled to Kabul again for talks after the December 2024 debacle. His visit paved the way for a visit of Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar to Kabul in April. Pakistan’s Foreign Office explicitly described Dar’s visit as part of its effort to develop “good, friendly, neighborly relations” with Afghanistan.
From May through August, Islamabad considerably intensified this diplomatic track with the involvement of China. In May, Pakistan, China, and Afghanistan held a trilateral foreign minister meeting in Beijing, where the three sides agreed to strengthen communication, economic cooperation, regional connectivity, and security cooperation. China and Pakistan also supported the extension of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) to Afghanistan.
This was the time when Pakistan and Afghanistan also agreed to upgrade diplomatic representation from chargé d’affaires to the ambassadorial level. Dar subsequently described the diplomatic interactions as laying the foundations for a “qualitative change” in Pakistan’s bilateral relations with Afghanistan.
On July 7, 2025, the two foreign ministries institutionalized another channel through an additional-secretary-level mechanism covering trade, transit, security, connectivity, and Afghan nationals. Dar made two back-to-back visits to Kabul in July and August to sign the framework agreement for a joint feasibility study of the Uzbekistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan railway and the sixth Pakistan-China-Afghanistan trilateral, respectively. Pakistan even provided Afghanistan with humanitarian assistance after the September 2025 earthquake.
Despite all this intense positive diplomacy, however, terrorist attacks inside Pakistan with purported links to Afghanistan continued. That is what has led Islamabad to treat coercion – not diplomacy with Afghanistan – as the primary option of choice since October 2025, even if the results of that change are highly debatable. As the escalation hurts populations on both sides of the border, there seems to be a perception among Pakistani policy circles that coercion is more likely to persuade the Afghan Taliban to quit supporting the TTP and its affiliated groups than diplomacy. And even if not, perhaps, at least Pakistan would be getting even with the Taliban.

AI generated
MOSCOW - Russia has singled out European firms in its latest drive to strip foreign owners of the right to manage their Russian assets, government and company sources said, with the Kremlin accusing the European Union of involvement in the war in Ukraine.
Russia placed the assets of Swiss food giant Nestle, German wholesaler Metro and French retailer Auchan under temporary management this month.
“The time has come for asymmetric measures. Let them think about what measures they are taking and what sanctions they are introducing,” a senior government source with direct knowledge of the measures told Reuters.
Asked which companies might be the next targets and whether the Russian units of Italian bank UniCredit and Austrian lender Raiffeisen could be placed under temporary management, the source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said: “Let them be scared.”
A Russian corporate source, who also spoke on condition of anonymity, accused European firms of deliberately stifling the development of their Russian units, ultimately harming the Russian economy.
A senior manager with a European company, part of a shrinking community of foreign businesses operating in Russia, told Reuters that European businesses expected the status quo to be maintained in the immediate future.
The Kremlin said on Sept 29 the decisions were driven by “the increasing level of involvement of these unfriendly countries in direct battlefield hostilities” against Russia, but suggested the moves were “reversible”.
“For now, we do not see any grounds for a reversal. We do not hear any reasonable voices calling for dialogue or for efforts to rectify the situation,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
The EU blames Russia for the failure to end the war, saying Moscow shows no real intent to engage in genuine peace talks, and last week renewed sanctions on more than 3,000 individuals and entities.
It did not immediately comment on Russia’s latest moves against European companies.
Peskov gave no evidence or details of how European countries were involved in military operations.
Russian officials have previously cited weapons supplies, including the manufacture of drones in the EU, as well as the provision of targeting and intelligence information.
“If you acknowledge that your weapons are being used against us, and we are shooting them down, call it whatever you want, but I have no doubt that this is a war being waged against us by Europe,” Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Sept 29.
Russia also criticises the EU for freezing about €210 billion (S$300 billion) of its sovereign assets in response to the war and for targeting assets belonging to Russian companies in Europe and other Western countries.
The EU, a staunch supporter of Ukraine during the more than four-and-a-half-year-old war, has accused Russia of carrying out attacks on European territory, while some government and intelligence officials have raised the prospect of a future Russian invasion. Moscow has denied the accusations.
Since the start of the war, Russia has introduced temporary administration at 135 firms affiliated with foreign companies, the vast majority of them from EU countries, including French food group Danone and Danish brewer Carlsberg, according to data compiled by Russian news agency TASS.
Prior to the latest moves, Russian law firm NSP put the number of affected Western firms at 22. In its latest annual report, the Association of European Businesses said it had 330 member companies with operations in Russia, down from 400 a year earlier.
No major US company has been targeted by similar measures, although some smaller firms, such as US private equity fund NCH Capital, whose Russian business includes agricultural assets, have also been placed under temporary administration.
The American Chamber of Commerce in Russia put the number of US companies still operating in Russia at around 300 this year. Russia and the United States have been in discussions on business opportunities once peace is restored in Ukraine. REUTERS

EU Commission unveils new measures to tackle mass arrivals at external borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:12:12 UTC
23:12:12 KST

The European Commission has proposed a five-point plan to help the EU prevent and respond to sudden, large-scale irregular arrivals at its external borders.
The proposal follows a surge in arrivals in Ceuta this summer, which the Commission said showed how quickly an emergency could develop despite irregular border crossings being at their lowest since 2021, according to a statement on Tuesday.
The plan calls for stronger cooperation with partner countries, reinforced external borders, improved early warning systems, action against migrant smuggling networks and more effective returns.
Among the proposals is a new European Emergency Response Framework for situations in which mass movements of people are “engineered and weaponised.”
The Commission also plans to propose a stronger mandate for the EU border agency, Frontex, including personnel and equipment that could be deployed immediately and a larger role in returns.
To improve early warning, the Commission wants Frontex to be able to monitor social media in connection with external border management. It also urged member states to report developments affecting the borders promptly through the EU’s surveillance system, EUROSUR.
The plan seeks closer cooperation with online platforms and financial institutions to identify smuggling activity and illicit financial flows. It also urges the Council to adopt a proposed sanctions regime allowing asset freezes and travel bans against migrant smugglers.
On returns, the Commission called for greater cooperation with countries of origin and transit on readmission and wider use of Frontex support.
“We will reinforce our foundation of strong external borders, effective migration diplomacy, the Pact on Migration and Asylum, and credible returns,” said EU Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner.
The plan will be presented to member states at the Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting October 1-2.

Israeli settlers attacked a Palestinian village in the northern occupied West Bank on Monday night, in the latest in a wave of anti-Palestinian pogroms across the territory.
Dozens of extremists stormed the village of Jalud, around 30 kilometres south of Nablus, setting fire to Palestinian homes and vehicles.
They torched two houses belonging to the Al-Tubasi family, who had returned to the village just hours earlier after being driven from the area by settlers two months ago, sources told Anadolu Agency.
"More than 100 Israeli rioters were present in the village, blocking roads, setting tyres on fire and throwing stones at security forces," the Israeli military said in a statement, adding that the terrorists had "set fire to Palestinian buildings in the village, torched vehicles and other property".
Three officers were reportedly "lightly injured", and a police vehicle was damaged during the violence, according to the military. Security forces made just two arrests.
Palestinian villagers attempted to confront the settlers but were prevented from doing so by Israeli soldiers, according to local sources, who they said provided cover to the terrorists.
The Al-Tubasi family had fled the village in July following months of harassment by extremist settlers. Hours before Monday night's attack, Israeli forces had allowed them to return following a court order.
A member of the family told Haaretz that settlers began gathering after they arrived in the village. Security forces later came under attack as they escorted the family out of Jalud to the nearby town of Qusra, the family member said.
The family's lawyer told Haaretz that the army "bears full responsibility" for the violence after leaving the houses exposed to the settlers.
Two other Palestinian villages were also attacked on Monday night.
Settlers assaulted several homes and torched vehicles in Al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah, during an Israeli raid on the village. In Qaryut, south of Nablus, an elderly Palestinian woman was assaulted by extremists.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) warned on Tuesday that surging settler violence and rapid settlement expansion were making life increasingly untenable for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
"The frequent and severe violence must be brought to an end," said Julien Lerisson, head of the ICRC’s delegation for Israel and the occupied territories. "Authorities have a responsibility to protect the population from violence, including when that violence is inflicted by settlers."
Explosion in settler terrorism
Since taking power at the end of 2022, Netanyahu's far-right government has presided over a surge in anti-Palestinian violence in the occupied West Bank, which Palestinians and rights groups have repeatedly accused Israeli forces of facilitating or failing to prevent.
The rate of settler terrorism has increased every year since 2023, reaching a record high this year, according to the UN.
The UN has documented more than 1,600 instances of settler violence between January and September this year, averaging 6.7 attacks per day.
Settlers killed almost two dozen Palestinians and injured more than 1,040 others during the first eight months of the year, according to UN figures. Tens of thousands of Palestinians have also been forcibly displaced from their homes amid settler attacks and Israeli military raids.
Israeli settlers are rarely prosecuted for violence against Palestinians.
Some of Israel's closest allies have stepped up criticism of the violence in recent weeks and announced measures targeting settlements.
The UK said this month it would cut ties with Israeli settlements and impose sanctions on companies involved in the settlement project. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accused members of the Israeli government of facilitating ethnic cleansing and encouraging settler terrorism.
Other Western countries, including France, Canada, the Netherlands, Ireland and Spain, have also announced measures targeting settlement trade.
Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador in Jerusalem and a staunch supporter of Israel, has also accused settlers of committing acts of terrorism.
Israel's defence establishment has increasingly warned that settler violence poses a major national security threat.
In a rare warning this month, the country's leading security think tank said the proliferation of "Jewish terrorism" risked triggering the collapse of state institutions and cementing the country's status as an international pariah.
Israeli political figures issued rare condemnations following Monday night's violence.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he "strongly condemned" the attack, blaming a "handful of rioters", whom two Israeli military divisions currently operating in the occupied West Bank seem incapable of controlling.
Gadi Eisenkot, one of Netanyahu's main rivals in the upcoming election, called the attacks "horrifying" and accused settlers of waging a "campaign of terror and violence".

SYDNEY, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Australia's New South Wales (NSW) Minister for Climate Change, Energy, Heritage and the Environment Penny Sharpe highlighted the contribution of Chinese business and technology to the state's energy transition.
Addressing a reception celebrating the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China held by the Consulate-General of China in Sydney on Monday, the minister said NSW could not undertake its energy transition without China.
Sharpe said the significant, long-standing relationship between NSW and China is rooted in the state's strong trade and investment ties with China, one of NSW's largest export destinations.
In his remarks, Chinese Consul General in Sydney Wang Yu noted that the achievements of Chinese modernization have created opportunities for the world, while the positive progress in China-Australia relations has benefited both peoples.
China's "new tech trio" of artificial intelligence, robotics and innovative pharmaceuticals is seeing strong export growth, and China has also remained the world's second-largest import market for 17 consecutive years, he said.
"This creates opportunities for countries around the world to develop together," Wang added. ■

Cyber fraud can outwit the tech-savvy too, IIT study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:06:58 UTC
23:06:58 KST

NEW DELHI: A career in IT and security did not save her from losing Rs 90 lakh to cybercrime. The professional, with 28 years of experience, was among 33 victims interviewed for an IIT Madras-led study that found technological familiarity could be overwhelmed by fear, urgency and psychological manipulation.Participants came from Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, New Delhi and Mumbai; the sample included 12 senior citizens. Participants included bankers, doctors, IT professionals and people with cybersecurity certifications. One reported a loss of Rs 1.12 crore even after recovering Rs 25 lakh.Published in Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, the qualitative study explores how victims were deceived, rather than measuring national risk. Its urban, professionally employed sample cannot establish that educated people are more vulnerable than others.Many participants were navigating illness in the family, retirement, job searches or workplace pressure. Fraudsters exploited these circumstances through investment promises, employment offers or threats to reputation. Some victims sought quick returns; others paid because they feared arrest or harm to relatives.
“The way they act and talk, you cannot believe that they are not police officers—they play a psychological game with you,” the IT and security professional said in the study.In “digital arrest” scams, victims described being confined to rooms, monitored over video and coached to mislead bank managers. A plastic surgeon said: “They emotionally manipulated and trapped me: every half an hour I had to send them pics that I am alone”.In task-based scams, criminals initially paid victims for simple online assignments to build trust, then pressed them to invest larger sums and borrow from relatives or friends when funds dwindled.The researchers also found neglected device updates and missing security software among participants. Their accounts suggest psychological manipulation can work alongside technical weaknesses. Some victims subsequently abandoned online payments and returned to cash.
The damage extended beyond bank balances. Victims reported sleeplessness, shame and strained family relationships. Institutional responses were uneven: some banks helped, while others blamed customers; some victims reported being sent between police stations.The researchers call for awareness campaigns explaining specific fraud tactics, stronger police expertise, faster bank detection and better coordination between banks, police and courts. “The response to cybercrime must move beyond blaming victims,” said IIT Madras adjunct faculty member P Kandaswamy in a statement.
Manash Pratim Gohain is a seasoned journalist with over two decades at The Times of India, where he has built a rich body of work spanning education policy, politics, and governance. Renowned for his incisive coverage of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, accreditation reforms, and skilling initiatives, he has also reported on student politics, urban policy, and social movements. His political reportage—both reflective and news-driven—adds depth to his writing, bridging policy with public impact. Through his 2,500 articles and related outlets, he has emerged as a trusted voice in national discourse, particularly in linking education reform to broader societal change.

A drone photo taken on July 22, 2026 shows completed vessels at the Hengli Heavy Industries industrial park in Dalian, northeast China's Liaoning Province. Located at the Changxing Island Economic Zone of Dalian City, Hengli Heavy Industries industrial park launched its "Ocean Factory," a green shipbuilding base, in early 2023. Its "Future Factory" was put into operation in early 2025, specializing in the manufacturing of high-value-added green vessels ranging from ultra-large oil tankers, ultra-large liquefied gas carriers to ultra-large container ships, alongside high-end marine engineering equipment.
At the industrial park, cutting-edge technologies such as welding robots, automated cutting, and dynamic automatic steel-plate marking are extensively deployed across the site. Numerous industrial data collection terminals have been installed throughout dry docks, workshops and quays. Leveraging advanced technologies such as industrial data acquisition, IoT sensing and on-site 5G private networks, the entire factory has realized digital capture of production-related factors as well as refined operational management. China Focus: China expects bumper 2026 grain harvest as agricultural, rural modernization gathers pace
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
22:06:51 CST
23:06:51 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on accelerating agricultural and rural modernization to drive all-round rural revitalization during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Jin Liangkuai)
BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China is on track for a bumper grain harvest in 2026 amid steady progress in agricultural and rural modernization, the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs said Tuesday.
This year, summer grain output exceeded 150 million tonnes for the first time, and early rice output remained above 28 million tonnes for the sixth consecutive year, the ministry said at a press conference.
Autumn crops, the mainstay of China's annual grain production, are now being harvested, with the planted area expanded and that of high-yielding crops, particularly corn, increasing notably, according to Zhang Zhu, minister of agriculture and rural affairs.
"Against the backdrop of increased volatility in global grain markets, China has a solid foundation and ample confidence to ensure stable grain production and supply," said Zhang.
SOLID FOUNDATION FOR FOOD SECURITY
Food security has long been an important priority for China, which feeds nearly one-fifth of the world's population with less than 9 percent of the world's arable land. Ensuring a stable food supply is becoming more challenging amid geopolitical uncertainties and increasingly frequent extreme weather events.
Despite the headwinds, China's annual grain output has remained above 700 million tonnes for two consecutive years of 2024 and 2025. Per capita grain availability has surpassed 500 kg, which is higher than the global average.
The country has achieved basic self-sufficiency in grains and ensured a secure supply of staple foods, Zhang said. "We are firmly holding the rice bowl of the Chinese people in our own hands."
Beyond grains, China is also expanding food sources to ensure a diverse and abundant supply of agricultural products.
Last year, China's meat production exceeded 100 million tonnes for the first time, with per capita meat availability reaching about 1.5 times the global average. Per capita egg availability exceeded the level in developed countries.
The country aims to ensure that its population of more than 1.4 billion has enough to eat and access to a healthier, more nutritious diet over the five years between 2026 and 2030, said Chen Bangxun, a spokesperson for the ministry.
Efforts will be made to advance modern facility-based agriculture, develop more food resources from fisheries, forests and grasslands, and use synthetic biology to create new sources of food, Chen added.
TECHNOLOGY DRIVES AGRICULTURAL MODERNIZATION
The role of technology in China's agricultural modernization continues to grow, according to the ministry.
The contribution of science and technology to agricultural development has now exceeded 64 percent, with innovations such as smart agricultural machinery and agricultural robots increasingly being applied in farming, according to Maierdan Mugaiti, vice minister of agriculture and rural affairs.
Such progress is supported by a series of policy measures. The outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) sets out specific measures to advance agricultural science and technology and modernize agricultural equipment.
The latest move in this regard is a plan for China's agricultural and rural modernization for the same period, which sets a target of raising the contribution of science and technology to agricultural development to 67 percent by 2030. It also calls for wider application of AI in agriculture and breakthroughs in developing new quality productive forces in the sector.
China will foster more agricultural technology companies and support them in taking on more research tasks addressing urgent industry needs, Mugaiti said.
The country will also accelerate the application of new technologies and the commercialization of agricultural research results to serve the industry and benefit farmers, he noted.
CONSOLIDATING POVERTY ALLEVIATION GAINS
Consolidating the gains from poverty alleviation and promoting rural development remain key priorities, with a focus on job creation, local industry development, and increasing farmers' incomes, according to the ministry.
By 2021, China had lifted 98.99 million rural residents living below the then poverty line out of poverty and announced the completion of its fight against absolute poverty. It then established a five-year transition period from 2021 to 2025 to consolidate and expand those gains and prevent people from falling back into poverty.
Over the past five years, development conditions in areas and among people lifted out of poverty have continued to improve, while their capacity for self-development has grown stronger, Zhang said.
With the five-year transition period wrapped up, China has entered a new stage of regular, targeted assistance. China has established a nationwide system covering all provinces and the entire rural population to identify people at risk of falling back into poverty and provide targeted assistance. So far, all 2.56 million people identified as being at risk have received assistance, Zhang said.
This year, the central government has allocated 177 billion yuan (about 26.26 billion U.S. dollars) to support rural industries, employment and development-based assistance in less-developed areas.
This has provided greater support for rural development and helped boost farmers' incomes. The per capita disposable income of rural residents in counties that have been removed from the poverty list rose from 12,588 yuan in 2020 to 18,627 yuan in 2025, achieving average annual growth of 8.2 percent, a State Council report revealed.
China is also developing local specialty industries to boost farmers' incomes, the ministry said. Efforts should be made to strengthen agricultural product processing, foster new industries and business forms and develop new types of rural services, said Mugaiti.
"We will continue to create more opportunities for farmers to benefit from rural industries, strengthen links between farmers and businesses, create more jobs in rural areas and ensure continued growth in farmers' incomes," he said. ■

China's World Internet Conference summit to focus on open-source AI
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
22:06:50 CST
23:06:50 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 World Internet Conference (WIC) Wuzhen Summit will put open-source AI and international cooperation on AI development and governance at the center of its agenda, organizers said Tuesday at a news conference in Beijing.
The summit will take place from Nov. 2 to 5 in Wuzhen, east China's Zhejiang Province, bringing together Chinese and international participants for discussions on innovation, security governance, cultural exchanges and international cooperation.
A dialogue at the main forum will gather executives from leading technology companies and developers of open-source large models to discuss how to build a global open-source AI ecosystem.
The summit will feature 27 sub-forums, with topics including trust, connectivity and interoperability among AI agents, as well as robotics, embodied AI and spatiotemporal intelligence. Cyberspace cooperation under the Global Governance Initiative will also feature in the discussions.
This focus on open-source cooperation follows broader Chinese efforts to promote international collaboration in AI.
An action plan issued at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai in July called for sharing open-source ecosystems, jointly developing rules and standards and strengthening cooperation on AI safety governance.
The theme of this year's Wuzhen Summit emphasizes open source, inclusiveness, joint contribution and shared benefits in building a community with a shared future in cyberspace.
Discussions will address both the principles and practical applications of open-source and inclusive AI development, as well as international concerns over its governance, according to the organizers.
Other events will include the WIC Awards for Pioneering Science and Technology, the WIC Distinguished Contribution Award, the Light of Internet Expo, and presentations of outstanding cases of jointly building a community with a shared future in cyberspace.
First held in 2014, the Wuzhen Summit brings together government officials, representatives of international organizations, technology executives and researchers to discuss the development and governance of the internet. The WIC was established as an international organization headquartered in Beijing in 2022.
The summit is organized by the WIC, with the Zhejiang provincial government responsible for local arrangements. ■

Interview: Chinese market is great opportunity for Spanish food products: ICEX executive
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
22:06:38 CST
23:06:38 KST

BARCELONA, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Food and drink products from Spain are growing ever more popular with consumers in China, and demand from importers and distributors is now extending to products that have yet to gain access to the Chinese market, a senior Spanish trade official has said.
"The reception in China has been spectacular," Maria Naranjo, director of the Agri-Food Industry at the Spanish Institute for Foreign Trade (ICEX), said in an interview with Xinhua on Tuesday.
However, she added: "One limitation is that there aren't more Spanish products that can be exported, because we're negotiating product by product. There are many well-liked products that Chinese importers and distributors are demanding from us, but which are not yet on the Chinese market."
Naranjo was speaking during this year's "Eat Spain, Drink Spain" campaign, a global initiative organized by ICEX together with the Spanish Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food. The campaign's China program was launched at the Spain Food Nation Summit in Shenzhen on Sept. 10.
According to Naranjo, the Chinese market for Spanish food is also expanding beyond restaurants specializing in Spanish cuisine.
"We have just 30 Spanish restaurants in China - a drop in the ocean - but we are seeing that there are now many hotels and restaurants that have Spanish products on their menu alongside Chinese food," she said.
Wine is another example of changing consumer tastes. Naranjo said renowned Spanish wines, including Rioja and Albarino, have attracted particular interest during this year's campaign.
"There are more and more wine lovers," she said, noting that wine is not traditionally part of Chinese gastronomy. In major cities, however, she sees a new generation of consumers, particularly young people with spending power who are developing an interest in wine.
Naranjo also attributed the growing awareness of Spanish food in China to the recovery and expansion of travel between the two countries.
According to Spain's national tourism agency Turespana, around 795,000 Chinese tourists visited Spain in 2025, up 22.6 percent year on year and 13.5 percent from 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic.
"I think the Chinese come to Spain and fall in love with the food," Naranjo said. While gastronomy may not initially be their main reason for visiting, she said, travelers discover "how varied and diverse Spanish gastronomy is."
Following the first "Eat Spain, Drink Spain" campaign last year, Spain in 2026 expanded the initiative in cooperation with the agriculture ministry. Its budget has risen to 2 million euros (2.3 million U.S. dollars), with activities covering 19 countries. ■

Asian Games | Olympic champions Chen, Wang lead China's diving gold haul
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
22:06:31 CST
23:06:31 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's Olympic champion Chen Yuxi delivered a dominant performance in the women's 10m platform on Tuesday, while two-time Olympic champion Wang Zongyuan completed a three-gold sweep as China continued its dominance of diving at the 2026 Asian Games.
Chen led from the opening round and pulled clear with two outstanding dives midway through the final, eventually taking gold with 432.65 points. Teammate Lu Wei finished second with 385.40, while DPR Korea's Jo Jin-mi took bronze with 363.80.
After scoring 76.50 and 86.40 on her opening two dives, Chen earned 92.40 for her third before producing the highlight of the final in the fourth round.
Her back 3 1/2 somersaults in tuck position earned 97.35 points, with several judges awarding perfect 10s for execution. Chen closed with 80.00 points on her final dive to comfortably secure the title.
"In the final, I kept telling myself that every dive had to be done cleanly. I had to stay relaxed without any hesitation," Chen said. "I'd rather pull off the dive decisively, imperfect as it might be, than hesitate halfway through."
Chen acknowledged that her final dive had not gone according to plan after she nearly over-rotated.
"I need to go back and train hard. After all, I still didn't do the 5253B well," she said.
The victory came five years after Chen won Olympic silver at the same venue.
"I had not competed in an individual event for almost a year. I hadn't fully adapted to the rhythm and state of competition," Chen said.
Asked to describe the five years between her two appearances at the venue in one word, Chen chooses "resilience."
"Over these five years, I have certainly encountered difficulties and moments when I wanted to give up. But in the end, I firmly chose to come back and keep going," she said.
Chen said her next major target was the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Lu, competing at her first Asian Games, said excitement had affected her control during the final.
"Overall, I felt pretty good about the competition, but in the afternoon I was very excited, and perhaps I had a little less control over my dives," the 16-year-old said.
Later Tuesday, Wang completed his three-gold campaign by winning the men's 3m springboard, adding the title to his victories in the men's 1m springboard and synchronized 3m springboard.
Wang led from his opening dive and remained on top throughout the final. He faltered with 68.40 points on his fifth attempt but responded with 85.50 on his last to seal the title.
"It was a challenge to compete in three events and fight for three gold medals, especially as I get older," the 24-year-old said. "I'm very happy that I managed to push through and accomplish the goal, although my overall performance was not perfect."
Teammate Zheng Jiuyuan recovered from two major errors to claim silver.
Zheng scored just 39.10 points on his opening dive and 43.20 on his fourth, but recovered with 74.10 on his fifth before producing the highest-scoring dive of the final. His final effort earned 93.60 points and lifted him to silver with 419.75.
Japan's Sakai Sho took bronze with 376.40.
"I was too excited at the beginning, but I forced myself to calm down and just follow what I do in training," said Zheng, who was competing at his first Asian Games.
Wang's victory in the men's 3m springboard was China's 98th Asian Games diving gold medal.
The final two diving titles will be decided Wednesday in the women's 3m springboard and men's 10m platform. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Seventeen-year-old sprint sensation Chen Yujie led China to gold in the inaugural mixed 4x100m relay on Tuesday, while South Korea's An Se-young became the first player to retain the badminton women's singles title at the 2026 Asian Games.

China's Wu Hongjiao won the women's 800m, while Japan's Ko Ochiai took the men's title in a Games-record 1:44.48. In the men's pole vault, Ernest John Obiena of the Philippines cleared a Games-record 5.91 meters to win gold, ahead of China's Yao Jie and Li Chenyang.

Surfing made its Asian Games debut at Aichi-Nagoya, with the men's and women's shortboard competitions also serving as qualifiers for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
China's first Olympic surfer, 17-year-old Yang Siqi, took silver in the women's shortboard after losing to Japan's Mirai Ikeda in the final. In the men's event, Japan's Tokyo Olympic silver medalist Kanoa Igarashi defeated Indonesia's I Made Pajar Ariyana to win gold.

China to implement mortgage interest subsidies from Oct. 1
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
22:06:28 CST
23:06:28 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China will implement interest subsidies for housing loans starting Oct. 1, 2026, with a tentative implementation period of one year.
During this period, for eligible first-time homebuyers, the fiscal authorities will provide an annualized subsidy of 1 percentage point, according to a notice jointly issued by the Ministry of Finance, the People's Bank of China and the National Financial Regulatory Administration on Tuesday.
This is the first time the central government has offered interest subsidies on commercial housing loans.
This interest subsidy policy is focused on first-time homebuyers. The floor area of each purchased unit must not exceed 120 square meters, and the purchase price must not surpass 1.5 million yuan (about 222,516 U.S. dollars).
Under this policy, the maximum amount of interest-subsidized loans can reach 1 million yuan, and the subsidy period can extend up to five years.
According to estimates, for a long-term 1-million-yuan commercial personal mortgage, the subsidies could help borrowers reduce cumulative interest payments by nearly 50,000 yuan.
By defining housing price, floor area and loan category, the policy aims to precisely benefit target groups and help lower-income families reduce their monthly mortgage burdens, the departments said.
The policy focuses on first-time buyers with essential needs, supporting families in purchasing small and medium-sized, and relatively low-priced homes, according to the departments. ■

Why Gaza Flotilla's Thiago Ávila is running for Brazil Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:06:22 UTC
23:06:22 KST

Breadcrumb
'We must fight imperialism': Global Sumud Flotilla's Thiago Ávila takes his fight to Brazil's Congress
For more than two decades, Brazilian socio-environmentalist and Palestine solidarity activist Thiago Ávila has campaigned against what he describes as imperialism, colonialism and the exploitation of people and nature.
Now, after years of activism and high-profile participation in Gaza-bound flotillas, he is taking that political struggle into Brazil's electoral arena.
A member of the Global Sumud Flotilla's steering committee, Ávila has helped organise a movement that expanded from more than 40 vessels in 2025 to more than 70 by May 2026, bringing together hundreds of activists from around the world.
He was also among those detained after the flotilla was illegally intercepted by Israeli forces near Crete on April 30, 2026. Along with Spanish-Swedish activist Saif Abukeshek, he was held without formal charges at the Shikma facility in Ashkelon and deported on May 10, 2026, following international pressure and a hunger strike.
Now, Ávila is running for a seat in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies with the green party REDE in São Paulo.
He says his potential term would bring his activism into parliament, with a particular focus on challenging what he describes as Israeli and Zionist influence over Brazilian policy.
"We believe that our candidacy and possible future term can accomplish an even more expressive role in the struggle for the Palestinian cause, in the fight against imperialism and colonialism," Ávila tells The New Arab.
"One of our key proposals is the rupture of all relations [with Israel]," he continues.
"We intend to establish a term that is vigilant to combat the Zionism lobby in our country, in our political process, and most importantly, in our elections. We are aware that Zionism uses scrutiny times to infiltrate, and that Brazil unfortunately has given in many ways, mostly associated with far-right-wing politicians."
Foreign influence in Brazilian politics
His remarks come days after ABIN, the Brazilian Intelligence Agency, forwarded a report on September 19 to the Supreme Electoral Court (TSE), the Presidency of the Republic, and the Ministry of Justice, pointing to the "risk of influence and interference from the United States of America in the upcoming Brazilian electoral process."
The information was released by Folha de S.Paulo and confirmed by O GLOBO. The report comes amid a wider pattern of closer US-Israeli alignment across Latin America, including the creation of the 'Shield of the Americas', a coalition of 18 Latin American countries plus the United States, which excludes Brazil's Lula and Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum.
The shift has also been reflected in relations between Israel and governments across the region.
Argentina's president Javier Milei has praised Benjamin Netanyahu and co-signed the 'Isaac Accords', a branch of the Abraham Accords aimed at furthering public diplomacy and cooperation between Israel and Latin American countries.
In Brazil, congresswoman Tabata Amaral of the Brazilian Socialist Party (PSB-SP) registered bill 1424/26, which supposedly criminalises anti-semitism and includes criticism of Israel as an anti-semitic practice, despite anti-semitism already being a crime in Brazil since 1988.
On September 21, President Lula told CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour that he was "deeply concerned" about possible interference from the United States in Brazil's democratic election process.
As a counterpoint, the United States spokesperson, Amanda Robertson, denied that the United States or its allies had meddled in Brazilian democracy.
Brazilian Zionist backlash
Political candidates who publicly support Palestine and oppose Israel's genocide in Gaza, like Thiago, are commonly attacked by local Zionist organisations.
These include StandWithUs Brazil and the Brazilian Israelite Confederation (CONIB). Journalist Caio Blinder and academic Samuel Feldberg, who are linked to these organisations, have publicly described Ávila as a "professional activist" whose advocacy is motivated by the pursuit of publicity and political gain.
"This sort of attack is not exclusive to Brazil or to me," Ávila explains.
"They attack all those who report on what is done in Palestine, who report on the genocide, and who report on Zionist infiltration in a wide range of countries — similarly how they attacked United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories, Francesca Albanese, environmental activist Greta Thunberg, and other prominent figures in the debate for Palestinian liberation," he adds.
"I treat these attacks as part of the process. Threats against me and other advocates have increased dramatically, and our democracy has largely deteriorated due to the influence of Trump and Netanyahu. This is evident in the growing number of far-right leaders occupying positions of power. We must confront these hateful ideologies with all our capacity."
Pathway as a social-environmentalist
Despite support from a significant portion of the Brazilian-Palestinian community and his role in past flotillas to Gaza, Ávila rejects claims that his advocacy for Palestine is motivated by political gain.
He says that, in the electoral process, voters will primarily consider his work as a social-environmentalist rather than his activism in defence of the Palestinian people.
He also adds that his candidacy rests on the intersection of social justice and environmentalism, and rejects claims of appropriation, pointing to the recognition of his advocacy by Palestinian-Brazilian organisations such as the Palestinian Federation and the Palestinian Front of São Paulo.
"I've been an activist for 22 years now, and for 22 years I have been fighting against exploitation, oppression, and the destruction of nature in order to build a 'well-living' society," Ávila tells The New Arab.
"Both environmental disaster and the war machine that profits from genocide originate in the same system. American imperialism, which provides over 80% of the bombs Israel uses in Gaza, is also involved in environmental damage all around the world," he adds.
"It's not a coincidence that the US military, as an institution, is one of the most prominent sources of pollution for the whole planet," Ávila adds.
"In Brazil, some right-wing state governments, but also certain so-called progressive ones, purchase weapons, espionage software, drones and hypersurveillance technology from Israel's arms industry. These are, logically, tools used for mass exploitation, agricultural deforestation, poaching, mining and many other destructive practices," Ávila tells The New Arab.
"The billionaires who profit from these violations, and those behind the legal frameworks that allow this technology to flow into Brazil and circulate around the globe, are the same."
With elections approaching on October 4, and the country’s sovereignty to choose its own leaders at stake, the open question remains: will Brazilian voters pick their representatives based on the Brazil they want to build for the future, or on the Brazil foreign powers want to build for them?
Rogger Oliveira is a multimedia journalist covering geopolitics and social issues in the Middle East and North Africa. He has a previous background as a translator and interpreter working in English, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, and French

"Today I truly felt what it means when dreams come true," Li said. "I came here aiming for the gold. I told myself to stay composed and step onto the platform steadily."
Li, the 2024 Olympic champion in the women's +81kg division, withdrew from the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023 because of an elbow injury.
Earlier Tuesday, China's Wu Yan won the women's 86kg title with a total of 273kg.

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China added three more golds in the women's hammer throw, 4x100m mixed relay and women's 800m as athletics concluded Tuesday at the 2026 Asian Games, while the Philippines' Ernest John Obiena set a men's pole vault Games record of 5.91m.
In the women's hammer throw, China's Zhang Jiale set a Games record of 78.27m to win gold, with compatriot Zhao Jie taking silver at 74.83m and Japan's Joy Iris McArthur claiming bronze.
The Chinese duo faced little challenge, as no other contender in the field had a personal best beyond 71 meters.
Zhang said her focus after the Asian Games is now reaching 80 meters, a mark no women's Asian thrower has hit. "My teammate Zhao and I both want to push toward that and bring Asia closer to the world's best," she said.
China then won the 4x100m mixed relay, with Chen Jinfeng, Liu Guoyi, Shi Junhao and Chen Yujie clocking 40.78 seconds. Thailand took silver and India bronze.
It was the third gold of the Games for Chen, who had already won the women's 100m and the women's 4x100m relay, along with a silver in the 200m.
Chen said running the anchor leg from behind was one of the more nerve-testing moments of her Games, but she trusted her technique.
"I've raced the Thai anchor before, so I know her rhythm well. As long as I could beat her over the final 100 meters, I knew we'd be fine," she said.
"What I achieved at the Games is a real motivator. Now that it's done, I can already start looking ahead to the next one," she said.
In the men's pole vault, Obiena was the only competitor to clear 5.75m. After two failed attempts at 5.80m, he raised the bar to 5.91m and cleared it to break the Games record and take gold. China's Li Chenyang and Yao Jie finished second and third.
Uzbekistan's Sayfullaeva Barnokhon cleared a personal best of 1.90m to win the women's high jump. Kazakhstan's Kristina Ovchinnikova took silver and India's Pooja took bronze, while China's Lu Jiawen and Jin Ruoxuan finished fourth and 10th, respectively.
In the women's 800m, China's Wu Hongjiao won gold in 2:04.49, ahead of Bahrain's Nelly Korir and the Philippines' Victoria Bossong.
Running from a boxed-in position, Wu moved up early and, with no one willing to push the pace, settled into a rhythm that suited her.
"Everyone seemed to be waiting, so I just ran however felt comfortable," she said, adding that nerves only crept back in the final 100 meters.
It was Wu's first Asian Games title after years of near-misses. "I figured if I beat the faster entries, that's a breakthrough. If I ran a personal best instead, that's a breakthrough too," she said.
Looking ahead, Wu said Asian middle-distance runners need to "dare to believe" they can compete with the world's best.
In the men's 800m, Japan's Ko Ochiai set a Games record of 1:44.48 to win gold, ahead of Iran's Ali Amirian and Qatar's Abubaker Abdalla. China's Xi Xiaoheng finished fourth.
Bahrain's Birhanu Balew won the men's 5,000m in 13:30.79, ahead of Japan's Tomonori Yamaguchi and India's Gulveer Singh.
India won the women's 4x400m relay, with Bahrain second and China third. Host Japan closed out the athletics program with gold in the men's 4x400m relay, ahead of Qatar for silver and India for bronze. ■

Symposium held to mark birth centenary of former senior Chinese legislator

Zhao Leji, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the National People's Congress (NPC) Standing Committee, attends a symposium to commemorate the 100th birth anniversary of Zou Jiahua, a late senior national legislator, in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 29, 2026. Zhao met with Zou's family ahead of the symposium. (Xinhua/Liu Weibing)
BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- A symposium was held in Beijing on Tuesday to commemorate the 100th birth anniversary of Zou Jiahua, a late senior national legislator.
Zhao Leji, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the National People's Congress (NPC) Standing Committee, attended the event and met with Zou's family ahead of the symposium.
The event hailed Zou as an outstanding CPC member, a time-tested and loyal communist fighter, and a proletarian revolutionary.
At the symposium, Vice Premier Zhang Guoqing, also a member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, paid tribute to Zou's life and called on people to learn from his political character, work style, striving spirit, and fine conduct.
The event was presided over by Ding Zhongli, vice chairman of the NPC Standing Committee.
During his life, Zou served as a member of the Political Bureau of the 14th CPC Central Committee, vice premier of China's State Council, and vice chairman of the Ninth NPC Standing Committee. ■
