Australian doctors censored for trying to speak about Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:32:13 UTC
21:32:13 KST

Breadcrumb
'We have been silenced': Australia doctors battle censorship on Gaza
Australian doctors are pushing back against a growing pattern of censorship of pro-Palestinian voices in the country’s healthcare system, after hospitals repeatedly cancelled events featuring medical professionals who have worked in Gaza or spoken about the devastation of its healthcare system amid Israel's genocidal war.
There are now calls for an investigation into restrictions on discussions of Palestine in Australian hospitals, with medical professionals warning that the pattern is preventing doctors from sharing first-hand experiences of treating Palestinian children and working inside Gaza’s devastated hospitals.
Perth Children’s Hospital (PCH) cancelled a ‘Children and War’ event just days before it was due to take place on 17 September, after senior management raised concerns about a perceived “pro-Palestinian bias” and discussed preventing Jewish staff from being “upset” by the session, Dr Sue Wareham told The New Arab.
The event was due to feature doctors with experience in Gaza, Afghanistan and Congo discussing the impact of armed conflict on children, but Wareham said Palestine became a central concern behind the hospital’s decision to pull the session.
Wareham, president of the Medical Association for Prevention of War (MAPW) Australia, told TNA that she was scheduled to speak at the event.
However, hospital management explicitly cited concerns about Palestine when explaining the cancellation.
“The initial reason I was told (on 12 September) for the cancellation was that there was concern about there being ‘any perception of pro-Palestinian bias’,” Wareham said.
“When I rang the Executive Director of Medical Services on 15 September, she repeated that concern to me and mentioned the need to prevent Jewish staff members being upset by the discussion.”
Emails shared with TNA reveal that PCH Executive Director of Medical Services Dr Clare Matthews reaffirmed her decision to cancel the session in writing on 11 September, while describing it as a “‘not now’, rather than a ‘not ever’ decision”.
Matthews also referred to the need to “address any perception of bias towards a pro-Palestinian position” before holding any future discussion, according to the correspondence.
The hospital has yet to announce another date for the event.
Wareham said Matthews had promised to respond to her concerns in writing but had not done so.
“Dr Matthews said she would reply in writing to my message, but I have not yet received anything in writing from her,” she told TNA.
Doctors push for investigation
Doctors are now pushing for scrutiny of a broader pattern of Palestinian voices and experiences being shut out of Australian healthcare institutions.
Wareham disclosed to TNA that MAPW sent Western Australia Health Minister Meredith Hammat a letter last Thursday raising concerns about PCH’s decision and its implications for medical education about children living through armed conflict.
Wareham described the cancellation as part of “a wider pattern of racism against Palestinian people”.
“The cancellation is a deeply disturbing politicising of the health and welfare of children,” she told TNA.
“When an event is cancelled on the basis of nationality – in this case so that the plight of Palestinian children remains hidden – this is a very dark development for the health professions.”
Trauma surgeon Martin Jarmin and general surgeon Dr Farah Abdul Aziz were also due to discuss their experiences working or volunteering across conflict zones including Afghanistan and the Democratic Republic of Congo as well as Gaza.
Wareham said organisers wanted to educate hospital staff about the dangers facing children in wars and the ethical responsibilities of medical professionals to protect them.
“One purpose was to alert hospital staff to the dangers faced by children in war zones and our professional and ethical responsibilities to speak out for their protection,” she said.
“An additional purpose was to provide some context for the clinical care of refugee children and adolescents in Australia (of whom there are over 5,000 in Perth alone) to help in their clinical care.”
Emails seen by TNA also detailed the proposed programme for World Patient Safety Day. Dr Mairead Heaney, a Perth-based paediatric anaesthetist and member of Doctors for Palestine, was due to coordinate the session.
Gaza surgeon planned to describe reality inside devastated hospitals
Abdul Aziz, a general surgeon who volunteered in Gaza, told TNA that she planned to show colleagues the severe injuries suffered by Palestinian children and the long-term physical and psychological consequences of Israel’s war.
She intended to “exemplify the cases that the doctors there and the volunteer doctors were dealing with and the injuries sustained by the children with short and long term psychological and physical effects”.
Her presentation would also have given medical staff a first-hand account of working inside Gaza’s devastated healthcare system, where doctors have operated through blackouts, damaged hospitals and acute shortages of basic equipment.
She planned to describe “the conditions that we were operating in, half bombed hospitals, blackouts, damaged equipments, doing bowel surgery with no staplers, minimal equipment and how as doctors we had to go back to basics and operate without our ‘toys’”.
Abdul Aziz also intended to discuss treating patients with multiple traumatic injuries and carrying out damage-control surgery, which she said would have provided valuable clinical education for surgeons attending the event.
Instead, PCH cancelled the session three days before it was due to take place, she said.
“We can’t discuss the medical consequences, treatment, prevention strategy etc. when it comes to Palestinian refugee children as we have been silenced and cancelled every time we try,” Abdul Aziz told TNA.
Gaza healthcare talks repeatedly cancelled
Wareham said PCH was not an isolated case, pointing to previous cancellations at Fiona Stanley Hospital in Murdoch, Western Australia, and the Royal Children’s Hospital in Melbourne involving events where doctors were due to discuss healthcare crises in Gaza and other war zones.
“In every case the cancellation has clearly been linked to the inclusion – in panels of diverse speakers with different perspectives – of medical doctors who have spoken out against the catastrophic destruction of health care in Gaza,” Wareham said.
“No other area of healthcare has been subject to such silencing.”
The string of cancellations has fuelled calls for scrutiny over whether Australian medical institutions are disproportionately restricting discussion of Palestinian suffering and the destruction of Gaza’s healthcare system.
MAPW is now pressing for action over the PCH cancellation, while Wareham’s letter to Hammat raises questions about the implications for medical education and healthcare professionals’ ability to discuss the treatment of children affected by war.
The New Arab contacted PCH and Western Australia Health Minister Meredith Hammat for comment but had not received a response at the time of publication.

Iranians stock up on food and medicine as fears of new US fighting grow
Stockpiling and calls for military action are among signs of increasing precarity as economy conditions worsen.
Tehran, Iran – Iranians are stocking up on food and medicines as fears grow that the country will face dire shortages as the United States tightens an embargo on the country.
The Iranian government had managed to keep household staples flowing during the early months of the war. But a US naval blockade and pivot to draconian sanctions have led to fears that imports will be limited.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iran touts Hormuz attacks as oil flows increase despite tensions
- list 2 of 3Flights between Iran and Iraq’s Najaf resumes amid US aviation sanctions
- list 3 of 3Iran’s Araghchi meets Qatari mediators as US calls for nuclear talks
More recently, the US announced a ban on Iranian airlines worldwide and is pressing other countries to cut trade ties with Iran in a bid to isolate the country.
Addressing the United Nations General Assembly last week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian condemned Washington for its blockade on his country, saying it will prevent food and medicine from reaching the Iranian people.
On Saturday, US President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s offer for a seven-day truce that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for economic relief and other conditions.
As the war enters its eighth month and hopes for a diplomatic solution dim, Al Jazeera looks at how some Iranians are faring under a US embargo.
Consumers
Tehran’s stores remain stocked, but shoppers are keeping an eye on shop shelves. Their anxiety has deepened since a flurry of social media posts urging people to ensure they have several days of food before a possible new round of fighting with the US.
At one shopping centre, Ali, 51, was loading a trolley packed with rice, flour, pasta, pulses, cooking oil and canned food.
He is stocking up because he is convinced that Iran’s adversary is seeking to “starve” the people to push them to turn on their government.
“This is not a war in the traditional sense. It targets the people to put pressure on the authorities,” he said.
With flights to some nearby countries suspended, imports of certain medicines and mobile phone headsets are hard to find. The prices of those still available in shops have been pushed up.
Haj Pasandideh, a 71-year-old grocer, said he believed warehouses were well-stocked with basic goods at the moment. But the problem lies in the daily price increases due to Iran’s weakening rial, prompting him to bulk-buy goods before the expected hikes.
He sometimes caps cooking oil at one bottle per sale to ensure as many customers can purchase the goods as possible.
Exporters crushed
Farmers are also on edge due to the embargo, unable to ship out their produce and forced to sell to local markets.
The war has worsened the economic situation, even after years of sanctions that have pushed the country from being a regional exporter of agricultural and food products to being one of the region’s main importers.
Mehran, an apple grower, told Al Jazeera that due to the difficulties of exporting, he had sold only a third of this year’s harvest, all of it inside Iran.
Some neighbouring countries have halted trade with Iran in recent months, he said, while trucks now spend days at crossings they once cleared in a day, causing fruit to spoil before it reaches buyers.
“The blockade has not only closed the sea and air but also the land routes but in an undeclared manner,” he said.
Pharmaceutical shortages
The war has also deepened an already-dire shortage of medications. Some pharmacies Al Jazeera visited in southern Tehran had run out of infant formula and dozens of other types of medications.
Although officials have assured Iranians that substitute products were available, pharmacy staff expressed concern about the increasing number of customers searching for infant formula in vain.
“Imported medicines are disappearing fast, and lately people have been coming in to buy certain items before they need them for fear they will run out in future,” Mahsa, a 23-year-old pharmacy assistant, told Al Jazeera.
She said the health authorities had introduced “smart systems” to track the quantity and type of medication each person buys.
Breaking the blockade
The prospect of a prolonged siege and deteriorating economic conditions have driven some Iranians to call for a military solution.
On Tehran’s main thoroughfare, several people told Al Jazeera that another round of fighting with the US was unavoidable. Some urged the government to break the blockade by force before it is tightened further.
Mohsen, a 23-year-old economics student, believes Washington’s goal is to strangle the Iranian economy and the cost will ultimately be felt by Iranian citizens.
Iran possesses many strong cards that it must use to break the air and sea blockade before they develop into a land blockade that would completely choke Tehran, he said.
Alireza Taghavinia, an Iranian international relations expert, told Al Jazeera that the gap between Washington and Tehran was too wide to be bridged. “The siege imposed by force will only be lifted by force,” he said.
In a worst-case scenario, falling living standards could bring protesters onto the streets, he added.
“The enemy is counting on stirring up chaos inside Iran because it believes no military strike will achieve its objectives without internal unrest,” he said.

What trap? US-China relations show conflict is far from inevitable

US Republicans Weren’t Happy With Trump’s Hosting of Xi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:30:00 UTC
21:30:00 KST

Surrounding Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington, D.C. – capped by a summit at the White House with U.S. President Donald Trump – was a spate of commentary from both sides of the political aisle. Clearly, not everyone was convinced of the need for Xi to visit in the first place.
Even Trump loyalists such as Louisiana Senator John Kennedy spoke out against having Xi at the White House. One of the Senate’s most colorfully spoken members, Kennedy made his point of view known in no uncertain terms, speaking on the Will Cain show.
Kennedy opined: “All four of them are the same. It’s like the same hooker in different dresses. They all lie like time share salesmen. You can’t trust ‘em. You can’t turn your back on any of ‘em, even if I thought, I knew they were two days dead.”
Kennedy was referring to the leaders of China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia – Xi Jinping, Masoud Pezeshkian, Kim Jong Un, and Vladimir Putin, respectively.
Kennedy went on to dub the quartet “a colony of reptiles,” giving Xi pride of place as the “chief reptile” and “quarterback.”
Taking a more serious approach from his powerful perch as chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, Mississippi Senator Roger Wicker, also a strong Trump supporter, forcefully stated his opposition to the state visit and summit. From the Senate floor, Wicker said, “Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party.”
The Senate Armed Services Committee carries enormous influence and prestige in Washington and beyond, and Wicker used that platform to call out Trump’s decision to bring Xi to Washington, and roll out the red carpet for him.
Key among the core functions of the committee itself is responsibility for aeronautical and space activities associated with the development of weapons systems, and for the Departments of Defense, Army, Navy, and Air Force. It also oversees military research and development.
With that authority behind him, Wicker said, “I want to take a moment to suggest a list of topics that the president might mention during the summit.”
“This summer,” he continued, “it was all over the press that China gave Iran satellite imagery intelligence, and that intelligence led to the death of American troops. So I would certainly suggest that the president try to get an answer to that.”
Wicker’s list continued. He wanted answers on the plight of the Uyghur people, along with Tibetan Buddhists, Christians, and Falun Gong practitioners. “Why not suggest,” Wicker reflected, “releasing all imprisoned Christians and allowing all people of whatever faith to worship freely?”
Finally, Wicker listed the abuses by China of its neighbors, of Taiwan, of Hong Kong, of African nations, of dissidents, and of Jimmy Lai, the 78-year old former Hong Kong newspaper publisher who ran afoul of security laws pushed through by Beijing and who is now serving a 20-year sentence for sedition and collusion with foreign forces.
Wicker continued, “During every minute of dialogue, our commander in chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America.”
Joining the chorus, North Carolina Republican Senator Thom Tillis told CBS News on September 24 – the day of the summit and state dinner – that Trump’s hosting of Xi was “bad timing.”
Calling the meeting a “WTF moment,” Tillis questioned why Xi had received a red-carpet welcome that surpassed those given to traditional U.S. allies.
Axios reported that Tillis was “worried about the trend of spending more time with despots and less time with democratic leaders of nations.”
“It’s not that Xi Jinping is coming here to learn how to become a democratic, capitalist nation,” Tillis said. “Xi Jinping is trying to understand how his opposition will ultimately embrace their worldview.”
Tillis went on to question what prompted the “sea change” he sees in Trump’s posture toward China after years of pledging to take a hard line against Beijing.
The White House downplayed the criticism from the Republican senators, with spokeswoman Anna Kelly pointing out that Trump was “reciprocating” the “hospitality” Xi showed when Trump visited China in May.
It could be argued that it is less hypocritical to honor Xi with a state dinner than not. The reasons are myriad. From 1990 through 2020, the United States invested $284 billion into Xi’s country, not including venture capital. And, according to the Global Times, there are over 84,000 U.S.-invested companies in China.
Notably, the United States has educated over 3 million Chinese students since visas became available in the late 1970s.
And, as strong as the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is, its belief and behavioral systems have had to radically alter in order to build an economy that serves the people well enough to keep the CCP in power.
The CCP has had to abandon the command economy that is central to communist countries in favor of a fusion economy that blends state-owned enterprises, private domestically owned enterprises, and importantly, foreign-owned enterprises. It is the latter, the foreign-owned enterprises, that have brought about profound changes to the mindset and living standards of much of the Chinese population. By manufacturing in China products never seen before in the country, whether for domestic use or export, or both, China experienced a rapid modernization by exposure to the products themselves, the processes and standards of quality required to manufacture them, and the labor standards and management styles that make those businesses profitable.
Perhaps, then, instead of focusing on a state dinner for a Chinese leader little trusted in the United States, it is more fitting to view that dinner and the pomp and ceremony that surrounded it as a state dinner in honor of the Chinese people. They have had to put up with a lot, and still do. They may not have had a seat at the table in the White House, but they will have viewed with pride the American treatment of a Chinese leader. Diplomatically, and historically, that goes a long way.

SpaceX's Starship engine failure could cause problem for NASA's 2028 moon mission objectives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:29:52 UTC
21:29:52 KST

The Starship engine failure that nearly foiled the orbital debut of SpaceX's next-generation spacecraft on its 14th uncrewed test flight may complicate NASA's ability to meet its time frame for astronaut missions to the moon.
Starship, designed in part to carry large payloads to space, is one of two vehicles vying to become the first craft that NASA will use as early as 2028 to land humans on the moon and bring them safely home, a feat last achieved in 1972 at the end of the Apollo era.
While Starship accomplished a number of key objectives in its latest test launch from Texas on Monday, the mission was cut short by several hours after a malfunction of its propulsion system.
Despite the unexpected shutdown of one of its three main Raptor engines following Starship separation from its lower-stage booster rocket, flight controllers proceeded with sending the spacecraft to orbit for its first-ever commercial satellite deployment.
Determining what caused the engine glitch remains critical to SpaceX's bottom line. But the stakes are potentially higher for NASA, as a Starship moon-landing vehicle would rely on the same engine system for transporting astronauts through space to and from the lunar surface.
How big a blow to Starship's development progress the engine snafu becomes depends on whether it turns out to be "a one-off failure of a single part" or points to a larger design problem that requires upgrades "across the fleet," said Dean Sladen, an aerospace engineer for Accu Components.
"Any engine fix that holds up the next flights, including the planned attempt to catch the ship with the launch tower's arms (after re-entry), eats into that schedule," he said.
NASA and SpaceX did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
'The real pressure is the moon'
A longer delay would pose not only a greater setback to SpaceX's commercial ambitions to rapidly expand its Starlink broadband satellite network, but its pivotal role in NASA's Artemis moon program.
"The real pressure is the moon. NASA needs Starship for Artemis III," an Earth-orbit test mission targeted as soon as next summer as a rehearsal flight for the program's actual first crewed lunar landing, Sladen said.
Raptor engine and propulsion-system issues have contributed to several previous Starship setbacks, including an engine that failed to ignite as planned during Starship's 12th flight in May. The methane-fueled engines are among the most complex and expensive components on the rocket.
During some previous flights, SpaceX scrubbed plans to test-ignite the Raptor engine in space. But all of the engines successfully fired during ascent on Starship's 13th flight in July.
SpaceX, the newly public venture founded by Elon Musk near Los Angeles in 2002, is competing with Blue Origin, the rival rocket company from fellow entrepreneur Jeff Bezos, to usher in an era of lunar exploration under NASA's Artemis program.
While SpaceX was originally contracted to provide the first crewed lunar lander for Artemis, the head of the US space agency, Jared Isaacman, said in April that NASA would go with whichever lander was ready to fly first. NASA saw the added competition as healthy for progress in light of mounting delays in Starship's test flight program.
NASA hopes to return to the moon's surface by 2028
NASA officially aims to return astronauts to the moon's surface by 2028 - a target widely seen as overly ambitious - to get there ahead of China, which plans a crewed lunar landing by 2030.
A functioning lunar landing craft also will be needed for the precursor Artemis III mission, as early as summer 2027, to test rendezvous and docking maneuvers in low Earth orbit.
SpaceX is developing a Human Landing System based on its Starship vessel, a towering stainless-steel vehicle far larger than any moon lander built before. Blue Origin is building its own Blue Moon lander, relying on a more traditional design philosophy.
If ready, both landers are likely to participate in the Artemis III mission, demonstrating orbital maneuvers using their in-space engines.
Isaacman went public with the competing lander strategy days after completion of NASA's Artemis II mission sending astronauts around the moon and back in what was the first crewed launch of NASA's Space Launch System rocket, built by Boeing and Northrop Grumman, and the Orion capsule, made by Lockheed Martin.

Israel should stop treating the Kurds as a temporary ally - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:29:23 UTC
21:29:23 KST

Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar delivered a timely and important message at the first Kurdish-Jewish Conference in London on September 6. He has once again clarified that Israel recognizes the Kurdish historical and ongoing predicament in the Middle East.
Sa’ar went beyond recognition and pointed out that the Kurdish-Jewish relationship in the Middle East is strategic.
His remark highlighted not only the Kurdish-Jewish relationship but also the Kurdish-Jewish alliance, neither invented nor merely a political construct, but a natural alliance rooted in the close ties between the Kurdish and Jewish peoples since the first Jewish deportation by the Assyrians around 720 BCE to Northern Mesopotamia, in contemporary Kurdistan.
This historical Jewish deportation overlaps with the beginning of the Kurdish calendar around 650 BCE.
This encounter laid the foundation for a Kurdish-Jewish relationship that is deeply rooted in the history and collective memory of both peoples.
To honor these close Kurdish-Jewish ties, Kurdish people hope that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as head of the cabinet and ultimate executive authority, will directly echo and institutionalize Sa’ar’s stance to build genuine, lasting trust among the Kurdish people.
Subsequently, Kurdish-Jewish solidarity can move decisively beyond an era in which Kurdish aspirations were treated as convenient rhetorical leverage against Ankara and Tehran rather than as the basis for enduring strategic commitments.
With the belief in this ancient relationship, Kurdish and Jewish academics, civil society representatives, and diaspora activists convened to discuss the shared challenges they face both in their homelands and across the diaspora. The Kurds welcomed the conference and warmly embraced Sa’ar’s message.
Similarly, Israeli media extensively reported on the gathering and its objectives. The conference underscored the strategic relationship between two indigenous peoples of the Middle East and their shared concerns regarding threats emanating from the Sunni and Shi’ite axes.
The strongest headwinds came, unsurprisingly, from the Turkish media and nationalist supporters of the self-appointed monarch Reza Pahlavi, who have circulated distorted narratives about the Kurdish people and their political movements.
These narratives target a people already enduring daily atrocities at the hands of the IRGC and the wider militarized forces of the Mullah regime.
The Kurdish people are a nation of over 50 million whose ancestral homeland was unjustly partitioned between the Iranian Safavid and Ottoman empires in 1639, and later between Arab states and Turkey following the post-World War I settlement of the Middle East in the 1920s.
The Kurds are an indigenous people with their own distinct language, history, culture, and territory, forming an ethnic peoplehood that is neither Turkish, Arab, nor Persian. As a separate nation with its own distinct identity, language, culture, and deep historical roots, the Kurdish people possess every legitimate right to demand full statehood.
Within this framework, self-determination and separatism remain their natural, inherent right under the principle of indigenous sovereignty. The Kurds have been denied their nation-state and, consequently, have suffered multiple genocides, ethnic cleansing, and forced displacement under successive Muslim regimes in Tehran, Ankara, Damascus, and Baghdad.
This history is inseparable from the contemporary debate over Iran. The divisive and accusatory rhetoric of contemporary monarchists recalls, in the eyes of many Kurds, the denial and repressive policies of the grandfather Reza Shah Pahlavi, following the collapse of the Qajar Empire in 1925.
Kurdish demand for recognition
The Pahlavi dynasty pursued a centralized Persian nationalist project that marginalized minority identities, including those of Kurds and Jews. Kurdish demands for recognition of their cultural and linguistic identities were denied.
Kurds were misrepresented as “mountainous Iranian people,” a policy that nationalist Turks adapted earlier in constructing a hegemonized Turkish national state. As part of these measures, Kurdish elites and leaders, including Simko Agha, were assassinated while Kurdish political movements were suppressed.
Jews endured a similar fate under the repression of the Pahlavi era. Jewish leaders suffered a similar fate: as part of Pahlavi’s nationalistic project, Shmuel Haim, a prominent Jewish leader and head of the Iranian Zionist organization, was arrested and executed in 1931 for allegedly promoting Zionist activities and encouraging Jewish emigration to Jerusalem.
The Pahlavi regime’s systematic repression and authoritarian policies toward minority communities had a lasting impact. In 1946, the government of Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the father of the current self-appointed Reza Pahlavi, crushed the short-lived Kurdistan Republic in Mahabad and executed its principal leaders.
The Pahlavi regime continued a repressive and authoritarian policy toward diverse minority communities, including the Kurds, which resulted in the emergence of the current Mullah regime in 1979. The Kurds have again remained a primary target of the new Mullah regime, facing daily executions and repression.
Kurdish leaders and activists have been executed in Iran and assassinated abroad, including in Vienna and Berlin. The regime continually scapegoats Kurds, justifying state crimes by alleging collaboration with Mossad.
The state murder of the Kurdish woman Jina Amini in the custody of Iran’s morality police became a defining example of severe repression against the Kurds. Since the February 28 war within Iran and across Iraqi Kurdistan, the regime has killed over 100 Kurdish people, mostly civilians, and wounded more than 1,000.
While Kurds face extreme atrocities by the Mullah regime, monarchist supporters of Reza Pahlavi attack Kurds in the diaspora and on social media, weaponizing accusations of separatism to delegitimize Kurdish autonomy.
However, they deliberately obscure a vital reality: although national self-determination and statehood remain their fundamental right, Kurdish leadership has actively chosen to pursue a democratic, decentralized, and federal Iran.
Members of the Kurdish coalition, including PDK-I, PJAK, Komala, and PAK, have voluntarily set aside unilateral separation to offer a shared future rooted in regional autonomy, civic equality, and collective liberation.
Similarly, at a Moshe Dayan Center panel, representatives of all Kurdish parties declared their readiness to cooperate with transformative forces, including Israel and the US, on regime change and democratization.
The accusations of separatism and attacks on Sa’ar are calculated attempts by Reza Pahlavi’s followers to create a rift between Kurds and Israel, undermining the forces actively resisting the regime. This divisive, chauvinistic policy fractures opposition solidarity, protects the Mullah regime from imminent collapse, and undermines those fighting for freedom.
Yet Sa’ar’s message in London was significant precisely because it recognizes the reality that Kurds and Jews, two peoples with ancient roots in the Middle East, have common interests in defending their identity, security, and peaceful future.
Strengthening the Kurdish-Jewish relationship is strategically important in confronting the challenges posed by authoritarianism and repression in the region.

Swiss archaeologists redraw Roman maps after drought discoveries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:27:53 UTC
21:27:53 KST

Swiss archaeologists redraw Roman maps after drought discoveries
AVENCHES, Switzerland, Sept 29 - Archaeologists are redrawing Roman maps of Switzerland after traces of long-buried ruins emerged as the country endured the hottest summer on record.
Drought can reveal hidden archaeological sites through "parch marks" created when vegetation above them withers, one of several effects of this year's heatwaves, which also exposed World War Two wrecks on river beds.
Alerted by a history enthusiast, archaeologists in the Swiss canton of Vaud used a drone to take daily images of fields around Aventicum, the former capital of Roman Helvetia, founded 2,000 years ago after Julius Caesar defeated local tribes. It is now the site of the small town of Avenches.
"These are the richest discoveries made there in the last 50 years, at least over the last two generations of archaeologists," said Jordan Anastassov, archaeologist for Vaud.
The images revealed traces of thermal baths, houses, roads and a possible temple that were previously unknown or dimly understood, many in never-before-excavated areas of the city, which thrived under Roman rule before gradually fading as Germanic incursions increased from the third century onward.
The team of five archaeologists superimposed the discoveries onto maps in purple, filling blank spaces and correcting mistaken markings.
"We are now asking really interesting questions we wouldn't otherwise be asking," said archaeologist Hugo Amoroso.
Some of the traces captured from June to August vanished after mowing and with lower temperatures, but the perimeter of a new pool in the baths is still visible in a partially withered alfalfa field as unseasonably warm weather has persisted in September.
Other buried historical remains have emerged elsewhere in Switzerland and Europe, but many are harder to interpret because they are isolated and lack dedicated researchers.
The Swiss archaeologists will present their findings to peers and may conduct targeted digs later.
"We aren't going to wish for droughts," said Pierre Blanc, director of excavations for the site. "But we're going to make the most of this and keep looking." REUTERS

Economic Watch: Multinationals double down on R&D in China to serve global markets
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
20:27:43 CST
21:27:43 KST

CHONGQING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- As foreign companies race to deepen their R&D footprint in China, tech firm HP has opened a new AI innovation center in southwest China's Chongqing Municipality, underscoring a broader shift from manufacturing to locally rooted research and development with global reach.
"Manufacturing was the starting point of our partnership. Innovation is its future," said Jonathan Jennings, HP's global chief procurement officer.
HP's launch of the new China AI innovation center reflects a wider trend among foreign companies operating in China. For decades, the country was best known as the world's factory, where global manufacturers built vast production lines to serve overseas markets. Now, many multinationals are moving research, design and product development closer to Chinese customers, suppliers and engineers, embedding innovation in China to serve global markets.
The scale of this shift is visible in data. Figures released by the Ministry of Commerce show that by the end of March 2026, Beijing was home to 332 foreign-funded R&D centers, with 55 added this year. Shanghai hosted 647, with 15 new ones established in the same period.
A recent survey of multinational executives in China revealed that 42 percent of companies plan to invest in China-based R&D that serves global markets over the next two years.
"Many multinationals' manufacturing bases in China are being upgraded into sources of innovation," said He Yadong, spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce, citing recent R&D investments by companies such as AstraZeneca, Philips and Schneider Electric.
For many executives, the main reason is speed. Chinese customers, supply chains and engineering teams allow new products to move from concept to market far faster than in many other regions.
"Our customers in China adopt new technologies in about 12 to 14 months, while it can take three to four years elsewhere," said Jerome Dorlack, president and CEO of Adient, a global leader in automotive seating. The company operates three global technology centers in China, including the largest one located in Chongqing.
The talent pool in China is another draw. "China has long emphasized university education for scientists and engineers, and the new generation of Chinese engineers and scientists has a strong mathematical foundation while becoming increasingly creative," said Michael Mertin, CEO of AT&S AG, an Austrian manufacturing company.
This talent advantage is now feeding into artificial intelligence (AI), which has become a focus for foreign companies in China. HP's Chongqing center is developing AI-powered inspection systems, while Adient is using AI vision to identify production defects earlier in the process.
The global reach of China-based R&D is already taking shape. Audi's innovation center in China is engineering luxury vehicles that could feed into Audi's global product portfolio, while Valeo is leveraging its R&D centers in China to deepen local innovation and export self-developed core new-energy technologies worldwide.
Policy support is reinforcing this trend. China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for attracting more foreign companies to establish regional headquarters and R&D centers, with many cities rolling out measures to support these efforts.
"The concentration of foreign R&D centers in China shows the country is moving up the value chain and global production networks are being redrawn," said Wang Lei, a professor at the School of Government of Beijing Normal University. "Deeper integration between foreign and local innovation will raise productivity, strengthen China's role in global innovation, and pave the way for shared growth." ■

Major water conservancy project begins power generation in China's Xinjiang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
20:27:35 CST
21:27:35 KST

URUMQI, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The first batch of generating units of the Dashixia Water Conservancy Project in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region was connected to the grid for power generation on Tuesday, its constructor said.
Located in Wensu Grand Canyon in Xinjiang's Aksu Prefecture, the 247-meter-high dam of this water conservancy hub is currently the world's highest concrete-faced sand-gravel dam, according to the constructor, China Gezhouba Group Co., Ltd.
When fully operational, the hub can generate over 1.89 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, capable of meeting the electricity needs of approximately 600,000 households.
It will also channel 3.42 billion cubic meters of water to the Tarim River each year, easing water shortages on more than 6.8 million mu (about 453,333 hectares) of farmland, while significantly boosting flood control capacity and greatly advancing agricultural modernization in southern Xinjiang.
During the construction process, blockchain technologies were applied to collect concrete data and manage transportation, making project quality controllable and traceable, noted Song Xiaojian, the project manager.
To mitigate the impact of the project on fish, the constructor also invested 65 million yuan (around 9.64 million U.S. dollars) in various ecological protection measures, which went into operation ahead of schedule, according to Yang Yanling, who is with the project's quality and environmental protection department.
So far, a total of 141,000 fish have been released through artificial propagation, Yang added. ■

TEKNOFEST Southeast to open Wednesday in Türkiye's Sanliurfa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:27:19 UTC
21:27:19 KST

Rauf Maltas, Cebrail Caymaz and Gizem Nisa Demir
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
The world's largest aviation, space and technology festival, TEKNOFEST, will open its doors to visitors Wednesday at Sanliurfa GAP Airport in Türkiye under the name TEKNOFEST Southeast, with the five-day event expected to feature air shows, technology competitions, exhibitions and educational activities.
The festival, which has welcomed nearly 12 million visitors since its launch, will be held from Sept. 30 to Oct. 4 in Sanliurfa, a southeastern province of Türkiye.
Anadolu is the festival's "Global Communications Partner."
Organized under the leadership of the Turkish Industry and Technology Ministry, the T3 Foundation, and Defense Technologies Engineering and Trade Inc. (STM), the festival will cover an area of 191,000 square meters at Sanliurfa GAP Airport.
Air shows, exhibitions and activities for all ages
TEKNOFEST Southeast will bring together activities for visitors of all ages throughout the five-day event.
The festival will feature air shows by Türkiye’s leading aviation and defense platforms, including SOLOTURK and the Turkish Stars, as well as fighter aircraft.
Visitors will also have the opportunity to see ATAK helicopters, HURKUS, ANKA, Bayraktar TB2, Bayraktar TB3, and Bayraktar AKINCI, alongside land and naval vehicles.
The program will include concerts, stage performances, exhibitions, educational workshops, simulation areas, a planetarium, science shows, the TEKNOFEST Time Tunnel, displays of domestically developed land, naval and air vehicles, trade fair activities and special first-flight experiences for students.
More than 1.6M contestants applied from 99 countries
TEKNOFEST Southeast will feature technology competitions aimed at supporting technological development in critical fields, with teams that advance through the preliminary stages receiving financial and other forms of support.
More than 1.6 million contestants and hundreds of thousands of teams applied to the technology competitions held as part of TEKNOFEST Southeast. Of more than 730,000 teams that applied, 2,000 advanced to the finals.
Successful contestants will receive more than 100 million Turkish liras in total support.
Applications to this year's TEKNOFEST Technology Competitions came from 99 countries, including the US, France, China and Japan.
Eleven new categories were added, including 5G, the Artificial Intelligence and Smart Road Safety Competition, the Technological Applications in Combating Addiction Competition and the Electronic Warfare Competition.
Finals of 14 technology competitions to be held in Sanliurfa
The finals of technology competitions in 14 categories will be held in Sanliurfa as part of TEKNOFEST Southeast.
These include the Technological Applications in Combating Addiction Competition, organized by the Turkish Green Crescent Society; the Blockchain Competition, organized by the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Türkiye (TUBITAK); the Steel Dome Air Defense Systems Competition and Mobile Satellite Terminal Competition, organized by ASELSAN; the Financial Technologies Competition, organized in cooperation with Takasbank and the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye; the HackMasters Southeast Competition, organized by the Cybersecurity Presidency; the International Invention Competition under ISIF, organized by the Turkish Patent and Trademark Office; the Mining Technologies Competition, organized by Turkish Gold Inc.; the Architectural and Visual Design Competition, organized by KUME Foundation; the 3T in Oncology Competition, organized by Cansagligi; the Agricultural Technologies Competition, organized by Bilişim Vadisi and TUME; the TEKNOFEST Drone Championship and World Drone Cup, organized by STM; and the TEKNOFEST Robolig Competition, organized by the T3 Foundation.
Online registration required
Admission to TEKNOFEST Southeast is free, but visitors must register online to enter the festival grounds.
Visitor entry and exit will be available between 9 am and 7 pm local time each day. Organizers recommend using public transportation to reach the festival area for faster and easier access.
Further information about TEKNOFEST Southeast and visitor registration is available at www.teknofest.org.

====================================================================================================

The horseshoe alliance: How America’s hard-left, far-right are converging on key issues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:22:45 UTC
21:22:45 KST

The political divide in a deeply polarised American society is becoming increasingly blurred as the country heads to crucial midterm elections that could impact the balance of power in Congress.
Progressive lawmakers with positions typically associated with the hard-left end of the political spectrum now find themselves in agreement with far-right commentators on a range of issues that have otherwise divided US society for decades.
Be it Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, unconditional military aid to Tel Aviv, yet another US war in the Middle East, the unrestrained power of AI platforms, or the accountability of those involved in Jeffrey Epstein’s paedophilia ring, the two opposite sides of the US political spectrum have taken increasingly identical positions.
The convergence of the ideological opposites has a textbook name: the horseshoe alliance.
It’s a theory derived from the U-shaped horseshoe – where the hard-left and the far-right bend toward each other and, on some key issues, stand closer to one another, far away from the political centre.
The so-called horseshoe alliance in the US is most visible on the issue of Israel’s relentless war in Gaza.
A Pew poll found earlier this year that six in every 10 Americans held an unfavourable view of Israel, including large majorities of Democrats and a rising share of Republicans under the age of 50.
Similarly, a Gallup poll showed that more Americans now sympathised with Palestinians than with Israelis – a first since the polling firm began asking this question in 2001.
Josef Gregory Mahoney, a professor of politics and international relations at East China Normal University in Shanghai, explains the shift through the prism of religion.
“What leads an American Catholic, an American Protestant, an American Jew, or an agnostic or atheist to support or oppose genocide in Gaza can be influenced by personal perspectives on religion,” he tells TRT World.
He says that political commentator Tucker Carlson – who has gained a massive following in the Global South because of his highly critical view of Israel and its expansionist policies – is an Episcopalian Christian who “publicly lauds Catholicism”.
“Both churches, distinct from white evangelicals, have expressed reservations about what Israel has done in Gaza,” he says.
Some American Jews object “either from similar moral concerns” or because they worry that Zionist excesses undermine Israel’s long-term security, he says.
“Most Americans are not that different from each other. It’s often the case that identity politics plays up those differences in extreme ways,” he says.
Douglas Rossinow, a history professor at Metro State University in Minnesota, says the political shift is generational, but other factors have also contributed to it.
Older members of the Democratic Party have indeed changed their view of Israel, he tells TRT World.
“For the Democrats, it is the party elites versus the party supporters on a popular level where Israel/Palestine is concerned,” he says.
That shift in public sentiment has finally reached Congress. In July, the House of Representatives rejected an amendment by Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky to end $3.3 billion in aid to Israel.
The move failed, but as many as 104 Democrats voted for the cut – a nearly three-fold increase from only 37 Democrats who backed a similar effort only two years ago.
According to Mahoney, the political overlap matters because it punctures the old claim that criticism of Israel’s war is a “fringe” position.
But he warns that the shift should not be construed as a new policy altogether.
“MAGA as a governing project is not an anti-Zionist project,” he says, while referring to the make-America-great-again movement that helped bring the Republican Party to power.
“Parts of it will still arm Israel… Other parts will say America First and mean: stop writing the cheques,” he says.
“Palestine should treat the second group as a tactical opening, not as a comrade,” he adds.
Rossinow says the future of US-Israel relations remains uncertain despite the emerging horseshoe alliance.
More important than any left-right partnership is the “broader alienation” of the general public from Israel, he notes.
“The Republicans have not faced as serious a backlash on this issue from primary voters yet, despite the prominence of Tucker (Carlson) and (Steve) Bannon,” he says, while referring to the two far-right pundits, who have railed against Israeli premier Benjamin Netanyahu for influencing US foreign policy.
Iran war: A betrayal of America First?
The Iran war is another flashpoint where the far-right and hard-left seem to be converging.
Isolationist voices on the Republican right have called the war a betrayal of “America First” because they believe Washington acted solely to protect Israeli interests.
On the left, anti-war progressives have opposed it as another imperial project meant to reorganise countries thousands of miles away.
Polls show the war is unpopular with a majority of Americans and especially with younger Republican voters.
But Mahoney warns against confusing this phenomenon with any well-thought-out strategy.
“They share a refusal to open another expensive war, while the domestic order is already straining,” he notes.
The overlapping positions in the two camps can “cancel a march to Tehran in a given month”, but are not enough to lift sanctions or produce a permanent settlement.
Rossinow describes the Iran war as one more source of “bitter disillusionment” among MAGA supporters, who had believed earlier Republican promises of non-intervention in the Middle East.
“The war against Iran was another betrayal,” he says.
United against AI oligarchs
The newest meeting point for the far-right and hard-left in the US is Big Tech.
Bannon, the far-right strategist, and Senator Bernie Sanders, a self-declared democratic socialist, spoke back-to-back at the same Washington conference on September 15 to condemn AI “oligarchs” and demand tighter control of the emerging technology.
They did not endorse one another’s programmes, even though each of them criticised the same AI platforms.
For Mahoney, Sanders’s position on AI is framed around “class and accountability” questions.
But Bannon’s scepticism of AI platforms is based on his views about “sovereignty and anti-oligarchy”, Mahoney says.
“They are not building a joint programme. They are hitting the same firms because those firms now sit on labour, information, and the means of political speech,” he says.
More than an electoral tactic?
Is the horseshoe alliance part of a tactical restructuring in the run-up to the mid-term elections?
Mahoney disagrees, saying it is not merely a midterm tactic.
“Tactics are there – they always are – but they are not what produced the overlap,” he says.
“There is no joint party, no shared theory of the state, no common programme for Palestine, Iran, or the dollar,” he notes.
What exists is a “conjunctural convergence” that can be “electorally useful” in 2026.
“It is not an electoral invention,” he says.
Rather, the overlap has imperial and fiscal roots.
“The US is having more difficulty sustaining imperial prerogative and paying off the domestic coalition that used to receive the spoils,” he notes.
When that happens, the opposing wings of the political spectrum discover that they can speak on the same stage “without first becoming friends”.
Rossinow says he is sceptical that the shift will last long.
That’s because the patterns of partisanship for party establishments are deeply ingrained, he says.
“Most of those on the US left do not want a left-right alliance,” he says, adding that cooperation on non-intervention, Epstein files, and even AI remains possible.
“But this will be sporadic,” he adds.
For the Global South, Mahoney’s advice is straightforward: do not mistake a crack in the US consensus for a new policy.
“Some Americans notice the moral obscenity. Some notice the fiscal and military overstretch. A few notice both. That is the horseshoe,” he says.
The horseshoe can constrain the worst impulses of the centre, he notes.
However, the horseshoe alliance cannot end Zionism as a political project, or defend Iran, he insists.
“Those remain tasks for the peoples actually under the bombs and the sanctions,” he says.

"After deliberate consideration of Christa Gail Pike’s request for clemency, and after a thorough review of the case, I am upholding the sentence of the State of Tennessee and do not plan to intervene," Gov. Bill Lee said in a statement released Monday.
Pike, 50, faces lethal injection at 10 am local time (1500GMT) at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. She was convicted and sentenced to capital punishment in 1996 for the 1995 slaying of Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville, remaining the only female prisoner on the state's death row.

A pending Supreme Court petition does not automatically stop an execution.

Private sector’s 5 demands for expansion of export
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:13:08 UTC
21:13:08 KST

Private sector’s 5 demands for expansion of export
TEHRAN- A member of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, emphasizing that the main problem of Iran’s exports is not a lack of production capacity, deemed it necessary to reform trade processes, reduce transaction costs, and create infrastructure for a sustainable presence in foreign markets.
Shahla Amouri, President of the Ahvaz Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, said that the problem of Iran’s exports is not a lack of production capacity; the problem is the inability to convert this capacity into a sustainable presence in the market. An economy that has supply capacity—from energy and raw materials to industrial and agricultural products—can use foreign trade for growth when an Iranian firm can deliver its product to the customer at a predictable cost, through a clear process, and in competitive time. The gap between these two points is where a significant part of Iran’s economic advantages is eroded.
Between producing a good and selling it sustainably in a foreign market lies a chain of decisions and processes: from financing and regulations to transportation, standards, insurance, market information, and distribution networks. Weakness in any link destroys part of the advantage created at the production stage.
In today’s trade, a foreign customer does not buy only goods; they also buy reliability. Continuous supply, consistent quality, on-time delivery, predictable prices, and after-sales services are part of the value of a transaction. Therefore, successful export is not the result of a single deal; it is the result of building trust and continuity in a trade relationship.
Khuzestan is a clear example of this reality. Having ports, a land border with Iraq, access to open waters, and diverse industrial and agricultural capacities has placed this province in a position where it can be one of the drivers of the country’s regional trade. But geography becomes an economic advantage only when infrastructure and trade governance can turn this capacity into an efficient path for firm activity.
Meanwhile, one of the less-seen issues is the difference between “the possibility of accessing the market” and “the ability to remain in the market.” The initial presence of a good in a foreign market may be formed by a single deal, but its continuation depends on understanding consumer behavior, standards, competitors’ prices, distribution channels, import regulations, and supplier credibility. Many small and medium-sized firms do not have regular and usable access to this information.
For this reason, trade development policy must move beyond providing general information and toward trade intelligence. A firm must know, in each target market, what product with what specifications, through what route, and to which customers can be offered. This information must be up-to-date, practical, and convertible into an economic decision.
On the other hand, the country’s foreign trade structure still faces a multiplicity of processes and scattered responsibilities. In a single chain, an exporter encounters multiple institutions and regulations, while the performance of these institutions has not always been designed around a common goal. The result is increased friction along a path that should be predictable for firms.
To reform this situation, five actions must be pursued as a single package: First, reducing administrative friction by integrating systems, exchanging information among agencies, and eliminating parallel controls; second, managing trade time and cost by setting specific indicators for core processes and continuously measuring performance; third, creating shared services for small and medium-sized firms in cargo consolidation, warehousing, packaging, transportation, and specialized consulting; fourth, launching a market intelligence system in border provinces to provide up-to-date information on demand, regulations, competitors, and distribution networks; and fifth, creating a clear mechanism for resolving trade problems by designating the responsible agency, a response deadline, and an evaluable result.
These five axes are in fact five links in a single reform: simplifying the path, reducing transaction costs, enabling the presence of small firms, gaining a more accurate understanding of the market, and turning unresolved issues into cases with a designated responsible party and timeframe.

Pakistan and Terrorism: When the Tables Turn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:12:00 UTC
21:12:00 KST

In his address to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif described Afghanistan as a haven for terrorist groups carrying out attacks against Pakistan. He specifically named Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or the TTP, and the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), and called on the Afghan Taliban to take decisive action to prevent Afghan soil from being used against Pakistan and other countries.
Coming from a Pakistani official, this demand raises many questions. The first is: since when has Pakistan decided that supporting armed groups in a neighboring country is dangerous? When the Taliban were fighting in Afghanistan against the Republic government and the Afghan people were the victims, where was this concern? Why does the same government that supported the Taliban for years now speak about terrorist sanctuaries as though it had no role in creating this situation?
Pakistan’s support for the Taliban is not merely an allegation made by Afghans out of anger or without grounding. Financial support, the training and recruitment of fighters, the transfer of ammunition and fuel, and cooperation between Pakistani military and intelligence officials and the Taliban have been extensively documented over the years by credible international organizations. For much of the last 25 years, Pakistan helped strengthen a force that imposed war and repression on the people of Afghanistan.
The Haqqani network is a clear example of this conduct. Its sanctuaries in North Waziristan and its ties to Pakistan’s intelligence apparatus have been the subject of reports and official objections for years. In 2011, Mike Mullen, then chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, described the network as effectively an arm of Pakistani intelligence, an allegation Islamabad denied. Now that Pakistan is complaining about sanctuaries across the border, it must explain why it refused to meet the same demand regarding the Haqqani network more than a decade ago.
Even after the Taliban returned to power in 2021, then-Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan spoke of Afghans breaking the “shackles of slavery.” The political meaning of this response was clear: the Taliban’s victory was welcomed in Islamabad. But now that the Taliban are not behaving as Pakistan expected, that same victory has become a threat. Has the Taliban’s nature only just become apparent, or has Pakistan’s calculation that it could control the Taliban’s behavior simply proved wrong?
To me, this reversal shows that the central problem is a selective definition of terrorism. When the Taliban were fighting in Afghanistan and helping expand Pakistan’s influence, justifications could be found for supporting them. Now that groups close to the Taliban are fighting against Pakistan, Islamabad is suddenly concerned about sanctuaries, support, and the responsibility of the host state. Human lives should not suddenly become valuable simply because the place where people are killed has changed.
Of course, the people of Pakistan are, indeed, the victims of terrorism. No disagreement with Islamabad’s policies can justify killing Pakistani citizens. The TTP is a real threat and must be confronted. But the same standard must also apply to victims in Afghanistan and India of groups supported by Pakistan. Pakistan’s government cannot use its own people’s suffering to erase its record of supporting forces that have devastated lives in other countries.
Pakistan’s hostility toward the TTP is not new. It has conducted operations against the TTP and other groups that target Pakistan. The issue, therefore, is not that Islamabad has never fought terrorism; it is why its response to armed groups has varied depending on where their attacks are directed. If opposition to terrorism is a matter of principle, networks that recruit fighters, raise funds and organize attacks against neighboring countries must be viewed as equally unacceptable.
As long as this contradiction remains, Pakistan’s statements about terrorism cannot be taken seriously. That can only change if Pakistan moves beyond general statements and actually fights terrorism, something it appears to have no intention of doing. Lashkar-e-Taiba is one of the clearest examples. The U.N. Security Council’s sanctions committee identifies this Pakistan-based group as responsible for numerous attacks against military and civilian targets, including the 2008 Mumbai attacks. The same records identify Jamaat-ud-Dawa, also based in Pakistan, as a front for financing, training and supporting Lashkar-e-Taiba.
Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) is another example. Founded by Masood Azhar after his release from prison in India, the group is on the U.N. sanctions list, too. The Security Council has documented its links with al-Qaida and the Taliban, as well as its role in attacks in Kashmir. In May 2025, JeM was reported to be based in Bahawalpur, in Pakistan’s Punjab province.
Hizbul Mujahideen is another longstanding group active in Kashmir, fighting to end Indian rule and unite the region with Pakistan. According to U.S. State Department reports, the group has carried out numerous attacks against Indian security personnel and politicians and has been involved in abductions and killings. Reports from June 2026 also describe its leader, Syed Salahuddin, as being based in Pakistan.
Harakat-ul-Mujahideen is another example of these cross-border networks. The Security Council’s records identify Muzaffarabad and Rawalpindi as bases for the group and record attacks against military and civilian targets in Kashmir, the training of fighters and cooperation with other groups. The hijacking of an Indian aircraft in 1999 has also been attributed to the group. This history shows that the connection between Pakistan-based groups and violence across the region has not been limited to the Afghan Taliban and stretched across decades.
In April 2025, Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Asif was asked in an interview with Sky News about the country’s history of supporting, training and financing terrorist groups. He replied: “We have been doing this dirty work for the United States for about three decades, and the West, including Britain.” He called this policy a mistake and spoke about its costs for Pakistan. But what about the price the people of Afghanistan have paid? How does pointing to the role of the United States and the U.K. remove the responsibility of Pakistani officials?
If Pakistan wants its words to be taken seriously, it must demonstrate at home the same thing it demands of the Taliban: action against international terrorism and measures that can be verified. The fight against terrorism has credibility when past political ties to a group do not stand in the way of action against it. Pakistan’s statements about terrorism can be taken seriously only when it acts to cut off funding, stop recruitment and dismantle the operational structures of known terrorist groups on its own soil.
Until then, these words will remain just words; neither the problem of terrorism in Pakistan nor the threat that has driven it to make these statements will go away. Otherwise, the very danger then U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton warned about in 2011 will persist: “You can’t keep snakes in your backyard and expect them only to bite your neighbors.”
It is the continuation of this same policy that makes Pakistan’s language about terrorism difficult to take seriously in 2026.
Islamabad wants an end to the threat directed at itself, but it must show that it judges its neighbors’ security by the same standard. Terrorism was no less dangerous or criminal when it helped extend Pakistan’s influence. To give its words credibility, Pakistan must demonstrate that its concern is terrorism itself, even when terrorists are fighting against another country.
So far, what we can see is that Pakistan’s current dispute with the Taliban does not, in itself, mean it has abandoned its longstanding policy of using armed groups to further its aims. The test of change is an end to the logic of using such groups. If Islamabad raises its voice only when these groups defy its wishes, what has changed is the relationship between the patron and the group; the value of human life is still judged by the same selective standard.
Before Sharif describes Afghanistan as a haven for terrorism, he must explain what role his own country has played in bringing Afghanistan to this point. The people of Afghanistan never invited Pakistan to support the Taliban, and they should not now have to pay the price for that failed calculation.

Referring to the increase in the volume of trade exchanges between the two countries, the Minister of Transport and Urban Development said: “In the past six months, despite the problems and conditions caused by the war in the region, we have witnessed an increase in the volume of trade exchanges between Iran and the Republic of Azerbaijan, and we are trying to continue this trend by developing infrastructure and removing obstacles.”
Sadegh, referring to the project to widen the Jolfa–Kalaleh route, said: “The Islamic Republic of Iran is seriously advancing this project, and widening this route can be effective in increasing the transport capacity and volume of trade exchanges between the two countries.”
In conclusion, the Minister of Transport and Urban Development emphasized: “Given the friendly and brotherly relations between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Republic of Azerbaijan, the ground is prepared for further development of cooperation between the two countries in various fields, and we will certainly witness the expansion of bilateral relations and cooperation in the future.”
Back in early September, Farzaneh Sadegh, and Shahin Mustafayev, Deputy Prime Minister of Azerbaijan, held a telephone conversation to review the latest developments in bilateral relations and explore ways to expand economic ties, particularly in transit, energy, and border infrastructure.
According to a report by IRNA from the Ministry of Transport and Urban Development, both sides assessed the growing trend in bilateral relations and emphasized the continuation of high-level consultations.
Farzaneh Sadegh, referring to specialized meetings held in gas, electricity, and transportation sectors, called for accelerating the formation of joint committees to follow up and implement the approvals from these meetings.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development, pointing to the damage caused by recent regional tensions to transportation infrastructure, stated: "Despite existing challenges, the reconstruction of damaged routes has been prioritized and the process of completing ongoing infrastructure projects continues without interruption."
She attributed the strengthening of relations between Tehran and Baku to the will of the presidents of the two countries and the close interaction of executive officials at various levels.
Shahin Mustafayev also expressed satisfaction with the progress of railway projects during the call, stating: "The railway route within Azerbaijan's territory up to the 'Aghband' region has been completed, and with the completion of the section within Iran, we will witness a significant transformation in the region's transit and logistics capacities."
Praising the professional performance of Iran's Ministry of Transport and Urban Development in addressing infrastructure damage, he added: "The Iranian government's determination to revive and activate transit corridors is a commendable approach."
At the end of the call, the two sides exchanged views on the latest regional developments and emphasized deepening strategic and economic cooperation as the main pillar of stability and development in the region.
In a decisive move that signals a new phase in regional economic integration, Iran and the Republic of Azerbaijan are rapidly expanding their bilateral trade and transit cooperation through a series of high-level agreements, infrastructure projects, and customs facilitation measures. The momentum, driven by political will at the highest levels and supported by tangible results at border crossings, positions the two neighbors as strategic partners in connecting the Caucasus, Central Asia, and the Persian Gulf.
At the heart of this economic rapprochement lies the Bileh Savar border crossing in Iran's northwestern Ardabil Province—a 24/7 customs post that has emerged as a vital artery for trade. Over the past year alone, the crossing recorded $268 million in exports, demonstrating its growing capacity to handle increased commercial volumes. This figure is particularly noteworthy given that the period coincided with external pressures and regional instability, underscoring the resilience of Iran's border economy and its ability to maintain trade flows even under challenging circumstances.

Iran, WHO join efforts to eliminate human rabies by 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:07:23 UTC
21:07:23 KST

Iran, WHO join efforts to eliminate human rabies by 2030
TEHRAN – The National Plan for the Elimination of Human Rabies 2026–2030 was formally countersigned at a seminar marking World Rabies Day, hosted by the Ministry of Health and Medical Education's Centre for Communicable Disease Control.
The initiative aims to strengthen national efforts to prevent and ultimately eliminate human rabies through coordinated measures in disease surveillance, prevention, public awareness, and timely access to post-exposure treatment.
Speaking at the event, Dr Jean Jabbour, WHO Representative in the Islamic Republic of Iran, emphasized the need for collaboration across human health, veterinary services, municipalities, communities and other sectors through a One Health approach. He also highlighted timely care after animal bites and dog vaccination as essential measures to prevent rabies deaths
Achieving the goal of zero human deaths from rabies by 2030 requires enhancing collaborations among the health system, veterinary, municipalities, and local communities within the framework of the “One Health” approach, Jabbour stated.
Dog bites contribute to 99 percent of human rabies cases. Despite being fatal, rabies is entirely preventable. However, no single organization can defeat the disease on its own, the health ministry’s website quoted Jabbour as saying.
The official made the remarks on the occasion of World Rabies Day, which is marked on September 28 every year.
Highlighting this year’s World Rabies Day theme, ‘Stronger Together’, he noted that rabies elimination needs ongoing multi-sectoral cooperation among physicians, veterinarians, health staff, municipalities, and local communities.
Referring to the number of animal bites in the country, he said over the past two decades there has been a fivefold increase in the number of reported cases. More than 441,000 individuals bitten by animals were referred to medical centers in the past Iranian year (March 2025 – March 2026). Twenty of them lost their lives, and it could have been prevented. Eleven individuals died without receiving any treatment.
The statistics indicate that, in addition to prompt presentation of the bitten person to medical centers, timely and appropriate post-exposure care and the raise of public awareness are critical, and every case of animal bite must be treated as a medical emergency. When a person is bitten or scratched by an animal, even if the bite looks small, they have to visit a healthcare provider right away, he added.
Noting that approximately four out of every five confirmed rabies deaths in Iran are due to dog bites, Jabbour stated that stray dogs alone account for more than half of these cases, while the rest are attributed to wild animals, including wolves and foxes.
The official underlined the role of One Health strategies for rabies control, including constant vaccination of dogs, effective management of stray dogs, and the promotion of close cooperation among the human health, environmental health, and veterinary sectors, he added.
Lauding the adopted measures in the country, Jabbour said some 729 rabies prevention and treatment centers are operating across the country, and post-exposure care services are provided in all provinces.
Around one million doses of human rabies vaccine and 180,000 vials of anti-rabies serum are procured for the national program, annually; Pasteur Institute of Iran helps diagnose confirmed cases of rabies as well as train physicians and health workers.
The official went on to say that the development of a national strategic document for rabies eradication is also a significant step toward aligning Iran with the global goal of “zero human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030”, adding that the WHO is committed to supporting Iran, through technical assistance and collaboration, in achieving the goal.
Why “Stronger Together”?
The 2026 theme, ‘Stronger Together’, highlights a simple truth: rabies elimination is only possible when we work together.
Expand access to life-saving dog vaccinations.
 
 Improve rabies surveillance and reporting systems.
 
 Strengthen public awareness and education.
 
 Support policies that protect both people and animals.
 
 Build sustainable community-led solutions.
 
 Rabies elimination depends on connected systems. Stronger partnerships create stronger outcomes!
We all have a role to play
From local communities and veterinary professionals to governments, healthcare workers, educators, and global partners, we all have role to play in making a world free from rabies a reality.
Communities: Communities are often the first line of defense against rabies. Education, awareness, and responsible animal care help prevent cases before they happen.
Veterinary Professionals: Mass dog vaccination remains the most effective way to stop rabies at its source.
Healthcare Workers: Timely treatment and accurate diagnosis save lives.
Governments and Policymakers: Strong legislation, investment, and national coordination are essential for long-term progress.
Global Partners: Collaboration across sectors helps share resources, expertise, and solutions that accelerate impact.
One Health in action
Rabies elimination depends on interconnected action. Education, vaccination, surveillance, and legislation cannot work in isolation, they must function as part of one coordinated system.
World Rabies Day 2026 reinforces the importance of a One Health approach, recognizing the connection between human, animal, and environmental health.

Hackers have stolen personal data from 150,000 members of the Jims fitness chain. Parent company Colruyt has confirmed the breach. The data theft dates back to this summer, but its true scale has only now become clear. The chain is now trying to warn all members about potential phishing messages.
Data breach at Colruyt’s Jims fitness chain much larger than thought
Initially, a “malicious party” was said to have been able to download customer data from “a limited group of customers” between 13 and 20 July.
The company added that the accounts affected had since been reset and given extra security measures. Colruyt also reportedly had the fraudulent email addresses and domain names used in the phishing attacks blocked.
Hack larger than anticipated

Their names, addresses, dates of birth, email addresses, membership details and, in certain cases, bank account numbers may have been stolen. The stolen data is already being offered for sale on the dark web. No passwords or health data have been leaked. Furthermore, data from other Colruyt systems is not believed to be affected.
“The Belgian Data Protection Authority was informed within the applicable timeframes, in accordance with legal obligations,” said Colruyt spokesperson Hanne Poppe. “We are also closely monitoring the situation with all parties involved, including the police, with whom we have lodged a formal complaint.”
Warning email on the way
Jims’ members are also due to receive an email today explaining the potential impact of the data breach. In it, Colruyt warns, amongst other things, about malicious emails or text messages.
“As the data in question was made available online, there is a risk that third parties may attempt to use it for fraudulent purposes, such as phishing via email, text message or telephone. As an active member of Jims, we advise you to be particularly vigilant regarding messages referring to your membership, payments, direct debits, refunds or changes to your account.”
