How AI is becoming a new battleground in Israel's election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:20:52 UTC
19:20:52 KST

Breadcrumb
How AI is becoming a new battleground in Israel's election
East Jerusalem - Like a scene from an action movie, Israeli political party leaders Gadi Eisenkot and Avigdor Lieberman descended an elevator shaft, tore off their spy gear, and tried to break into the prime minister’s office.
When their attempts failed, Eisenkot said to Lieberman in Hebrew, “I have the master [key],” and the video cut to Israeli MP and leader of the United Arab List (Ra'am), Mansour Abbas, waving a giant set of pliers with a sinister grin.
In fine print in the top right-hand corner of the video, it reads 'AI: This content was created through a digital medium and is not original.'
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu posted the AI-generated video on his X account with the caption, “Eisenkot will form a left-wing government with [Israeli Democrats’ leader] Yair Golan and the Arab parties”.
It’s one of a myriad of images Netanyahu and other Israeli politicians have shared ahead of Israel’s national elections scheduled for 27 October.
In fact, Netanyahu’s Likud Party leads in the amount of AI-generated content they’ve distributed throughout this election cycle.
According to the “Ze Be AI” project by Israel’s Open University, 13 per cent of content published by politicians and political parties was created with artificial intelligence. Of that number, 70 per cent of the AI content came from Likud.
Highlighting their opponents’ willingness to work with Palestinian parties is a common theme for these AI campaign adverts.
AI becomes a new political weapon in Israel
In a video posted by Itamar Ben Gvir, Israel’s National Security Minister and leader of the Jewish Power Party, former police officer Yoav Segalovitz is seen wearing the flag of the Al-Qassam Brigades, Hamas’ military wing, while handing out pastries to a smiling queue of Palestinian prisoners.
In the preceding scene, Abbas kisses Segalovitz while draping him in the green sash. Segalovitz joined Abbas’ party last month, prompting Ben Gvir to release the AI-generated video with the caption, “Marhaba (hello in Arabic), ya Segalovitz. The Eisenkot brothers and [former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali] Bennett are proud of you,” in Hebrew.
Another AI video, posted by Bezalel Smotrich, Israeli Finance Minister and leader of the Religious Zionism party, portrays a phone conversation between a Palestinian in the occupied West Bank and a Palestinian citizen of Israel, with the West Bank resident warning that Smotrich is going to Judaize the Naqab (Negev) and Galilee, just as he did with the West Bank.
“Over here it is all lost. They don’t let you run wild anymore and build without stopping,” the character, Ahmed, says.
Using AI, Smotrich, Ben Gvir, and Netanyahu are attempting to instil fear in Israeli voters that their opposition - in collaborating with Palestinian parties - will lead to terrorism, and that under their leadership, Israel’s expansionism will thrive.
In response to several controversies surrounding the use of AI-generated campaign materials, including a Likud video showing Eisenkot running into the arms of Abbas after snubbing an individual resembling his son, who was killed in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, authorities have stepped in.
Israel’s Central Elections Committee has mandated the aforementioned AI label to be displayed on all AI-created campaign content that “could appear to have been authentically documented when it was not,” meaning not all AI images have to be disclosed.
“It's not real, it's an AI. So when we cannot tell what is true and what is generated any longer because of AI slop, people’s minds become very weary. They don't have the energy to start determining what is real and what is not,” Dr Sharon Haleva Amir, a communications professor at Bar-Ilan University, told The New Arab.
“What it causes is that you can no longer say what is true and what is false in the general sense - to an ad or a statement or an agenda. You just don't believe anything anymore.”
Changing the way Israelis vote
A month after Israel’s last election, in November 2022, ChatGPT debuted, and subsequently unleashed a swarm of AI tools into the public sphere.
Almost four years later, this is Israel’s first election in the age of AI and will test how much influence the technology has - not just over day-to-day lives, but politics as well.
“These things meddle with your brain in ways that the people don't understand or perceive in real time,” Haleva Amir said. “From a democratic point of view, AI pulls the rug out from under your feet because this is not really your decision. Your mind is being played with.”
And with AI distorting reality, Dr Tal Elovits, a political analyst and communications lecturer at Reichman University, explained it reinforces the scepticism that Israeli society was already experiencing in the aftermath of the coronavirus pandemic and Hamas’ 7 October 2023 attack.
“Conspiracy theories that are blending with political campaigns and with the generated AI content, which looks good, have a tremendous effect,” Elovits said. “It makes the whole information environment become untrustworthy. For the general public, if you don't know where the truth lies, if you don't know how you can search for the truth, it makes political convincing and political competition very, very difficult.”
In addition to increasing the level of distrust in the public, AI also risks compromising election integrity.
“One of the affordances of AI-generated content is that you can prepare a lot of versions. Different people can receive different ads,” Haleva Amir said.
“Like we have with search engine optimisation, today there are also firms that do large language model [LLM] optimisation, and in this way, we cannot even know what people are being fed with because these things are behind the scenes.”
AI has become so advanced that its messages are no longer simply tailored to individual commercial interests.
“We are no longer talking about a single ‘campaign ad’ for everyone, but an emotional pressure point that speaks directly to the fears, anger, or hopes of a specific individual,” Dr Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler, head of the Israel Democracy Institute’s in the Digital Age Program, wrote.
As politicians use AI to influence, Israeli voters are expected to use it in their decision-making.
Through a survey, the Israeli Internet Association found that a quarter of Israelis are considering or intending to use AI to determine who they should vote for.
“If the information is not correct and since people do not check anymore, then the [LLMs] can circumvent the way voters think,” Haleva Amir told The New Arab.
While AI has sparked alarm in the run-up to the election, it also poses a threat on Election Day as robocalls could disseminate false information to voters.
Similar to Netanyahu’s infamous 2015 rallying cry that falsely claimed, “Arab voters are coming out in droves to the polls,” AI bots could spread propaganda designed to manipulate votes.
Possible violations, like these, of the Central Elections Committee’s new AI law can be reported to the committee through a petition and if the material does breach the law, the content will be removed. Experts stress, though, it’s a little too late once the material is published.
“The content itself is already living online. It already has multiplied itself,” Elovits said. “So the damage was already done even before the committee was able to discuss if it's illegal.”
Amid weak election oversight, Haleva Amir advises that the public should become more informed on the capabilities and dangers of AI.
“Laws will not be enough or sufficient because technology always exceeds the law,” Haleva Amir said.
“The real answer to all these things should come from the people…by raising awareness and educating people and giving them tools to criticise and reflect and understand AI literacy.”
Jessica Buxbaum is a Jerusalem-based journalist covering Palestine and Israel. Her work has been featured in Middle East Eye, The National, and Gulf News
Follow her on Twitter: @jess_buxbaum

Era of Iraq without US troops begins as combat presence ends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:20:13 UTC
19:20:13 KST

Breadcrumb
End of an era as US-led coalition forces withdraw from Iraq
Baghdad and other Iraqi provinces hosting military bases used by foreign and US forces are entering a new chapter with the end of the "combat and operational presence" of US forces and the international coalition.
Baghdad no longer has any field barracks or combat camps after Lt Gen Abdul Amir Al-Shammari, director of the office of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces and head of the Iraqi government, announced that the Victory military base, located near Baghdad International Airport west of the capital, is now completely free of US personnel as part of the withdrawal of foreign forces from Iraq.
A new framework based on the bilateral security and political relationship between Baghdad and Washington is set to follow after the withdrawal.
Iraq says it will work to cover the shortfall in military aviation capabilities that will follow the departure of the international coalition, stressing that there will be no foreign combat forces or military bases in the country after 30 September.
Years of US forces in Baghdad
For years, the US military and security presence was distributed across strategic sites inside and around Baghdad, including the Victory military base complex, the largest operations management centre near the capital.
Victory housed headquarters for the general staff, reconnaissance centres, and facilities securing air and logistical transport, as well as advisory headquarters in Baghdad's "Green Zone", the government district.
These forces focused on coordination through the Joint Operations Command to protect the area around the US Embassy and nearby institutions.
In Anbar province in western Iraq, Ain al-Asad airbase was a vital artery for air support, radar systems and supplying equipment and support to fronts near Baghdad.
Harir Airbase in Erbil, the centre of the Kurdistan Region in northern Iraq, emerged as a hub for technical support and logistical movements in the north. Its various roles included intelligence gathering, intelligence coordination through unmanned aircraft, providing air cover, training and equipping Iraqi forces, and carrying out targeted strikes against remnants of the Islamic State.
Iraqi government military spokesman Sabah al-Numan announced on Monday, 28 September, that the international coalition forces had begun withdrawing from the base, saying in press statements that the withdrawal would be completed by 30 September.
Under the 2008 security agreement between Baghdad and Washington, US forces completed their full withdrawal from military bases and cities in December 2011.
The final convoys crossed the southern border into Kuwait, with Baghdad announcing at the time that it had taken over the sites and bases from the Americans and established national sovereignty.
But Iraq soon became compelled to submit an official request to Washington for training and air support after Islamic State occupied about 30 per cent of the country in 2014, amid a security and military collapse of the Iraqi army and armed forces that continues to raise questions without answers.
As a result, the US-led international coalition was formed, comprising 89 countries and international organisations such as the European Union and NATO.
US advisory and combat groups returned to scattered bases, including in Baghdad and Anbar.
The role of the international coalition and US forces in the war against Islamic State from 2014 to 2017 contributed to providing air cover and carrying out direct strikes against the group's headquarters and movements, as well as coordination through reconnaissance aircraft, intelligence gathering and identifying field targets, and training Iraqi military forces, equipping them with modern equipment and weapons, and providing advice on managing battles.
The role of Iraqi forces and Popular Mobilisation Forces brigades was to conduct direct ground combat and carry out raids and operations to liberate villages and cities that had been under the group's control.
But the assassination of Jamal Jaafar, known as Abu Mahdi Al-Muhandis, deputy head of the Popular Mobilisation Forces, and Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani near Baghdad International Airport on 3 January 2020 marked a decisive strategic turning point like the relationship between armed factions close to the "Axis of Resistance" and US forces and the international coalition in Iraq.
These factions chose to apply political pressure and launch continuous and systematic military campaigns.
This translated into parliamentary demands to expel foreign and US forces as "occupiers", alongside moves to launch strikes and attacks against the US Embassy in Baghdad and vital military bases, including "Victory, Asad and Harir", using missiles and drones.
These attacks led to a state of isolation and heightened security precautions inside headquarters and bases.
The movement of US forces in the field was restricted, and Washington was often forced to redeploy its forces and withdraw some personnel from secondary bases, consolidating them in more heavily fortified camps.
The tensions pushed forward negotiations to restructure the military presence and shift it entirely towards an advisory and bilateral framework.
Baghdad and Washington announced the end of combat missions at the end of 2021, with the missions changing from combat to advisory and training roles, without ground combat forces on the ground.
This followed lengthy rounds of dialogue conducted by the Joint Higher Military Committee between the two sides, which established timetables for evacuating sites, dismantling combat infrastructure and returning full management of the airspace and bases to Iraqi military forces.
In this context, Iraqi Security Media Cell chief Lt Gen Saad Maan said the international coalition had handed over all its bases and headquarters to the authorities and that there would be no coalition combat or training forces after the end of this month.
Maan added that Iraqi security forces were ready to take over the security file and capable of managing it after the international coalition withdrawal.
He said in a press statement that "relations with coalition countries after their withdrawal will become bilateral".
Optimism and objections
For his part, Ali Al-Fatlawi, a member of the Coordination Framework alliance, said to The New Arab, "Iraq's sovereignty is indivisible, and we see ending any US military presence inside Baghdad and its bases as an inevitable step that has been long awaited."
"Previous experiences, beginning with the 2011 withdrawal and the return under the pretext of the Islamic State in 2014, taught us that real stability is not achieved through the presence of foreign forces but through complete reliance on Iraqis," he said. "the withdrawal of the international coalition's combat forces and the complete clearing of Baghdad and its headquarters of any field barracks is a national achievement that reflects the high readiness of Iraqi forces".
"The security situation today is under the full control of our security institutions, and what the agreement stipulated is a smooth and carefully planned transition from a direct military and field role to an equal bilateral security relationship based on training, arms supplies and intelligence sharing to ensure that Islamic State threats do not return," he added.
"Clearing the capital of signs of foreign and US military presence represents a pivotal turning point in the history of security alliances in the region," researcher Adnan Al-Kinani told TNA. "This shift from a field combat presence to institutional partnership tests the state's ability to control the pace of the domestic security scene and remove political and weapons-related pretexts."
"Iraqi forces now face the challenge of proving their direct field capacity to manage the vacuum and sustain stability without direct foreign support," Kinani added.
Despite optimism in Baghdad over the departure of US forces and the announcement of a three-day public holiday after 30 September to mark "Sovereignty Day", the Kurdistan Regional Government has openly expressed its concerns over the US withdrawal.
Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani described the US military withdrawal from Iraq as "shameful" and said it would leave Washington's Kurdish allies without protection.
He warned that US President Donald Trump risked repeating the mistake of the administration of President Barack Obama, which withdrew in 2011 before being forced to return.
Barzani warned in an interview with the Financial Times that "the US withdrawal is happening at a particularly turbulent time in the region".
"We are weak, and we are under attack. To be left alone now without any proper defence system is shameful," he continued. "And when we are prevented from buying the sufficient weapons needed against these missiles, drones and advanced systems, we naturally become more vulnerable by design."
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

UK expands Israel arms export ban from 30 to over 80 licences - report
Unknown

2026-09-29

- i24NEWS

- Europe
- UK expands Israel arms export ban from 30 to over 80 licences - report
UK expands Israel arms export ban from 30 to over 80 licences - report
Britain reportedly suspended or refused more than 80 export licences for items that could be used by the IDF in Gaza, nearly three times the number affected when restrictions began in September 2024
The UK government has suspended or refused more than 80 export licences for items that could be used by the IDF in Gaza, up from roughly 30 licences suspended when restrictions were first introduced in September 2024, the Jewish Chronicle reported. More than 50 new applications have been refused since then.
The government continues to approve licences that meet its "Strategic Export Licensing Criteria," with all licences kept under review.
Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty said additional measures introduced on September 8, when the government classified the occupation as illegal, tightened restrictions further. "The new decisions that we took on September 8 mean there's effectively now a double lock on arms exports. They have to be considered both in relation to the existing conditions that we set in relation to international humanitarian law violations," Doughty said.
British components in the international F-35 fighter jet program remain largely exempt from the restrictions, though direct F-35 exports to Israel have been halted. Doughty defended the exemption, saying pulling British-made spares from the global F-35 supply chain "would potentially have very serious implications to the whole program" and is "crucial to our security and that of our allies."
Foreign Affairs Select Committee chair Emily Thornberry pushed back, arguing the UK could continue supplying the F-35 program while marking components as barred from use in aircraft sent to Israel, similar to an approach used by the Netherlands.
The expanded restrictions follow a broader shift under Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government toward a more confrontational stance on Israel.

Early birds for Wang Fuk Court buy-back get first pick of subsidised houses
Some residents pleased with new homes offered under schemes, with others calling for stamp duty waivers to help ease financial burden
Residents who lost their homes in Hong Kong’s deadly Tai Po fire started choosing their replacement flats on Tuesday, with some calling on authorities to introduce stamp duty waivers to help ease their financial burden.
After last November’s blaze at Wang Fuk Court, authorities rolled out a HK$7.8 billion (US$994 million) plan to buy back flats at the eight-block subsidised housing estate.
Under the scheme, participants can use the cash compensation to buy a flat on the private open market or join a special sales exercise to purchase new subsidised housing under the government’s “flat-for-flat” arrangement.

Spain to ban evictions till 2030 as ousted 87-year-old considers offer to return home
- Spain's coalition government proposes banning evictions until 2030 and implementing rent freezes to tackle the housing crisis, following protests over an elderly woman's forced eviction.
- New measures include extending contract renewals until 2028, banning vulture funds from the housing market, and stricter regulation of short-term rentals, but face parliamentary challenges.
- The evicted 87-year-old woman may return home under an agreement to pay 30% of her pension in rent, highlighting the broader struggle between tenants and investment funds in Spain.
AI generated
MADRID – Spain’s coalition government said it had agreed on proposals including banning evictions until 2030 to address the country’s housing crisis, as the 87-year-old woman whose forced removal last week triggered protests was considering an offer to return home.
Hundreds of people remained camped in one of Madrid’s main squares on Sept 29 to protest against Maricarmen Abascal’s removal from her home on a stretcher six days earlier. They are demanding legal reforms, including a rent freeze and the automatic renewal of leases without abusive rent hikes.
Health Minister Monica Garcia said the ruling Socialists reached an agreement on Sept 29 with junior partners Sumar for a decree. New measures include rolling over contracts until 2028 and banning so-called vulture funds from the housing market, though the minority government faces an uphill battle to secure support in a fragmented Parliament.
The government was seeking to broaden the definition of what constitutes a vulture fund beyond large private equity funds to any fund or company that buys housing for speculation, Housing Minister Isabel Rodriguez told a news conference, naming UrbaGestion, the small company that evicted Abascal, as an example of a firm that might fall into that category.
The measures will be divided into two decrees to be voted in parliament on Oct 2, with the majority in a first decree. The “final sticking point” of automatic contract rollover is in a second decree, Social Affairs Minister Pablo Bustinduy told a news conference.
‘Time to intervene’
“It is time to intervene in the speculative housing market and start striking a balance between ordinary citizens and vulture funds,” Garcia wrote on X.
The government has 30 days from the decree’s publication to reach a consensus with allies in congress. Junts, the Catalan pro-independence party that would need to back the decree for it to pass, said on Sept 29 it was still far from agreeing to it and wanted protection for small landlords, who make up the vast majority of property owners in Spain.
“We all agreed that evictions – where the property is owned by a fund, a vulture fund, run by someone managing millions of euros – obviously need to be stopped,” Junts parliamentary spokeswoman Miriam Nogueras said on RTVE.
“Lumping together in this category those who have invested their savings in a flat, a restaurant or a property – putting them all in the same basket – is a mistake,” she added.
Other measures approved in a Cabinet meeting on Sept 29 included stricter regulation of short-term and by-the-room lets, automatic renewal of contracts and limiting rent increases, Garcia said.
Madrid’s Tenants’ Union criticised the government’s decision to split the measures into two decrees and said the Madrid encampment and others across Spain would continue until their full demands were met, with further demonstrations planned.
Abascal’s lawyer said on Sept 29 that UrbaGestion, the fund that owns her apartment, had offered a preliminary agreement late on Sept 28 that could allow her return to her home if she agrees to its terms, which would imply paying 30% of her pension over the next eight years, equivalent to around €500 (S$725) a month.
This would see her paying a similar level as prior to the eviction.
“She should never have been forced to leave,” Beatriz Duro told reporters. “I hope this case serves to provide a collective response to the housing crisis.”
The tenants’ union had said Abascal’s monthly rent was earlier hiked by 275 per cent to €2,650. REUTERS

What to Know About the Pentagon Breach Affecting Millions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:15:05 UTC
19:15:05 KST

A reported monthslong breach in the Defense Department’s human resources database exposed personal information of millions of military personnel and those related to them, including their Social Security numbers and job details.
A Pentagon official confirmed to TIME Tuesday that some 2.76 million “living individuals” and 294,000 “deceased individuals” have been affected by the breach at the Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC).
The breach was first reported by defense-focused news publication Military Times on Thursday, citing a breach notification letter to a person whose information was in the affected files.
It remains unclear what particular files were accessed and who was behind the incident. The Defense Department official told TIME that individuals whose personal information were accessed had been notified by mail.
The length of the breach and the amount of personal information exposed present a security risk for many personnel linked with the department, and some experts say it makes other security compromises, like phishing attempts, easier for bad actors.
What we know about the breach
The DMDC collates personnel, manpower, training, financial, and other data for the Defense Department for healthcare, retirement funding, and other administrative needs. Its website says that based on FY2024 data, it has the records of more than 60 million people—including the military, civilians, contractors, family members, retirees, and veterans.
But the Military Times reviewed a Sept. 18 letter from the DMDC notifying its recipient of a data breach. The letter reportedly said it discovered on July 16 a security vulnerability in the center’s file-sharing system.
The notice reportedly details that between October 2025 and the time of discovery, some “unauthorized users” accessed files on a server containing the personal information. The type of personal information varies from names to dates of birth, contact information, and others.
DMDC then said it updated the file-sharing system to address the vulnerability. The letter reportedly added that there has been no indication of misuse of the recipient’s information.
Not the first hack
The latest incident involving Pentagon data emerged as the FBI confirmed it was looking into criminal hacking group ShinyHunters’s apparent attack on its jobs website. The group claimed to have stolen “very sensitive data” on nearly all agents and job applicants in response to an FBI notice about them issued in May. (ShinyHunters were also behind a high-profile hack in May of education platform Canvas.)
It’s still unclear how massive the previous FBI breach was, but a New York Times analysis found that it may have involved the stealing of home addresses, Social Security numbers, and job assignments, on top of other personally identifiable information. Reuters reported last week that the hackers claimed they have obtained about 2-3 terabytes of data. Some of the data Reuters reviewed also revealed details of assignments to specific field offices, as well as FBI units engaged in high-stakes intelligence, security, or counterespionage work, which risks endangering national security.
In a statement to 404 Media and the Times, the FBI said it was “working around the clock to investigate the cyber incident involving FBIJobs.gov and is in regular communication with anyone who may be impacted—including multiple bureau-wide communications within 24 hours of public reporting.”
The FBI incident also follows a breach that may have exposed more than 153 million driver’s licenses in the U.S. and Canada.
What affected personnel can do
Security experts have previously warned that access to troves of records poses a massive security risk, especially if these fall into the hands of foreign actors.
Justin Sherman, a senior associate at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote about the license data breach earlier this month: “It can be tempting to dismiss the next hack of a database as ‘just another data breach.’... But breaches do not exist in a vacuum.”
The DMDC said in its notice to affected personnel that it was offering year-long credit monitoring and identity-restoration services through IDX, a private firm contracted by the department. The defense official said in a statement to TIME that individuals with questions should contact IDX at https://response.idx.us/DMDC or 1-855-744-4556.
According to the Federal Trade Commission, anyone could place a free credit freeze with each of the three major credit bureaus—Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.
Active duty personnel and National Guard members could also get free electronic credit monitoring to spot problems that could stem from identity theft.

A Pentagon Influencer Called Liberal Women a ‘Pestilence’ Who Will End Western Civilization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

A retired Army colonel turned social media influencer, who has worked with the Pentagon to promote Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s agenda, has a history of praising dictators, denigrating women and minorities, and suggesting that only people with children should be allowed to vote.
Kurt Schlichter has over 620,000 followers on X and has regularly posted in support of Hegseth’s anti-woke agenda. Last month, as part of an investigation into the Pentagon’s employment of influencers in civilian roles, The Washington Post found that Schlichter was one of several individuals to be given active government email addresses at the time and assigned to the undersecretary of defense for personnel and readiness’s office. According to reporting from the Post, Schlichter appears in the government database with the designation of “HQE,” which could stand for “highly qualified expert.”
Schlichter confirmed that he was a civilian government employee, working as part of a task force rooting out so-called woke ideologies at the military’s war colleges.
What wasn’t reported, however, were Schlichter’s posts on social media and other platforms in recent years that highlight extremist, anti-democratic worldviews. WIRED has reviewed many of these posts.
“The Department was proud to have a group of patriotic civilians and veterans like Kurt Schlichter contribute to our Senior Service College Task Force. Nothing is more important than the formation of our future military leaders," Kingsley Wilson, the Pentagon’s press secretary, tells WIRED. Schlichter did not respond to requests for comment. It’s not clear if Schlichter is still working with the Pentagon. Wilson herself shared extremist content and an antisemitic conspiracy theory prior to joining the Pentagon.
In an August 2021 thread on X, Schlichter demanded an authoritarian crackdown on “liberals.”
“We must, by any means necessary, force them to be like us. No quarter. No compromise,” Schlichter wrote. In the thread, he advocates for banning everything from masks and unions to critical race theory and “leftist media.” (Last year, Hegseth’s Department of Defense required journalists to sign a pledge that would prevent them from gathering certain information. Most major journalists refused to sign the pledge and left the Pentagon.)
In the same thread on X, Schlichter also suggested that people who don’t have children, who do not serve in the military, and who don’t own property should not be allowed to vote. “Penalize barren, non-familial lifestyles through taxes and disqualification from political participation,” Schlichter wrote. “Establish property and military service qualifications for voting.” Posts in the thread were shared a combined 10,000 times.
Schlichter has also repeatedly expressed appreciation of murderous dictators like Chile’s Augusto Pinochet and Spain’s Francisco Franco. “Pinochet was too soft,” Schlichter wrote on X in April 2024. In May 2025, he quoted a post on X that called on Trump to offer asylum to Spanish fascists, writing: “Franco did nothing wrong.” In December 2025, Schlichter called Franco “a Spanish patriot.” (Under Pinochet’s dictatorship, tens of thousands of his citizens were tortured while thousands of his political opponents disappeared. During the Spanish Civil War, Franco’s Nationalists executed tens of thousands of dissidents while systematically raping women.)
Schlichter has also repeatedly lashed out at women and minorities. In an article for conservative website Townhall, published in July 2026, Schlichter suggested that “liberal women” could bring about the end of Western civilization.
“These self-righteous crones are a pestilence, a plague upon Western society, a group of doggedly ignorant feminist/chauvinists playing out their personal psychodramas on the world stage whose antics, if unchecked, will inevitably lead to the fall of civilization,” he wrote. Taiwan extends paid marriage leave to 14 days

19:13:14 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan will extend paid marriage leave from eight to 14 days on Thursday, with the government reimbursing employers for wages paid during the six additional days, the labor ministry said Tuesday.
The ministry announced the measure after amending the Regulations of Leave-Taking for Workers and issuing guidelines for a wage subsidy program. The new rules and application system will take effect on Oct. 1.
Employers must pay workers their regular wages throughout the 14 days of marriage leave. They may then apply to the Bureau of Labor Insurance for full reimbursement of wages covering days nine through 14.
Employers may apply after a worker has completed the leave or, if the employment contract ends before then, after paying the wages required for the additional days. Applications can be submitted through the bureau’s online service system using an organization’s digital certificate.
Employers may also download an application form from the bureau’s website and submit it by registered mail or in person.
The bureau expects to issue the first payments for eligible applications submitted in 2026 by the end of January 2027. Applications received from January 2027 onward will generally be paid by the end of the following month. Payments are contingent on passage of the 2027 budget.
Employers must apply within two years of paying wages for the additional marriage leave. The bureau has established an online information section containing application instructions, subsidy details, frequently asked questions and a one-minute tutorial video.
The ministry said the policy would give workers more time to prepare for marriage and adjust to a new stage of life while reducing the financial burden on employers.
The measure is part of the government’s population strategy, which seeks to strengthen workplace support for marriage, pregnancy, childbirth and parenting.

Iraq War film 'Atonement' tells story of US Marine seeking Iraqi family's forgiveness

Iraq War film 'Atonement' tells story of US Marine seeking Iraqi family's forgiveness
TORONTO, Sept 29 - Three generations of an Armenian-Christian family were driving home in Baghdad in April 2003 when US Marines in a firefight with Iraqi forces fired on their cars, killing three men.
Almost a decade later, two women who survived the attack sat down in their Glendale, California, living room with one of the Marines who pulled the trigger.
That encounter serves as the climax of "Atonement," writer-director Reed Van Dyk's feature debut, which had its North American premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival this month and opens in theaters on Friday.
Based on a 2012 New Yorker article by Dexter Filkins, the film stars Kenneth Branagh as Michael Reid, a journalist who reported on the gunfight and arranged the meeting. Hiam Abbass portrays Mariam, the family matriarch whose husband and two sons were killed, while Boyd Holbrook is Lou D’Alessandro, the former Marine seeking forgiveness. The names were altered from the real-life characters: former Marine Lu Lobello, Margaret Kachadoorian and Filkins.
Van Dyk, speaking to Reuters during an interview with the cast, said Iraqi characters in typical Iraq War films are "viewed through sniper scopes or in the background," and he set out to invert that perspective.
"It was really exciting for me to centralize these people who were affected deeply by this instance and by war in general," he said.
After returning from Iraq, Lobello struggled with post-traumatic stress disorder, haunted by the memory that his unit had killed civilians that day.
"This bullet goes both ways, and you’re really seeing Lou grapple with that," Holbrook said, echoing a line from the film.
Lobello eventually asked Filkins to connect him with the Kachadoorians. The family agreed to meet, and they forgave him.
Abbass said that, in portraying Mariam, she channeled her experience as a mother and a Palestinian woman who grew up around wars. She said she was struck by her capacity for forgiveness.
"This woman was able to forgive, but imagine how many people on Earth that lived that situation are incapable to ... forgive," she said.
Branagh called the film's central interaction an "extraordinary act of vulnerability" and praised the willingness of both sides to have a conversation without a clear resolution.
"You’re left with a tremendous sort of interchange between people in impossible situations with difficult answers to find — if they can be found," he said.
"Atonement" opens in select theaters on October 2, expanding widely on October 9. REUTERS

Taiwan flu activity remains above epidemic threshold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:12:48 UTC
19:12:48 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Influenza activity in Taiwan remained stable but above the epidemic threshold last week, with 138,654 outpatient and emergency visits for flu-like illnesses, according to the Taiwan Centers for Disease Control.
Visits declined 3.2% from the previous week, partly because clinics were closed during the holiday period, per CNA and UDN.
The CDC said influenza activity was expected to remain elevated until mid-October before beginning to decline. Weekly visits could reach between 150,000 and 160,000.
Health authorities reported 87 new cases of severe influenza complications and 30 deaths last week. Influenza A remained the predominant virus type in the community, with A(H1N1) accounting for 87.7% of detected strains.
CDC Director-General Lo Yi-chun (羅一鈞) said A(H1N1) infections carry a relatively high risk of becoming severe. Previous flu seasons dominated by the strain also recorded comparatively high numbers of severe cases, per CNews.
Since the current flu season began, Taiwan has recorded 1,673 severe cases and 334 deaths. People aged 65 and older accounted for 65.9% of severe cases, while 83.4% of patients had chronic illnesses and 67.7% had not received this season’s flu vaccine.
With influenza activity remaining high, the CDC has extended expanded eligibility for government-funded antiviral medication through Oct. 31.
The agency urged people experiencing warning signs—including rapid or labored breathing, bluish skin, bloody sputum, chest pain, altered consciousness or low blood pressure—to seek medical attention promptly.
As temperatures begin to fall, the CDC also advised the public to wash their hands regularly and observe proper cough etiquette. People with fever, coughing or other flu-like symptoms should wear a mask and seek medical attention early.

Anti-South Asian online hate has escalated sharply across social media platforms and fringe forums, driven by generative artificial intelligence, incendiary political rhetoric and targeted harassment campaigns, according to a report released Monday by the Center for the Study of Online Hate (CSOH).
The study documented more than half a million hateful posts on X between January 2025 and June 2026. Monthly hate volume on the platform grew 75% during the study period and 240% since January 2024, with five of the six highest-volume months occurring between November 2025 and June 2026. On fringe platforms including 4chan, 8chan and Gab, researchers identified 397,522 hateful mentions in 2025 alone.
Posts portraying South Asians as invaders, job thieves and demographic threats accounted for 45% of anti-South Asian hate on X, with H-1B visas and immigration serving as primary drivers.
These narratives frequently invoked "Great Replacement" and "remigration" rhetoric, while fringe platforms overlapped with antisemitic conspiracy theories.
Dehumanizing language and slurs pervaded every platform analyzed. The slur "pajeet" and its variants appeared in 30% of all posts on X and 45% of mentions on fringe platforms. Hygiene-based dehumanization marked the fastest-growing category on X, surging 171%.
Researchers warned that generative AI is "industrializing visual hate," generating caricatures at unprecedented speed that depict South Asians as vermin, scammers and sexual predators.
Digital hostility has also moved directly into physical spaces. A network of X accounts routinely doxxes South Asians over alleged visa fraud or job competition, while right-wing influencers film harassment encounters at targets' homes and workplaces.
In Texas, influencers produced documentary-style videos framing local neighborhoods, businesses, and temples as evidence of a foreign "takeover."
South Asian public figures across party lines, including Republican politicians, faced coordinated attacks framing their civic participation as an invasive threat.
The report also detailed attacks on Hindu, Sikh and Muslim religious practices, calls to destroy temples and the weaponization of British grooming-gang cases into broad smears against all South Asians.
CSOH attributed the overall surge to six converging drivers: racist policies and incendiary rhetoric, xenophobic nationalism, racial hostility, growing South Asian political visibility, economic resentment and digital amplification.
"Anti-South Asian hate deliberately and intentionally targets the community; it is manufactured, it is articulated to provoke resentment, anger, panic, and outrage, it is strategically circulated, and it is amplified online," the report stated.
It also noted that digital hostility reinforces physical violence, citing a September incident in Wyoming where a Sikh truck driver was stabbed 17 times.
The researchers linked the rise in targeted hostility to federal policy decisions and rhetoric from the Trump administration.
On Feb. 5, 2025, 104 undocumented Indian nationals were deported to India. Data from Stop AAPI Hate cited in the report indicates South Asian deportations under the current administration rose roughly 14 times above levels recorded during the previous administration.
The report also highlighted policy shifts surrounding the H-1B visa program alongside inflammatory public statements. These include remarks by White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller accusing India of “cheating on immigration policies,” and statements by President Donald Trump referring to Indian immigrants as “gangsters with laptops.”
"Online hate does not exist in isolation from offline forms of hostility," the report warned, noting that digital algorithms and political discourse continue to reinforce real-world abuse.

Using old election playbook, Netanyahu projects image as Israel’s protector despite Hamas attack

Using old election playbook, Netanyahu projects image as Israel’s protector despite Hamas attack

JERUSALEM – Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is using the same campaign playbook that has served him for decades as he tries to retain power in an election in October, presenting himself as the only person who can keep Israelis safe in a hostile region.
But four weeks before the election, he is struggling to salvage his security credentials, shattered by Hamas' surprise attack on southern Israel on his watch on Oct 7, 2023 — one of the country’s worst security breaches.
The Oct 27 election is Israel’s first since its single deadliest day and the worst attack on Jews since the Holocaust, masterminded by a Palestinian militant group that caught the Middle East’s most powerful military off guard.
“Netanyahu does not surrender” is the official slogan for Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party, which most opinion polls predict will lose around a third of its parliamentary seats.
In speeches and short campaign videos, Netanyahu portrays his political rivals as weak leftists who lack the resolve to wage war on Israel’s enemies and the backbone to stand up to its critics abroad.
But whether Netanyahu, who turns 77 days before the election, can still present himself as best equipped to navigate Israel on matters of national security and diplomacy is a big question, said Yohanan Plesner, President of the non-partisan Israel Democracy Institute.
In recent weeks, Netanyahu has been forced to deny media reports that his Middle East partners warned him of a potential Hamas attack, allegations seized on by his political rivals.
“This is a new thing. Mr Netanyahu ran in elections, but never after overseeing such a dramatic security failure,” said Plesner.
“It’s in many ways a referendum on the incumbent, his responsibility for the failure, the government’s responsibility and the way they carried out the Israeli response.”
Netanyahu takes on the world
Hamas’ assault precipitated a multi-front war in which Israel’s military had some success against the Palestinian group and its allies Hezbollah and Iran, but made few strategic gains. Netanyahu says the conflict has, and still will, transform the region.
But Israel’s conduct in the war in Gaza, with tens of thousands of Palestinians killed and much of the enclave in ruins, has led to deeper diplomatic isolation. Dozens of delegates at the United Nations walked out of the hall when he began his speech to the General Assembly meeting of world leaders last week.
Support for Israel has fallen even in its most important ally, the United States.
Netanyahu’s last campaign in 2019 featured Donald Trump shaking hands with Netanyahu on election billboards. This time, the US president’s image has been absent from Likud’s campaign videos.
Nonetheless, Israel’s longest-serving leader – first elected prime minister in 1996 – has not strayed from campaign tactics that have kept him in power almost consecutively since 2009.
A source close to Netanyahu said the prime minister approaches all elections as though he is going to lose – and that this was one of the reasons he has often won, even when the odds were against him.
Another source briefed on his campaign said Netanyahu’s team appears focused, showing no sign of panic or disarray despite the opinion polls.
Netanyahu’s address at the UN in which he mounted a forceful defence of Israel’s actions in the region and berated critics, featured heavily on his Telegram channel, a platform largely used for political messaging.
He posted six teasers before the address, with one video saying he was “proud to represent you to the world, about to get on (podium) to fight for Israel against the UN,” and five excerpts of his speech.
The link to the full address was captioned in Hebrew: “Netanyahu takes on the world.”

Another familiar theme in Netanyahu’s campaign has stoked fear among parties representing Israel’s Arab minority by warning that if his political rivals win the election, they will form a government with Arab factions that will be too soft on the Palestinians and compromise security.

Since Sept 26 alone, Eisenkot has featured in four Likud posts, including AI-generated images, portraying him with Arab party leaders.
“There is no straight. Yashar is a bluff. There’s either left or right. That is the essence of this election. Do you want a Palestinian state? (or) do you want a Jewish state?” Netanyahu said in a campaign video on Sept 18.
But Netanyahu’s use of familiar tactics against Eisenkot might be a long shot, said Amotz Asa-El, political analyst at Shalom Hartman Institute, given Eisenkot’s security background and centre-right party candidates.
Though election polls have often been inaccurate, Netanyahu knows he is unlikely to command a parliamentary majority allowing him to form Israel’s next government.
“It seems that Netanyahu’s strategy is to simply win enough to prevent the emergence of an alternative government and emerge with some kind of a stalemate that will leave him as an interim prime minister en route to another election,” said Asa-El. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Puja after paribartan: What is changing in West Bengal’s biggest festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:07:56 UTC
19:07:56 KST

One of the enduring memories of the Mamata Banerjee era in West Bengal will be the elaborate Durga Puja carnival, where handpicked baro pujos (marquee pujas) would parade along Red Road with tableaux before the CM and other dignitaries in an almost Republic Day-esque procession. It would often end with Mamata Banerjee doing an impromptu jig with the crème de la crème of the Bengali film industry.The carnival has been scrapped. Instead, a pre-Puja event will be held at the iconic Eden Gardens on Mahalaya, October 10, which Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to attend. These and many other changes are expected as West Bengal counts down to the homecoming of the Goddess.This year marks a significant break in Bengal's politics. The BJP government took office on May 9, making this its first Durga Puja in power in the state. And some changes are already in motion. Beyond the cosmetic, is Bengal's intrinsic style of celebrating Durga Puja going to change?The number of pujas continues to grow. As of September 24, 2,318 Durga Pujas had already registered on Kolkata's Sahaj single-window permission portal, including 270 new applicants, with more applications still expected. In 2025, the final tally of 2,936 applications was the highest ever. Across Bengal, the state power department expects the number of community pujas to cross 65,000 this year, an estimate based partly on demand for temporary electricity connections.
Durga Puja Carnival-has been scrapped
The barowari, or community-puja, tradition in Bengal is generally traced to late-18th-century Guptipara, although historians differ over the precise year and even whether the earliest community celebration there was Durga Puja or Jagaddhatri Puja. The word barowari is generally traced to baro yaar, or "twelve friends". From the patronage of zamindars to that of influential political leaders, Durga Puja's format has constantly changed, though it remains the cornerstone of Bengal's annual cultural calendar.
From ek-chalar thakur, where the divine family is presented within a single frame, to multi-part installations; from sabeki pratima, or traditional-style idols, to theme pujas; from sholar saaj to idols made from unconventional materials, creative people have continually found new ways to express their love and reverence for Goddess Durga.In the run-up to Mahalaya, Kumartuli, north Kolkata's famous idol-making quarter, draws growing crowds of photographers, selfie-seekers and curious visitors into its narrow lanes. The adjoining Kumartuli Ghat is now adding another attraction. A Rs 10-crore redevelopment of a 300-metre stretch of the Hooghly riverfront, with viewing areas, walkways and improved public facilities, is expected to add to the draw.
Change in Durga Puja patronage
The most visible change this year is in the patronage of Durga Pujas. For years, the names of influential Trinamool leaders were virtually interchangeable with those of Kolkata's marquee pujas. There was Sujit Bose's Sreebhumi, Arup Biswas's Suruchi, Firhad Hakim's Chetla Agrani and Partha Chatterjee's Naktala Udayan Sangha, among others.Along with these, many up-and-coming political leaders ensured that relatively unknown Durga pandals shot to fame with innovative themes. Often, hosting a large-scale Durga Puja became a proxy for growing political clout.That competition for spectacle and social ownership, however, long predates contemporary party politics. Kaliprasanna Sinha's 19th-century Hutom Pyanchar Naksha used Durga Puja to lampoon Calcutta's babu culture, its display, extravagance and social pretensions.At Sreebhumi Sporting Club, the extravaganza that became synonymous with former Trinamool minister Sujit Bose is being prepared by a new committee. BJP leader Kanak Debnath has become president, with the organisers promising to retain the puja's grandeur while ending prolonged road blockades.
Sreebhumi Puja in 2025
At Suruchi Sangha, for years associated with Arup Biswas and his brother Swarup, BJP MLA Sourav Sikdar is now secretary. Suruchi's new committee has replaced the Biswas brothers, although the transition was accompanied by protests from residents. At Tala Prattoy, which has been delivering extremely eye-catching themes over the last few years, much of the previous organising set-up has changed, with Sushanta Shibani Pal handling this year's theme.The organisational change is extending beyond individual clubs. A new statewide coordination platform, Paschim Banga Durga Puja Samannay Samiti, or West Bengal Durga Puja Coordination Committee, is taking shape, with Kartik Maharaj as chairman and BJP MLA Rudranil Ghosh as chief adviser. It could emerge as an alternative pole to the established Forum for Durgotsab, which represents hundreds of committees.The churn has reached venues old and new. Known for its elaborate Christmas and New Year celebrations, Park Street will host a Durga Puja at Allen Park for the first time this year. Without missing a beat, Kolkata Sanatani Sangha, fronted by BJP leader Shankudeb Panda, will be organising it.At Mohammad Ali Park, competing committees put up banners under different names after BJP councillor Meena Devi Purohit proposed renaming the historic venue Mahabali Park. The iconic Bagbazar Puja, meanwhile, landed in trouble over a deadlocked committee election before the courts sorted it out.The financial machinery behind Durga Puja is also being recalibrated. The Mamata Banerjee government introduced annual assistance to puja committees at Rs 10,000 in 2018 and increased it over the years to Rs 1.1 lakh in 2025. The new BJP government has announced Rs 1 lakh for 2026, while chief minister Suvendu Adhikari has appealed to big-budget organisers to leave the assistance for smaller celebrations that need it.During TMC rule, BJP leader Sajal Ghosh's Santosh Mitra Square was something of a 'rebel' puja, refusing to take grants. With power having changed hands and TMC virtually disintegrating, there are no such rebel pujas this time, at least publicly.Several prominent committees have agreed to forgo the grant, in line with the government's appeal. The BJP government has also asked electricity suppliers to provide free power to organisers; under the previous government, the waiver in 2025 was 80%.In Birbhum, BJP district president Uday Shankar Banerjee told puja committees that clubs taking the 2026 government grant must display the chief minister's photograph or face action, a claim promptly shot down by minister Dilip Ghosh.
Navratri tradition in Durga Puja?
It is perhaps on food that the focus will be most intense.In late August, Swami Nirgunananda, a member of the VHP's central advisory council, suggested that non-vegetarian food should be kept away from the immediate puja space, while acknowledging that Bengal's Durga Puja has never been exclusively vegetarian. VHP leaders subsequently clarified that there was no official or binding directive banning non-vegetarian food during Durga Puja.Days later, religious preacher Dhirendra Krishna Shastri, popularly known as Bageshwar Baba, went considerably further. He criticised the consumption of non-vegetarian food during Durga Puja, describing those who did so as pakhandis, or hypocrites.The remarks provoked criticism, including from within the BJP. State party president Samik Bhattacharya defended Bengal's food traditions, while Adhikari subsequently visited Kalighat temple and consumed traditional prasad that included fried fish, fish head and basanti pulao. At Suruchi Sangha, where BJP MLA Sourav Sikdar is now secretary, organisers have said mutton and hilsa will continue to be served at the Maha Navami feast. Many housing societies where community Durga Pujas take place have also affirmed that their Puja feasts aren't going to change and will remain largely non-vegetarian, barring Maha Ashtami.In large parts of north India, abstaining from meat during Navratri is commonplace. Critics of the BJP have expressed concern that such a food culture could gradually be pushed on Bengal. There is no evidence of any government plan to impose such a restriction. But the effect could be subtler than a formal ban.Some organisers are already drawing a firmer boundary around the immediate sacred space. Thakurpukur SB Park and Chaltabagan have announced restrictions on visitors entering while eating, while the new Allen Park puja will have no food stalls inside the park, TOI has reported previously.There is a perception that, at many pandals, egg-roll stalls and other non-vegetarian food outlets will be stationed farther away from the main arena where the Goddess will be placed.
To theme or not to?
Theme pujas have not been barred, but organisers have been asked to ensure that idols and themes do not hurt religious sentiments or undermine what the new government describes as Sanatani traditions. That has prompted some artists and organisers to tread more cautiously.However, social and experimental subjects continue this year too, including themes around care workers, gender identity and ecology. What is changing is the political vocabulary surrounding them. At the same time, several high-profile pujas this year are invoking patriotism, nationalism and Hindu cultural identity.There is no official census separating theme pujas from traditional ones.Santosh Mitra Square, whose committee is headed by BJP MLA Sajal Ghosh, has chosen Vande Mataram. New Town Sanatani Durga Puja, whose leadership includes chief ministerial adviser Subrata Gupta and Kartik Maharaj, is exploring what its organisers describe as the relationship between ancient Indian traditions and modern science.
Santosh Mitra Square in 2025 showing Operation Sindoor
The use of Goddess Durga as a political or nationalist metaphor is hardly new. In Bankimchandra Chattopadhyay's Amar Durgotsav (My Durga Puja), included in Kamalakanter Daptar, an opium-addled Kamalakanta looks at the Durga image on Saptami and eventually sees in her Bengal itself (Banga Janani, Mother Bengal), invoking the Goddess as an image of collective strength and awakening.Nazrul would later take the idea in another direction. In his Durga and Agomoni compositions, the rebel poet repeatedly invoked the Goddess as Shakti, or living power, rather than merely an image of clay. His 1922 poem Anandamoyeer Agamane used Durga's arrival as an anti-colonial metaphor so explicitly that the British prosecuted him for sedition.The VHP's Nirgunananda, though, has argued for a more explicitly religious ownership of the festival. At an August meeting with Puja organisers, he rejected the formulation that "religion belongs to individuals, but festivals belong to everyone", arguing instead that festivals primarily belong to followers of the faith, while people of other religions were welcome to visit.That marks a clear difference in outlook, which may well become one of the faultlines around Bengal's Durga Puja celebrations.
'Sharadotsav' coinage contested
Pandal-hopping has also traditionally been an easy way to get a crash course in political history.The Left Front's stalls, where the para-r communist kaku would be stationed selling books on Markshiyo Darshan, or Marxist philosophy, were hard to miss. Seeing them, the TMC also started its Jago Bangla stalls, though Didi, a skilled politician, never quite got the stamp of approval from Bengalis for her literary exploits.This year, though, the Left may face problems putting up some of those stalls.The name Sharadotsav, synonymous with Durga Puja, is facing questions. Chief minister Suvendu Adhikari has asked committees not to accommodate CPI(M) bookstalls that describe the festival as "Sharadotsav" instead of "Durga Puja", arguing that the terminology dilutes its religious identity.Interestingly, Rabindranath Tagore wrote Sharadotsav, a play celebrating the autumn season, way back in 1908, a point also raised by Left leaders in response to the controversy. A puja committee at Kamardanga in Tangra has gone further, announcing that it will not allow stalls run by CPI(M), DYFI, SUCI or other Left-wing organisations at its celebration. The committee has appealed to other organisers to follow suit, while CPI(M) has criticised the move.
How the calendar is changing
The Red Road immersion carnival, first held under Mamata Banerjee's government in 2016, has been discontinued. In its place comes a grand Mahalaya celebration at Eden Gardens on October 10, 2026, one week before Maha Shashthi on October 17. The programme is expected to feature traditional performers, thousands of dhakis, fireworks and a drone show. Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to attend and virtually inaugurate prominent Kolkata pujas from the programme. The Eden Gardens presentation aims to recreate important events and rituals associated with Durga Puja.Mahalaya holds a very special significance. Beyond tarpan, the ritual offering to one's ancestors, Birendra Krishna Bhadra's recitation in the Mahishasuramardini radio programme, which became associated with Mahalaya from the 1930s, has itself become a ritual. Hosting such a gala event on that day gives the new government a prominent ceremonial role at the opening of Bengal's Puja season.
Tarpan in Mahalaya
There are changes for ordinary pandal-hoppers too. The new government has said Puja pandals will not be allowed to be inaugurated before Mahalaya. Maha Ashtami will be a dry day, with liquor sales prohibited. DJs have been banned during Puja celebrations and immersion processions, while organisers have been instructed to avoid prolonged road blockades and complete immersions within the prescribed period.Even the appearance of Kolkata Police's crowd-management volunteers is set to change, with police floating a tender for orange T-shirts and caps to replace the familiar white-and-blue attire.There is not much clarity yet about how active the TMC will be during Durga Puja. But one thing Kolkata will surely be revisiting through reels is Mamata Banerjee's one-liners and gestures, from her suggestion that kash, the tall white kans grass associated with the Bengali autumn, could be used as stuffing for pillows to her symbolic chokhu daan.
File Image of Mamata Banerjee doing chokhu daan
What no government can legislate
So will Bengal's intrinsic style of celebrating Puja change? The answer may lie in how varied that style has always been.There has never been one compulsory Bengali Puja menu, or even one compulsory visual grammar. Mahendranath Datta, the younger brother of Swami Vivekananda, recorded striking differences between Durga images in Shakta and Vaishnava households. In Shakta homes, he wrote, Durga's lion had the conventional lion's face; in Gosain or Vaishnava homes, the lion had a horse-like face, apparently marking a distinction between the two traditions. On food too, practices differed. At Brahmin homes, guests could be served rice, five vegetable dishes, curd and payesh; in Shakta Brahmin households, he noted, fish was also permitted, while Kayastha homes served luchi.The traditions that have survived in Bengal's old family pujas are equally difficult to squeeze into a single dietary rule. The Sabarna Roy Chowdhury family continues to offer katla as Nabami bhog.
At Chorbagan Chatterjee Bari, fish is offered during the Puja days. At the Janbazar home of Rani Rashmoni's descendants, on the other hand, the Goddess receives vegetarian bhog even as non-vegetarian food is served to guests, reported TOI previously.There is no quick primer on how to be Sanatani across Bengal's myriad Durga Puja traditions. The pandals may change hands, and the colour of uniforms may change. But beneath the contest for ownership lies a diversity of practice too old and too deep-rooted.Perhaps the more things change, the more they stay the same.

Beril Canakci
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
FIFA has accused UEFA of conducting a “misinformation campaign” and seeking to influence its upcoming presidential election amid an escalating legal dispute over the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) project.
In a filing submitted Monday to the US District Court for the Southern District of Florida, FIFA opposed UEFA’s request for the disclosure of evidence and documents related to the project.
European football’s governing body accused FIFA President Gianni Infantino of “criminal mismanagement” and promoting what it called “a fraudulently off-market price” for his own benefit in connection with the FFE proposal.
In its response, FIFA said UEFA’s filing contained “numerous false or misleading statements about FIFA and Infantino.”
“With no basis whatsoever, UEFA suggests that Mr Infantino sought to profit personally from the FFE proposal,” FIFA said, according to a BBC report.
“UEFA’s suggestions that Mr Infantino violated any law or ethical principle are categorically without merit.”
FIFA also described UEFA’s request for documents as “farcically overbroad” and argued that courts had rejected similar applications.
The FFE proposal was shelved following widespread opposition. UEFA has been among the leading critics of Infantino over the project, while calls have also been made for him to step down.
On Monday, The Athletic reported that Infantino had signaled support for distributing more money to member associations from FIFA’s $6 billion reserves.
Infantino told the presidents of FIFA’s six continental confederations that proposals for additional funding would be considered by the FIFA Council at its Oct. 15 meeting, according to the report.
The FIFA chief is expected to seek another term as president in March 2027, with potential challengers having until Nov. 18 to enter the race.

Israel revokes aliyah of Jewish left-wing activists after initial approval
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:06:53 UTC
19:06:53 KST

Israel’s Population Authority (PIBA) has revoked the aliyah approval of two Jewish activists in their 20s, both active in pro-Palestine advocacy in the West Bank.
This was first reported by Ha’aretz on Monday, but The Jerusalem Post spoke with one of the individuals – British national Lawrence Shenkin – who said the details of the report are correct. The story of the other individual – an American woman – mirrors Shenkin’s.
These are believed to be the first known cases where halakhic Jews without criminal records have been denied the right to immigrate to Israel.
Shenkin grew up in a Modern Orthodox family in Golders Green. He was raised Zionist and has already lived in Israel for five years.
He moved to Israel at 18 to attend yeshiva, intending the stay and live in the country permanently. During this time, Shenkin joined the left-wing religious organization Bnei Avraham in 2023. As such, he has been involved in protecting Palestinian communities in the West Bank from alleged Israeli settler harassment.
In November 2025, on the cusp of finishing his university studies, he started the process of Aliyah.
He submitted all his files to PIBA and, in January, received an email saying, “Due to a change in the circumstances of your case, your ETA has been revoked.” In lieu of citizenship, an ETA is required to enter Israel.
Shenkin said he didn't think much of it, assuming the ETA revocation was a simple response to his Aliyah.
However, months went by, and he still hadn't heard any update on his Aliyah.
He then traveled to the UK to visit his family for Passover, and applied for a new ETA to return, which was again denied.
“I couldn’t really think of what was happening,” Shenkin told the Post. “Friends then told me that lots of left-wing activists have had their ETAs denied and had their ETAs revoked and that maybe it was related to that.”
He decided to stay in the UK and finish his Aliyah from there. In July, he received an email from the Jewish Agency congratulating him on his successful Aliyah.
Peace activists' aliyah denied over 'Section 40'
“I was elated. I sent my passport to the consulate to receive the visa because that’s what they said to do. “About three weeks later, I got an email from the Jewish Agency saying, 'Based on information received from the Population and Immigration Authority, and in accordance with Section 40 of the Entry into Israel Law, the approval of your eligibility for aliyah is currently under review by the Authority and is temporarily revoked.”
Shenkin’s lawyer said there is no Section 40 of the Entry into Israel Law. There is an amendment 40, which denies entry to people who denied October 7th or who call for the prosecution of Israeli soldiers, which Shenkin has not done.
“I was quite offended at the notion that it could be me. I’ve never done something like that ever at all,” he told the Post.
Shenkin’s lawyer informed him that Israel could not legally deny him Aliyah, given he is halachically Jewish, and has “never committed a crime.”
“I don’t know under what grounds they denied me.”
“I’ve been torn away from my homeland, which I love and whose welfare I’m only looking to contribute to. Israel is truly one of my greatest loves.”
Shenkin describes himself as a “very passionate religious Zionist.”
“I believe that, you know, there’s a mitzvah to be living in the land of Israel,” he said.
He, however, also believes that it is his religious duty to protect Palestinians from “settler violence” and “ethnic cleansing.”
He cited the Torah as commanding Jews to care for the welfare of the ger and the toshav.
“This is a Torah commandment, and the people who are committing this violence, often they’re wearing kippot and tzitzit and peyot; they are committing horrific acts that bring a terrible name onto Israel and onto my community of religious Zionists.”
Advocacy with Bnei Avraham
This informs much of his advocacy with Bnei Avraham.
“We’re a religious Jewish organization interested in creating a positive relationship between Palestinian communities and the religious Jewish community in Israel and in trying to prevent settler violence against Palestinians,” he said. I have been active with the group since late 2023, early 2024.”
“In 2025, our focus was on two villages that we had a connection with in the South Jordan Valley, Ras Ein al-Auja and Mu’arrajat. We would regularly go to these villages. And when settlers would come there, we went in principle, our hope was we were going to spend time with our friends who live in this village. These two villages no longer exist because they were ethnically cleansed as a result of settler violence. Every time we went every day, they suffered some kind of incident interaction with hilltop youth where they would get harassed, we would get harassed.”
“Violent incidents are very common. And so we would go because we wanted to stand in solidarity with them. And also we felt that as Israelis, oftentimes the police took us more seriously than they would take the Palestinians.”
He claimed that neither he nor anyone in Bnei Avraham “has ever been involved in a violent incident in the West Bank or a criminal incident in the West Bank of any type.”
“We are very careful about obeying the law and being respectful human beings,” he added.
When pressed by the Post on whether this activism and rhetoric may fuel the fire of anti-Israel hate and misconceptions around all settlers being violent, Shenkin said that idea is a “misrepresentation.”
“We were in the Palestinian village of Ras al-Ain. Okay. Where people not from that village came to invade private property and harass the people who lived on that property. These are people who have come and established an outpost with the goal of expelling the people there, explicitly the goal of coming to expel the people there. That is what they pursued and did.”
“If the state of Israel believes that non-criminal activity–activity that is in line with the biblical Torah commandments of caring for the welfare of non-Jews in the land of Israel–doing that in a way in a pacifistic way that does not involve violence, if they believe that–it is a serious offense that denies a person the rights that are codified in the Torah.”
“If that’s the case, it’s a total outrage, and that’s why this is a big story.”
Shenkin hopes that with public interest in the story it will be resolved.
“What’s happening here is anti-Zionist. After all, the whole promise of Israel is that any Jew can move there simply because they’re Jewish. And now there’s this new idea that you have to support a certain agenda, or else we don’t want you.”
PIBA told the Post that “The requests have been received and are being reviewed individually on their own merits. There is no freeze whatsoever.”
The Jerusalem Post was unable to reach the Jewish Agency for comment; however, the organization told Ha’aretz: “The Population and Immigration Authority is the government body responsible for implementing the Law of Return. In light of this, and for reasons of privacy, we cannot comment on the details of the cases.”
