Chancellor questions Rydman’s STEA funding criteria
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:57:52 EEST
18:57:52 KST

Finland’s Chancellor of Justice has criticised Social Affairs and Health Minister Wille Rydman and his ministry over the preparation of new criteria for state grants to social welfare and health organisations, saying their wording risked giving a false impression of how funding decisions would be made.
Chancellor of Justice Janne Salminen issued his decision on Tuesday after receiving several complaints concerning the criteria for grants distributed by the Funding Centre for Social Welfare and Health Organisations, known as STEA.
The dispute centres on funding for 2027. STEA announced in June that continued grants would not be awarded to organisations whose activities focused on social advocacy or advisory work. The criteria also targeted organisations whose work focused mainly on one specific background or identity group without a health-related basis.
Salminen found the wording problematic because applicants might have understood that some types of organisations had been excluded before officials assessed individual applications.
“The setting of such restrictive criteria risks undermining confidence in the impartiality of the authority,” the Chancellor of Justice said in his decision.
Salminen said the preparation of state grants must comply with non-discrimination requirements and must also appear impartial from outside the administration.
The decision does not state that Rydman lacked authority to set priorities for STEA funding. Salminen said the minister had the power to provide more detailed direction on the activities eligible for grants.
That authority has limits. Funding criteria must comply with legislation and government decrees and must not introduce restrictions that legislation does not provide for, according to the Chancellor.
STEA changed its approach before the application process proceeded. Its September call for applications states that officials will disregard the disputed provision concerning organisations focused mainly on a particular non-health-related background or identity group.
Salminen also addressed how officials assess applications. Equal treatment requires officials to examine every application under the same criteria announced in advance. He questioned explanations suggesting that officials might rely on grounds that did not appear in the published call for applications.
The Chancellor also criticised the way the ministry prepared and recorded the criteria.
Rydman and the Ministry of Social Affairs and Health told the Chancellor that officials had not made a formal administrative decision when setting the criteria. Salminen accepted that such a decision was not necessarily required.
He said the criteria still carried major consequences for applicants. The ministry should therefore have used a formal presentation procedure when preparing and approving them, providing a record of the grounds behind the minister’s decision.
Such documentation supports transparency, external oversight and applicants’ legal protection, the Chancellor said.
The criteria became a source of dispute within Prime Minister Petteri Orpo’s government during the summer. Parliament also held a confidence vote concerning Rydman.
The government had agreed on €84 million in cuts to STEA grants. In August, the government approved changes to the decree governing how the funding is distributed after Orpo called for changes to the framework.
Rydman’s June announcement drew criticism in particular over the provision concerning organisations serving individual background or identity groups. Previous criticism focused on the effect the rules might have on organisations working with immigrants, asylum seekers and sexual and gender minorities.
The Chancellor’s decision does not prevent the government from setting funding priorities. It requires those priorities to remain within the legal framework governing state grants and calls on Rydman and the ministry to observe state-aid legislation and the legal principles governing public administration.

Breadcrumb
US tells Lebanon Hezbollah disarmament efforts 'not enough'
Lebanon has received negative signals from the United States over its efforts to bring Hezbollah's weapons under state control, with Washington warning that Israel intends to continue its military operations in the south, The New Arab has learned.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam received several messages while in New York on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, including warnings from US officials that Israel intends to maintain the security zone it has established in southern Lebanon.
Washington conveyed that Israel would continue its operations "as long as the Lebanese state does not take serious action to disarm Hezbollah", according to information obtained by TNA, and that it remains determined to destroy the group's military infrastructure.
US officials also told Salam that the steps taken by the Lebanese government so far were insufficient and that efforts to bring all weapons under state control must be accelerated.
According to the information obtained by TNA, Washington called for a firmer approach to the issue, warning that the situation could deteriorate further otherwise.
The warnings come as southern Lebanon faces near-daily Israeli escalation, with Israel stepping up its operations and insisting on maintaining the security zone it has established in the south.
Prospects for a solution are meanwhile receding, at least until Israel's parliamentary elections on 27 October.
Salam also received several messages of support, particularly from Arab and European countries, backing the government's decisions and Lebanon's demands for Israel to halt its attacks and withdraw from occupied Lebanese territory.
There was also support for the need to fill any security vacuum in southern Lebanon if the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) expires without renewal, with efforts expected to intensify in the coming period to find a solution to the crisis.
Hezbollah sets conditions for weapons talks
Attention is meanwhile turning to Hezbollah and whether the group could enter into a confrontation with Israel, particularly if Israeli military operations intensify.
Such a scenario remains unlikely in the near term, however, as Hezbollah is currently looking to developments between the US and Iran, with Tehran making Lebanon a key issue in its negotiations.
Hezbollah parliamentary sources told The New Arab that the group was "monitoring all developments, and its eyes will remain on the field. Iran remains committed to the Lebanon issue and will not abandon it, which is what should be relied upon rather than direct negotiations with the enemy".
They added that the Lebanese state should return to indirect negotiations with Israel and correct the course of the talks.
The sources said Hezbollah was open to discussing the issue of its weapons domestically and as part of a national defence strategy.
However, they said a complete halt to Israeli attacks and Israel's withdrawal from all Lebanese territory must come first.
Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem on Sunday renewed his call for Lebanese authorities to end what he described as concessions and review the course of negotiations, calling for direct talks to be suspended in favour of indirect negotiations.
His comments came on the second anniversary of the assassination of former Hezbollah secretary-generals Hassan Nasrallah and Hashem Safieddine.
"Let it be clear, Lebanon without resistance will disappear; the enemy wants all of Lebanon," Qassem said.
"Lebanon can only remain through its liberation and unity and the cooperation of its components. Whoever bets on retaining a part of Lebanon in exchange for abandoning the other part of the land or people is deluded."
Israel steps up attacks on southern Lebanon
Israeli forces carried out a series of attacks on several areas of southern Lebanon in recent hours, including the use of an Apache attack helicopter in a strike for the first time during the latest escalation.
The helicopter struck a commercial centre on the main road between the towns of Shoukine and Mifdoun in the Nabatieh district.
Israeli forces also carried out air strikes on Wadi Zibqin, Talouseh, Mais al-Jabal and the Al-Dabsh area, while artillery fire targeted Wadi Saluki, the outskirts of Kfar Tibnit and Nabatieh al-Fawqa, Al-Mansouri and Wadi Zibqin.
Israeli forces also opened machine-gun fire towards the outskirts of Kfar Shuba in the Azrael area, as well as Sarbin and the Al-Sadana area.
An explosion was also carried out by Israeli forces in Mais al-Jabal, while illumination flares were fired over Hadatha-Haris and Wadi Saluki.
The escalation comes as Israeli media reports suggest southern Lebanon could enter a new phase in the coming days following the completion of what Israel described as "clearing" operations on the Ali al-Taher heights and the destruction of Hezbollah infrastructure in the area.
Direct negotiations remain suspended despite Washington previously announcing that talks would take place in October.

Raytheon expands Sidewinder supplier base in U.S., Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:40:11 UTC
18:40:11 KST

The U.S. Navy is paying Raytheon up to $30.2 million to line up additional suppliers for key parts of the AIM-9X Sidewinder air-to-air missile, including the cooling engine for its heat-seeking sensor and its warhead components.
The undefinitized contract modification, announced by the U.S. Department of War, covers engineering work to qualify new manufacturing sources for several AIM-9X components. Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, awarded it without competition, and the work is due to be finished in February 2030.
Qualifying a second source means testing and approving another factory to make a part that currently comes from only one supplier, so that production does not stop if that supplier falls behind or shuts down. The notice lists the parts involved: the cryoengine, which cools the missile’s infrared seeker so it can detect a target’s heat; connectors and wiring harnesses; sensor platform and warhead components; components of the optical target detector, which senses when the missile is close enough to its target to detonate; and parts of the inertial measurement unit, which tracks the missile’s movement in flight.
The work will be spread across the United States and Europe. About half, 51%, will take place at Raytheon’s missile plant in Tucson, Arizona. Another 19% is set for Schrobenhausen, Germany, 12% for Anaheim, California, and 8% for Heilbronn, Germany, with smaller shares in Camarillo, California; Delémont, Switzerland; Midland, Ontario; and Logan, Utah.
The modification is a cost-plus-incentive-fee arrangement, meaning the government covers Raytheon’s costs and pays a fee that depends on performance. Because it is undefinitized, work can begin before final prices and terms are agreed, up to a $30.2 million ceiling. The Navy committed $29.6 million in fiscal 2025 weapons procurement funds at the time of award.
The AIM-9X is the latest version of the Sidewinder, a short-range, heat-seeking missile carried by U.S. and allied fighter jets and also fired from the ground by the NASAMS air defense system. The U.S. Navy leads the program jointly with the U.S. Air Force, and more than 35 allied and partner nations use the missile.
In June 2026, the U.S. Navy awarded Raytheon a $1.1 billion contract for more than 1,900 AIM-9X Block II missiles, including 1,653 for U.S. inventories and 336 for foreign customers, with work running through September 2029. That followed another $1.1 billion AIM-9X award in June 2025, then the largest in the program’s history. Raytheon says it is raising AIM-9X production capacity to about 2,500 missiles a year.

Mistry also allegedly helped siphon off funds from bank accounts of dummy companies in the UAE.The charge-sheet in the case has been filed before the competent court, the CBI said.
Red Notice issued in July
At the CBI’s request, an Interpol Red Notice was published against Mistry in July 2026. He was subsequently traced and arrested by UAE authorities, following which the deportation process was initiated.The CBI said Mistry was brought back to India within around two months of the notice being issued, following coordination among the agencies concerned.
Bank of India case against Nirav Modi
Separately, a London court has ordered Nirav Modi to pay more than $10.7 million to Bank of India over a loan extended to Firestar Diamond FZE, a Dubai-based company promoted by him.The loan facility was extended in 2012, and Nirav Modi had executed a personal guarantee in favour of the bank on August 3 that year. Under the guarantee, he was personally responsible for repayment in case of a default by the borrowing company.Nirav Modi challenged the recovery proceedings, arguing that the guarantee was unenforceable and that the bank had not made a valid demand for payment. He also claimed that he had not received notices issued in April 2018 and October 2025.
The court rejected his arguments and held that the notices had been properly served. It also observed that his legal representatives had received a copy of the April 2018 notice in 2019.The court concluded that Bank of India was entitled to seek repayment, accelerate the loan and enforce the personal guarantee.Nirav Modi has been lodged in a London prison since 2019 and is contesting extradition proceedings initiated by India in connection with the alleged multi-billion-dollar PNB fraud. He is also pursuing legal remedies before the European Court of Human Rights, ANI reported.

The movement in the lycees, which handle the final years of school in France, started in the Ile-de-France region around Paris, where blockades in some 10 schools were reported by education authorities on Sept 29. It has now spread to other cities nationwide.

At the Lamartine school in Paris, around 80 students gathered outside brandishing slogans like “more hours of lessons than sleep” and “8am to 6pm, are we pupils or under arrest?”

Tens of thousands were expected to rally in Paris and other cities, with teachers and fire services striking nationwide although with public transport not badly affected.
“The anger is immense. I warn the government: It must address the demands and revise the draft budget, which is dangerous for the country and is driving us straight into the wall of recession at 200 kilometres an hour,” the head of the hardline CGT union Sophie Binet told BFM TV.

“We are also there to support our teachers who have a crazy amount of work compared to what they earn,” she said.

What is Medicare for All, and how is it growing in US midterms?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:34:29 UTC
18:34:29 KST

Breadcrumb
What is Medicare for All, and how is it a growing movement in US midterms?
Medicare for All is proposal for a national universal healthcare plan for US residents that would eliminate the need for private insurance and payments for doctors’ visits and procedures. Once a largely left-wing position, support for the plan is becoming increasingly mainstream amid rising healthcare costs.
It is one of the top policy platforms for progressive candidates running in the 2026 midterms. It affects the vast majority of Americans currently living under a system in which they can go bankrupt over one medical bill.
National public healthcare is often referred to as “single payer healthcare” with the idea being that the government would be the one entity paying the cost of healthcare.
What is Medicare?
Medicare is a healthcare plan that covers US seniors (both citizens and residents). Its purpose is to financially cover healthcare for those over 65. It was established in 1965 under then-US President Dwight Eisenhower to support seniors, who, at the time, were paying far more for healthcare than their younger counterparts.
Along with Social Security (in which Americans collect a pension after retirement), Medicare has long been one of the most popular government programmes in the US. This was confirmed by a 2023 YouGov poll, which found that among members of both major parties these two programmes were the most popular of all social welfare plans.
Why has Medicare for All become so important in US politics?
Americans pay more per capita for healthcare than anyone else in the world. Despite this, the country ranks low among developed nations in key metrics, such as life expectancy and overall health.
Over the past several years, with skyrocketing healthcare costs, the popularity of Medicare for All has surged.
A 2025 survey conducted by Data for Progress found that 65 percent of US voters (including 79 percent of Democrats, 71 percent of Independents and 49 percent of Republicans) support a Medicare for All system that would replace the current private for-profit insurance plans.
This survey was conducted prior to the 2026 rise in healthcare premiums, in which subsidies were removed and many enrollees saw a 60 percent increase in monthly dues. Rates are expected to spike again in 2027.
What would Medicare for All mean?
Medicare for All would mean the phased transition from private health coverage to a government-funded system similar to what exists in much of the rest of the world. The proposed US model has often been compared to that of Canada and Taiwan.
Who supports it?
Medicare for All has the support of at least 136 members of Congress – 19 in the Senate and 117 in the House of Representatives, all of them Democrats (except for Bernie Sanders of Vermont, an Independent who caucuses with the Democrats). They are co-sponsors of a bill that would require the government to provide health coverage.
The politician who has most actively advocated for it is Bernie Sanders, who had it as one of his main platforms in his 2016 and 2020 presidential runs. In the current midterm cycle, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, a doctor and a former public health director who wrote a book on Medicare for All, also has it as one of his main campaign platforms.
Who opposes it?
The main opponents of Medicare for all are health insurance companies and others who benefit from the current system. Perhaps surprisingly, given the plan’s popularity, Democratic House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries has been a vocal opponent of it.
What are the main obstacles to passing it?
At present, there are not enough votes in Congress to pass Medicare for All. At the same time, the healthcare industry remains the biggest lobby group in US politics, spending around $6.4 billion on lobbying between 1998 and 2025, according to Investopedia.

UK nearly triples blocked arms export licences to Israel as policy tightens over Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:30:49 UTC
18:30:49 KST

Britain has sharply expanded restrictions on military exports to Israel, suspending or refusing more than 80 licences for items that could be used by the IDF in Gaza, nearly three times the number affected when the policy was introduced in September 2024.
UK Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty said more than 50 additional export applications had been refused since the initial suspension of around 30 licences, part of what he described as a tougher system for assessing exports to Israel.
The original September 2024 decision suspended roughly 30 of about 350 licences after the British government concluded there was a “clear risk” that certain military exports could be used to commit or facilitate serious violations of international humanitarian law in Gaza. The affected equipment included components for military aircraft, drones, naval systems and targeting equipment.
Doughty said additional measures adopted this month had created what he called a “double lock” on approvals. Export applications must now be considered both under the existing international humanitarian law criteria and in light of Britain’s position on the legality of Israel’s presence in the Palestinian territories.
“We have suspended or refused over 80 licences now,” Doughty said, adding that he had personally reviewed each licence.
F-35 components remain largely exempt
Despite the broader restrictions, British components entering the international F-35 fighter jet supply chain remain largely exempt.
The UK government has maintained that stopping British-made parts from entering the global F-35 pool could undermine the wider program and have serious consequences for the security of Britain and its allies. Direct exports of F-35 components intended specifically for Israel remain suspended.
Doughty defended the continued supply of components through the international program, arguing that halting them could have serious implications for the broader European and allied security architecture.
Foreign Affairs Committee chair Emily Thornberry challenged that position, arguing that the issue was political rather than purely legal.
She suggested adopting an approach similar to the Dutch model, under which components entering the international supply chain could be marked as not intended for aircraft destined for Israel.
The initial suspension was introduced under then-Foreign Secretary David Lammy in September 2024. Lammy stressed at the time that the measure did not constitute an arms embargo and applied only to items assessed as potentially usable in military operations in Gaza.
The policy has since been tightened under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Miliband signals tougher line on Israel
The expanded export restrictions come as the Burnham government adopts a more confrontational policy toward the Israeli government.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband received strong applause at Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool after sharply criticizing the Netanyahu government’s policies and defending Britain’s decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
Miliband accused Israel of war crimes in Gaza and said the British government had heard public anger over the conflict.
“We hear you. You were right,” he told delegates.
The tougher rhetoric and widening export restrictions mark a clear shift from the narrower 2024 policy, when Britain suspended around 30 licences while emphasizing that it was not imposing a general arms embargo on Israel.

Plastic Is Melting Onto Corals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Marine plastic pollution is rampant. That’s nothing new. Plastic waste has been found in a variety of marine ecosystems, including beaches, coral reefs, and even some of the ocean’s farthest depths. While a precise measurement is difficult, it’s estimated that several million metric tons of plastic lie on the seafloor.
Scientists have been recording marine animals entangled in or consuming plastic debris for over half a century, some even proposing the term “Plastocene” (the Plastic Age) to denote the geological epoch spanning from the 1950s onward. And now researchers have discovered a new way these substances are polluting the environment: Plastic is fusing with corals.
The discovery of this conglomerate—which researchers have dubbed “plasticoral”—was made during a survey of the beaches of the Ryukyu Islands in southern Japan. The scientists noticed small, brightly colored spots embedded in the white coral gravel. They collected samples from three beaches on the main island, Okinawa, and brought them to the lab where spectroscopic analysis revealed there were polymers derived from common household plastics.
Using micro-CT scans, the researchers determined that the polymers had melted into the microscopic pores in the fragments of coral skeleton, becoming so integrated that the two could no longer be separated.
This is also not the first time plastic has been found enmeshed with the natural world, though this phenomenon usually involves nonliving things like rocks. In 2019, another group of researchers found a thin layer of degraded plastic coating mussels and large algae in tide pools, which they called “plastiskin,” but this new study marks the first time plastic has been seen fused with corals.
And while coral rubble is no longer itself a living organism, even after being washed ashore, it often returns to sea later and plays an important role in coral reef ecosystems. It forms a stable foundation for new corals to settle on, and the irregular shapes make essential hiding places for small marine organisms to protect themselves from strong currents and predators.
How exactly the plasticorals may impact their living bretheren is unknown, though previous research has shown that some chemicals that can leach from common plastics inhibit coral reproduction. Other studies have found that plastic fragments can carry pathogens to corals.
Scientists are also not yet certain how the plastic is fusing with the corals. Though the temperatures of our oceans are ever increasing, they’re not quite hot enough yet to melt plastic. Ultraviolet radiation can also contribute, but the researchers consider beach bonfires to be the leading candidate.
Further investigation is needed to confirm this, but given plastic’s pervasiveness as a pollutant, it’s not unlikely that fires in even seemingly pristine areas are creating unintended fusions.
This story originally appeared in WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

About 1,500 refugees are to be sent back in the first phase, despite criticism from rights groups.
Malaysia has begun sending nearly 1,500 Rohingya refugees back to Myanmar, describing their return as voluntary despite warnings from the United Nations and rights groups that Myanmar remains unsafe for them.
Dozens of buses arrived under police escort at a stadium near the Lumut naval base in northwestern Malaysia on Tuesday, the AFP news agency reported. Journalists were barred from the grounds. The passengers were expected to be processed before being taken to the base and transported to Myanmar by ship.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items

- list 2 of 4Malaysia offers to invite Myanmar leader in Rohingya repatriation push
- list 3 of 4Myanmar’s Van dominates Pantoja to retain flyweight belt in UFC 331

The Myanmar army has repeatedly cracked down on the country’s Rohingya minority, including a wave of violence in 2017 that many rights groups have described as genocide, and which set off a major refugee crisis, with hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fleeing to Bangladesh, Malaysia, India and other neighbouring nations. Myanmar does not officially recognise the Rohingya as an ethnic community with local roots, instead describing them as “Bengalis” — in effect, calling them Bangladeshi migrants.
As of February 2026, Malaysia had more than 126,144 Rohingya refugees. Bangladesh hosts the most Rohingya refugees — more than 1.2 million.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said in July that Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya, leaving a question about who is being sent back. The nearly 1,500 picked for repatriation on Tuesday are part of the group. The Ministry of Home Affairs said two Myanmar naval warships and a hospital ship would be used.
The UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said it had no role in the operation and warned that continuing conflict and violence in Myanmar meant conditions for safe and dignified returns did not exist. “Any refugee return must be voluntary, based on an informed decision, and take place in conditions of safety and dignity,” it told the Reuters news agency.
Malaysia’s Home Ministry declined to comment on the warning, referring to its earlier statement that the returns were voluntary.
Rights advocates question whether people held in detention can freely choose to return to a country they fled.
“The genocide has never stopped. Sending Rohingya back to this is not repatriation,” Nay San Lwin, cochair of the Arakan Rohingya National Council (ARNC), a group representing the Rohingya, told Al Jazeera. “It is sending people back to a killing field. We call on Malaysia to halt all returns of Rohingya to Myanmar until it is safe.”
He argued that Malaysia’s decision to send refugees back to Myanmar came at a time when intense fighting was taking place between the army and rebel groups, including the Arakan Army.
“The Myanmar military has lost control of much of the Rohingya homeland, and its fighting with the Arakan Army is still ongoing, with Rohingya caught in the middle. Both the military and the Arakan Army are committing atrocities against the Rohingya,” he said.
Ro Mayyu Islam, founding Chair of the Center for Rohingya Crisis Studies based in Cox’s Bazaar, Bangladesh, also opposed the repatriation under the present conditions.
“Do not confuse repatriation with resolution. Moving Rohingya from Malaysian detention centres to Myanmar does not solve the Rohingya crisis. Address the conditions that forced us to flee, and then make the return genuinely safe, voluntary and sustainable,” he told Al Jazeera from Cox’s Bazaar.
“We are not asking the world to keep us refugees. We are demanding the right to return home as equal human beings with citizenship, security, dignity and fundamental rights.”
Meanwhile, Doctors Without Borders (MSF) has urged Malaysia to halt the returns and disclose who was being sent back and what risks each person faced. “Refugees should not be returned to places they’ve fled and where their lives are at risk,” the organisation said.
More than 160 civil society organisations also called for the repatriation to stop, citing violence and the risk that Rohingya could be pressed into armed groups. Their warning comes as Myanmar’s military fights the Arakan Army in Rakhine state, the region from which many Rohingya fled.
Myanmar’s government has promised “safe and dignified” returns for the Rohingya. Meanwhile, Malaysian Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil has said the country would not return people if they faced persecution or threats to their lives.
For Rohingya who have already gone back, the question is what awaits them after arrival. Ismail, 25, told AFP he left his work at a fish market in Malaysia amid arrests and rising hostility towards Rohingya. Now jobless in Yangon, he relies on relatives and still lacks full citizenship. “We are the most discriminated people,” he said. In Rakhine, a Rohingya activist identified as Mohammad feared returnees could be sent to displacement camps in a region still affected by fighting and disease.
The returns follow growing pressure on Rohingya in Malaysia. In July, authorities detained more than 100 people who gathered outside UNHCR’s office in Kuala Lumpur after facing eviction from an informal settlement in Penang. They were later released when officials confirmed they held UN documents, AFP reported. Malaysia is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention and does not formally recognise refugee status.
Anwar has said he intends to invite Myanmar’s Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, who led the military during the 2017 crackdown, to Malaysia to help accelerate the returns.

UAE admits Netanyahu made unannounced visit for talks with MBZ
The United Arab Emirates confirmed that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Abu Dhabi and met President Mohammed bin Zayed, a day after Israeli media revealed the previously secret trip.
The UAE's official WAM news agency confirmed the visit late on Monday, saying Mohammed bin Zayed had received Netanyahu during his trip to the country on Sunday.
The two leaders discussed relations between the UAE and Israel and "ways to strengthen and develop them", according to WAM.
Netanyahu's office also confirmed the visit, saying the talks focused on strengthening relations between the two countries and regional challenges.
The acknowledgement came after Israeli media reported on Sunday that Netanyahu had secretly travelled to Abu Dhabi, met Mohammed bin Zayed and returned to Israel the same day.
The visit comes less than a month before Israel's 27 October parliamentary election and amid controversy over reports that Mohammed bin Zayed warned Netanyahu shortly before the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack that a major operation could be imminent.
Haaretz reported earlier this month that Mohammed bin Zayed spoke to Netanyahu roughly 10 days before the attack and warned him that then-Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a "huge surprise".
The newspaper reported that the UAE had previously passed a warning to Israel's Shin Bet security agency.
Netanyahu’s office has denied that he had received such a warning. Netanyahu has also threatened legal action against Haaretz, accusing the newspaper of publishing a "fabricated" and "politically motivated" report.
The UAE subsequently said security matters with other countries are handled through the relevant agencies and that details of this kind are not discussed at the level of national leaders.
Meeting reportedly held at airport
Haaretz, citing Emirati sources, reported on Monday that Sunday's meeting took place at the airport and that Netanyahu asked Mohammed bin Zayed to deny reports concerning their alleged pre-7 October phone call.
According to the newspaper, Netanyahu also asked the Emirati president to deny other details relating to 7 October that could cause him political embarrassment and sought what was described as "moral support".
Israeli newspaper Maariv separately reported that Netanyahu had exerted considerable pressure on the UAE to arrange a visit before the election.
Emirati sources cited by the newspaper described the pressure as "very heavy", reportedly involving telephone calls, approaches through associates and international intermediaries, and references to future security cooperation.
Another visit had been fully arranged several days earlier, according to Maariv, but was cancelled shortly before Netanyahu was due to depart.
The Emirati side reportedly told Israel that Mohammed bin Zayed was not in the country, although subsequent checks indicated that the UAE president was in Abu Dhabi at the time.
A source cited by Maariv said Mohammed bin Zayed did not want to become part of Netanyahu's election campaign.
Despite the cancellation, Israeli efforts to secure the meeting continued, culminating in Sunday's visit.
Israel's Channel 12 was among the first outlets to disclose the trip. Israel's Shin Bet subsequently filed a complaint with the country's military censor over the report, arguing that its publication endangered Netanyahu and exposed the security agency’s operational methods, according to the Associated Press.
Netanyahu's visit comes as Israel and the UAE maintain diplomatic relations established under the US-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020.
The latest meeting was held around six months after Netanyahu's office claimed he had made another secret visit to the UAE during the war with Iran. Abu Dhabi publicly denied that visit at the time, saying reports of unannounced visits or undisclosed arrangements were unfounded unless officially announced by Emirati authorities.

Defence chief Vansina on fears Russia will overstep the line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:26:44 UTC
18:26:44 KST

With hybrid attacks on the rise, Russia is attempting to undermine European support for Ukraine, both directly and indirectly, says Belgium’s Chief of Defence Frederik Vansina. “So far, Russia has always remained below the threshold set by Article 5 of the NATO Treaty, which equates an attack on one NATO country with an attack on all. But there is a fear that sooner or later they will cross that threshold.”
On Friday, Belgium’s National Security Council will meet to examine the so-called hybrid warfare threat. The federal security services and the relevant ministers are working on a plan to better protect Belgium against potential incidents.
“We have certainly seen these incidents escalate since the start of the year,” says Frederik Vansina, Chief of the Defence Staff. “That is why the government is convening the National Security Council.”
At present, there is no specific cause for concern or concrete threat to Belgium, says Vansina. “Intelligence from our eastern allies points to an increase. It is important to piece everything together and gain a better picture of the situation.”
Is Russia testing Europe?
In the incidents of recent months, the focus has mainly been on Russia. It is sometimes said that Russia is ‘testing’ Europe. What are we to make of that?
‘Russia is now in its fifth year of the war. They are relatively bogged down in the Ukrainian mud, but they are making slow yet steady progress,’ says Vansina. ‘Ukraine really needs Western support – particularly from Europe – to keep up the fight.’
“And Russia, of course, wants to undermine that support. Directly, as we saw in an incident at Leipzig Airport, for example, but also indirectly – by undermining the resolve of Ukraine’s allies and the support of public opinion.”
Russia is “sensible enough” to stay just below the threshold of NATO’s Article 5, says Vansina. That article states that an attack on one NATO member state is an attack on all member states, and that NATO will respond.
What is Belgium doing?
Belgium is sometimes referred to as an ‘interesting’ target for hybrid attacks. “Belgium is home to NATO headquarters, Euroclear (a company that manages funds and investments, including frozen Russian assets), the ports, key military bases, …” Vansina dishes up a long list.
“Belgium is also a logistical transit country. In the event of a conflict, many reinforcements would arrive via Belgian ports and airports.”
So, we are an attractive target for adversaries, but we are extremely vigilant, says Vansina. “We already have a high level of security in place, depending on the sensitivity of the military bases.”
Vansina refers, amongst other things, to the additional investment in the capacity to detect and intercept drones. At the end of last year, the government brought forward investment in its anti-drone plan, following reports of drones flying over military bases and airports.
‘An accelerated investment of 50 million euros was made, enabling us to improve the security of our bases,’ says Vansina. ‘Most of that equipment has now been delivered and put into service. Our bases are now better protected against drones than they were a year ago.’
“We are also currently working on integrating sensors from other organisations, such as air traffic control provider Skeyes, into our air command centre,” says Vansina. “We are constantly taking measures to improve the security of our installations, and therefore also that of the public.”

U.S. to send Philippine Coast Guard three spy-equipped planes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:26:17 UTC
18:26:17 KST

- Technology Service Corp. received a $39.6 million contract to supply the Philippine Coast Guard with three pre-owned King Air 350 aircraft by September 2028.
- Two of the aircraft will carry surveillance sensors, and the deal is funded entirely with foreign military sales money.
The United States will supply the Philippine Coast Guard with three secondhand King Air 350 turboprop aircraft, two of them fitted with surveillance sensors, under a $39.6 million contract that finalizes a deal the two countries signed in February.
The U.S. Department of War announced the firm-fixed-price award to Technology Service Corp., a small business based in Arlington, Virginia. The company will provide three pre-owned, extended-range King Air 350 Maritime Domain Awareness aircraft, along with sensor operator training, ferry flights to the Philippines, technical manuals and training materials. Work is scheduled to be completed in September 2028.
The King Air 350 is a twin-engine turboprop built by Textron Aviation’s Beechcraft brand and widely used for patrol, surveillance and medical evacuation. Two of the three aircraft will receive intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance equipment and mission management software, which lets crews track ships, collect imagery and share what they see. The third will not carry the sensor suite.
An earlier notice from the Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division said all three aircraft would get extended-range fuel tanks, a gross weight increase, Garmin G1000 NXi avionics and high-frequency radios, and that the two surveillance aircraft would carry the King Air 350 Maritime Domain Awareness, or KAMDA, sensor package. Neither notice lists the specific sensors.
The contract is paid for entirely with foreign military sales funds, the money a partner country uses to buy U.S. defense equipment through the U.S. government. All $39.6 million was committed at the time of award. The contract was not competed. The Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division at Patuxent River, Maryland, is managing it.
Most of the work, 70%, will take place in Crystal City, Virginia, with the rest spread across sites in New Century, Meriden and Wichita, Kansas; Manila; Concord, North Carolina; and New Smyrna Beach, Florida.
Philippine Coast Guard Commandant Adm. Ronnie Gil Gavan and U.S. Assistant Secretary of War for Indo-Pacific Security Affairs John Noh signed the letter of offer and acceptance for the aircraft on Feb. 16 in Makati City. At the time, the coast guard said the planes would strengthen its ability to watch Philippine waters and respond faster to emergencies at sea, after the capsizing of the bulk carrier M/V Devon Bay and the January sinking of the ferry M/V Trisha Kerstin 3 off Basilan, which left dozens dead. The coast guard also cited the need for sustained surveillance in the West Philippine Sea, the Philippine name for the parts of the South China Sea it claims.
The two officials also discussed a U.S. Coast Guard search planning program that uses environmental modeling to predict where people lost at sea are likely to be found. This year, the Philippine Coast Guard became the first foreign coast guard to take part in the U.S.-led Rim of the Pacific exercise in Hawaii.

LANG’s los angeles flagship layers fragments of hong kong into a former warehouse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:25:36 UTC
18:25:36 KST

LANG’s los angeles flagship layers fragments of hong kong into a former warehouse
a mix of fashion, exhibitions, and gathering, the space uses everyday references and tactile materials to create a place for cultural exchange.
Paul Chan turns cultural memory into a retail interior
Studio Paul Chan completes LANG’s 110-square-meter flagship at ROW DTLA in Los Angeles, transforming a former industrial warehouse into a fashion store and cultural venue shaped by the experience of living between cultures. Founded by Hong Kong-born Kayla Wong, LANG focuses on Asian-founded fashion brands while hosting exhibitions, artist talks, performances, and community gatherings. The interior uses material, craft, and everyday rituals to consider how cultural identity can be rebuilt through migration and adaptation.
For architect Paul Chan, who was also born in Hong Kong, the project begins with memory but does not end in nostalgia. ‘Much of our generation exists between cultures,’ says Chan. ‘The goal was never to recreate Hong Kong, but to ask how memories of one place can evolve into something entirely new when they meet another. Los Angeles isn’t the backdrop for that conversation, it is where entirely new cultural identities are formed.’ Studio Paul Chan treats cultural identity as something that changes and accumulates over time. Instead of recreating Hong Kong, the interior brings together familiar materials, objects, and spatial references, reworking them through a Los Angeles context.
LANG’s row dtla flagship is organized around discovery
Paul Chan divides the former warehouse into smaller environments. Velvet curtains replace permanent walls, allowing the layout to change between shopping, exhibitions, talks, performances, and gatherings. Mirrored partitions conceal rooms and create moments of discovery as visitors move through the store. The arrangement draws on the experience of Hong Kong’s layered neighborhoods, where narrow passages, changing scales, and unexpected interiors can produce a sense of spatial discovery. This approach gives the store a degree of flexibility. Retail is one activity among several, with the architecture accommodating the social and cultural programming that has become part of LANG’s identity.
The material palette combines custom mahogany shelving with mauve moiré wallcovering, hand-brushed aluminum clothing shelves, vintage textiles, polished mirrors, handmade paper, and the retained concrete shell. Warm timber sits alongside industrial aluminum, while the roughness of the existing structure is placed against more tactile and decorative surfaces. Studio Paul Chan allows these differences to remain visible. A similar logic appears in the Washi Table, part of the studio’s Domestic Ritual furniture collection. Its surface is assembled from handmade papers sourced across East and Southeast Asia, including Hong Kong, China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines. Different fibers, textures, degrees of translucency, and cultural histories become one continuous surface. The table offers a useful parallel for the larger project. Identity here is not represented by a single material or symbol, but constructed through accumulation.
ordinary objects become collective references
At the center of the store, a circular upholstered lounge occupies nearly half of the floor area, making gathering as important to the plan as retail display. Its custom upholstery, developed with Los Angeles textile studio SUAY, takes its colors from Hong Kong’s familiar red, white, and blue woven utility bags. These bags are associated with hardware stores, construction sites, and street markets, but the project does not reproduce them literally. Their palette becomes an architectural surface instead. Cushions referencing the striped towels of traditional cha chaan teng cafés add another everyday reference. These details shift the focus away from iconic representations of Hong Kong toward objects associated with ordinary routines and shared memories.
Above the lounge, four tiers of handmade paper lanterns are individually painted with colloquial Cantonese sayings. Inspired by weathered lanterns found outside Cantonese opera houses and neighborhood festivals, the installation functions simultaneously as lighting, a visual marker, and a social focal point.
Hidden behind mirrored partitions, the fitting room uses reflections to dissolve the apparent boundaries of the room, while a luminous ceiling produces an even, diffuse light. The effect is intentionally ambiguous. Familiar references elsewhere in the store give way to a space where orientation becomes less certain, turning the fitting room into a more direct spatial expression of the project’s interest in inhabiting multiple cultural contexts. Another installation draws from Hong Kong neighborhood newsstands. Instead of reconstructing one of the compact kiosks literally, Studio Paul Chan layers vintage advertisements and printed ephemera to evoke their informal atmosphere. The reference locates cultural memory in everyday urban rituals: buying a newspaper, browsing printed material, exchanging a few words, or simply encountering other people alongside commerce.

Japan remained the largest Asian source of visitors to the US, followed by China, South Korea, India and Taiwan.

Taiwan university develops underwater vehicle monitoring system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:24:36 UTC
18:24:36 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — National Kaohsiung University of Science and Technology has developed a system that monitors the structural condition of underwater vehicles in real time, the Ocean Affairs Council said Wednesday.
The council funded the research to address the difficulty of monitoring pressure hulls during extended deep-sea operations, according to a press release.
Fiber-optic sensors installed at key locations collect data that the system uses to generate three-dimensional maps of stress and deformation across the pressure hull. A digital twin identifies damaged areas, while an AI model estimates the structure’s remaining service life to help operators determine when maintenance is required.
The researchers also developed a nontoxic biomimetic coating to prevent marine organisms from accumulating on the vehicle without harming the surrounding environment. High-pressure packaging and a corrosion-resistant biomimetic coating allowed the sensors to withstand pressure-chamber testing and sea trials at a depth of 300 meters.
The council said the technology could reduce the risk of sudden structural failure during underwater missions by more than 90% and cut maintenance and operating costs by about 30%.
The system could also be used to inspect and monitor underwater infrastructure at offshore wind farms, the council said.

Germany's persistence in debating the consequences of denying Israel's right to exist is not meant to create more nuance and force the pro-Palestine movement to make its stances, chants, and slogans clearer. Soldiers and mercenaries killed at least 34 civilians in Mali, Amnesty report says
DAKAR, Sept 29 - At least 34 civilians were killed in seven incidents during military joint operations in Mali by the army and Russia's Wagner mercenary group between June 2023 and December 2025, Amnesty International said in a report on Tuesday.
• The human rights organization documented the deaths of 34 people, who it said were not participating in hostilities, in incidents across Mali's Segou, Mopti and Timbuktu regions along the Mauritanian border.
• It said the victims were mostly members of pastoralist communities who were attacked based on their ethnicity and their presence in areas where jihadist groups were active.
• Mali's military-led government, which took power after coups in 2020 and 2021, has denied killing civilians in its fight against jihadists. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment, nor did Moscow.
• "These murders were deliberate: the victims were shot, had their throats cut, or were burned alive," Amnesty's report said, adding that acts described in the report amounted to war crimes.
• Those interviewed for the report told Amnesty they were tortured mostly by Wagner members during patrols or during their detention at military bases. Others described civilians being hit in drone strikes and the destruction of civilian property.
• "In their minds, all herders are terrorists, and as a result they do not hesitate to burn people and property," a herder who has taken refuge in Mauritania told Amnesty.
• The Wagner mercenary group left Mali in 2025. But the Africa Corps, which is made up of many former Wagner fighters, still operates there.
• Amnesty said it shared the report's findings with the Malian authorities on August 3 but did not receive a response at the time of publication. REUTERS

Pentagon orders more fuzes to turn Hydra rockets into drone killers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:19:43 UTC
18:19:43 KST

The Pentagon has ordered another $52.3 million worth of L3Harris proximity fuzes that turn laser-guided APKWS rockets into drone killers, more than doubling the value of a fuze contract signed just four months ago.
The firm-fixed-price modification, announced by the U.S. Department of War, adds to a contract the Naval Surface Warfare Center Indian Head Division awarded L3Harris Fuzing and Ordnance Systems in late May. The work will be done in Cincinnati, Ohio, and is due to be finished by November 2027. The notice does not say how many fuzes the money buys.
A proximity fuze sets off a warhead when it senses a target nearby, so the rocket does not have to hit a small, fast-moving drone directly to destroy it. L3Harris calls the product its Mechanical Proximity Fuze, also known as the FALCO fuze, after the Fixed Wing, Air Launched, Counter-Unmanned Aircraft Systems Ordnance program. It combines radio-frequency sensor electronics from Technology Service Corporation with an L3Harris safe-and-arm device.
The fuze is fitted to the Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System, or APKWS, a BAE Systems guidance kit that turns ordinary 70 mm (2.75-inch) Hydra rockets into laser-guided weapons. The rockets are far cheaper than air-to-air missiles, and a single F-16 carrying six seven-tube launchers can hold 42 of them.
U.S. Air Force F-16s began using proximity-fuzed APKWS rockets to shoot down Houthi one-way attack drones over the Red Sea in 2024. In testing at Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona, APKWS rockets with the L3Harris fuze destroyed Group 3 drones, the larger class of unmanned aircraft, every time, The Defence Blog reported in May. The same fuze arms rockets fired by L3Harris’ VAMPIRE, a truck-mounted counter-drone launcher that Ukraine has used against Russian drones since 2023.
The original May contract was worth $48.5 million, with options that could raise it to about $98 million and deliveries running through July 2027. L3Harris has said demand is pushing it to increase proximity fuze production sevenfold. Most of the new money, $44.8 million, or 86%, comes from fiscal 2026 Defense-wide operations and maintenance funds. Another $3.8 million comes from fiscal 2025 funds of the same type, which expire at the end of the current fiscal year on Sept. 30, and $3.7 million comes from fiscal 2026 U.S. Army ammunition procurement funds. The notice does not say which units will receive the fuzes.
The Pentagon is also developing a newer air-to-air version of APKWS. In February 2026, the U.S. Air Force awarded BAE Systems a contract worth up to $145 million for an APKWS variant with a long-wave infrared seeker and a proximity-fuzed warhead, which lets the rocket home in on a drone’s heat without a pilot having to keep a laser on the target. That version is planned for U.S. Air Force F-16s and U.S. Navy MH-60 helicopters.

Argentina’s Milei threatens legal action over Falklands oil project
Argentina gives UK two weeks to cease operations or face maritime court action.
Argentinian President Javier Milei has threatened the British government with legal action unless it stops an oil project off the disputed Falkland Islands, the British-administered territory over which Buenos Aires claims sovereignty.
Milei gave the United Kingdom a two-week ultimatum on Monday evening, saying it must halt all work on the Sea Lion oil project or Argentina will ask the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, a maritime court in Hamburg, Germany, to order a stop to the project.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Why is Argentina reigniting the Falklands dispute?
- list 2 of 3Why do the Falkland Islands matter to the UK and Argentina so much?
- list 3 of 3Milei says UN ‘looking the other way’ on Falkland Islands dispute
He called the operations “the illegal plundering of our resources” and declared “Argentina will not stand idly by” as the UK causes “irreversible and irreparable” damage.
The companies developing the project, Israel’s Navitas and Britain’s Rockhopper, have shrugged off Argentina’s threats, insisting they have valid exploration licences issued by the UK.
The tribunal, an independent court established under the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, can issue legally binding emergency orders. But even if it ordered the UK to halt the project, it has no means of forcing the government to comply.
The UK rejects Argentina’s sovereignty claim, arguing that the islanders have the right to determine their own future and develop their natural resources. In a referendum in 2013, residents of the Falklands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory. Argentina says the islands were populated illegally.
Milei’s administration has already taken legal action against the project authorised by Britain, arguing it violates a United Nations resolution calling for both sides to desist from unilateral actions in the islands until their dispute is resolved.
Buenos Aires has doubled down on its claim over the Falklands since United States President Donald Trump said Washington was open to reviewing its historically neutral stance on the territory.
The British government for its part has said it stands behind the businesses operating near the Falklands.
The dispute over the Falkland Islands led to a war between Britain and Argentina in 1982. It killed 649 Argentinian soldiers, 255 British soldiers and three islanders after Argentina invaded the archipelago that year.

Germany’s potential next leader holds talks in Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:14:53 UTC
18:14:53 KST

Hendrik Wüst, the premier of Germany’s most populous state and the country’s potential next leader, has begun his three-day visit to Türkiye on Sept. 28. (AA Photo)
Hendrik Wüst, the premier of Germany’s most populous state and the country’s potential next leader, has called for a “new chapter” in ties with Türkiye as he began a three-day visit to the country on Sept. 28.
Wüst, the conservative premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, arrived in the Turkish capital Ankara with a large delegation that included senior business representatives.
He was received by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan shortly after landing.
The visit comes as Germany and Türkiye mark the 65th anniversary of the 1961 labor recruitment agreement that brought Turkish “guest workers” to West Germany.
Around 3 million people of Turkish origin currently live in Germany, according to the country’s Federal Statistical Office, with slightly more than half holding German citizenship.
Wüst highlighted the strong links between Türkiye and North Rhine-Westphalia, noting that roughly one-third of Germany’s population of Turkish origin lives in the state.
“They are naturally part of our state,” Wüst said, becoming the first premier of North Rhine-Westphalia to make an official visit to Türkiye.
The 51-year-old politician has repeatedly rejected speculation that he could seek to replace Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose government has come under pressure.
“I want to remain premier of North Rhine-Westphalia,” Wüst told German broadcaster ZDF before departing for Türkiye, adding that his priority was to help “get the federal government firing on all cylinders again.”
During his first day in Ankara, Wüst was scheduled to visit a Henkel facility belonging to the Düsseldorf-based company before paying his respects at the mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder of modern Türkiye.
He was also due to meet Turkish business representatives.
On Sept. 29, Wüst is expected to hold political meetings in Ankara before traveling to Istanbul.
His Istanbul program includes a business conference and a ceremony honoring former Germany football captain İlkay Gündoğan with an award recognizing tolerance and intercultural reconciliation.
Speaking ahead of the trip, Wüst said he wanted to concentrate on areas where Germany and Türkiye could deepen cooperation, arguing that difficult issues could be addressed more effectively through a close partnership.
“No [German] region is as closely connected to Türkiye, socially and economically, as North Rhine-Westphalia,” he said.

The Samir Kassir Award for Freedom of the Press has named Ali Al-Ibrahim, co-director of OCCRP member center Siraj, and Syrian investigative journalist Mais Katt as joint winners in its investigative reporting category. The award recognizes their September 2025 cross-border investigative project, “Syria’s Stolen Children: How the Assad Regime Turned Detainees’ Children into Hostages Between Intelligence Agencies and Orphanages.”
Published a year ago following the fall of Bashar al-Assad in late 2024, the investigation documents how officials from al-Assad’s security services abducted hundreds of Syrian children of political detainees and hid them inside children’s charities in order to coerce and intimidate their families. The investigation exposed the complicity of several care institutions, including facilities run by the major European charity SOS Children’s Villages, whose leadership knew about the abuses for years and remained silent.
The Samir Kassir Award, which has been presented by the E.U. since 2006, selected the investigation from 194 submissions across 11 countries in North Africa, the Middle East and the Gulf.

Iran parliament speaker warns no one in region will sell oil if Tehran cannot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:12:50 UTC
18:12:50 KST

Mohammad Sio
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf warned Tuesday that no country in the region would be able to sell oil if Iran were prevented from doing so, according to the state-run IRNA news agency.
“The US and other countries should know, as we have said, that in a region where we cannot sell oil, no one will sell oil,” Qalibaf said.
His warning comes as Iran faces severe restrictions on its oil exports amid the ongoing conflict with Washington and US sanctions.
Iran’s Central Bank governor said in August that the country’s oil exports had fallen to zero, saying Tehran was no longer exporting crude because of the war and sanctions.
The US military, meanwhile, said on Sept. 19 that more than 1 billion barrels of crude oil had passed through the Strait of Hormuz in recent months with US military assistance, while claiming Iran had exported “zero barrels” under what Washington calls its “ironclad blockade.”
“If our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will be safe,” Ghalibaf said.
Earlier this month, Qalibaf warned that US energy infrastructure and assets around the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz could face Iranian retaliation if Washington attacked Iran’s oil and gas facilities.
Qalibaf also referred to recent remarks by US President Donald Trump concerning the Strait of Hormuz and the passage of vessels through the waterway, describing them as a repetition of earlier US claims.
Trump on Saturday rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to normal commercial traffic within seven days, saying Tehran’s conditions were unacceptable and claiming Washington already had “total control” of the waterway.
Under Tehran’s proposal, Washington would release frozen Iranian assets, lift oil sanctions and end the US naval blockade on Iranian ports, after which Iran would move to reopen the strait and talks on a final agreement would begin.
Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz restricted while demanding that Washington fulfill commitments under a June memorandum of understanding. Iran says that the waterway will not fully reopen until Iran’s conditions are met and US commitments are implemented.
On Monday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that Qatari mediators will present the US with new ideas discussed with Tehran on how to meet Iran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Qalibaf also warned Washington against further pressure on Tehran, saying Iran will not retreat in the face of what he described as “air or commercial blockades.”
His comments come as Washington has expanded economic pressure beyond Iran’s oil and maritime sectors to civil aviation.
“The leaders of the White House should know that Iran, a wise nation that has made history, will never retreat because of lines being drawn, speeches, or air or commercial blockades,” Qalibaf said.
He added that Iran’s response to “any threat or adventurism” would be “regrettable and swift.”
In February, the US and Israel launched a war against Iran, which responded with attacks on Israel and US targets in the region before a ceasefire agreement was reached in April.
Washington and Tehran later signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, but implementation stalled over disagreements related to security in the strategic waterway as tensions continue to escalate between the two sides.

Honeywell gets $25.6M for nuclear-tough navigation gyro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:08:21 UTC
18:08:21 KST

- The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory awarded Honeywell $25.6 million to mature a compact, radiation-hardened strategic gyroscope, with work due by July 2029.
- The contract follows a $41.6 million laboratory award in 2020 for Honeywell to design a Compact Strategic-Grade Gyroscope.
The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory has awarded Honeywell Aerospace $25.6 million to keep developing a small, radiation-hardened gyroscope accurate enough for “strategic” use, the class of navigation sensor that has to work in space and survive the effects of a nuclear environment.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee contract covers what the Pentagon calls the compact strategic gyroscope maturation project, the U.S. Department of War said. Honeywell will do the work in Clearwater, Florida, and is expected to finish by July 1, 2029. The laboratory’s office at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico, is managing the contract.
Combined with accelerometers in an inertial navigation system, it lets a missile, satellite, ship or aircraft work out where it is and which way it is pointing without GPS or any other outside signal. “Strategic-grade” refers to the most accurate class of these sensors, used where drift has to stay extremely low for long periods, such as in ballistic missile guidance and satellite pointing. Radiation hardening means the sensor and its electronics are built to keep working when hit by the radiation found in space or produced by a nuclear blast.
The notice does not say which weapon or spacecraft the gyroscope is intended for.
The award builds on earlier Air Force Research Laboratory work with the same company. In early 2020, the laboratory’s Space Vehicles Directorate at Kirtland gave Honeywell a $41.6 million contract to design a Compact Strategic-Grade Gyroscope, Military & Aerospace Electronics reported. That five-year effort, carried out at Honeywell’s Phoenix site, called for building and testing four prototypes, refining the design into six strategic-grade units, developing a radiation-hardened custom chip and software for the gyro, flying it on an experimental satellite for a one-year mission in low Earth orbit, and laying out a path toward a gyroscope that could keep operating through the radiation and electromagnetic pulse of nuclear explosions. The earlier contract was scheduled to run through August 2025.
The Department of War did not say how much of the first project’s goals were met or whether the space flight took place. The new work is described as “maturation,” which in defense research usually means taking a design that has been shown to work and making it more reliable, easier to build and closer to use in a real system.
The contract was competitively awarded, and the government received two offers. Only $500,000 in fiscal 2026 research and development money was committed at the time of award, with the rest of the $25.6 million to be added in later years.
Honeywell’s Clearwater site is one of the company’s main centers for navigation and inertial sensor work. The notice did not name the second bidder.

Turkish trade minister to visit US to tackle food security, overproduction and more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:07:44 UTC
18:07:44 KST

Seda Tolmac and Emir Yildirim
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Turkish Trade Minister Omer Bolat is traveling to the US on Wednesday to attend the G20 trade ministers’ meeting and the Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity (GFSEC) in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.
The two-day summit, hosted under the American G20 presidency, will gather trade ministers at a time when world trade is navigating fragmentation risks and geopolitical tensions.
The agenda will focus on combating the weaponization of food supplies via coercive trade decisions, eliminating forced labor within global supply chains and addressing structural production overcapacity.
The event will also involve talks on potential updates to the most-favored-nation (MFN) principle, which has served as a foundational pillar of the multilateral trading system.
Participating ministers will outline their national policies on these agenda items and explore strategies to boost global economic cooperation.
Meanwhile, the GFSEC will address chronic overproduction issues that have consistently strained the global metals trade.
The forum will evaluate the multifaceted economic impact of market excesses and involve talks to determine actionable steps to resolve the root causes of industrial overcapacity.
Bolat will express Ankara’s strategic perspectives and specific concerns over the proposed changes to global trade at the gathering, according to the Turkish Trade Ministry.
The minister will also hold a series of bilateral meetings with senior representatives from the US, the EU, Canada, the UK, Poland, South Korea and Saudi Arabia on the sidelines of the G20 summit.
The diplomatic talks will constitute a platform for officials to evaluate ongoing bilateral economic initiatives and track the progress of mutual trade deals while providing Türkiye with a dedicated stage to address geopolitical and commercial issues currently dominating its mutual agenda with key global partners.

Genes may influence fruit, vegetable intake: twin study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:07:28 CST
18:07:28 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- An international twin study found that genetic differences contribute to fruit and vegetable intake, highlighting the complex mix of biological, social and environmental factors that shape people's diets.
The research challenges the idea that healthy eating is simply a matter of willpower, finding that genetics may help explain why some people find it easier than others to maintain healthy dietary habits, according to a statement released Tuesday by the Center for Healthy Brain Ageing (CHeBA) at Australia's University of New South Wales.
The study, published in Behavior Genetics, examined 5,789 twins aged 45 to 90 from four international community-based studies.
Researchers estimated that fruit consumption was 25 percent heritable and vegetable consumption 17 percent heritable, meaning genetic differences accounted for about one-quarter of the variation between individuals in fruit intake and around one-sixth of the variation in vegetable intake.
"Dietary behavior is far more complex than people think," said lead author Annabel Matison, a postdoctoral research fellow at the CHeBA, adding, "Genetics is one of many factors that may contribute to what we eat, alongside food availability, culture, cost, personal preferences and our individual life experiences."
However, the findings showed that genetic influence should not be viewed as "genetic destiny," noting that most of the variation in dietary intake was attributable to non-genetic influences.
The study also found a positive genetic correlation between fruit and vegetable intake, suggesting some genetic factors influencing fruit consumption may also influence vegetable consumption. ■

Türkiye must take center stage as global trade routes shift, sector body says

Gokhan Ergocun
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
The Foreign Economic Relations Board of Türkiye (DEIK) report revealed that China shifts its trade routes to alternative markets, creating new opportunities for Türkiye amid changing global trade balances.
 
DEIK prepared an analysis covering the transformation in Chinese foreign trade and its possible consequences for Türkiye after the US implemented additional customs tariffs.
 
The document showed that China's export share to the US decreased to 11.14% in 2025 from 14.68% in 2024.
 
DEIK Chair Nail Olpak stated on Tuesday that protectionist policies in global trade reshaped global routes instead of just affecting two countries.
 
Olpak noted that the decline in the US market drove China to create new trade channels across a wide geography from Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to Africa.
 
China increased its exports to Africa by 25.9%, the Middle East by 9.7% and the EU by 8.6% in the 2024-2025 period, he said.
 
The analysis highlighted Nigeria in Africa, the UAE in the Middle East and Germany in the EU as prominent markets for China.
 
The president mentioned that Türkiye must closely monitor the geographic diversification in Chinese exports.
He stated that China heavily targeted Africa, the Middle East and Europe to compensate for its loss in the US market.
Olpak added that these regions represent areas where the Turkish business world traditionally maintains a strong presence or aims to expand.
The report indicated that the production capacity, geographic location and logistics advantages of Türkiye provide significant benefits during this global trade restructuring.
Chinese exports to Germany, the largest export market for Türkiye, increased by 10.55% during the 2024-2025 period.
The existing data showed that the rise of China in the German market did not pose a direct threat to Türkiye yet.
The DEIK report warned that Türkiye should closely monitor the increasing competition in the African and Middle Eastern markets.
China exported goods worth $20 billion to Egypt in 2025, while Turkish exports to the country stood at $4 billion.
 
Olpak stressed that Türkiye established multi-dimensional relations in Africa involving contracting, investments and industrial cooperation beyond simple price competition.
Chinese exports to the UAE surged to $72.9 billion in 2025, whereas Türkiye recorded $9.3 billion in exports to the same market.
 
He urged Turkish companies to focus on greater value-added production, stronger brands and innovation against China's strong position in electrical devices.
The president highlighted that global trade started to experience a rising competition of trust alongside the traditional price and technology rivalry.
 
Olpak concluded that Türkiye aimed to become a reliable partner that takes a proactive position in the new trade architecture instead of just watching the changes.

U.S. Air Force pays $64 million for secretive balloon project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:00:56 UTC
18:00:56 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded Aerostar a $64.4 million sole-source contract for Swamp Gas, a prototype for an urgent high-altitude balloon need.
- The contract runs through March 2028, and the balloon's mission, users and payloads have not been disclosed.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded balloon maker Aerostar a $64.4 million contract to quickly build a prototype for an urgent high-altitude balloon requirement under a project called Swamp Gas.
The contract covers development of a “minimum viable product” prototype, meaning an early working version with just enough capability to be tested and used, to support what the Pentagon called a “High-Altitude Balloon Operational Urgency.” Operational urgency is the term the military uses for a need from the field that has to be met faster than normal acquisition allows.
The notice does not say what the balloon is meant to do, which U.S. military command or unit asked for it, what it will carry or where it could be used. Work will be done in Arlington, Virginia, and is scheduled to finish by March 23, 2028.
Aerostar Technical Solutions received the contract without competition. Nearly all of the money was committed at once: $57.7 million in fiscal 2025 research and development funds and $6.3 million in fiscal 2026 funds, about $64 million of the $64.4 million total. The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, is managing the contract.
The project name has an unusual history. In 1966, U.S. Air Force consultant J. Allen Hynek suggested that “swamp gas” could explain a wave of UFO sightings in Michigan, an explanation that became a lasting punchline in the UFO world. The Air Force did not say why it chose the name.
Aerostar builds stratospheric balloons that fly far above commercial airliners. Its larger Thunderhead balloon operates between about 16,800 and 22,900 m (55,000 and 75,000 feet), can stay aloft for 60 days or more and can carry up to about 90 kg (200 pounds) of equipment, according to the company. It also makes a smaller balloon, Lightning, designed to carry a single payload and be launched by a small team without a runway.
The company has worked with the Pentagon on balloons for years. In 2021, the Defense Innovation Unit hired Aerostar to demonstrate how stratospheric balloons could carry communications relays and sensors for U.S. forces. More recently, Aerostar has paired its balloons with the solar-powered Apollo-R drone built by Icarus, with the balloon lifting the drone into the stratosphere before it flies on its own. Aerostar executive Russ Van Der Werff told The War Zone in July that its balloons carry radio links with ranges beyond 160 km (100 miles) and that a Thunderhead could act as a “mothership” for several drones.
The U.S. Army has tested balloon-carried drones in at least three exercises this year, most recently launching micro high-altitude balloons, one carrying an Apollo-R, on Japan’s Hokkaido island on Sept. 18 during Exercise Orient Shield 26. Earlier launches took place off Morocco during African Lion 26 and on Guam during Valiant Shield 2026.
High-altitude balloons drew wide public attention in February 2023, when a U.S. Air Force F-22 shot down a Chinese balloon off South Carolina after it drifted across the United States. Supporters of the technology argue that balloons are cheaper than satellites and aircraft such as the Global Hawk and can linger over an area for weeks.
